# ↩

赞誉

say what you mean

说出你的意思

“By the time we reach adulthood, most of us have learned to operate through such deeply engrained patterns of language and behavior that virtually all of our communication involves projection, assumption, and bias. No wonder we often feel so cut off and all alone! Mr. Sofer deftly weaves together his mindfulness practice and principles of Nonviolent Communication to help us learn how to find one another again. This is a powerful guidebook to thinking, speaking, and listening with authenticity and care. Bravo!”

“当我们步入成年，大多数人已经习惯了根深蒂固的语言和行为模式，以至于我们几乎所有的沟通都离不开投射、假设和偏见。难怪我们常常感到如此孤立无援！索弗先生巧妙地将他的正念练习和非暴力沟通原则融合在一起，帮助我们重新建立彼此之间的联系。这是一本指导我们如何以真诚和关怀的态度思考、说话和倾听的有力指南。太棒了！”

—Sharon Salzberg, author of Real Happiness and Real Love

——莎伦·萨尔茨伯格，《真正的幸福》和《真正的爱》的作者

“This tremendous book addresses one of the biggest challenges in any relationship: how to combine heart with strength, compassion with assertiveness. Written with great warmth and clarity, it brings together well-researched principles, effective tools and suggestions, powerful experiential practices, and many examples. It is down-to-earth and completely accessible while also being so deep, even profound. If I had just one book to recommend about interpersonal communication, it would be this one.”

“这本杰出的著作探讨了人际关系中最大的挑战之一：如何将温情与力量、同情与自信结合起来。它以温暖而清晰的笔触，汇集了经过充分研究的原则、有效的工具和建议、强有力的实践练习以及大量案例。它既通俗易懂，又深刻隽永。如果只能推荐一本关于人际沟通的书，我会毫不犹豫地选择它。”

—Rick Hanson, PhD, author of Resilient: How to Grow an Unshakable Core of Calm, Strength, and Happiness

——里克·汉森博士，《韧性：如何培养坚不可摧的平静、力量和幸福核心》一书的作者

“Oren Jay Sofer’s eloquent book Say What You Mean could just as well be titled Living What You Mean. Going beyond the surface level of communication, he describes our relational journey together in its inherent connections with how we behave, how we express, perceive, and meet the needs of ourselves and others, how we engage with difference and even conflict, how we negotiate love and anger—in sum, how to fully live this complex life. Sofer gives essential frameworks, perspectives, and skills for our shared humanity.”

奥伦·杰伊·索弗的著作《言行一致》（Say What You Mean）或许更应名为《活出真我》（Living What You Mean）。他超越了沟通的表面层面，描述了我们共同的人际关系之旅，以及它与我们行为方式、表达方式、感知方式和满足自身及他人需求方式、处理差异乃至冲突的方式、调和爱与愤怒的方式——总之，是如何充分体验这复杂人生的内在联系。索弗为我们共同的人性提供了至关重要的框架、视角和技巧。

—Larry Yang, Buddhist teacher and author of Awakening Together: The Spiritual Practice of Inclusivity and Community

——拉里·杨（Larry Yang），佛教导师，《共同觉醒：包容与社群的灵性实践》作者

“Words have tremendous power—both to harm, and to heal. In Say What You Mean, Oren shares a three-part process for communicating with mindfulness, clarity, and compassion and creating more connection and understanding in our relationships. In these times of turbulence and conflict, we need this more than ever before.”

“语言拥有巨大的力量——既能伤人，也能治愈。在《直言不讳》一书中，奥伦分享了一个三步沟通法，帮助我们以正念、清晰和同理心进行沟通，从而在人际关系中建立更多的联结和理解。在当今动荡和冲突不断的时代，我们比以往任何时候都更需要这种方法。”

—Chris Kresser, MS, LAc, New York Times best-selling author of The Paleo Cure and Unconventional Medicine

——克里斯·克雷瑟，理学硕士，针灸师，《纽约时报》畅销书《原始人疗法》和《非常规医学》的作者

“Meeting the enormous challenges of living in these times calls for an integration of inner practices of mindfulness with outer practices of communicating with honesty, vulnerability, strength, care, and empathy. Oren shows us a way to do just that.”

“应对当今时代的巨大挑战，需要将内在的正念练习与外在的沟通实践相结合，例如以诚实、坦率、坚强、关怀和同理心待人。奥伦向我们展示了如何做到这一点。”

—Miki Kashtan, Certified Nonviolent Communication Trainer and author of Spinning Threads of Radical Aliveness

——米基·卡什坦，认证非暴力沟通培训师，《编织激进生命的线索》作者

The fish trap exists because of the fish;

鱼笼的存在是因为鱼的存在；

once you’ve gotten the fish you can forget the trap.

一旦你钓到了鱼，就可以把陷阱忘掉。

The rabbit snare exists because of the rabbit;

兔子陷阱的存在是因为兔子；

once you’ve gotten the rabbit, you can forget the snare.

一旦你抓住了兔子，就可以把陷阱忘掉。

Words exist because of meaning.

词语之所以存在，是因为它们具有意义。

Once you’ve gotten the meaning you can forget the words.

一旦理解了它的含义，你就可以忘记那些词语了。

Where can I find a man who has forgotten words,

哪里能找到一个忘记了词语的人？

so I can have a word with him?

那我跟他单独谈谈吗？

—CHUANG TZU

foreword

# ↩

前言

IN ONE WAY or another, we spend our lives communicating. For most of us, the predominant mode of communication is speech, the words we use and the emotional tone underlying our words. Interaction forms the bedrock of all our relationships, and the patterns through which we engage in conversation determine, to a large extent, the quality of our lives. What’s more, our habits in communication establish a template for our relationship with ourselves, and with our society at large.

无论以何种方式，我们一生都在与人沟通。对大多数人来说，主要的沟通方式是言语，包括我们使用的词语以及词语背后蕴含的情感语调。互动是我们所有关系的基础，而我们进行对话的模式在很大程度上决定了我们生活的质量。此外，我们的沟通习惯也为我们与自身以及与整个社会的关系奠定了基础。

In this wonderful book, Oren Jay Sofer explores the many nuances of the way we speak, illuminating the patterns that foster well-being and harmony, and those that simply lead to greater frustration and distress. The perspectives and methods in this book also hold an essential key to the healing and radical transformation that is so desperately needed—not only in our lives as individuals but collectively in our communities and on our planet. Drawing from his extensive training in mindfulness practices, somatic healing, and Nonviolent Communication, Oren provides both the insight and the skill necessary for us to transform communication into a vehicle for greater intimacy, honesty, and compassion, and to point our social lives toward greater equity and peace.

在这本精彩的书中，奥伦·杰伊·索弗深入探讨了我们说话方式的诸多细微差别，阐明了哪些模式能够促进幸福与和谐，哪些模式只会导致更大的挫败感和痛苦。本书的视角和方法也蕴含着一把关键钥匙，它能帮助我们实现迫切需要的疗愈和根本性转变——这不仅关乎我们个人的生活，也关乎我们所在的社区乃至整个地球。凭借在正念练习、身体疗愈和非暴力沟通方面的丰富经验，奥伦为我们提供了必要的洞察力和技巧，使我们能够将沟通转化为增进亲密、真诚和同情心的途径，并引导我们的社会生活走向更加公平与和平。

Through clear theoretical frameworks and a wealth of stories and examples, Say What You Mean offers an array of useful tools for strengthening awareness of our habitual patterns, as well as many specific suggestions for how to communicate with greater care and effectiveness. Oren discusses the essential role of empathy in listening to others and proposes, in very precise ways, how to cultivate it. As he writes, “Communication practice is not about what we say. It’s about where we’re coming from and how we say it.”

《直言不讳》通过清晰的理论框架和丰富的案例，提供了一系列实用工具，帮助我们更好地觉察自身的习惯模式，并就如何更用心、更有效地沟通提出了许多具体建议。奥伦探讨了同理心在倾听他人时的关键作用，并以非常精准的方式提出了培养同理心的方法。正如他所写：“沟通实践的关键不在于我们说了什么，而在于我们的出发点以及我们如何表达。”

He also clearly describes practices for recognizing and understanding our thoughts, perceptions, and emotions, and how they influence, often unconsciously, the words we use and the motivations behind them. Without this understanding, we often find ourselves caught in the many tangles of our conditioning, not seeing our way to greater connectedness and inner freedom.

他还清晰地阐述了如何识别和理解我们的思想、感知和情绪，以及它们如何（通常是无意识地）影响我们使用的语言及其背后的动机。缺乏这种理解，我们常常会发现自己深陷于各种固有观念的束缚之中，无法找到通往更深层次联结和内心自由的道路。

Besides being a detailed and comprehensive roadmap for cultivating wise communication, there are also many little gems in this work that can act as reminders through the day. One of my favorites is the simple understanding that “we have more clarity and power when we use fewer words with more sincerity.”

除了提供一份详尽全面的培养明智沟通技巧的路线图之外，这本书中还蕴含着许多精辟的见解，可以作为我们日常生活中的提醒。我最喜欢的一点是，它提出了一个简单的道理：“当我们用更少的文字表达更真诚的想法时，我们就能拥有更清晰的思路和更强的力量。”

One of the foundations of this book is that communication, like any other art, takes practice. Once we have the basic skills, we can begin to expand the ways we think, speak, and interact, making our speech a pathway to greater harmony and insight in our lives.

本书的核心观点之一是，沟通和其他任何艺术一样，都需要练习。一旦掌握了基本技能，我们就能拓展思考、表达和互动的方式，使言语成为通往生活中更大和谐与深刻洞见的途径。

I’ve known Oren for many years, since the early days of his meditation practice. It brings me great joy to see him integrate the deep awareness of his meditative insights with his profound understanding of communication in an accessible method of training. This book, with his characteristic warmth and lucidity, is a great gift to anyone seeking more connection, clarity, and compassion in their life.

我认识奥伦很多年了，从他开始冥想练习的早期就认识他了。看到他将冥想中深刻的领悟与他对沟通的深刻理解融会贯通，并以一种易于理解的方式呈现出来，我感到非常欣慰。这本书以他特有的热情和清晰的语言写成，对于任何渴望在生活中获得更多联结、清晰的思路和慈悲心的人来说，都是一份珍贵的礼物。

—Joseph Goldstein

——约瑟夫·戈尔茨坦

acknowledgments

# ↩

致谢

SKILLFUL COMMUNICATION RESTS upon a profound recognition of our interdependence. Like so much in life, this book is the work of many hands and the result of countless interactions.

娴熟的沟通技巧建立在对我们相互依存的深刻认识之上。如同生活中的许多事情一样，这本书也是多人合作的成果，是无数次交流的结晶。

For the insight that I hope graces these pages, I am deeply indebted to my teachers. Acarya Anagarika Munindra and Godwin Samararatne opened my eyes and revealed what was possible in this life. Robert Pryor’s humble and steady work shepherded so many of us to the Dharma. Venerable Ajahn Sucitto, Joseph Goldstein, and Michelle McDonald: your wisdom, generosity, and skillful guidance has helped me to mature and understand what it is to be human. Sarah Doering believed in me and offered support during a difficult time.

我希望本书能为读者带来深刻的洞见，而这一切都源于我师们的悉心教导。阿查里亚·阿那加里卡·穆宁德拉和戈德温·萨马拉拉特内开启了我的双眼，让我领悟到此生无限的可能。罗伯特·普赖尔谦逊而坚定的修行引领我们许多人走向佛法。尊贵的阿姜·苏吉托、约瑟夫·戈德斯坦和米歇尔·麦克唐纳：你们的智慧、慷慨和精妙的指导帮助我成长，让我更深刻地理解人性的真谛。莎拉·多林在我人生低谷时给予我信任和支持。

I am equally indebted to my Nonviolent Communication teachers for guiding me to translate the beauty of the Dharma into action, and for teaching me how to say what I mean. Marshall B. Rosenberg’s vision, clarity, and warmth touched me deeply. I learned a great deal from Inbal Kashtan, who died too early of cancer. (I miss you, Inbal.) I especially want to express my sincere appreciation to my friend and colleague Miki Kashtan, whose uncompromising commitment to the values and vision of NVC continues to push me beyond my edges, and who offered penetrating comments on key portions of the text. Kathy Simon gave essential input on short notice. I’m also grateful to Penny Wassman, whose care and enthusiastic endorsement welcomed me into the Certified Trainer community, and to my colleagues at BayNVC, whose authenticity has taught me something valuable about how to embody these skills.

我同样感激我的非暴力沟通老师们，是他们引导我将佛法的精髓转化为实际行动，并教会我如何表达自己的真实想法。马歇尔·B·罗森伯格的远见卓识、清晰的思路和温暖的品格深深地打动了我。我从英巴尔·卡什坦身上学到了很多，可惜她因癌症英年早逝。（英巴尔，我非常想念你。）我尤其要真诚地感谢我的朋友和同事米基·卡什坦，她对非暴力沟通的价值观和愿景的坚定不移的信念不断激励我超越自我，并对本书的关键部分提出了精辟的见解。凯西·西蒙在短时间内提供了至关重要的帮助。我也感谢佩妮·沃斯曼，她热情的关怀和支持让我加入了认证培训师的行列；感谢湾区非暴力沟通中心的同事们，他们的真诚让我受益匪浅，让我更深刻地理解了如何将这些技能融入到我的生活中。

Steve Hoskinson and Anthony “Twig” Wheeler provided gentle support in service of my well-being and wholeness. David O’Neal, senior editor at Shambhala, saw potential in my writing and reached out. Editor Matt Zepelin’s intelligence has enhanced the manuscript. Joe Kelly offered to help and edited several chapters after a serendipitous walk.

史蒂夫·霍斯金森和安东尼·“特威格”·惠勒给予了我温和的支持，帮助我保持身心健康。香巴拉出版社的资深编辑大卫·奥尼尔看到了我写作的潜力，并主动联系了我。编辑马特·泽佩林的智慧提升了稿件的质量。乔·凯利在一次偶然的散步后主动提出帮忙，并编辑了几个章节。

I am fortunate to be part of a thriving community of spiritual friends, who continue to challenge me lovingly and show me what kindness really means. Several colleagues also offered useful feedback on various chapters: Matthew Brensilver, Donna Carter, Derek Haswell, Sumi London, Ali Miller, Donald Rothberg, Ben Rubin, and Aaron Soffin. My mother, father, and brother humored and loved me through many awkward moments as I learned NVC. Evan A. Wong offered steady, tender encouragement through many long days and late nights at the computer.

我很幸运能成为一个充满活力的灵性朋友群体的一员，他们不断以爱挑战我，并向我展现了真正的善意。几位同事也对本书的各个章节提出了宝贵的意见：Matthew Brensilver、Donna Carter、Derek Haswell、Sumi London、Ali Miller、Donald Rothberg、Ben Rubin 和 Aaron Soffin。在我学习非暴力沟通的过程中，我的父母和兄弟包容我，在我经历许多尴尬时刻时给予我爱。Evan A. Wong 在我无数个日夜伏案工作时，给予我坚定而温柔的鼓励。

I also want to thank the many folks on my email list and social media accounts, who followed along and cheered me on through the process. This book also would not be possible without the students who have attended my workshops, classes, and retreats, whose genuine feedback inspired me to write and whose fortitude and courage inspire me daily.

我还要感谢邮件列表和社交媒体账号上的各位朋友，感谢你们一路以来的关注和鼓励。这本书的出版也离不开参加过我的工作坊、课程和静修营的学生们，你们真诚的反馈激励着我写作，你们的坚韧和勇气也每天都在激励着我。

Any errors are my own. Thankfully, life is a process of learning.

任何错误均由我本人承担。所幸，人生就是一个学习的过程。

# ↩

introduction

# ↩

介绍

WHAT WE SAY matters. We’ve each felt the power that words have to heal, soothe, or uplift us. Even one caring remark can make the difference between giving up and finding the strength to face life’s challenges.

我们所说的话至关重要。我们每个人都曾感受到语言的力量，它能治愈、抚慰或鼓舞我们。哪怕一句温暖的话语，也能改变一个人是选择放弃还是重拾力量去面对生活的挑战。

We each also know something of the great harm that can be inflicted through speech. Sharp words laced with anger or cruelty can break a relationship and burn for years. Language can be used to manipulate and coerce on a mass scale, to fuel fear, war, and oppression, and to advance political agendas of genocide or terror. Few things so powerful are also so commonplace.

我们每个人都深知言语能造成多么巨大的伤害。尖刻的言辞，夹杂着愤怒或残忍，足以破坏一段关系，其带来的伤痛甚至会持续多年。语言可以被用来大规模地操纵和胁迫他人，煽动恐惧、战争和压迫，并推进种族灭绝或恐怖主义等政治议程。如此强大的力量，却又如此司空见惯，实属罕见。

Words are woven into the fabric of our lives. Your first love. Your first job. Your last goodbye to someone you love. Our beginnings and endings and the countless moments in between are punctuated by a play of words as we share our thoughts, feelings, and desires.

文字早已融入我们生活的方方面面。你的初恋，你的第一份工作，你与挚爱之人最后的告别。我们的开始与结束，以及其间无数的瞬间，都因文字的交织而熠熠生辉，我们用文字分享着彼此的思想、情感和渴望。

My parents tell me that I was a gregarious child. “E-A-T, O-R-E-N,” they would spell out at meals, trying to redirect the stream of questions that bubbled from my small body as they reminded me to eat. My fascination with words began at an early age. I still recall the thrill of discovering the meaning of simple compound words such as seaweed or sunset —that moment of realization when abstract sounds were suddenly transformed into their more familiar parts.

父母说我小时候是个很爱交际的孩子。吃饭的时候，他们会拼读“吃，吃”，试图阻止我那滔滔不绝、一连串的问题，提醒我吃饭。我对文字的迷恋始于幼年。我至今仍记得发现像“海藻”或“日落”这样简单复合词含义时的兴奋——那一刻，抽象的声音突然被分解成更熟悉的组成部分，我恍然大悟。

Words are a kind of magic. To be alive and self-aware on this remarkable planet with its forests and lakes, its oceans and mountains, in this vast universe with billions of galaxies, is mysterious enough. What a marvel to be able to look into each other’s eyes for an instant and form words that tell something of our lives.

文字是一种魔力。在这个拥有森林、湖泊、海洋和山脉的奇妙星球上，在这个拥有数十亿星系的浩瀚宇宙中，能够活着并拥有自我意识，本身就已足够神秘。而能够瞬间与彼此对视，并用文字诉说我们的人生，这又是多么奇妙的事情啊！

The creation myths of many cultures and religions through time—East, West, and Indigenous—recognize the generative power of words, giving the potency of speech a key role in the beginning of the cosmos. Indeed, words have the power to shape our reality. As we think, so we perceive; as we perceive, so we act. Moreover, the teachings of all world religions reflect a universal understanding about the ethical implications of language—its potential for good or harm—and include moral guidelines around the appropriate use of speech.

纵观古今，东方、西方以及原住民等众多文化和宗教的创世神话都认可语言的创造力量，赋予语言在宇宙起源中关键的地位。的确，语言拥有塑造我们现实的力量。我们的思想决定了我们的感知；我们的感知决定了我们的行动。此外，世界各大宗教的教义都体现了对语言伦理意义的普遍理解——语言既能行善也能作恶——并包含着关于如何恰当使用语言的道德准则。

My childhood fascination with language crystallized into a firm commitment to understand how to use words wisely when I attended a meditation retreat with the Vietnamese Zen master, poet, and peace activist Thich Nhat Hanh. His modern rendering of the Buddha’s guidelines on “Right Speech” struck a chord deep within, motivating me to learn as much as I could about communication. It still inspires me today:

我从小就对语言着迷，而参加越南禅师、诗人兼和平活动家一行禅师的禅修营后，我对如何明智地运用语言产生了坚定的追求。他对佛陀“正语”教义的现代诠释深深触动了我，激励我尽可能多地学习沟通之道。时至今日，它依然激励着我。

Aware of the suffering caused by unmindful speech and the inability to listen to others, I am committed to cultivating loving speech and deep listening in order to bring joy and happiness to others and relieve others of suffering. Knowing that words can create happiness or suffering, I am determined to learn to speak truthfully, with words that inspire self-confidence, joy, and hope. I will not spread news that I do not know to be certain and will not criticize or condemn things of which I am not sure. I will refrain from uttering words that can cause division or discord, or words that can cause the family or the community to break. I am determined to make all efforts to reconcile and resolve all conflicts, however small. 1

我深知不经思考的言语和缺乏倾听会造成痛苦，因此我致力于培养充满爱意的言语和深切的倾听，以便为他人带来喜悦和幸福，并减轻他人的痛苦。我明白言语可以带来快乐，也可以带来痛苦，因此我决心学习真诚地说话，用能激发自信、喜悦和希望的言语。我不会传播未经证实的消息，也不会批评或谴责我不确定的事情。我不会说出可能造成分裂或不和，或导致家庭或社区破裂的言语。我决心尽一切努力调解和解决所有冲突，无论大小。

What we say matters—perhaps now more than ever.

我们所说的话很重要——或许现在比以往任何时候都更重要。

We live in times of great change, in which much is being asked of us. We live at a time when we are less and less able to listen and really hear one another in society, at a time when those with different views, beliefs, or backgrounds are (once again) so easily cast as the “other.” At this time when great forces of political, social, economic, and environmental change are sweeping the globe and intensifying our separation from self, others, and life, we need to learn how to speak and listen in a new way. We need to learn how to reperceive our world with fresh eyes, beyond inherited historical and economic structures of competition and separation that can so easily determine our relationships. True dialogue is more than the mere exchange of ideas. It is a transformative process based on trust and mutual respect, in which we come to see another in new and more accurate ways. As theologian David Lochhead explains, “it is a way of knowing truth that neither party possesses prior to the dialogue.” 2

我们生活在一个剧烈变革的时代，肩负着诸多重任。在这个时代，我们越来越难以倾听彼此，也越来越难以真正理解彼此；在这个时代，那些持有不同观点、信仰或背景的人（再一次）如此轻易地被贴上“他者”的标签。当政治、社会、经济和环境的巨大变革力量席卷全球，加剧我们与自我、他人和生活的疏离时，我们需要学习如何以一种全新的方式说话和倾听。我们需要学习如何用全新的视角重新审视我们的世界，超越那些轻易就能决定我们人际关系的、根深蒂固的历史和经济竞争与隔离结构。真正的对话不仅仅是思想的交流，它是一个基于信任和相互尊重的变革过程，在这个过程中，我们能够以全新且更准确的方式看待他人。正如神学家大卫·洛克黑德所解释的那样，“这是一种在对话开始之前双方都不具备的认识真理的方式。”

It is heartbreaking to know the good of which we are capable yet to see so much destruction and violence. In Japan, there is a saying: the cherry blossoms are beautiful because they are fleeting. We each have an opportunity to use the time and energy we are given with integrity. My hope is that this book might, in some small way, help us begin to realize our potential for good as humans by learning to bring more compassion, wisdom, and kindness to how we navigate the relationships that make up our everyday lives. I hope that it might help us to transform the mechanisms of thought and perception that make violence seem like a viable strategy, that it be one step in creating a world that works for all.

明知我们拥有行善的能力，却目睹如此多的破坏和暴力，这令人心碎。在日本，有句谚语说：樱花之所以美丽，是因为它们转瞬即逝。我们每个人都有机会以正直的态度利用我们所拥有的时间和精力。我希望这本书能以某种方式，帮助我们开始意识到作为人类的向善潜能，让我们学会将更多的同情、智慧和善意融入到日常生活的人际关系中。我希望它能帮助我们转变那些将暴力视为可行策略的思维和认知机制，并成为我们迈向一个对所有人都有益的世界的第一步。

A Confluence of Waters

水流交汇处

In my mid-twenties, toward the end of a ten-day retreat with Marshall B. Rosenberg, the founder of Nonviolent Communication, I had breakfast with Dr. Rosenberg and his wife. I had met Rosenberg a few years prior and was eager to share my gratitude for the profound changes I was experiencing in my life due to his system of communication. Being a longtime meditator, I was also keen to offer my perspective on how meditation could support the NVC process. *

二十五六岁的时候，在参加完马歇尔·B·罗森伯格（非暴力沟通创始人）为期十天的静修营即将结束时，我和罗森伯格博士及他的妻子共进早餐。几年前我曾见过罗森伯格博士，我非常渴望表达我对他的沟通体系给我的生活带来的深刻改变的感激之情。作为一名长期冥想者，我也很乐意分享我对冥想如何辅助非暴力沟通过程的看法。

This was in the early 2000s, before mindfulness exploded into the public sphere. I explained how mindfulness practice developed inner awareness, a prerequisite for being able to identify and stay conscious of feelings and needs—the core of Nonviolent Communication—and therefore a key missing piece in the NVC model. I was excited and a bit stunned when he completely agreed! He shared, with a bit of dismay, that he’d been trying to figure out how to teach people to meditate for some time using a baby giraffe hat, a modified version of one of his signature puppets. Looking at me across the table with a wry smile, he said, “Maybe that’s your work to do.”

那是在2000年代初期，正念还没有像现在这样在公众领域迅速普及。我解释了正念练习如何培养内在觉察力，这是识别并保持对自身感受和需求觉察的先决条件——也是非暴力沟通的核心——因此也是非暴力沟通模式中缺失的关键一环。他完全同意我的观点，这让我既兴奋又有些惊讶！他略带沮丧地告诉我，他一直在尝试用一顶小长颈鹿帽子（他标志性玩偶的改良版）来教人冥想。他隔着桌子看着我，带着一丝苦笑说：“也许这就是你应该做的。”

Thus began a journey of nearly two decades in which I have worked to integrate my understanding of Buddhist meditation and Nonviolent Communication. The material I share with you in these pages is a synthesis of three distinct streams of practice. The first primary stream is mindfulness, coming out of the Theravada Buddhist tradition (specifically the texts and practices of Burmese Satipaṭṭhāna and the Thai Forest tradition). The second is the system of Nonviolent Communication developed by Dr. Rosenberg, whose seminal book Nonviolent Communication: A Language of Life has sold over one million copies worldwide. 3 NVC has been used for international conflict resolution and nonviolent social change, interpersonal communication and mediation, as well as for personal growth and healing. The last methodology that informs this book is my training in a therapeutic technique designed by Dr. Peter A. Levine called Somatic Experiencing, which emphasizes the role of nervous system regulation in resolving trauma.

于是，我开启了一段近二十年的旅程，致力于将我对佛教冥想和非暴力沟通的理解融会贯通。本书所分享的内容，是三种不同修行流派的综合。第一种主要流派是正念，源自上座部佛教传统（特别是缅甸四念处和泰国森林禅修的经典和修行）。第二种是罗森伯格博士创立的非暴力沟通体系，他的开创性著作《非暴力沟通：生命的语言》在全球销量超过百万册。非暴力沟通已被应用于国际冲突解决、非暴力社会变革、人际沟通和调解，以及个人成长和疗愈。本书的最后一个方法论，是我接受的由彼得·A·莱文博士创立的“躯体体验疗法”的培训，该疗法强调神经系统调节在创伤疗愈中的作用。

I have found that these three streams form a powerful vehicle for deepening self-understanding and transforming our habits of communication. In the early years of my practice, I discovered many synchronicities between these methods and their respective underlying theories. My passion led me through various mental contortions as I attempted to map one method onto the other, seeking a coherent master system that would encompass all that I was learning. It took time for the perspectives to settle into my body and to recognize that they were simply different ways of understanding human experience. They overlapped in some areas but didn’t need to fit together perfectly to function simultaneously or be mutually supportive.

我发现这三种方法构成了一个强大的载体，能够帮助我们加深自我理解，并转变沟通习惯。在实践的早期，我发现这些方法及其各自的理论基础之间存在诸多共通之处。出于对它们的热情，我尝试将一种方法映射到另一种方法上，寻求一个能够涵盖我所学一切的连贯体系，这期间我经历了各种思维上的挣扎。我花了很长时间才将这些视角融入自身，并意识到它们仅仅是理解人类经验的不同方式。它们在某些方面有所重叠，但并不需要完美契合才能同时发挥作用或相互支持。

When streams in a watershed run together to form a river, you can no longer distinguish the waters of one from the other. In some sense, these three systems and their corresponding practices can live as one river, a seamless whole, each describing and supporting different facets of a holistic experience of being alive.

当流域内的溪流汇聚成河时，你便无法再区分它们之间的差异。从某种意义上说，这三个系统及其相应的实践可以像一条河流一样共存，成为一个浑然一体的整体，各自描述并支撑着生命整体体验的不同层面。

As such, my presentation of the material in this book is holistic. While I don’t discuss the Dharma explicitly, those familiar with Buddhist teachings will recognize clearly the presence of its wisdom in different sections. Similarly, my exposition of Somatic Experiencing is more tangential (save for one important section in chapter 13 on challenging situations). Rather than try to parse the waters from this stream or that, I have instead focused on creating what I hope is an accessible guide to the basics of interpersonal communication that can be used to create concrete shifts and changes in one’s life.

因此，本书的内容呈现方式是整体性的。虽然我没有明确讨论佛法，但熟悉佛教教义的人会清楚地感受到佛法智慧贯穿于各个章节之中。同样，我对躯体体验疗法的阐述也较为间接（除了第十三章中关于挑战性情境的重要部分）。我并没有试图从不同的角度去分析各种理论，而是专注于创作一本易于理解的人际沟通基础指南，希望它能帮助读者在生活中带来切实的改变。

Three Steps, Three Foundations

三步走，三大基石

Human communication is complex. There are a myriad of factors in any interaction. Our emotions, ideas, and beliefs come into play both verbally and nonverbally. We have to negotiate patterns of relating that have been established, whether between two individuals or between the groups and communities to which we belong. Yet, in all of this, there are certain consistent foundations to skillful communication.

人际沟通十分复杂。任何互动都涉及诸多因素。我们的情感、想法和信念都会以语言和非语言的方式发挥作用。我们必须在既定的关系模式中寻求平衡，无论是在两个人之间，还是在我们所属的群体或社群之间。然而，在所有这些因素中，有效的沟通都遵循着某些始终如一的基础。

The overarching framework for this book is taking three steps to create effective conversation. The steps themselves are simple enough:

本书的核心框架是分三步进行有效对话。这三步本身非常简单：

1. Lead with presence.

1. 以身作则。

2. Come from curiosity and care.

2. 源于好奇心和关爱。

3. Focus on what matters.

3. 专注于重要的事情。

Each step is part of a much more thorough and profound training. Like three firm, solid stones placed in the middle of a fast-flowing stream, each step is only as stable and useful as the foundation upon which it rests. Thus to show up and be fully in the moment rests on training ourselves in the first foundation of mindful communication: presence. Coming from curiosity and care is rooted in the foundation of our intention. Focusing on what matters is about honing our attention, training our mind’s capacity to discern what’s essential and shift its focus in a nimble and responsive manner. The first three sections of this book correspond to our training in each of these foundations, while the fourth and final section explores how they all fit together.

每一步都是更为全面和深刻的训练的一部分。如同三块坚实的石头放置在湍急的溪流中央，每一步的稳定性和有效性都取决于其所依附的基础。因此，全然地活在当下，关键在于训练我们掌握正念沟通的首要基础：临在。好奇心和关怀源于我们的意图。专注于重要之事，意味着磨练我们的注意力，训练我们心智辨别本质的能力，并能灵活敏捷地转移注意力。本书的前三部分分别对应着我们对这些基础的训练，而第四部分，也是最后一部分，则探讨了它们如何相互关联。

How to Use This Book

如何使用本书

Reading a book on communication is a bit like reading a manual on how to swim. No matter how clear and detailed the text, you won’t learn to swim without getting in the water. This book is meant to be used in your life; consider it a field guide for conversations, a map that describes a landscape as you travel. It is likely to serve you best if you go slowly, taking time to integrate each section as you read. Every concept, analogy, or idea is meant to be tested in your life. Try it out, bash it around, and see what works.

阅读一本关于沟通的书有点像阅读游泳手册。无论文字多么清晰详尽，不下水你永远学不会游泳。这本书旨在应用于你的生活中；不妨把它看作是一本对话指南，一张为你描绘旅途风景的地图。细细品读，花时间理解和消化每一部分内容，对你最有帮助。书中的每一个概念、比喻或想法都旨在在你的生活中得到检验。不妨尝试一下，反复推敲，看看哪些方法行之有效。

In each chapter, you will find practical suggestions for how to implement the tools and concepts. Start small, in lightweight, low-stakes situations. To return to the swimming analogy: one doesn’t learn to swim by leaping into the ocean on a stormy day. Sure, you might make it, but not without struggling and swallowing a fair amount of salt water. What’s more, you’re less likely to want to go swimming again! It’s much easier if one begins in the shallow end of a pool, preferably on a warm day.

每一章都会提供一些实用建议，指导你如何运用这些工具和概念。从小处着手，在轻松、风险较低的情境中练习。回到游泳的例子：你不可能在暴风雨天直接跳进大海就学会游泳。当然，你或许能游到海里，但肯定会挣扎一番，而且会呛到不少海水。更重要的是，你可能以后就不想再游泳了！最好是从泳池的浅水区开始，最好是在温暖的日子里。

In the same way, I don’t recommend attempting to apply these tools immediately to the most difficult conversations or relationships in your life. First learn to swim; build some capacity. Whenever possible, seek out situations where it will be easiest to practice and where you are most able to experiment and learn without too much resistance. You may want to read the book with someone else, so you have a partner with whom to practice the exercises. Or try the tools with a close friend or family member who can humor you as you stumble through the awkwardness of learning a new language.

同样，我也不建议你立刻将这些技巧运用到生活中最棘手的对话或人际关系中。先学会“游泳”，积累一些经验。尽可能寻找最容易练习、最能让你轻松尝试和学习的情境。你可以找人一起阅读这本书，这样就有了可以一起练习的伙伴。或者，你也可以和亲密的朋友或家人一起尝试这些技巧，让他们在你磕磕绊绊地学习新语言时给予你理解和包容。

For that’s what it’s like: learning communication skills is remarkably akin to learning a new language. It takes repetition. The more frequently you practice, the more quickly you will become fluent. Knowing even a few words of a new language will help you begin to say what you mean. So I encourage you to practice a little every day, whether through formal exercises or informal conversations. Even five minutes of intentional, daily practice will have an effect over time.

学习沟通技巧与学习一门新语言非常相似，都需要反复练习。练习越频繁，你就能越快流利地运用。即使只掌握一些新语言的词汇，也能帮助你开始表达自己的想法。所以我鼓励你每天都练习一会儿，无论是正式的练习还是非正式的对话。哪怕每天只练习五分钟，日积月累也会有所成效。

At the end of each chapter you will find a summary of key points and a series of questions and answers. Many of these questions are based on transcripts from students at actual workshops and retreats. They’re meant to address some of the most common challenges that you may encounter along the way. (Certain names or details of stories have been changed to honor requests for privacy.) Throughout the text you’ll find key terms related to mindful communication. These are italicized on first use, and their definitions can be looked up in the glossary. Notes at the end of the book offer further reflections and references that may be of interest. The “Further Resources” section contains suggestions to continue your training, including a link to companion guided meditations for select practices.

每章末尾都附有要点总结和一系列问答。其中许多问题都取材于学员在实际工作坊和静修营中的访谈记录，旨在解答您在学习过程中可能遇到的一些常见挑战。（为尊重隐私，部分人名或故事细节已作更改。）文中会穿插一些与正念沟通相关的关键术语。这些术语首次出现时以斜体字标出，其定义可在词汇表中查阅。书末的注释提供了一些您可能感兴趣的延伸思考和参考资料。“拓展资源”部分包含一些继续学习的建议，包括部分练习的配套引导冥想链接。

Finally, I want to point out a key distinction that runs throughout the book. In each chapter you’ll find principles, which capture the underlying ethos or aim of a certain aspect of communication. You’ll also find practices, which are specific tools meant to help you learn how to bring the principles into your life in concrete ways. For example, you’ll encounter principles such as, “The more aware we are, the more choice we have.” You’ll also find correlating practices—some you can do as you read, others you can take into your practice of communication in daily life. In this instance, one practice to support this principle of awareness might be instructions for mindfulness of breathing.

最后，我想指出贯穿全书的一个关键区别。每一章都包含原则，这些原则概括了沟通某一方面的核心理念或目标。同时，你也会看到实践方法，这些具体工具旨在帮助你将这些原则切实地融入到生活中。例如，你会遇到这样的原则：“我们越有觉察力，就越有选择。”你还会找到与之相关的实践方法——有些可以在阅读时进行，有些则可以运用到日常沟通实践中。就此而言，支持“觉察力”这一原则的一种实践方法可能是正念呼吸练习。

The danger in any communication training is that we mistake the practice for the principle and begin to speak in rigid or robotic ways in an attempt to adhere to some kind of dogma or system. While systems are incredibly useful (and the exploration of Rosenberg’s NVC comprises a major part of this book), I’m less interested in following a system than I am in learning how to understand and respond dynamically to the moment.

任何沟通培训的危险在于，我们常常把实践误认为原则，为了遵循某种教条或体系而开始用僵化或机械的方式说话。虽然体系非常有用（本书很大一部分内容就是对罗森伯格非暴力沟通的探讨），但我更感兴趣的是学习如何理解当下情境并做出动态的回应，而不是遵循某种体系。

In other words, try not to get hung up on any one way of speaking. To offer another analogy: it’s a bit like learning an instrument. Playing scales is essential, but the aim is to make music. The tools and practices here will be invaluable for retraining your communication habits, but the aim is to relax and be in the flow of conversation with ease.

换句话说，不要过于执着于某种固定的说话方式。再举个例子：这有点像学习乐器。练习音阶固然重要，但最终目标是创作音乐。这里介绍的工具和练习对于重塑你的沟通习惯至关重要，但最终目的是让你放松下来，轻松地融入对话之中。

What to Expect

预期情况

The field of communication encompasses a wide range of areas: personal and professional relationships, higher-level skills such as group facilitation and mediation, and strategic applications such as diplomacy and nonviolent resistance. This book won’t cover everything, nor is it intended to do so. Its primary focus is interpersonal communication in social and intimate relationships. If you’re interested in taking your training further, the tools you learn here will provide an indispensable foundation for other applications.

沟通领域涵盖广泛：人际关系（包括个人关系和职业关系）、更高层次的技能（例如团体引导和调解）以及战略应用（例如外交和非暴力抵抗）。本书并非旨在涵盖所有内容，也并非意在面面俱到。本书主要关注社交和亲密关系中的人际沟通。如果您有兴趣进一步提升沟通技巧，本书所教授的工具将为其他应用奠定不可或缺的基础。

This book is directly informed by my personal life experience, which means that it will also be limited by that experience in some ways. In particular, aspects of my conditioning as a heterosexual, Jewish, middle-class white male have left me ill-prepared to realize the vision that Marshall Rosenberg articulated for his work. I still get chills when I consider what he said in 2005, at a retreat in Switzerland:

这本书直接取材于我的个人生活经历，这意味着它在某些方面也会受到这些经历的限制。特别是，作为一名异性恋、犹太裔、中产阶级白人男性，我所受到的某些熏陶使我难以理解马歇尔·卢森堡在其著作中所阐述的愿景。每当我想起他在2005年瑞士的一次静修会上所说的话，我仍然会感到不寒而栗：

If I use Nonviolent Communication to liberate people to be less depressed, to get along better with their family, but do not teach them at the same time to use their energy to rapidly transform systems in the world, then I am part of the problem. I am essentially calming people down, making them happier to live in the systems as they are, so I am using NVC as a narcotic. 4

如果我运用非暴力沟通帮助人们减轻抑郁，改善家庭关系，却不同时教导他们如何运用自身能量迅速改变世界体系，那么我就是问题的一部分。我本质上是在安抚人们，让他们更乐于接受现有的体系，所以我把非暴力沟通当作了一种麻醉剂。

Teaching is humbling; I know I have more to learn, particularly around the blind spots of my own privilege . 5 To the extent that I have managed to see beyond my own conditioning, the text and its ideas may support others across different social locations to learn how to liberate themselves from their own conditioning, and to step more fully into the interdependent dance of communication. Nothing would please me more. To the extent that I haven’t seen beyond my own conditioning, I continue my practice of mindful communication as a lifelong path of learning and transformation.

教学让我感到谦卑；我知道自己还有很多东西要学，尤其是在克服自身特权带来的盲点方面。如果我能超越自身的局限，那么这篇文章及其理念或许能够帮助不同社会阶层的人们学习如何摆脱自身的局限，并更充分地融入相互依存的沟通之中。没有什么比这更令我欣慰的了。如果我仍无法超越自身的局限，我将继续践行正念沟通，将其作为终身学习和转变的道路。

Such an enduring commitment is the most helpful way to approach this practice. Learning to communicate skillfully is not something we complete in a weekend workshop, a six-week class, or a four-part book. It takes patience, interest, dedication, and humility. It’s common to feel completely and utterly inept at various stages in the process. At times, it can even feel as if one were better off before trying these tools!

这种持久的投入是练习沟通技巧最有效的方式。学会有效沟通并非一个周末工作坊、六周课程或一本四卷本的书籍就能完成的。它需要耐心、兴趣、奉献和谦逊。在学习过程中，感到自己完全无能是很正常的。有时，甚至会觉得尝试这些技巧之前反而更好！

All of this is to be expected. Learning anything is a process of making mistakes. Expect to fall flat on your face sometimes. It doesn’t matter how many times you fall down; what matters is whether or not you get back up again. Remember that each small success, every interaction in which you are able to implement one of the tools or principles, will build confidence and lay down a new pattern in your mind.

这一切都在意料之中。学习任何东西都是一个不断犯错的过程。做好跌倒的准备吧。跌倒多少次并不重要，重要的是你是否能重新站起来。记住，每一次小小的成功，每一次你运用这些工具或原则的互动，都会增强你的信心，并在你的脑海中形成新的模式。

Changes to communication don’t happen overnight. It took time to learn the habits we have. It will take time to unlearn them and become proficient at something new. But every minute you spend learning is worth it. It will pay off in the quality of your relationships, the amount of well-being in your life, and your ability to engage effectively in the world.

沟通方式的改变并非一朝一夕就能完成。我们养成的习惯需要时间，而摒弃旧习惯、掌握新技能也需要时间。但你花在学习上的每一分钟都物有所值。它将提升你的人际关系质量，增强你的生活幸福感，并提高你有效融入社会的能力。

Learning to Ride a Bike

学习骑自行车

I remember well my enthusiasm and curiosity as a kid, but I also recall having a very hard time getting a word in edgewise during the fast-paced, animated dialogue of our family dinners. I have a visceral memory of sitting at that black kitchen table with a heavy sensation in my chest, a hard knot in my throat, and tears of frustration burning beneath the surface as the rest of my family plowed through the conversation, leaving little space for my voice.

我清楚地记得小时候的热情和好奇心，但也记得在家人热烈的餐桌对话中，我很难插上一句话。我至今仍清晰地记得，坐在那张黑色的餐桌旁，胸口像压着一块石头，喉咙哽咽，沮丧的泪水在眼眶里打转，而其他家人却滔滔不绝地谈论着，几乎不给我留下任何发言的空间。

Finding your voice, learning how to say what you mean and how to listen deeply—this is one of the most rewarding journeys you can take. When you have developed your capacity to speak wisely and listen well, you possess an inexhaustible resource with which to navigate and transform the world. Rather than turning your conversations into a bland, neutral wash of “being nice,” the skills in this book will help you feel more alive and engaged.

找到自己的声音，学会如何表达真我，学会如何深度倾听——这将是你人生中最有意义的旅程之一。当你培养出智慧表达和善于倾听的能力时，你就拥有了取之不尽的资源，可以用来驾驭和改变世界。本书中的技巧将帮助你摆脱平淡乏味、敷衍了事的“客套话”，让你的对话更加生动鲜活，更能全身心投入其中。

When I was a kid, I owned a blue Schwinn dirt bike with a red seat and red handlebars. On many a summer evening after dinner I would ride my bike around our block in suburban New Jersey again and again, jumping curbs and racing along the sidewalk beneath old oak and sycamore trees.

小时候，我有一辆蓝色的施文牌越野自行车，红色的车座和红色的车把。很多个夏日的傍晚，晚饭后，我都会骑着它绕着新泽西郊区的街区转悠，时不时地跳过路沿，沿着人行道在古老的橡树和梧桐树下飞驰。

Learning to communicate mindfully has a lot in common with riding a bike. It takes time. In the beginning, it’s helpful to have training wheels to guide you as you find your balance. Having someone else to cheer you along tends to make the process safer and more fun. And when you take the training wheels off, you need to be prepared to take a few bruises and skin a knee or elbow. But once you learn, you never forget how to ride. It can take you great distances, and the exhilaration and joy of getting there is all the fun.

学习用心沟通与骑自行车有很多相似之处。这需要时间。一开始，辅助轮能帮助你找到平衡，这很有帮助。有人为你加油鼓劲，会让过程更安全、更有趣。当你摘掉辅助轮时，就要做好磕磕碰碰的准备，膝盖或手肘可能会擦破皮。但一旦学会，你就永远不会忘记如何骑行。它可以带你走很远的路，而到达目的地的兴奋和喜悦才是最大的乐趣。

* I often refer to Nonviolent Communication by its acronym, NVC. If you’d like information about NVC and Rosenberg’s work, see the “Further Resources” section in the back of the book.

* 我经常用缩写 NVC 来指代非暴力沟通。如果您想了解有关 NVC 和罗森伯格著作的信息，请参阅本书末尾的“延伸阅读”部分。

# ↩

part one

# ↩

第一部分

the first step

第一步

lead with presence

以气场引领

EFFECTIVE COMMUNICATION DEPENDS on our ability to be present. Speaking openly and honestly, listening deeply, and navigating the inevitable twists and turns of a conversation all require a high degree of self-awareness. To say what we mean, we must first know what we mean. To know what we mean, we must listen inwardly and discern what’s true for us.

有效沟通取决于我们能否全神贯注。坦诚直言、认真倾听、应对对话中不可避免的曲折变化，都需要高度的自我认知。要表达清楚自己的意思，首先必须明白自己的意思。要明白自己的意思，就必须倾听内心的声音，辨别哪些话对我们而言才是真实的。

The first step of mindful communication is to lead with presence, which means that we show up as fully and completely as possible. If we’re not here, we’re probably on automatic. And if we’re on automatic, we’re less likely to remember the tools we’ve learned, come from our best intentions, or access our own wisdom.

正念沟通的第一步是保持临在，这意味着我们要尽可能全身心地投入。如果我们不在状态，很可能就处于自动状态。而一旦进入自动状态，我们就更难想起我们学到的技巧、我们出于好意的初衷，或者运用我们自身的智慧。

Leading with presence is a rich practice with many dimensions. In part one , we’ll explore this primary foundation of skillful communication: our ability to be present. We’ll look at the nature of human communication, its central role in our lives, and how we can cultivate awareness in ourselves and in conversation.

以临在感引领是一种蕴含丰富内涵的实践，涵盖诸多层面。在第一部分，我们将探讨有效沟通的根本基础：临在感。我们将审视人类沟通的本质、它在我们生活中的核心作用，以及我们如何在自身和对话中培养这种觉察力。

# ↩

1

the center of our lives

我们生活的中心

Language is very powerful. Language does not just describe reality. Language creates the reality it describes.

—DESMOND TUTU

语言拥有强大的力量。语言不仅描述现实，它还能创造它所描述的现实。——德斯蒙德·图图

WE ENTER THIS world vulnerable, completely dependent, and primed for language. From the moment we’re born, communication sits at the center of our life.

我们生来脆弱，完全依赖他人，并且天生渴望语言。从我们出生的那一刻起，沟通就占据了我们生活的中心。

A human baby is born with the innate ability to learn any of the world’s seven thousand languages. In the first weeks and months, though, we are given just two tools to communicate our needs: crying and smiling. From there our brains develop, neurons primed to discern the rhythm, sound, tone, and volume of human language. And at this early age we pick it up very quickly—whichever language circumstance (or fate) drops us into.

人类婴儿天生就具备学习世界上七千多种语言中任何一种的能力。然而，在最初的几周和几个月里，我们只有两种表达需求的工具：哭泣和微笑。之后，我们的大脑开始发育，神经元逐渐被激活，能够辨别人类语言的节奏、声音、语调和音量。在这个早期阶段，无论我们身处何种语言环境（或者说命运的安排），我们都能很快掌握它。

Along with this system of sounds, words, and grammar, we learn how to express emotions, how to ask for what we need, and ways to try to get what we want. Eventually, if all is functioning well, we learn how to read and use more complex social cues; we learn metaphor, idiom, and humor. We learn all of this through listening, inquiry, observation, and repetition.

伴随着这套由声音、词汇和语法构成的系统，我们学会了如何表达情感，如何提出需求，以及如何努力争取自己想要的东西。最终，如果一切顺利，我们会学会解读和运用更复杂的社交信号；我们会学习比喻、习语和幽默。所有这一切都是通过聆听、探究、观察和重复来学习的。

As we enter the human family with language, we naturally pick up whatever patterns of communication happen to come along with our family of origin, ethnic group, class, gender, society, and the dominant culture. Some of us learn that it’s not safe to express our needs, so we try to ensure we’ll be cared for by taking care of others. Some of us learn to get what we want by using force, so we assert ourselves and try to appear the strongest or smartest. Some of us learn that our needs aren’t valued by our society, and so we harden inside and disconnect from our vulnerability. And at times, we may learn that there’s space to ask for what we need and still stay connected to others, working things out together.

当我们带着语言进入人类大家庭时，我们自然而然地会习得原生家庭、种族、阶级、性别、社会以及主流文化所带来的各种沟通模式。有些人学会了表达自己的需求并不安全，所以我们试图通过照顾他人来确保自己得到关爱。有些人学会了用武力来获得想要的东西，所以我们会强势地表现自己，力求显得最强大或最聪明。有些人学会了不重视自己的需求，所以我们变得内心冷漠，与自己的脆弱隔绝。而有时，我们或许会发现，即使表达了自己的需求，仍然可以与他人保持联系，共同解决问题。

Most of us learn some combination of these approaches to meeting our needs, yet we’ve all had communication training. Generally it’s just been unconscious and unintentional. The context of our social location and cultural milieu set the frames and beliefs, and our life experiences confirm and reinforce them. That is, until something wakes up inside and says, “This just isn’t working!” This realization could be sparked by a failed relationship or marital problems, a fight that results in the loss of a friendship, ongoing communication issues at work, the struggle to survive in a system that isn’t designed to meet human needs, the plight of our world and breakdown of social institutions, or simply being fed up with the tyranny of the voice in our own head.

我们大多数人都会学习运用这些方法来满足自身需求，但我们都接受过沟通方面的训练。通常情况下，这些训练都是无意识的、非刻意的。我们所处的社会环境和文化背景塑造了我们的思维框架和信念，而我们的生活经历则不断印证并强化这些框架和信念。直到内心深处某个声音觉醒，发出“这样行不通！”的呐喊。这种觉醒可能源于一段失败的感情或婚姻问题、一场导致友谊破裂的争吵、工作中持续不断的沟通障碍、在一个无法满足人类需求的体制中挣扎求生、我们所处世界的困境和社会制度的崩溃，或者仅仅是厌倦了内心独白的束缚。

The good news about all this is that since language is learned, since our communication patterns and the emotional habits that drive them are trained, they can be unlearned, retrained. We can learn to speak and listen in a new way that’s more conducive to the kind of life we want to live and the society we want to create. *1 We can find our voice, learn to say what we mean, and discover how to listen deeply.

好消息是，语言是学习而来的，我们的沟通模式和驱动这些模式的情感习惯都是后天习得的，因此它们也可以被改变、被重新训练。我们可以学习用一种全新的方式说话和倾听，这种方式更有利于我们想要的生活和想要创造的社会。我们可以找到自己的声音，学会表达自己的想法，并学会如何深入倾听。

Finding My Way with Words

用文字寻找方向

For me, the turning point came in my early twenties. After a couple of failed romantic relationships, lost friendships, and my parents’ divorce, I turned to Buddhist meditation to sort out some of the inner turmoil. After college, I ended up living and working at the Insight Meditation Society in rural Massachusetts. Buddhist teachings helped me come to terms with things and mature some. Yet I noticed that the values of clarity, kindness, and compassion I felt so strongly while meditating would often evaporate when, for example, a conflict arose with a coworker. They were even less accessible when I spoke with my family.

对我来说，转折点出现在二十出头。经历了几段失败的恋情、失去的友谊以及父母的离婚后，我开始接触佛教冥想，试图理清内心的种种困扰。大学毕业后，我最终在马萨诸塞州乡村的内观禅修协会生活和工作。佛教教义帮助我接受现实，也让我变得更加成熟。然而，我发现，我在冥想中强烈感受到的清明、善良和慈悲这些价值观，在例如与同事发生冲突时，往往会消失殆尽。而当我与家人交谈时，这些品质就更难寻觅了。

I remember one particularly devastating argument with my older brother, which ended with me, pushed to the limits of frustration, lifting a chair and smashing it against the floor in my grandmother’s living room. Dramatic, I know—but it happened.

我记得和哥哥有过一次特别激烈的争吵，最后我被逼到了忍无可忍的地步，在奶奶家的客厅里，我拿起一把椅子狠狠地摔在了地板上。我知道这很夸张——但它确实发生了。

It wasn’t until a staff communication training at the meditation center that I realized I could study and improve my habits of speech. After that first half-day workshop, I was hooked. I took an eight-week course in a small college town nearby and pretty soon found my way to Dr. Marshall B. Rosenberg.

直到在冥想中心参加了一次员工沟通技巧培训后，我才意识到我可以学习并改善自己的说话习惯。第一次半天的培训结束后，我就彻底着迷了。我在附近的一个大学城参加了一个为期八周的课程，很快就找到了马歇尔·B·罗森伯格博士。

As I explored the intersection of contemplative awareness and communication, I found that my years of mindfulness practice provided a fertile ground in which to grow new communication habits. Later contact with Dr. Peter A. Levine’s Somatic Experiencing added a new dimension to my understanding of human behavior. I began to see our patterns of relating as part of our hardwiring for self-protection, survival, and social connection. 1 I developed a more nuanced ability to observe how these basic evolutionary mechanisms play out in dialogue and how to help people shift out of habitual patterns that no longer serve them. Through all of this, I’ve come to a much greater, more profound appreciation for the power and complexity of human interaction and communication.

在探索冥想觉知与沟通的交汇点时，我发现多年的正念练习为我培养新的沟通习惯提供了沃土。后来接触到彼得·A·莱文博士的躯体体验疗法，为我理解人类行为增添了新的维度。我开始意识到，我们的人际交往模式是我们与生俱来的自我保护、生存和社会联结机制的一部分。我逐渐培养出更敏锐的观察力，能够洞察这些基本的进化机制如何在对话中发挥作用，以及如何帮助人们摆脱不再适用的习惯模式。通过这一切，我对人际互动和沟通的力量与复杂性有了更深刻的理解。

The Universe of Communication

沟通的宇宙

Communication is much broader than its rudimentary components of speaking and listening, much richer than the mere exchange of supposedly objective information. Whether one’s aim is strategic (to achieve a certain end) or relational (to connect), communication involves a meaningful exchange that leads to understanding.

沟通远比基本的说话和倾听更为广泛，也远比单纯交换所谓的客观信息更为丰富。无论沟通的目的是战略性的（达成特定目标）还是关系性的（建立联系），它都包含着有意义的交流，最终促成理解。

Communication is a process of interaction or exchange creating understanding.

沟通是产生理解的互动或交流过程。

This isn’t unique to human beings. Most (if not all) forms of life have some kind of “language,” some system for transmitting information. Humans have developed this capacity to send and receive messages to an extraordinary degree. It’s part of what’s allowed us to cooperate and create in such astonishing ways, for good and for ill.

这并非人类独有。大多数（如果不是全部）生命形式都拥有某种“语言”，某种信息传递系统。人类已经将这种发送和接收信息的能力发展到了非凡的程度。正是这种能力使我们能够以如此惊人的方式进行合作和创造，无论好坏。

Yet human communication involves so much more than what we say. It includes how we speak—our tone of voice, volume, and pace—which transmits a wealth of information about how we’re feeling, what we think of one another, how much power we do or don’t have, and so on. It’s also about why we speak. What do we want? What’s our motivation? And, of course, it includes listening: how we listen, why we listen, or if we’re even listening at all.

然而，人际沟通远不止于我们说了什么。它还包括我们如何说话——我们的语气、音量和语速——这些都传递着丰富的信息，例如我们的感受、我们对彼此的看法、我们拥有或不拥有的权力等等。它还关乎我们为什么说话。我们想要什么？我们的动机是什么？当然，它也包括倾听：我们如何倾听、为什么倾听，或者我们是否真的在倾听。

In addition to speaking and listening, awareness is another primary component at play when we communicate. Successful communication depends on our ability to pay attention. For “message sent” to equal “message received,” we need presence, to be fully here, aware of self and other.

除了说话和倾听之外，觉察力也是沟通中另一个至关重要的因素。成功的沟通取决于我们集中注意力的能力。为了确保“发出的信息”与“接收的信息”一致，我们需要全然地投入其中，完全觉察自身和他人的存在。

We can see this in the simplest of moments. Ever speak to someone who was reading or watching TV, and they don’t hear you? You’re speaking the same language; their ears are functioning fine—but their mind’s attention isn’t directed to listening. There’s no awareness of you or your words so communication doesn’t occur.

我们甚至在最简单的时刻都能看到这一点。你有没有过这样的经历：跟正在看书或看电视的人说话，结果他们听不见？你们说的是同一种语言；他们的耳朵也听得很清楚——但他们的注意力并没有集中在听你说话上。他们没有意识到你的存在，也没有听到你的话，所以沟通就无法进行。

This simple truth is so obvious we often overlook it. Awareness is the primary foundation for all communication. If communication is about creating understanding, mindful communication is about creating understanding through awareness. We could say that the opposite is mindless communication —we’re either running on automatic or we’re consumed by an inner narrative of judgments, criticism, planning, and mind wandering. It happens more often than we’d like to admit!

这个简单的道理如此显而易见，我们却常常忽略它。觉察是所有沟通的基础。如果沟通的目的是为了建立理解，那么正念沟通就是通过觉察来建立理解。我们可以说，反之亦然，那就是无意识沟通——我们要么机械地重复着对话，要么被内心的评判、批评、计划和思绪游离所吞噬。这种情况发生的频率远超我们的想象！

Presence is one of those things that’s hard to pinpoint with language, yet it makes a huge difference in the quality of our life. I define presence as the experience of being fully aware and sensing one’s body in the present moment. I’ve found presence to be so important to communication that I begin all my trainings by pointing this out and giving participants a taste of what it’s like to be present in dialogue.

临在感很难用语言准确描述，但它对我们的生活质量却有着巨大的影响。我将临在感定义为完全觉察并感受当下身体的体验。我发现临在感对沟通至关重要，因此我会在所有培训课程的开头强调这一点，并让学员体验在对话中保持临在感的感觉。

Presence is embodied awareness of our direct sensory, mental, and emotional experience.

临在感是对我们直接的感官、心理和情感体验的具身觉知。

In one of the first exercises I teach, I invite participants to share a short story with one another. We begin with a few moments of quiet to feel what it’s like to be fully here, aware of the body. One person listens while the other person shares their story, both aiming to maintain present-time awareness.

在我教授的第一个练习中，我会邀请参与者彼此分享一个短故事。我们先安静片刻，感受全然地活在当下、觉察身体的感觉。一人倾听，另一人分享自己的故事，双方都努力保持对当下的觉察。

After a minute or so I ring a bell and ask everyone to pause—midsentence, wherever they are. I invite them to return to that sense of presence and to notice what’s happening in their bodies. After a short period of silence, they continue, then trade roles so that all participants have a chance to experience pausing in the middle of things. Without fail, nearly everyone who does this exercise remarks on two things: (1) how quickly they lost touch with their body and (2) how stirred up they felt inside when they paused.

大约一分钟后，我摇铃，请大家停下来——无论他们正在说什么，都要停下来。我邀请他们重新感受当下，并觉察自己身体的感受。短暂的沉默后，他们继续，然后交换角色，让所有参与者都有机会体验在事情进行到一半时停下来的感觉。几乎每个做这个练习的人都会提到两点：（1）他们多么容易就与自己的身体失去联系；（2）停下来时，他们内心感受到的那种悸动。

Having presence for a moment is easy and readily accessible for most people. Staying connected to presence continually is harder—frankly, it takes training. Maintaining awareness in conversation is even more challenging. The tendency to lose presence is strong: we often leave it as soon as we open our eyes. Indeed, it’s amazing how difficult it is to stay here once we open our mouths!

对大多数人来说，短暂地保持觉察很容易，也很容易做到。但要持续地保持觉察就难多了——坦白说，这需要练习。在交谈中保持觉察则更具挑战性。我们很容易失去觉察：通常一睁眼就离开了。的确，一旦开口说话，想要保持觉察是多么困难！

Of course, there are common exceptions: the intimacy we feel in romantic relationships or moments of heightened awareness in nature. In these moments we often feel a profound sense of connection. It is precisely the combination of deep presence in relation to another or our surroundings that creates the potency of these experiences.

当然，也有一些常见的例外：比如我们在浪漫关系中感受到的亲密感，或者在大自然中高度觉察的时刻。在这些时刻，我们常常会感受到一种深刻的联结感。正是这种与他人或周围环境的深度联结，造就了这些体验的强大力量。

Bringing presence to relationship is a powerful practice. It means that we really show up for ourselves, the other person, and whatever happens between us. Yet there are several reasons why it’s hard to have presence while speaking and listening:

在人际关系中保持专注是一种强大的修行方式。它意味着我们真正地投入到自己、对方以及我们之间发生的任何事情中。然而，在说话和倾听时保持专注却并非易事，原因有很多：

• It’s vulnerable to be face-to-face with another human being.

• 与另一个人面对面交流是件很危险的事。

• Social engagement can activate the nervous system, putting us on edge. 2

社交活动会激活神经系统，使我们感到紧张不安。

• We tend to focus our attention outward, on the other person, or inward, on our thoughts—thus losing the sense of relatedness and connection.

• 我们往往会将注意力集中在外部，集中在他人身上，或者集中在内部，集中在自己的想法上——从而失去关联感和联系感。

• We haven’t practiced it.

• 我们没有练习过。

In nature, eye contact among primates can be a sign of aggression. In spite of our large brains, when face-to-face with another human we still share that old, edgy conditioning. In an instant of contact, our biology is gauging our safety: “Is this a friend, a foe, or a mate?”

在自然界中，灵长类动物之间的眼神交流可能是一种攻击性信号。尽管我们的大脑容量很大，但当我们与另一个人面对面时，我们仍然保留着那种古老的、紧张的本能。在接触的瞬间，我们的生物本能会评估我们的安全：“这是朋友、敌人还是伴侣？”

Though often below the threshold of consciousness, this conditioning is operating to some degree as we enter most interactions. Part of transforming our communication patterns is to recognize this fundamental uncertainty in our nervous system and have a means to ground and soothe ourselves. (We’ll look at some methods for doing that in chapter 3 ).

虽然这种条件反射通常处于意识层面以下，但在我们进行大多数互动时，它都会在一定程度上发挥作用。改变我们沟通模式的一部分，就是要认识到我们神经系统中这种根本性的不确定性，并找到让自己平静下来、安抚情绪的方法。（我们将在第三章探讨一些方法。）

The Human Voice, Breath, and Identity

人声、呼吸与身份

Another reason why communication can be such a charged area has to do with how our hearing evolved. Our ears are tuned to a very specific range of sound and are particularly sensitive to one narrow frequency: the human voice. (Many animals share this attunement to a particular range of sound. The oceanic calls of whales and the deep rumblings of elephants occur at frequencies inaudible to the human ear.) Have you ever heard someone shrieking with laughter or tears and experienced an uncertain yet pressing urge to find out which it was? Or heard a pack of coyotes howling that sounded so much like humans you couldn’t quite be sure?

沟通之所以会成为如此敏感的话题，另一个原因与我们听觉的进化方式有关。我们的耳朵只对特定范围的声音敏感，尤其对一个狭窄的频率——人声——格外敏感。（许多动物也对特定范围的声音有这种敏感度。鲸鱼的海洋鸣叫和大象的低沉咆哮都发生在人耳听不到的频率范围内。）你是否曾经听到过有人发出尖叫般的笑声或哭声，并感到一种难以分辨却又迫切想要弄清楚究竟是哪种声音？或者听到过一群郊狼的嚎叫，听起来如此像人类的叫声，以至于你无法确定它们究竟是什么？

This is tens of thousands of years of evolution at work. In order to care for our young and protect our kin, the inner architecture of our ears developed to attune precisely to the human voice and pick up immediately on sounds of human distress. 3 Remember that baby, smiling or crying? The conditioning to respond to those signals remains deep within us.

这是数万年进化的结果。为了照顾幼崽和保护亲人，我们耳朵的内部结构进化得能够精准地感知人声，并立即捕捉到人类的痛苦声音。还记得那个婴儿的笑容或哭声吗？对这些信号做出反应的本能反应仍然深深地存在于我们的体内。

Listening uses this same architecture and therefore carries a dual potential. Hearing the human voice can activate our nervous system’s fight-flight-freeze mechanisms, or it can activate the social engagement system that reassures, connects, and soothes. 4

聆听也运用了同样的架构，因此具有双重潜能。听到人声可以激活我们神经系统的战斗-逃跑-僵住反应机制，也可以激活社交互动系统，从而带来安慰、联结和抚慰。

How we speak adds another dimension to why words can be so charged. Humans produce verbal language by controlling the flow of air over the voice box and vocal cords. Our words are carried on a wave of breath, the same breath that feeds the cells of our body with oxygen from the moment we are born until the moment we die. Pause to take this in for a moment: we use the same physiological process to speak as we do to sustain our life energy.

我们说话的方式为语言为何如此充满力量增添了另一层含义。人类通过控制气流流经声带和喉部来发出语言。我们的话语承载着呼吸的波浪，而这呼吸也正是从我们出生到死亡，为我们身体细胞提供氧气的那股力量。请稍作停顿，仔细体会：我们说话所用的生理过程，与我们维持生命能量所用的生理过程是相同的。

It goes even further. Our breath (and therefore our speech) is directly linked to our nervous system in a reciprocal relationship: a change in one affects the other. When we feel excited, anxious, afraid, or aggressive (any degree of sympathetic activation ), our breathing quickens. When we feel relaxed, at ease, or settled (any degree of parasympathetic deactivation ), our breathing slows and deepens.

不仅如此，我们的呼吸（以及由此而来的言语）与神经系统之间存在着直接的相互作用：一方的变化会影响另一方。当我们感到兴奋、焦虑、恐惧或好斗（任何程度的交感神经激活）时，呼吸会加快。当我们感到放松、自在或平静（任何程度的副交感神经抑制）时，呼吸会减慢并加深。

This is partly due to the unusual position the breath occupies in our autonomic nervous system, which regulates the basic functions of our body. 5 Breathing is both voluntary and involuntary. It operates automatically, and it’s also subject to our will. Speech is one of the most common ways in which we consciously and intentionally manipulate the breath.

这部分原因在于呼吸在我们自主神经系统中的特殊地位，自主神经系统调节着我们身体的基本功能。呼吸既是自主的，也是非自主的。它既可以自动进行，也可以受我们意志控制。说话是我们最常有意识地控制呼吸的方式之一。

All of this holds particular significance for our training in mindful communication. When we understand the relationship between our breath, our words, and our mental-emotional state, we gain more mastery over our experience and self-expression. At various points in our exploration, I’ll offer suggestions on how you can use your awareness of the breath to hold a listener’s attention, manage strong emotions, and steady yourself in tense situations.

这一切对我们正念沟通的训练都至关重要。当我们理解呼吸、言语和心理情绪状态之间的关系时，就能更好地掌控自身体验和自我表达。在接下来的探索过程中，我会提供一些建议，帮助你运用对呼吸的觉察来吸引听众的注意力、管理强烈的情绪，并在紧张的情况下保持内心的平静。

Resting on top of this physiology is the intricate connection between the breath, the voice, and our sense of identity. Our voice is one of the most intimate and personal aspects of who we are. For most of us, it’s our primary means of expression, a kind of aural signature by which we are known and recognized. Of all the things that change over the course of a life—our aging bodies; our weathered, wrinkled visage—once we enter adulthood it’s our voice that changes the least and the slowest. Our sense of who we are often can become closely tied with our voice.

建立在这一生理结构之上的是呼吸、声音和自我认同感之间错综复杂的联系。声音是我们最私密、最个人化的特质之一。对大多数人来说，它是我们主要的表达方式，一种独特的听觉印记，让我们被他人认识和辨认。在人生的各个阶段，许多事物都会发生变化——衰老的身体、饱经风霜、布满皱纹的面容——但一旦步入成年，声音的变化却是最小、最慢的。我们对自我的认知往往与声音紧密相连。

Beyond the unique music of our voice, consider how we identify ourselves to others. One of the most common mechanisms by which I’m known is my first name—a word representing who I am. When in conflict, challenges to our identity or self-image can be the most painful and hardest to navigate.

除了我们独特的嗓音之外，还要思考我们如何向他人表明自己的身份。我最常用的识别方式之一就是我的名字——一个代表我是谁的词。当遭遇冲突时，对我们的身份或自我认知的挑战往往是最痛苦、最难应对的。

In addition to these root physiological and psychological components of communication, realms of emotion, class, culture, and even mystery are at play in this daily activity of speaking and listening. Considering all the layers that are present in a simple exchange, it’s no wonder our communication cuts so close to the core.

除了这些基本的生理和心理沟通要素之外，情感、阶级、文化，甚至神秘感等因素也在日常的听说活动中发挥作用。考虑到一次简单的交流中蕴含着如此丰富的层次，我们的沟通能够如此直击人心也就不足为奇了。

A Multidimensional, Holistic Experience

多维度、整体性的体验

As I hope you are beginning to appreciate, human communication is more than just a linguistic exchange. It’s a multidimensional, embodied, lived experience that involves all of our being: feelings, thoughts, memories, and history. It is at once verbal, mental, emotional, and somatic.

我希望你已经开始意识到，人类沟通不仅仅是语言的交流。它是一种多维度的、具身化的、鲜活的体验，涉及我们存在的全部：情感、思想、记忆和经历。它同时包含语言、心理、情感和身体层面。

Communication includes how we use our voice—the tone, volume, and pace at which we speak. It includes body language and touch. We communicate with silence: what we don’t say, or how we use verbal space. It includes our internal dialogue: how we think and speak to ourselves. Even our social conditioning and cultural history are present in our interactions.

沟通包括我们如何运用声音——说话的语调、音量和语速。它包括肢体语言和触摸。我们通过沉默进行沟通：我们不说的话，或者我们如何利用语言空间。它包括我们的内心对话：我们如何思考和与自己对话。甚至我们的社会制约和文化背景也体现在我们的互动中。

There is also a root somatic element to communication: the vibration of our words and the physicality of our subjective experience. Communication is dynamic, changing in real time. Skillful communication requires that we attune to our inner and outer world, continually adjusting to the moment.

沟通中也蕴含着一种根深蒂固的身体因素：我们言语的振动以及我们主观体验的物质性。沟通是动态的，实时变化。娴熟的沟通技巧要求我们与内在和外在世界保持协调，并不断根据当下情况做出调整。

Communication is also holistic; it crosses all the boundaries of our lives. We may compartmentalize our time, dividing our lives between personal, social, and professional realms, but these distinctions are only relative. We live one life. The various roles we play—parent, child, friend, teacher, student, employee—are interconnected facets of one whole person. We may speak or behave differently in different environments, but the fundamental programs running the show are the same.

沟通也是整体性的，它跨越了我们生活的方方面面。我们或许会把时间划分成不同的领域，比如个人、社交和职业，但这些区分只是相对的。我们拥有的是同一个生命。我们扮演的各种角色——父母、子女、朋友、教师、学生、员工——都是同一个人相互关联的不同面向。我们在不同的环境中可能会有不同的言行举止，但驱动这一切的基本机制却始终如一。

We can use this holistic nature to our advantage; changes in one area can transfer to other contexts of our lives. While doing simple exercises, it’s common for participants in my workshops to have powerful insights into core patterns in their lives. After practicing with the pause at a recent retreat, one woman realized how much of her speech was driven by mild social anxiety. Pausing helped her choose more carefully what she wanted to say and why.

我们可以利用这种整体性；一个领域的改变可以迁移到我们生活的其他方面。在我的工作坊里，学员们在做一些简单的练习时，常常会对自身生活的核心模式产生深刻的领悟。最近一次静修中，一位女士在练习了停顿技巧后，意识到自己很多话语都受到轻微社交焦虑的驱使。停顿帮助她更谨慎地选择自己想说的话以及想说的原因。

When we learn new ways to communicate, we engage with this entire rich, multilayered realm and all the years of conditioning that we carry within it. To make lasting changes in these habits of communication, it will help to make small, incremental shifts that we can sustain over time.

当我们学习新的沟通方式时，我们便会接触到这个丰富而多层次的领域，以及我们多年来积累的各种思维模式。为了持久地改变这些沟通习惯，循序渐进地做出一些小的改变，并长期坚持下去，将会大有裨益。

Principle: Given the complexity of communication, transformation occurs most readily through small shifts sustained over time.

原则：鉴于沟通的复杂性，变革最容易通过长期持续的小幅改变来实现。

Human beings are complex, living systems. When dealing with complex systems, a small change can have far-reaching effects. It’s like trying to turn a cargo ship at sea. A vessel that large with that much momentum can’t make sharp turns. However, a one- or two-degree course correction of the rudder, if held steady, will take that ship in a very different direction over time.

人类是复杂的生命系统。面对复杂的系统，一个微小的变化就可能产生深远的影响。这就像试图在海上调转一艘货轮的航向。如此庞大、动能巨大的船只无法进行急转弯。然而，如果舵的调整幅度保持稳定，哪怕只有一两度，假以时日，也能使这艘船驶向截然不同的方向。

Training Our Words, Training Our Minds

训练我们的语言，训练我们的思想

Contemplating the vast extent of human communication, it can be daunting to take in the scope of the project to retrain ourselves. How are we to deal effectively with something as fundamental as the core patterning through which we relate to the world?

考虑到人类交流的广袤无垠，重新训练自身的工作量之大可能会令人望而生畏。我们该如何有效地应对像我们与世界互动的核心模式这样根本性的问题呢？

Fortunately we have everything we need to do this—the insights of modern neuroscience and psychology, a clear method, and a fulcrum on which to turn knowledge into practice. The method is our three-step training in presence, intention, and attention. The fulcrum is mindfulness, our ability to steady awareness and see clearly.

幸运的是，我们拥有实现这一目标所需的一切——现代神经科学和心理学的洞见、清晰的方法，以及将知识转化为实践的关键所在。这方法就是我们关于临在、意图和专注的三步训练。关键所在则是正念，即我们稳定觉知、清晰观察的能力。

The need to transform these patterns is clear. If we are to live more meaningful lives, and if we are to work together to meet the radical changes occurring on our planet, in our governments, economies, and the environment, we must learn how to hear one another and communicate more effectively.

改变这些模式的必要性显而易见。如果我们想要过上更有意义的生活，如果我们想要携手应对地球、政府、经济和环境正在发生的剧变，我们就必须学会倾听彼此，并进行更有效的沟通。

Over the course of this book I’ll be encouraging you to investigate your thinking, listening, and speaking with the aim of making small shifts in your understanding and habits. If you sustain these shifts, they will lead to lasting change in your words, your relationships, and your life.

在本书中，我将鼓励你审视自己的思考、倾听和表达方式，旨在让你的理解和习惯发生细微的改变。如果你能坚持这些改变，它们将为你的言辞、人际关系和生活带来持久的改变。

PRINCIPLES

原则

Given the complexity of communication, transformation occurs most readily through small shifts sustained over time.

鉴于沟通的复杂性，变革最容易通过长期持续的小幅改变来实现。

KEY POINTS

要点

Bringing presence to communication can be challenging for many reasons:

在沟通中展现临场感可能面临诸多挑战：

• We haven’t practiced it.

• 我们没有练习过。

• It puts us in touch with our vulnerability.

它让我们意识到自身的脆弱。

• It can stimulate evolutionary drives for safety.

• 它可以激发人们对安全的进化动力。

• Eye contact in primates can signal aggression.

• 灵长类动物的眼神交流可以发出攻击信号。

• Hearing a human voice can be soothing or threatening.

• 听到人声可能会让人感到安慰，也可能会让人感到威胁。

• Verbal communication links our breath, nervous system, and sense of self.

• 语言交流将我们的呼吸、神经系统和自我意识联系起来。

Communication is multidimensional and holistic. It includes:

沟通是多维度、整体性的，它包括：

• A linguistic exchange of information

• 语言信息交流

• Nonverbal communication

• 非语言沟通

• Our internal dialogue (cognitive experience)

• 我们的内心对话（认知体验）

• Our emotional, affective experience

• 我们的情感体验

• Our somatic, embodied experience

• 我们的身体体验，具身经验

• Personal, psychological, social, and cultural conditioning

• 个人、心理、社会和文化条件

QUESTION & ANSWER *2

问答 *2

Q: I find it easier to stay present when I am speaking and harder to stay present while listening. Is that normal?

问：我发现自己说话时更容易集中注意力，而听别人说话时则比较难集中注意力。这正常吗？

It’s different for everyone. I find it fascinating how presence can feel more natural for some in the receptive mode and for others in the expressive mode. If you pay attention, you might even notice that it changes when talking with different people. Regard it as useful information. We want to build on our strengths and develop our capacity to be equally present with both speaking and listening.

每个人的情况都不一样。我发现，有些人更容易在倾听模式下自然地保持专注，而有些人则更容易在表达模式下自然地保持专注，这真是太有趣了。如果你仔细观察，甚至会发现，和不同的人交谈时，这种专注也会有所不同。把这当作有用的信息吧。我们希望发挥自身优势，提升在说话和倾听时都能保持专注的能力。

Q: You mentioned pausing. I don’t think I could do that in most conversations. I’m afraid I’d lose my turn to speak!

问：你提到了停顿。我觉得在大多数对话中我都做不到这一点。我怕那样会错过发言的机会！

Having trust and confidence in our own voice, that we can take up space and speak our mind, is really important. I want any communication tools to support that kind of internal ease. Pausing in a deliberate, extended way is more of a training exercise. There may be certain conversations or relationships where it would work to take a long pause, but generally it helps to make pauses short and less conspicuous.

对自己声音的信任和自信至关重要，我们能够畅所欲言，表达自己的想法。我希望所有沟通工具都能帮助我们建立这种内心的自在感。刻意地、长时间地停顿更像是一种训练。在某些对话或关系中，长时间的停顿或许会有帮助，但通常来说，短促而自然的停顿更为有效。

*1 On the collective level, since our social institutions are formed by (and simultaneously reinforce) the patterns of thought and perception that drive our communication, an essential aspect of working to transform them must be the parallel inner work of transforming our consciousness. Otherwise we run the risk of recreating the very systems we seek to change.

*1 从集体层面来看，由于我们的社会制度是由驱动我们沟通的思维和感知模式形成（并同时强化这些模式）的，因此，致力于变革这些制度的一个重要方面，必须同时进行我们意识的内在转变。否则，我们就有可能重塑我们试图改变的制度本身。

*2 Many of the questions found in the Question & Answer at the end of each chapter are based on transcripts from students at actual workshops and retreats.

*2 每章末尾的问答中出现的许多问题都是根据实际研讨会和静修活动中学生的记录整理而成的。

# ↩

2

the power of mindfulness

正念的力量

There is something mysterious and sacred about being alive. It’s an awareness of something that is too important to forget.

—CHRISTINA FELDMAN

活着这件事本身就充满神秘和神圣。它是一种对某些重要事物的觉察，而这些事物太过重要，不容遗忘。——克里斯蒂娜·费尔德曼

MY FATHER GREW up in the 1940s in a one-room shack in British Palestine. His mother raised chickens, goats, and rabbits while his father worked plastering walls and running a kiosk selling magazines, candy, and fresh juice. (They’d come from Belarus and Poland in their teens looking for a new life.) The oldest of three children, he was sent to a kibbutz when he turned thirteen so there would be one less mouth to feed.

我父亲在20世纪40年代的英属巴勒斯坦长大，住在一间简陋的小屋里。他的母亲养鸡、养羊、养兔，父亲则靠粉刷墙壁和经营小卖部为生，卖杂志、糖果和鲜榨果汁。（他们十几岁时从白俄罗斯和波兰来到这里，寻求新的生活。）他是家中三个孩子中的老大，13岁时被送到基布兹，这样家里就少了一张嘴要养。

He recently told me how during the first few weeks at the kibbutz, he would stand in his room each evening and watch the sun set over the fields. He told me how beautiful those sunsets were and how peaceful he felt. “A few months later, I was in my room when I looked up and realized that the sun was setting. I’d stopped noticing it.” He paused and grew quiet. “It’s always bothered me. Why did I stop noticing it?”

他最近告诉我，在基布兹的头几个星期，他每天晚上都会站在房间里，看着夕阳西下。他告诉我，那些日落多么美丽，他感到多么平静。“几个月后，我像往常一样待在房间里，抬头一看，才意识到太阳正在落山。我竟然不再注意到它了。”他停顿了一下，沉默不语。“这件事一直困扰着我。为什么我会不再注意到它呢？”

So much of the time we’re not actually here; we’re disconnected from our senses and the direct experience of being alive. Our attention is elsewhere, thinking of the past or the future—planning, worrying, remembering, regretting. My father’s story marks a key moment that each of us faces many times in our life—when we notice that we’re not living with awareness, what do we do about it?

很多时候，我们其实并不在当下；我们与感官脱节，无法直接体验生命。我们的注意力游离于外，沉湎于过去或未来——计划、担忧、回忆、后悔。我父亲的故事标志着我们每个人一生中都会多次面临的一个关键时刻——当我们意识到自己没有觉知地生活时，我们该如何应对？

The Ground for Connection

连接的基础

Mindfulness gives us back our lives. It’s what allows us to enjoy the beauty of a sunset, the wonder of an old tree, or the mystery and delight of human intimacy. In such experiences, we are wholeheartedly present. The force of their intensity induces a state of natural awareness in which we are deeply here, connected with ourselves and the world around us.

正念让我们重拾生活。它让我们能够欣赏日落之美，感受古树的奇妙，体验人与人之间亲密关系的神秘与喜悦。在这些体验中，我们全心全意地活在当下。它们带来的强烈感受会诱发一种自然的觉知状态，在这种状态下，我们深深地活在当下，与自我和周围的世界紧密相连。

This state of mindful presence is available to us at all times. It brings richness to ordinary experience, be it preparing a meal, talking to a family member, or feeling the morning air on our skin. It allows us to appreciate life and to move through the difficult parts with grace.

这种正念觉知的状态我们随时随地都可以拥有。它能丰富平凡的体验，无论是准备饭菜、与家人交谈，还是感受清晨的微风拂过肌肤。它让我们懂得欣赏生活，并优雅地度过人生中的艰难时刻。

As I’ve mentioned, mindful presence also plays an essential role in communication for the simple fact that we need to be here first to understand anything. Have you ever tried to converse with someone who was distracted? Or had someone pull out their smartphone in the middle of a conversation? (Maybe you’ve done the same when a conversation lagged.) How many arguments have you had simply because one person wasn’t listening? Or because someone couldn’t pause and hold their tongue? We can avoid many of the difficulties we have in dialogue simply by slowing down and being more present.

正如我之前提到的，专注当下在沟通中也扮演着至关重要的角色，原因很简单：我们首先需要集中注意力才能理解任何事情。你是否曾经尝试与心不在焉的人交谈？或者遇到过有人在谈话中途拿出手机的情况？（也许当谈话陷入僵局时，你也曾这样做过。）你经历过多少次争吵，仅仅是因为一方没有认真听？或者因为有人无法停下来，克制住自己的冲动？我们只需放慢语速，更加专注当下，就能避免对话中遇到的许多困难。

Mindfulness is being aware of what’s happening in the present moment in a balanced and nonreactive way.

正念是指以平衡、不反应的方式觉察当下正在发生的事情。

The role of awareness goes beyond being a prerequisite for understanding. Presence lays the ground for connection. We feel it when someone is engaged and listening. Presence is inviting. It gives others space, and it opens the door for them to engage with us. This kind of real-time awareness is a foundation for effective, healthy conversation. Without it, we’re running on automatic at best, and we may be unintentionally sowing seeds of disconnection. (If we’re not mindful, chances are we’re being mindless.)

觉察的作用远不止是理解的前提。临在感为联结奠定了基础。我们能感受到对方的投入和倾听。临在感令人感到亲切。它给予他人空间，也为他们与我们互动敞开大门。这种实时觉察是有效、健康对话的基础。缺乏觉察，我们充其量只能机械地运转，甚至可能在无意中埋下隔阂的种子。（如果我们不保持觉察，很可能就会变得麻木。）

Principle: Presence lays the ground for connection.

原则：在场是建立联系的基础。

The irony is that being mindful doesn’t actually require that much extra effort. In the long run, we may find being mindful actually conserves energy, compared to how we waste energy when mindless.

讽刺的是，保持正念其实并不需要付出太多额外的努力。从长远来看，与漫无目的、浪费能量相比，保持正念实际上可能更能节省能量。

How often do we take the time to begin a conversation by meeting the other person with presence? Rushing through the day, we barrel into conversations and wonder why we keep crashing. What would it be like instead to start from a place of clear, grounded self-awareness? To bring composure and respect to the process of making contact with another human being?

我们多久才会花时间以专注的态度去开启一段对话？我们匆匆忙忙地度过每一天，一头扎进对话，然后纳闷为什么总是以失败告终。如果我们能从一个清晰、踏实的自我认知出发，又会是怎样一番景象呢？如果我们能以沉着和尊重的态度去与他人建立联系，又会是怎样一番景象呢？

Leading with presence is the first step to effective conversations; is a rich and deep practice with many dimensions. Most fundamentally, it means that we enter conversations from the simplicity and strength of our own presence.

以临场感引领是有效对话的第一步；它是一种丰富而深刻的实践，包含诸多层面。从根本上讲，这意味着我们以自身临场感的简洁和力量开启对话。

To lead with presence also means that we strive to maintain awareness throughout a conversation. It’s a continual process in which we return to presence again and again, listening and speaking from awareness as much as possible. To be able to do this takes practice, especially in the heat of a difficult exchange. When we’ve developed this skill, our nervous system remembers how to return to presence. Like a gyroscope finding its center, we notice more quickly when we’re on automatic or caught in a reaction, and we readjust accordingly.

以临在感引领对话也意味着我们要努力在整个对话过程中保持觉察。这是一个持续的过程，我们需要不断地回归临在，尽可能地在觉察的基础上倾听和表达。做到这一点需要练习，尤其是在激烈的交流中。当我们掌握了这项技能后，我们的神经系统就会记住如何回归临在。就像陀螺仪找到中心一样，我们会更快地察觉到自己何时处于自动状态或陷入反应，并做出相应的调整。

So what is mindful presence? Put simply, mindfulness means knowing what’s happening right now in a balanced and nonreactive way. It’s the keen, observing eye of the naturalist who studies their subject patiently, with clarity, interest, and wonder. *1

那么，什么是正念临在呢？简单来说，正念就是以平衡且不带反应的方式觉察当下正在发生的事情。它就像博物学家敏锐的观察眼，耐心、清晰、饶有兴趣且充满好奇地研究他们的对象。

Mindfulness is not a purely mental experience. It is an intimate, embodied awareness of the richness of life: sensations, emotions, sounds, sights. To counter our tendency to associate mindfulness with a mental exercise, I use the word presence to refer to the experience of being mindfully aware. 1

正念并非纯粹的心理体验。它是一种亲密的、具身化的觉察，感受着生命的丰富性：感觉、情绪、声音、景象。为了避免我们将正念与心理练习联系起来，我用“临在”一词来指代这种正念觉察的体验。

To give you a taste of what I’m talking about, let’s try a simple experiment.

为了让你们体会一下我的意思，我们来做一个简单的实验。

PRACTICE : Sensing the Body

练习：感知身体

Right now, as you read, can you be aware of the sensations of your body sitting? Perhaps you feel some heaviness or pressure where your body contacts the chair or the touch of your feet on the floor. Keep bringing your attention to those places of contact. Were you aware of these sensations a few moments ago, before I suggested it? How difficult was it to become aware of your direct, present-moment experience?

现在，当你阅读时，你能觉察到身体坐着的感觉吗？也许你会感觉到身体与椅子接触的地方有些沉重或压迫感，或者感觉到双脚触地。请持续将注意力集中在这些接触点上。就在几分钟前，在我提出这个建议之前，你是否觉察到这些感觉？觉察到你当下的直接体验有多难？

Mindful presence also helps us investigate our experience. Like a sturdy magnifying glass, it’s an instrument we can use to refine our vision. It allows us to observe the actual process of communication: our speech, our listening, even our inner world of thoughts, perceptions, and emotions.

正念觉察也能帮助我们审视自身的体验。它就像一面坚固的放大镜，是我们用来提升洞察力的工具。它让我们能够观察沟通的实际过程：我们的言语、倾听，甚至我们内心的思想、感知和情感世界。

Mindfulness includes a certain staying power, the ability to keep being aware. It helps us remember the tools we’ve learned. We can know all manner of communication skills, but if we can’t remember to use them they won’t do us much good!

正念包含一定的持久力，即保持觉察的能力。它帮助我们记住已经学到的技巧。我们可以掌握各种沟通技巧，但如果我们记不住如何运用它们，它们对我们毫无用处！

It’s easy to be mindful for a moment, as you just experienced. What’s challenging is to make that awareness continuous, sustaining it over time. Are you still aware of your body sitting? This is where practice comes in, actively strengthening presence through patient, gentle repetition.

像你刚才体验的那样，保持片刻的觉察很容易。难的是让这种觉察持续下去，并长期保持下去。你现在还能感受到自己坐着吗？这就需要练习了，通过耐心、轻柔的重复练习来积极地增强觉察力。

Building on Our Strengths

发挥我们的优势

Increasing our capacity for presence begins with identifying our strengths and any areas we may need to develop.

提高我们的存在感，首先要找出我们的优势以及我们需要发展的领域。

PRACTICE : Reflection on Presence

实践：反思临在

What helps you stay connected to presence? What disconnects you from presence? Take some time to think about these, making a list of each.

什么能帮助你保持与当下的连接？什么会让你与当下断开连接？花点时间思考这些问题，并把它们列出来。

The longer you spend contemplating each question, the more surprised you may be at what you discover. You might find that you already know quite a bit about presence! Here are a few examples of things people commonly mention.

你花在思考每个问题上的时间越长，你的发现可能就越会让你感到惊讶。你或许会发现，你其实已经对“临在感”了解颇多！以下是一些人们常提及的例子。

MAY CONNECT YOU TO PRESENCE

或许能让你与存在感相连。

• Slowing down

• 减速

• Breathing

• 呼吸

• Time with a friend

• 与朋友共度时光

• Being in nature

• 置身于大自然中

• Touch

• 触碰

• Music

• 音乐

• Sunshine

• 阳光

• Rain

• 雨

• Beauty

• 美丽

MAY DISCONNECT YOU FROM PRESENCE

可能会使你与存在脱节

• Stress

• 压力

• Feeling tired

• 感觉疲倦

• Being hungry

• 饥饿

• Rushing

• 冲刺

• Fear

• 害怕

• Wanting something

• 想要某样东西

• Impatience

• 不耐烦

• Perceived threat

• 感知到的威胁

• Lack of safety

• 缺乏安全性

The more familiar we are with the particular conditions that connect or disconnect us from presence, the easier it becomes to spot them in our lives. For example, I tend to lose presence when I’m rushing. This means that I’m more apt to make physical or relational blunders: I might drop something in the kitchen, forget my lunch, or even say something sharp.

我们越熟悉那些让我们保持或脱离专注当下状态的具体因素，就越容易在生活中察觉到它们。例如，我匆忙的时候就容易失去专注力。这意味着我更容易犯一些身体或人际关系上的错误：比如在厨房里掉东西、忘记带午饭，甚至说出一些不中听的话。

I learned a painful lesson about this a few years ago. I was at a farewell party for my girlfriend, Evan, who had just finished a year of service at a meditation retreat center. We had plans to drive north up the coast of California after the party, and I’d made an appointment to install a car radio for the trip. In that classic, romantic way, I wanted everything to be perfect.

几年前，我在这方面吸取了一个惨痛的教训。当时我参加了女友埃文的欢送会，她刚刚结束了在一家冥想静修中心为期一年的服务。我们计划在欢送会结束后开车沿着加州海岸线一路向北，为此我还预约了安装车载音响。出于那种典型的浪漫情怀，我希望一切都完美无缺。

As our departure time approached, I grew more and more anxious about missing the appointment. With no sign of a formal send-off, I finally spoke up and said that we needed to leave soon. To avoid any awkwardness, Evan went along with my request, but she was in tears by the time we arrived at the auto shop. She was incensed at me for cutting short a meaningful experience and at herself for not speaking up. In my fixation to create “the perfect trip,” I’d missed the fact that she was already enjoying herself.

随着出发时间的临近，我越来越担心会错过预约。由于没有正式的送别仪式，我最终开口说我们得赶紧走了。为了避免尴尬，埃文同意了我的请求，但当我们到达修车厂时，她已经泪流满面。她既生我的气，怪我匆匆结束了这段意义非凡的旅程，也怪自己没有早点开口。我一心想打造“完美旅程”，却忽略了她其实已经很享受这段时光的事实。

I reflected a lot on that incident, how losing presence had unintended, painful consequences. 2 In the larger scheme of things, it’s a benign example. Recognizing the cost of rushing, I’m now more attuned to it. That inner pressure acts as a signal that says, “Watch out—you’re losing presence!” Instead of blocking presence, it reminds me to be here.

我反复反思了那件事，反思了失去专注力所带来的意想不到的痛苦后果。 2 从更宏观的角度来看，这只是个无害的例子。意识到匆忙的代价后，我现在更加注意这一点。那种内在的压力就像一个信号，提醒我：“小心——你正在失去专注力！”它并没有阻碍我保持专注，而是提醒我活在当下。

Almost everything in our civilization points away from presence. The pressures of earning a living in modern society place extraordinary demands on our time and energy—demands that leave little space to cultivate mindful awareness.

我们文明中的几乎所有事物都指向远离当下。现代社会谋生的压力对我们的时间和精力提出了极高的要求——这些要求让我们几乎没有时间去培养正念觉知。

Our instant, touchscreen culture bombards us daily with messages pointing to the future, trying to convince us that our happiness lies in the next hit of pleasure, a new gadget, or tantalizing experience. Our newsfeeds are programmed with algorithms to maximize engagement, leading to further distraction. In this blitz of information and consumption, face-to-face human interaction is becoming less a part of life. Ever notice how many people are glued to screens in public, even in parks and restaurants? Yet, no matter how long we spend meandering online or getting lost in thought, we all eventually come back to presence, here in our body.
