我们身处的即时触屏文化每天都在向我们灌输指向未来的信息，试图让我们相信幸福在于下一次的快感、一件新奇的小玩意儿或一次诱人的体验。我们的信息流被算法操控，旨在最大限度地提高用户参与度，但这反而让我们更加分心。在这场信息爆炸和消费狂潮中，面对面的人际互动正逐渐淡出我们的生活。你是否注意到，即使在公园和餐厅等公共场所，也有很多人低头盯着屏幕？然而，无论我们在网上漫无目的地游荡多久，或者沉浸在自己的思绪中多久，最终我们都会回到当下，回到我们自己的身体里。

Recognizing Presence

识别存在

Our natural state of being is a relaxed, open alertness characterized by contentment and well-being. This is innate. Evolutionarily we’re wired to be here in a profoundly attuned way. Even in our modern world with all its hurries and distractions, presence doesn’t need to be a random occurrence. We can actively enhance our ability to rest in this balanced state, to recognize when we’ve left, and to return more reliably.

我们自然的状态是一种放松、开放的觉察，以满足和幸福为特征。这是与生俱来的。从进化角度来看，我们天生就具备与当下深度契合的能力。即使在充满匆忙和干扰的现代世界，这种临在感也并非偶然。我们可以积极地提升自己保持这种平衡状态的能力，觉察自己何时偏离了这种状态，并更可靠地回归其中。

*2 PRACTICE : Orienting

*2 练习：定向

Use the following basic exercise to return to a state of natural presence.

通过以下基本练习，恢复到自然专注的状态。

Take a few minutes to look around where you are. Let your eyes explore with curiosity whatever you see. Is there anything new or different you notice? Let your head and neck move with your eyes as you look around.

花几分钟时间环顾四周。让你的目光带着好奇心去探索你所看到的一切。你有没有注意到什么新鲜事物或不同之处？环顾四周时，让你的头部和脖子随着眼睛一起转动。

Notice the bare experience of seeing: shapes, color, light, lines. Where are your eyes naturally drawn? If there is anything of interest, allow your gaze to linger there. Continue to explore at your own pace.

注意观察事物本身：形状、色彩、光线、线条。你的目光自然而然地被吸引到哪里？如果有任何吸引你的地方，就让你的目光停留在那里。继续按照你自己的节奏去探索。

Notice how you feel after looking around. You may notice yourself taking a spontaneous, deep breath or exhaling as your body settles. Using the eyes, head, and neck in this manner activates the ventral vagus nerve and signals to our hardwired protection mechanisms that we’re safe from danger in our immediate physical surroundings. Try this orienting practice out anytime, looking around and noticing the effect on your mind and body.

环顾四周后，留意一下你的感受。你可能会注意到自己不自觉地深吸一口气，或者随着身体放松而呼气。这样运用眼睛、头部和颈部，可以激活腹侧迷走神经，并向我们与生俱来的保护机制发出信号，表明我们周围的环境是安全的。你可以随时尝试这种定向练习，环顾四周，感受一下它对你身心的影响。

Honesty: Presence Means Being Real

诚实：存在意味着真实

Leading with presence doesn’t mean feeling a specific way—if it did, it would be quite limited. Presence means being real. It’s a willingness to be honest with ourselves about what’s happening, just as it is.

以临在感引领并非指某种特定的感受——如果真是如此，那它的意义就太局限了。临在感意味着真实。它是一种愿意坦诚面对当下一切的意愿，如实地接受它。

Sometimes we feel distinctly ungrounded. We might be nervous, angry, or agitated. The great strength of mindfulness is that it’s not about having a particular experience. Rather, it’s the capacity to know and feel whatever is happening directly, without getting caught in our reactions. Bringing presence to a conversation means accepting what arises in our experience: “This is truth. This is what’s happening right now.”

有时我们会感到极度不安。我们可能会紧张、愤怒或烦躁。正念的强大之处在于，它并非着眼于某种特定的体验，而是让我们能够直接觉察和感受当下发生的一切，而不被自身的反应所束缚。在对话中保持觉察意味着接纳我们体验中出现的一切：“这就是真相。这就是此刻正在发生的事情。”

This doesn’t mean that we condone harmful actions or automatically agree with another’s position. It doesn’t preclude taking strong action, and it doesn’t mean necessarily saying everything on our mind. (“Well, I was just being honest.”) It means that we acknowledge the reality of what’s happening. If we can’t be honest with ourselves about what’s going on, how can we hope to hear one another, much less find resolution to a difficult situation?

这并不意味着我们纵容有害行为或自动同意他人的立场。这并不排除采取强有力的行动，也不意味着我们必须把心里话说出来（“我只是实话实说。”）。这意味着我们要正视现实。如果我们都无法坦诚面对自己的处境，又怎能指望彼此倾听，更遑论找到解决困境的办法呢？

This kind of honesty provides reliable information about what’s happening inside and around us. We learn to access our own feelings and needs in real time and to read others’ experience more accurately. This in turn helps us know what we need to say to feel heard, to move forward, or to resolve a difference.

这种坦诚能让我们更可靠地了解自身内外正在发生的事情。我们学会实时感知自己的感受和需求，也能更准确地理解他人的经历。反过来，这又能帮助我们明白该如何表达才能被倾听、才能继续前进、才能化解分歧。

Principle: Lead with presence; begin conversation with awareness, return to and strive to maintain that awareness, and be honest with oneself about what’s happening.

原则：以临在感为先导；以觉察力开始对话，回归并努力保持这种觉察力，并对自己正在发生的事情保持诚实。

The Oil Light: Presence and Reactivity

油光：存在与反应性

I used to teach mindfulness to elementary school kids in the inner city of Oakland, California. I heard many stories from the children about how mindfulness helped them handle strong emotions. One boy explained he got so mad he wanted to kick his sister! “Then I remembered my mindful breathing, took a few breaths, and calmed down.”

我曾在加州奥克兰市中心的一所小学校教孩子们正念。我听孩子们讲过很多关于正念如何帮助他们应对强烈情绪的故事。有个男孩说他当时气得想踢他妹妹！“然后我想起了正念呼吸，深呼吸了几次，就平静下来了。”

When tensions run high, presence grounds us. The more familiar we are with how it feels to be present, the more easily we detect the signs of being activated. It’s like noticing the low-oil light in an automobile. If we catch that early warning signal, we can avoid a lot of trouble. What happens when you’re angry, scared, or hurt? Does your breath quicken? Does your jaw clench? Do you feel hot or cold? Do you start to space out? Instead of “kicking your sister,” you can use mindfulness to catch these signals and create the space inside to choose how you respond.

当情绪紧张时，正念能让我们脚踏实地。我们越熟悉正念的感觉，就越容易察觉到自己情绪激动的迹象。这就像注意到汽车的低油量指示灯一样。如果我们能及早发现这个预警信号，就能避免很多麻烦。当你生气、害怕或受伤时，会发生什么？你的呼吸会加快吗？你的下巴会紧绷吗？你会感到忽冷忽热吗？你会开始走神吗？与其“踢妹妹”，不如运用正念来捕捉这些信号，并在内心创造空间，选择如何回应。

Principle: The more aware we are, the more choice we have.

原则：我们越了解自己，就越有选择。

Feeling activated isn’t “bad”—it’s a healthy part of being alive. It’s only problematic if we lose awareness. Yet for many of us, the pace of modern life has us running on sympathetic arousal all the time. Whether it’s the stress of commuting, the volume of tasks we manage, or even the caffeine we consume, we can live in a constant state of low-grade panic, always on alert. When unchecked, this can lead to unnecessary interpersonal conflicts. As we practice mindfulness, we learn how to calm and steady the agitation of being overactivated. Even something as simple as taking a long, slow outbreath can begin to settle our nervous system.

保持警觉并非“坏事”，而是健康生命的一部分。只有当我们失去觉察时，才会出现问题。然而，对我们许多人来说，现代生活的快节奏让我们时刻处于交感神经兴奋状态。无论是通勤的压力、繁重的工作量，甚至是摄入的咖啡因，都可能让我们长期处于一种轻微的恐慌状态，时刻保持警惕。如果不加以控制，这会导致不必要的人际冲突。通过练习正念，我们学会了如何平静和稳定过度活跃带来的焦虑。即使是像深长而缓慢的呼气这样简单的动作，也能帮助我们的神经系统平静下来。

Training in Mindful Presence

正念训练

I love how portable and adaptable presence is. You can do it anytime, anyplace, without any special equipment or conditions. No one even needs to know. You can practice mindfulness—feeling your breath and body; noticing sounds, thoughts, or feelings—in the midst of ordinary life.

我喜欢“临在”的便携性和适应性。你可以随时随地练习，无需任何特殊设备或条件。甚至无需让任何人知道。你可以在日常生活中练习正念——感受你的呼吸和身体；觉察声音、想法或感受。

When it comes to conversation, it’s important to have a lightweight, nimble tool such as mindfulness. I recommend taking some time every day for formal mindfulness practice. It’s like having a master key that opens many doors in your heart and mind. Even a few minutes of practice can have a positive effect on your day, bringing renewed energy, clarity, and a sense of purpose.

在沟通中，拥有像正念这样轻便灵活的工具至关重要。我建议每天抽出一些时间进行正式的正念练习。它就像一把万能钥匙，可以打开你心灵深处的无数扇门。即使只是几分钟的练习，也能对你的一天产生积极的影响，带来新的活力、清晰的思路和目标感。

One of the most reliable methods for cultivating presence is to anchor our attention with sensations in the body. As we move through the world and interact with others, our attention usually rushes out to sights and sounds or gets consumed by thoughts of the past or future. Anchoring attention in the body counters these tendencies by giving our awareness a place to rest. Sensations only occur here and now. Whenever you bring your attention to a sensation, you are—for that moment—present.

培养临在感最可靠的方法之一，就是将注意力锚定在身体的感受上。当我们穿梭于世间，与他人互动时，注意力往往会被眼前的景象和耳边的声音所吸引，或者被对过去或未来的思绪所占据。将注意力锚定在身体上，能够帮助我们克服这些倾向，为我们的意识提供一个休憩之所。感受只存在于此时此地。每当你将注意力集中于某种感受时，在那一刻，你就真正地活在当下。

Here I’ll share four primary methods for cultivating presence. Each of them uses a specific sensory experience—called a reference point, or an anchor —to ground attention in the body: weight, the centerline, breathing, and touch points such as the hands or feet.

在这里，我将分享培养专注力的四种主要方法。每一种方法都利用特定的感官体验——称为参考点或锚点——将注意力集中在身体上：体重、中线、呼吸以及手或脚等接触点。

An anchor is a reference point to which we return to strengthen mindful presence.

锚点是我们回归的参照点，以此来加强正念觉察。

The aim isn’t to master all of these; it’s to find one or two that help you feel more alert and grounded in the midst of your life. Experiment with the instructions below. You can do each practice individually, or as a series flowing from one to the next. As you practice, consider which is easiest for you. The best method is the one that connects you with presence.

目标并非掌握所有这些方法，而是找到一两种能让你在生活中保持清醒和踏实的方法。请尝试以下说明。你可以单独练习每一种方法，也可以将它们串联起来，依次进行。练习时，思考哪种方法对你来说最容易。最好的方法是让你与当下连接的方法。

PRACTICE : Grounding in the Body

练习：身体接地

Method 1: Finding Gravity

方法一：寻找重力

Sit comfortably. Start by taking a few moments to orient to your surroundings, looking around the room. Find a posture that’s upright yet relaxed. Gently close your eyes and take a few deep breaths to help you settle in.

舒适地坐下。先花几分钟时间熟悉一下周围环境，环顾四周。找到一个既挺直又放松的姿势。轻轻闭上眼睛，深呼吸几次，帮助自己放松下来。

Feel any sensations of weight or heaviness in your body. You might notice your body’s contact with the chair, any hardness or give in the surface you’re sitting on. You might feel the sense of your whole body sitting, its mass, or warmth. Let your attention rest with these sensations of weight. Can you feel the downward force of gravity?

感受一下身体是否有重量或沉重感。你可能会注意到身体与椅子的接触，以及你所坐表面的硬度或弹性。你可能会感觉到整个身体坐在椅子上的感觉，它的质量或温度。让你的注意力停留在这些重量感上。你能感觉到重力的向下作用力吗？

When you notice your attention has wandered, gently let go and bring it back to the feeling of weight or heaviness in your body. Anchor your awareness there.

当你注意到自己的注意力游离时，轻轻地放开它，将它拉回到身体的重量感或沉重感上。将你的意识锚定在那里。

Method 2: The Centerline

方法二：中心线

Next, bring your attention to your upper body. Sense how your torso rises up from your waist and pelvis. Can you feel your back, shoulders, and neck? See if you can sense the midline or centerline of your upper body. Try feeling your spine, running from your tailbone, through your back, up to the base of your head. Or try imagining a line down the middle of your torso, halfway between your front and back, in the middle of the left and right sides of your body.

接下来，将注意力集中在你的上半身。感受一下你的躯干是如何从腰部和骨盆向上延伸的。你能感觉到你的背部、肩膀和颈部吗？试着感受一下你上半身的中线或中心线。试着感受一下你的脊柱，从尾骨开始，穿过你的背部，一直延伸到你的后脑勺。或者试着想象一条线从你的躯干中间穿过，位于你身体前后两侧的中间位置。

Moving your torso can help reveal the centerline. Rock forward and backward slightly, until you feel the balance point in the middle. Do the same from side to side. Finally, rotate your shoulders and upper body one or two degrees to either side. Can you feel the axis around which the body is turning? That’s the centerline. See if you can rest your attention here, on the centerline of your body. Can you feel how your body is upright?

移动躯干有助于找到身体的中心线。轻轻地前后摇晃身体，直到找到身体中间的平衡点。左右摇晃也一样。最后，将肩膀和上半身向两侧各旋转一到两度。你能感觉到身体围绕哪个轴旋转吗？那就是中心线。试着将注意力集中在身体的中心线上。你能感觉到身体是如何保持直立的吗？

Method 3: Breathing

方法三：呼吸

As you sit quietly, tune in to the sensations of breathing. See if you can allow your attention to rest with the sensations of breathing in and breathing out. You don’t need to block out other sensations, sounds, or thoughts. Just tune in to the steady rhythm of breathing in and breathing out, much as you might listen to waves crashing on a beach. Let your breath come into focus naturally.

静静地坐着，感受呼吸。试着将注意力集中在吸气和呼气的感觉上。你不需要屏蔽其他感觉、声音或思绪。只需专注于呼吸的节奏，就像聆听海浪拍打沙滩的声音一样。让你的呼吸自然而然地成为你的焦点。

It’s normal for the mind to wander to thoughts, sounds, or other experiences. Whenever you notice, gently bring your attention back to feeling your breath, appreciating that mindfulness is growing.

思绪游离到其他想法、声音或其他体验上是很正常的。每当你注意到这一点时，轻轻地将注意力拉回到感受呼吸上，并体会到正念正在增强。

Method 4: Touch Points

方法四：触点

Now explore specific areas in your body that tend to be rich in sensation. First, put all your attention in your hands. Feel any sensations there: warmth or coolness; tingling, pulsing, or heaviness; maybe moisture or dryness. Rest your attention on any sensations you can feel in your hands. You might feel the sensations of your hands touching or resting in your lap.

现在，探索一下你身体上那些感觉丰富的特定区域。首先，将全部注意力集中在你的双手上。感受一下那里的任何感觉：温暖或凉爽；刺痛、脉动或沉重感；或许是湿润或干燥。将注意力集中在你双手上的任何感觉上。你可能会感觉到双手接触或放在腿上的感觉。

Now shift your attention to your feet, feeling any sensations there: temperature, weight, texture, the contact with the floor, the pressure of your shoes. Rest your attention with any sensations in your feet.

现在将注意力转移到你的双脚上，感受那里的一切感觉：温度、重量、质地、与地面的接触感、鞋子的压力。将注意力集中在双脚的各种感觉上。

You can try this with any other part of your body that has strong sensations, such as your lips, tongue, or eyes. When your mind wanders, gently bring it back to one of these places.

你可以用身体其他感觉强烈的部位来尝试这种方法，比如嘴唇、舌头或眼睛。当你的思绪游离时，轻轻地将它拉回到这些部位之一。

Shifting Your Attention

转移你的注意力

Finally, try shifting your attention between these four areas: gravity, the centerline, breathing, and a touch point (hands, feet, lips). Which is most readily accessible? Which helps you connect most naturally with presence, that sense of being here in a relaxed and embodied way?

最后，试着将注意力在以下四个方面之间切换：重力、身体中线、呼吸以及一个接触点（手、脚、嘴唇）。哪个最容易做到？哪个最能帮助你自然地与临在感连接，让你以一种放松和身心合一的方式感受到自己身处此地？

When you’re ready, open your eyes. Look around the room, reorienting to your surroundings. Take a few moments to reflect on this exercise. Which of these four ways of training in presence would you like to practice this week?

准备好后，睁开眼睛。环顾四周，重新适应周围的环境。花几分钟时间反思一下这个练习。这四种正念训练方法中，你本周想练习哪一种？

Each method has its own strength. The downward force of gravity tends to balance the stimulating, upward movement of attention in conversations. The centerline can bring a sense of inner strength and clarity. Breathing can soothe us, while touch points can dissipate the intensity of emotions. You also can get creative and explore your own ways of strengthening presence. Some people keep a smooth stone in their pocket, using its weight and softness as a literal touchstone.

每种方法都有其优势。重力的向下作用力有助于平衡对话中注意力向上集中带来的刺激感。中心线可以带来内在的力量和清晰的思路。呼吸可以舒缓我们的情绪，而触觉点则可以消散强烈的情绪。你也可以发挥创意，探索自己增强临场感的方法。有些人会在口袋里放一块光滑的石头，利用它的重量和柔软度作为精神的象征。

Bringing Presence to Life

赋予生命以临在感

You probably read the previous pages in a matter of minutes, but to incorporate these practices into your life takes time. Choose one method to start and try practicing in three distinct areas: on your own (formal meditation), during transitions (waiting in line, commuting), and in conversations (initially while listening).

你可能只用了几分钟就读完了前面几页，但要将这些练习融入你的生活需要时间。选择一种方法开始，并尝试在三个不同的领域进行练习：独自练习（正式冥想）、在过渡场景中练习（排队等候、通勤）以及在对话中练习（最初是在倾听时练习）。

When on your own, give 100 percent of your attention to the anchor. During transitions, place as much of your attention there as feels appropriate to the context. When you’re interacting, put just 10 or 20 percent of your awareness there. At first it may be awkward to do during a conversation. It can feel as if your attention is flipping back and forth between what’s happening and your anchor. This is completely normal. Over time, your mind will learn how to balance external sensory data with a grounded internal presence and maintain a light awareness of your body during conversation.

独处时，将百分之百的注意力集中在你的“锚点”上。在过渡场景中，根据情境适当地将注意力集中于此。与人互动时，只需将10%到20%的注意力放在此即可。起初，在对话中这样做可能会有些不习惯。你会感觉自己的注意力在周围发生的事情和你的“锚点”之间来回切换。这完全正常。随着时间的推移，你的大脑会逐渐学会如何在外部感官信息和稳定的内在状态之间取得平衡，并在对话中保持对身体的轻微觉察。

Initially, much of the work is simply remembering to be present. One way to support this is to take a few moments each morning to set an intention and then to reflect on how things went at the end of the day. This practice can be as brief as two minutes, or longer if you have the time.

最初，大部分功课都在于记住要活在当下。一个有效的方法是每天早上花几分钟时间设定一个目标，然后在一天结束时反思一下事情的进展情况。这个练习可以短至两分钟，也可以更久一些，如果你有时间的话。

PRACTICE : Beginning and Ending the Day

练习：一天的开始和结束

MORNING : Soon after rising, take a few breaths to settle your mind and feel your body. Connect your attention to the reference point with which you’re working: gravity, the centerline, breathing, or a touch point. Notice how it feels to be present right now. Then, set a clear intention to return to this reference point as a support for presence as often as you can during your day. Imagine situations where you want to practice: on your commute, in a meeting, with someone specific.

早晨：起床后不久，深呼吸几次，让思绪平静下来，感受身体。将注意力集中在你正在使用的参照点上：重力、身体中线、呼吸或某个接触点。留意当下这种专注的感觉。然后，设定一个明确的目标，在一天中尽可能多地回到这个参照点，以此来保持专注。想象一下你想练习的场景：通勤途中、会议中、与特定的人相处时。

EVENING : At the end of the day, take some time to reflect. Did you remember? When? What was the effect? Bring an attitude of curiosity and warmth to your reflection, being wary of any self-judgment. What would you like to do differently tomorrow? Do you have ideas for ways you can remember to lead with presence?

晚上：一天结束时，花点时间反思一下。你还记得吗？是什么时候？有什么影响？带着好奇和温暖的态度进行反思，注意不要自我评判。明天你想做出哪些改变？你有什么方法可以提醒自己要以专注的态度领导？

This structured daily practice can be incredibly useful for training your mind. As you explore the suggestions throughout this book, you can use this same process to develop any of the three foundations of mindful communication and its associated tools.

这种结构化的日常练习对训练思维非常有益。当你探索本书中的建议时，你可以运用同样的方法来培养正念沟通的三大基础及其相关工具。

The Doorway to Resilience

通往韧性的大门

At one workshop, a participant raised her hand and asked with a pained expression, “What about when it hurts to be here?” Sometimes returning to presence can feel like stepping on the wrong end of a rake: all of a sudden, you get hit in the face. We’ve been going ninety miles per hour; when we finally slow down to reconnect with ourselves, we can be met with a backlog of physical discomfort, stress, or emotional pain.

在一次工作坊上，一位学员举手，带着痛苦的表情问道：“如果身处当下反而感到痛苦怎么办？” 有时，回归当下就像踩到耙子的另一头：突然间，脸上挨了一记重击。我们一直以每小时九十英里的速度飞驰；当我们终于慢下来，重新与自己连接时，却可能面临积压已久的身体不适、压力或情绪痛苦。

We often seek relief from pain and discomfort through distraction or pleasure. This can help rebalance a beleaguered nervous system. The danger is when the choice to seek relief becomes a chronic reflex to anything uncomfortable. Over time, we can become incapable of tolerating even the smallest amount of pain without immediately doing something to change it.

我们常常通过转移注意力或追求享乐来缓解疼痛和不适。这或许有助于平衡疲惫的神经系统。然而，危险在于，当寻求缓解成为一种对任何不适的慢性反射时。久而久之，我们甚至无法忍受哪怕是最轻微的疼痛，必须立即采取行动来改变现状。

But when pain is met with genuine care and presence, something amazing can happen—healing. With patient, steady attention, emotional pain eases. Consider how it feels to be received with empathy and presence in a moment of distress.

但当痛苦得到真诚的关怀和陪伴时，奇迹就会发生——疗愈。只要有耐心、持续的关注，情感上的痛苦就会减轻。试想一下，在痛苦的时刻，被同理心和陪伴所接纳，会是怎样的感受。

I was nineteen when I started studying Buddhism in a monastery halfway around the world in India. I was quite homesick, and our study-abroad director encouraged me to speak to one of the meditation teachers about how I was feeling.

我十九岁那年，远在地球另一端的印度，开始在一座寺院学习佛教。我非常想家，我们的留学项目主任鼓励我跟一位禅修老师谈谈我的感受。

Godwin Samararatne was a tall Sri Lankan man with soft eyes and a playful laugh. His deep brown skin cut a sharp contrast with his traditional white garments. We sat across from one another in a sunny room, Godwin listening as I talked about missing my family and my girlfriend. After a while he tilted his head slightly and asked, “Where does it hurt?” I pointed to the center of my chest and began to feel the pain directly.

戈德温·萨马拉拉特内是一位身材高大的斯里兰卡男子，眼神温柔，笑声爽朗。他深棕色的皮肤与身上传统的白色服饰形成鲜明对比。我们坐在阳光明媚的房间里，戈德温静静地听我倾诉对家人和女友的思念。过了一会儿，他微微歪着头问道：“哪里疼？”我指了指胸口正中央，顿时感到一阵剧痛。

Tears welled up as the ache moved from my heart to my throat. Godwin held my gaze, nodding slowly. The hurt grew more intense for a moment, then faded and passed. I beamed and thanked him, believing he had done something miraculous. It was a long time before I understood what had actually happened: his compassion had invited me into presence, to feel the pain and let it pass.

泪水涌上眼眶，痛楚从心底蔓延至喉咙。戈德温凝视着我，缓缓点头。疼痛瞬间加剧，随后又消散。我绽放出笑容，向他道谢，觉得他做了一件奇迹般的事。过了很久我才明白究竟发生了什么：他的同情心引导我正视痛苦，感受它，并让它过去。

As we delve into the patterns that drive our communication habits, we may discover difficult emotions or painful memories. Presence is an essential resource to navigate these places. It is a doorway to resilience, helping us access the innate healing and self-regulatory capacities of our mind and body. Just as our cells know how to heal a cut, our psyche possesses the intelligence to heal emotional wounds. With time, support, and caring presence, our heart can mend.

当我们深入探究驱动沟通习惯的模式时，可能会发现难以承受的情绪或痛苦的回忆。临在是应对这些困境的关键。它是通往韧性的门户，帮助我们开启身心与生俱来的疗愈和自我调节能力。正如我们的细胞懂得如何愈合伤口，我们的心灵也拥有治愈情感创伤的智慧。只要有时间、支持和关爱的陪伴，我们的心就能愈合。

Creating a Positive Feedback Loop

建立正反馈回路

As you endeavor to bring more presence to life, you may notice how hard it is. One of my first meditation teachers was fond of saying, “Mindfulness practice is simple, but not easy.” We can go an entire day without remembering to be present once! When we do remember, our response is often self-critical.

当你努力让生活更加鲜活时，你可能会发现这有多难。我的一位冥想老师常说：“正念练习很简单，但并不容易。”我们可能一整天都想不起要活在当下！即使想起来了，我们的反应往往也是自我批评。

We can have such unreasonable expectations of ourselves, as if we’re supposed to be experts from day one. It’s entirely normal to forget. Expect to forget a lot. Put another way: remembering is kind of amazing. Our communication habits have great momentum; recall the analogy of turning a ship at sea. Our job is to find ways to “hold the angle” of the rudder. Bringing even a small amount of presence to conversation will lead to profound changes over time.

我们常常对自己抱有不切实际的期望，仿佛从一开始就应该成为专家。忘记事情完全正常，而且要做好忘记很多事情的准备。换句话说：记住事情本身就很神奇。我们的沟通习惯具有很强的惯性；想想在海上调转船舵的比喻。我们的任务是找到保持舵角的方法。即使只是在对话中投入一点点专注，假以时日也会带来深远的影响。

Instead of berating ourselves for forgetting, the key to success is to appreciate remembering. Every moment of mindfulness strengthens awareness. This is cause for celebration rather than judgment. We learn more through warmhearted encouragement than bitter criticism. If you’re teaching a child math and you get angry every time they make a mistake, how much will that child learn? Will they even want to study mathematics?

与其责备自己遗忘，成功的关键在于珍惜记忆。每一次正念练习都能增强觉察力。这值得庆祝，而非评判。我们从温暖的鼓励中学到的东西远比尖刻的批评要多。如果你教孩子数学，每次他们犯错你就生气，那孩子能学到多少？他们还会想学数学吗？

If you can take this understanding to heart, you’ll find mindfulness grows more quickly, with more joy and ease. The secret is patient and kind persistence. Lead with presence as often as you remember, and let the rest unfold naturally.

如果你能将这种理解铭记于心，你会发现正念会增长得更快，也更容易获得喜悦和轻松。秘诀在于耐心和善意的坚持。只要记得，就尽可能多地以觉察为先，其余的就顺其自然吧。

The Power of Presence

临场感的力量

We can be such articulate creatures, and yet words often fall short of expressing the most meaningful things in life. In moments of great love and intimacy as in moments of great loss and tragedy, our simple, enduring presence sometimes says the most.

我们或许能言善辩，但言语往往不足以表达生命中最深刻的意义。在充满爱与亲密的时刻，以及在经历巨大失去与悲剧的时刻，我们简单而持久的陪伴有时胜过千言万语。

One of the most difficult things I’ve ever done in my life was saying goodbye to Safta, my dad’s mom. I was fourteen when her cancer metastasized; I joined my father for the trip back to Israel.

我一生中最艰难的事情之一就是和萨夫塔（我父亲的母亲）告别。她癌症扩散时我才十四岁；我陪父亲一起回以色列。

Safta and I never spoke the same language, but we had shared many loving moments over the years, playing card games or simply holding hands and laughing. She had the most amazing hands. They were small and rugged, hands that could snap a chicken’s neck or caress my face. The skin on Safta’s hands somehow managed to be plump and wrinkled at the same time. I can still feel the warmth and vitality of those hands.

萨夫塔和我语言不通，但这些年来我们一起度过了许多美好的时光，玩纸牌游戏，或者只是牵着手开怀大笑。她有一双令人惊叹的手。它们小巧而粗糙，既能轻易扭断鸡的脖子，也能温柔地抚摸我的脸庞。萨夫塔的手部皮肤奇妙地兼具了丰润和皱纹。我至今仍能感受到那双手的温暖和活力。

My father and I visited her in the nursing home every day. On our last visit, all three of us spent some time together in the courtyard and then went back to her hospice room. I spoke through tears as I told her in broken Hebrew that I loved her and would miss her. Then we just held hands for a long, quiet moment. It was a wordless goodbye and the most meaningful one I could have asked for.

我和父亲每天都去养老院看望她。最后一次探望时，我们三人一起在院子里待了一会儿，然后一起回到她的临终关怀病房。我含着泪，用不太流利的希伯来语告诉她，我爱她，我会想念她。然后，我们只是静静地握着她的手，度过了漫长而宁静的时光。那是一场无言的告别，也是我所能期盼的最有意义的告别。

Sometimes it’s our presence that says the most.

有时候，我们的存在本身就足以说明一切。

PRINCIPLES

原则

Presence lays the ground for connection.

陪伴是建立联系的基础。

Lead with presence; begin conversation with awareness, return to and strive to maintain that awareness, and be honest with oneself about what’s happening.

以专注的态度引领；以觉察力开始对话，回归并努力保持这种觉察力，并对自己正在发生的事情保持诚实。

The more aware we are, the more choice we have.

我们越了解情况，就越有选择。

KEY POINTS

要点

Presence has a range of benefits:

出场有诸多好处：

• It gives us back our life, waking us up to the present moment.

• 它让我们重获新生，唤醒我们活在当下。

• It helps us remember to use the communication tools we’ve learned.

• 它帮助我们记住如何使用我们已经学到的沟通工具。

• It gives us important information about ourselves and others.

• 它为我们提供有关我们自己和他人的重要信息。

• It gives us early warning signs if we feel activated or upset.

• 它会在我们感到烦躁或不安时发出预警信号。

• It provides a container to manage reactivity.

• 它提供了一个用于管理响应式的容器。

• It helps us heal places of emotional pain or wounding.

• 它帮助我们治愈情感上的痛苦或创伤。

Presence is our natural state. We can develop presence by:

临场感是我们的自然状态。我们可以通过以下方式培养临场感：

• Orienting to our surroundings in an alert and balanced way

• 以警觉和平衡的方式感知周围环境

• Identifying what helps us stay connected to and what disconnects us from presence

• 找出哪些因素帮助我们与临在保持联结，哪些因素使我们与临在断开连接。

• Practicing mindfulness of the body, grounding with an anchor: gravity, the centerline, breathing, touch points such as the hands or feet

• 练习觉察身体，通过锚点扎根：重力、中线、呼吸、接触点（例如手或脚）。

• Beginning and ending the day with an intention

• 以意图开始和结束一天

• Creating a positive feedback loop by appreciating when we remember to be present rather than judging ourselves

• 通过欣赏自己活在当下而不是评判自己，来创造一个积极的反馈循环。

QUESTION & ANSWER

问答

Q: Sometimes I feel really present with what someone is saying, but I might not be aware of my body. Is that still presence?

问：有时我感觉自己完全沉浸在别人说话的内容中，但我可能没有意识到自己的身体。这还能算是专注吗？

There are many ways to be present. We can be present cognitively, with the intellect; emotionally, with our feelings or needs; and somatically, in an embodied way. We are aiming to integrate all three of these domains. Using the body as a basis for presence lends a kind of wholeness and provides a basis for developing the other forms of presence.

活在当下的方式有很多种。我们可以认知地活在当下，运用理智；我们可以情感地活在当下，感受或满足我们的需求；我们也可以身体地活在当下，以具身的方式体验当下。我们的目标是将这三个方面整合起来。以身体为基础来体验当下，能带来一种完整性，并为发展其他形式的当下奠定基础。

Q: I tried being more present and aware when talking to a family member, and I felt so much that it made it hard to even talk or listen. It almost seemed like I got more reactive. What’s going on?

问：我试着在和家人交谈时更加专注和清醒，结果却感觉情绪波动很大，甚至难以开口说话或认真倾听。我似乎变得更加容易做出过激反应。这是怎么回事？

It can be overwhelming to feel what’s going on inside, especially if it’s a difficult conversation. Sometimes, being more present can reveal feelings or dynamics that have been going on under the surface. Other times, we may feel more open and vulnerable. Any of this can lead to a sense of disorientation. I encourage you to keep being present. Do your best to stay balanced with whatever comes up, because the alternative is being on automatic. If things start to feel overwhelming, you can always let the other person know: “I’d like to keep talking but I notice I’m feeling a little overwhelmed. Would it be all right if we took a break for a bit?”

感受内心的种种情绪可能会让人不知所措，尤其是在进行艰难的对话时。有时，更加专注当下能够揭示一些隐藏在表面之下的感受或动态。有时，我们可能会感到更加坦诚和脆弱。所有这些都可能导致迷失方向的感觉。我鼓励你保持专注当下。尽力保持平衡，应对任何突发情况，因为否则就会陷入机械式的反应。如果感觉难以承受，你可以随时告诉对方：“我很想继续聊下去，但我感觉有点不知所措。我们休息一会儿可以吗？”

Q: A lot of the time I don’t feel safe enough to relax and be present. How can I practice this if I don’t feel safe?

问：很多时候我感觉不够安全，无法放松身心，活在当下。如果我感觉不安全，我该如何练习放松和专注呢？

I feel really touched when I hear this question. To me, it points to both our longing to connect and our vulnerability. So much about our society doesn’t support the kind of familiar relaxation that our organisms long for: the ease of warm social connections and a sense of place. I want us to be able to understand our individual experience in the context of the larger structures of our society, otherwise we tend to view all our challenges personally, thinking they’re somehow our fault.

听到这个问题，我深受触动。在我看来，它既揭示了我们渴望联结的内心，也暴露了我们的脆弱。我们社会的很多方面都无法提供我们身体所渴望的那种熟悉的放松：轻松自在的温暖社交关系和归属感。我希望我们能够从社会整体结构的角度来理解个人经历，否则我们往往会将所有挑战都归咎于自身，认为这一切都是我们自己的错。

When we factor in how disconnected modern culture is from a sense of community and belonging, as well as how economic pressures minimize time for healthy attachment bonding between parents and children, of course we don’t feel relaxed and safe! We may have internalized a lack of safety from negative experiences based on our gender, sexual orientation, race, class, or other aspects of our social location. It’s important to identify places where we may need to get support, seek resources, and work to address the structural causes of these issues.

当我们考虑到现代文化与社群感和归属感的脱节，以及经济压力如何压缩父母与子女之间建立健康依恋关系的时间时，我们当然不会感到放松和安全！我们可能已经内化了因性别、性取向、种族、阶级或其他社会地位因素而产生的负面安全感缺失。因此，找到我们可能需要寻求支持、资源的地方，并努力解决这些问题的结构性根源至关重要。

It’s also important to investigate our assumptions. Our sense of safety can become reduced to a narrow attachment to emotional comfort. Safety is illusory. We do all we can to prevent harm and stop abuse while recognizing that the world isn’t safe physically or emotionally. Rather than contributing to our fear, this understanding can lead to great vitality and freedom.

审视我们的假设也至关重要。我们对安全的感知可能会被简化为对情感慰藉的狭隘执着。安全感只是一种幻觉。我们竭尽所能地防止伤害和制止虐待，同时也要认识到，这个世界在物质和情感上都并非绝对安全。这种认识非但不会加剧我们的恐惧，反而能带来巨大的活力和自由。

The tools and perspectives I’m sharing can help us build a stable base of ease and self-connection so that our sense of safety is sourced from within rather than without. The “shallow end of a pool” training principle is essential here. Look for people or situations where you feel a little bit safer, a little more relaxed, and start to practice there—even if that’s with your pet or a favorite tree. Our nervous systems long for the soothing effects of friendly, social engagement. We’ve been doing this for millennia, and our bodies will remember how to connect, share, and listen if we create the right conditions and give them a chance.

我分享的工具和视角可以帮助我们建立稳定的自在感和自我联结，使我们的安全感源于内心而非外在。“浅水区”训练原则在这里至关重要。寻找那些让你感到更安全、更放松的人或环境，并在那里开始练习——即使只是和你的宠物或你最喜欢的一棵树在一起。我们的神经系统渴望友好社交互动带来的舒缓效果。千百年来，我们一直在这样做，如果我们创造合适的条件并给予机会，我们的身体就会记住如何联结、分享和倾听。

*1 Due to the lack of a gender neutral, singular personal pronoun in English, I have chosen to use they throughout the text to be more inclusive.

*1 由于英语中缺乏性别中立的单数人称代词，我选择在全文中使用“他们”，以体现包容性。

*2 This symbol indicates a companion guided audio practice at OrenJaySofer.com/book-audio . See the index of practices on page 271 .

*2 此符号表示可在 OrenJaySofer.com/book-audio 上找到配套的引导音频练习。练习索引见第 271 页。

# ↩

3

relational awareness

关系意识

All real living is meeting.

—MARTIN BUBER

真正的生活就是相遇。——马丁·布伯

WHEN IT COMES to conversation, the force of our habits and the pressure of social settings can make it exceedingly difficult to maintain presence. Here, our internal practice serves as a basis. We use the arena of conversation itself as a training ground for presence, using techniques to anchor awareness within the midst of exchange and developing the capacity for relational awareness.

在交谈中，习惯的力量和社交环境的压力会让我们难以保持专注。此时，内在的练习就显得尤为重要。我们可以将交谈本身作为训练专注力的场所，运用各种技巧在交流中锚定觉察力，并培养关系觉察能力。

When I came to communication training after five years of dedicated mindfulness practice, I noticed certain changes emerging. I naturally began bringing more awareness to when I chose to speak and listen. I also began to make simple adjustments in the flow of my speech, taking pauses or making subtle shifts in my pace to modulate my nervous system. Eventually I learned to widen my awareness from my own sense of embodiment to include the other person, our connection, and the space around us.

在进行了五年专注的正念练习后，我参加了沟通技巧培训，并注意到一些变化开始出现。我自然而然地开始更加觉察自己何时选择说话和倾听。我也开始对说话的节奏进行一些简单的调整，比如停顿或略微改变语速来调节我的神经系统。最终，我学会了将觉察范围从自身的身体感知扩展到对方、我们之间的联结以及我们周围的空间。

Choice Points: Speaking or Listening

选择题：口语还是听力

Consciously choosing when to speak and when to listen is essential for meaningful conversation. In some respects, it’s the most basic communication skill. How many times have you said something only to wish you could take it back moments after the words left your mouth? Or hit “send” on an email when it might have been better to let things cool off? It’s equally important to have the courage to say our piece. When we don’t speak up, we can feel as if we’ve let ourselves or our loved ones down.

有意识地选择何时发言、何时倾听，对于有意义的对话至关重要。在某种程度上，这是最基本的沟通技巧。你是否曾说过一些话，却在话出口后后悔不已？或者，你是否曾在明明应该冷静下来再发送邮件的情况下，却按下了“发送”键？同样重要的是，我们要有勇气表达自己的想法。如果我们选择沉默，就会感到辜负了自己或我们所爱的人。

Conversation is a dynamic interplay between each person’s choice to speak or listen. When those choices are conscious and respectful, conversations tend to be more productive and enjoyable. If those choices are unconscious or impulsive, conversations tend to be less productive and more stressful.

对话是每个人选择说话或倾听之间动态互动的结果。当这种选择是自觉且尊重的，对话往往会更高效、更愉快。如果这种选择是无意识的或冲动的，对话往往会效率更低，压力更大。

I call this juncture the “choice point” between speaking and listening. With presence, every moment offers a choice. One of my NVC colleagues uses the acronym WAIT to remind himself of this. “Why Am I Talking?” he asks, pointing to how quickly and easily we tend to open our mouths. “What Am I Thinking?” he inquires, tracking the mental process that spurs our speech.

我把这个交汇点称为说话和倾听之间的“选择点”。只要保持觉察，每个瞬间都提供了选择的机会。我的一位非暴力沟通（NVC）同事用“WAIT”这个缩写词来提醒自己这一点。“我为什么说话？”他问道，指出我们往往多么轻易地、多么迅速地张开嘴。“我在想什么？”他追问，追踪促使我们开口说话的心理过程。

A choice point is a moment of awareness in which we decide whether to speak or listen.

选择点是指我们意识到自己应该说话还是倾听的时刻。

Our ability to maintain presence at the choice point takes practice. Sometimes the moment of choice races by like a road sign while we are doing seventy-five miles per hour on the freeway. The impulse to speak can be so strong that it impels us to verbalize simply to release the internal pressure. If we tend toward the quieter side, it can feel as if those openings in a conversation disappear before we can muster our voice.

在抉择时刻保持专注需要练习。有时，抉择的时刻就像高速公路上飞驰而过的路标一样转瞬即逝。说话的冲动如此强烈，以至于我们不得不开口，仅仅是为了释放内心的压力。如果我们倾向于沉默寡言，就会感觉那些对话的机会在我们鼓起勇气开口之前就消失了。

This is where mindfulness comes in. In meditation, we learn how to observe unpleasant sensations (knee pain, a sore back) without immediately reacting. We develop the capacity to be aware of an impulse without acting on it.

这就是正念的作用所在。在冥想中，我们学习如何观察不愉快的感受（比如膝盖疼痛、背痛），而不立即做出反应。我们培养出觉察冲动而不付诸行动的能力。

The anxiety we feel in conversation is usually rooted in deeper needs to be seen or heard, needs for safety, acceptance, belonging, and so on. The less confident we feel in meeting those needs, the more pressure we will experience to speak up or remain silent. We might fear that if we don’t say something right now we’ll never be able to do so. Or if we do say something, disaster or disconnection will surely ensue.

我们在交谈中感受到的焦虑通常源于更深层次的需求，例如被关注、被倾听、安全感、认同感、归属感等等。我们越缺乏满足这些需求的信心，就越会感受到开口说话或保持沉默的压力。我们或许会担心，如果现在不说，以后就永远没机会说了。或者，如果我们说了，肯定会引发灾难或导致关系破裂。

The more ways we find to meet those needs (and to handle them skillfully when they aren’t met), the less pressure we feel to speak or remain silent; we can relax into the flow of a conversation. There’s no danger in speaking our mind and no rush to say it all at once. If it’s important, we’ll find the right time and way to say it.

我们满足自身需求的方式越多（以及在需求无法得到满足时能够巧妙应对），我们就越不会感到说话或保持沉默的压力；我们就能放松地融入对话之中。表达自己的想法并没有什么危险，也不必急于一次性说完。如果这件事很重要，我们自然会找到合适的时机和方式来表达。

This capacity builds slowly. As we practice honoring our needs, we learn to trust ourselves. Paying attention to any small successes helps our nervous system settle and reset. With a new baseline of ease, it can stop setting off false alarms that impel or prevent us from speaking, and our ability to make more conscious choices grows. We can then discern what’s going to be most helpful to move a conversation forward and how to balance all the needs on the table.

这种能力是慢慢培养的。当我们练习尊重自己的需求时，我们学会了信任自己。关注任何小小的成功都有助于我们的神经系统平静下来并重新调整。有了新的放松状态，它就不会再触发那些驱使我们或阻止我们开口的错误警报，我们做出更清醒选择的能力也会增强。然后，我们就能分辨出什么最有助于推进对话，以及如何平衡所有需要兼顾的需求。

PRACTICE : Choice Points

练习：选择点数

To practice, choose someone with whom you feel relatively comfortable. This familiarity makes it easier to learn the tool. During a conversation, notice when you choose to speak. If you find yourself talking without having consciously chosen to do so, try stopping and leaving space for the other person to continue. Notice what it’s like to actively choose to say something rather than doing so automatically. Pay particular attention to any urgency or reluctance to speak or any sensations of internal pressure. Use that pressure as a signal to make a more conscious choice.

练习时，选择一个让你感觉比较自在的人。这种熟悉感会让你更容易掌握这个技巧。在对话过程中，注意你何时主动开口。如果你发现自己无意识地说话了，试着停下来，给对方留出空间继续说下去。感受一下主动选择说话和自动说话的区别。特别留意任何说话的紧迫感、犹豫感或任何内心的压力感。把这种压力感当作信号，促使你做出更清醒的选择。

Meetings

会议

There tends to be more freedom to remain silent in meetings than during one-to-one conversations. The next time you are in a meeting, notice how the impulse to speak can rise and fall as the conversation unfolds. If there is an important point you’d like to make, choose when to do so. You can always begin, “I’d like to go back to something we were talking about a few moments ago.” Notice how it feels after you speak. Is there relief? Anxiety or self-doubt?

在会议中，人们往往比在一对一谈话中更容易保持沉默。下次开会时，注意一下随着谈话的进行，你想要发言的冲动是如何起伏变化的。如果你有重要的观点想要表达，要选择合适的时机。你可以这样开头：“我想回到我们刚才讨论过的一个话题。” 注意一下你发言后的感觉。是如释重负？还是焦虑或自我怀疑？

Written Communication

书面沟通

Experiment with making conscious choices about when you check your inbox or social media feeds (“listening”). When you do engage, pause before replying to consider whether or not you want to “speak.” Is this the right time? Would it be useful to wait or to say nothing at all?

尝试有意识地选择何时查看收件箱或社交媒体动态（“收听”）。当你参与互动时，在回复之前先停顿一下，思考一下你是否真的想“发言”。现在是合适的时机吗？等待片刻或者保持沉默是否会更好？

Part of this investigation is getting to know our own patterns. Do we tend to speak easily and freely, finding it harder to leave space for others? Is it more comfortable for us to listen, finding it challenging to come forward?

这项调查的一部分是了解我们自身的行为模式。我们是否倾向于轻松自如地发言，而难以给别人留出空间？我们是否更习惯于倾听，而觉得发言有挑战性？

Most of us tend to be stronger in one area. Circumstances and events tied to our gender, race, class, or other aspects of our social location tend to mold how we show up relationally. We’ve all received messages—explicitly and implicitly, personally and through media, stories, and culture—about how we are expected to behave. Through various cues of approval or disapproval, inclusion or exclusion, we learn what’s safest based on our role and the expectations of others.

我们大多数人往往在某个领域更擅长。与性别、种族、阶级或其他社会地位相关的境遇和事件，往往会塑造我们在人际关系中的表现方式。我们都曾接收到关于自身行为规范的信息——无论是明确的还是隐含的，无论是通过个人经历还是媒体、故事和文化。通过各种赞许或不赞同、包容或排斥的信号，我们根据自身角色和他人的期望，学习如何做到最安全。

Our work is to uncover these patterns and develop an authentic freedom of expression. There is no ideal way to be, no one thing to do in all circumstances. The goal is dynamic flexibility through presence, choosing to speak or listen as needed.

我们的工作是揭示这些模式，并发展一种真正自由的表达方式。没有理想的生存之道，也没有适用于所有情况的固定做法。目标是通过临在感实现动态的灵活性，根据需要选择发言或倾听。

The Power of Pace: Pausing

节奏的力量：暂停

If I could teach people only one tool for training in presence it would be to pause. The space of one pause can make a world of difference. A colleague who teaches meditation to incarcerated youth tells a story about working with men in prison. He asks how much time they’re doing; their sentences often total well over one hundred years. Then he asks, “How long did you think about it before committing the crime that landed you here?” The combined total is often less than two minutes. Facing this stark disparity, my colleague explains to the youth, “Mindfulness helps you pause between an impulse and your reaction, so that you can have more choice about what you do with your life.”

如果我只能教人们一种提升觉察力的方法，那就是暂停。一次暂停就能带来巨大的改变。一位教授青少年冥想的同事讲述了他与狱中服刑人员共事的经历。他问他们服刑多久；他们的刑期加起来往往超过一百年。然后他又问：“在犯下让你身陷囹圄的罪行之前，你思考了多久？”答案往往不到两分钟。面对如此巨大的反差，我的同事向这些年轻人解释说：“正念能帮助你在冲动和反应之间稍作停顿，从而让你在人生道路上拥有更多选择。”

The pause is pregnant with possibility. In one breath, we can notice thoughts, feelings, and impulses, and choose which ones to follow. It’s like a mini-meditation, an infusion of presence to help stay clear and balanced. What happens during the space of that pause is quite open. We may ground our attention in the body or relax some inner tension, return to a specific intention, handle our emotions so they don’t spill out unskillfully, or gather our thoughts about how to proceed.

停顿蕴藏着无限可能。只需一口气，我们就能觉察到各种念头、感受和冲动，并选择跟随哪些。这就像一次迷你冥想，注入正念，帮助我们保持清醒和平衡。在停顿的这段时间里，一切皆有可能。我们可以将注意力集中在身体上，放松一些内在的紧张，回到某个特定的意图，妥善处理情绪，避免失控，或者整理思路，思考下一步该怎么做。

Pausing is both a support for and a natural expression of mindful presence. The more aware I am of my body, the more I notice any agitation in my nervous system and corresponding changes in my pace or volume. I can ride that wave of energy (say, expressing enthusiasm or frustration) or apply the brakes. As with choice points, the aim is not to become monotone, flat, or speak calmly all the time but rather to develop skill and proficiency in a wider range of circumstances.

停顿既是对正念的一种支持，也是正念的一种自然表达。我越觉察自己的身体，就越能注意到神经系统的任何波动，以及随之而来的语速或音量的变化。我可以顺应这股能量的起伏（比如表达热情或沮丧），也可以及时刹车。就像选择点一样，其目的并非变得单调、平淡，或者总是平静地说话，而是要在更广泛的情境中培养这种技巧和能力。

The pause is flexible, varying in length depending on the situation. One can take a micropause: an almost imperceptible gap in the flow of speech. It gives just enough time to ground your attention in the body or readjust your intention.

停顿是灵活的，其长度会根据情况而变化。我们可以进行微停顿：在言语流中几乎难以察觉的短暂停顿。这恰好给了我们足够的时间将注意力集中在身体上，或者重新调整我们的意图。

PRACTICE : Pausing

练习：暂停

If you have a practice partner for this book, set a timer for five minutes and discuss something you did recently that you enjoyed. See if each person can pause for the space of one breath each time before speaking. Try pausing for a moment during a sentence or between thoughts. During the pause, bring your attention back to a reference point in your body or your overall sense of presence.

如果你有练习伙伴，可以设定五分钟的计时器，然后分享最近让你感到愉悦的事情。尝试每次发言前，每个人都能停顿一下，深呼吸一次。也可以尝试在句子中间或思路之间稍作停顿。停顿期间，将注意力重新集中到身体的某个部位，或者感受一下自身的存在感。

This should slow the pace of the conversation considerably, and it will probably feel unnatural. This is a training exercise to explore pausing and returning to presence in a deliberate way, just as one might practice a tennis stroke in slow motion.

这会大大放慢谈话节奏，而且可能会感觉不太自然。这是一次训练练习，旨在探索如何有意识地停顿并重新集中注意力，就像慢动作练习网球击球一样。

You can also experiment with taking deliberate pauses in low-stakes conversations. Try pausing for the space of a breath before you speak or respond, as a way of gathering your attention and grounding in the body. This doesn’t mean acting oddly and taking slow, deep breaths! Just slow things down a bit, pausing to consider.

你也可以尝试在无关紧要的对话中刻意停顿。试着在说话或回应之前，先停顿一下，深呼吸片刻，以此来集中注意力，让自己感觉更踏实。这并不意味着要做出奇怪的举动，或者进行缓慢而深长的呼吸！只是稍微放慢节奏，停下来思考一下。

Try this in dialogue in a less obvious way, pausing a few times—for a moment before you begin speaking or for a beat between ideas. What is the effect on your state of mind? On the quality of connection?

尝试在对话中以一种不那么明显的方式运用这种技巧，比如时不时停顿一下——在开口说话前稍作停顿，或者在表达不同观点之间稍作停顿。这对你的心态有什么影响？对沟通质量有什么影响？

Pausing isn’t always easy to do. Even when we remember, it can be hard to insert space into a conversation or to find a way to do so that’s socially acceptable. We may feel concerned that we’ll lose our turn to speak or appear disinterested. Here are some specific ways to create a pause or to signal that you’re taking one:

停顿并不总是那么容易做到。即使我们记得要停顿，也很难在对话中插入停顿，或者找到一种符合社交礼仪的停顿方式。我们可能会担心失去发言机会，或者显得不感兴趣。以下是一些具体的停顿方法，或者可以借此表明你正在停顿：

• Take a deep, audible breath (especially an outbreath).

• 深吸一口气，发出清晰可闻的声音（尤其是呼气）。

• Use a short verbal cue to indicate you are thinking, such as “Hmm…”

• 使用简短的口头提示来表示你在思考，例如“嗯……”

• Use a visual cue, such as looking up and to the side or furrowing your brow.

• 使用视觉提示，例如抬头看向侧面或皱起眉头。

• “I’m not sure. I’d like to think about that.”

“我不太确定，我想考虑一下。”

• “Let me think about that for a moment.”

• “让我考虑一下。”

• “Can we pause for a moment? I want to gather my thoughts.”

• “我们能暂停一下吗？我想整理一下思路。”

• “This sounds important. I’d like to give it some time.”

• “这听起来很重要。我想花点时间考虑一下。”

• “I’d really like to consider this more carefully. Can I get back to you on it?”

• “我真的想更仔细地考虑一下。我可以稍后再回复你吗？”

When all else fails, create a distraction. If you’re out for a meal or in a meeting, excuse yourself to the restroom. I even heard of one fellow who would drop his keys or some loose change to insert a pause in conversation! Get as creative as you need to buy yourself some time and return to presence.

如果其他方法都无效，那就制造一些干扰。如果你正在吃饭或开会，就借口去洗手间。我甚至听说有人会故意掉落钥匙或零钱来打断谈话！发挥你的创造力，为自己争取一些时间，重新集中注意力。

Sometimes we need a longer pause. If we determine that the conditions aren’t right for a successful conversation, we may want to take a break for a day, a week, or longer. In these instances, how we pause is important. If we simply say, “I can’t talk about this now,” our conversation partners are left to interpret our behavior on their own. They may think we’re not interested, that we don’t care, or that we’re avoiding them. To increase the chances that our break will be productive, we need to share the reasons behind our choice. Here are a few examples:

有时候我们需要更长时间的停顿。如果我们觉得目前的条件不适合进行有效的对话，我们可能需要休息一天、一周甚至更长时间。在这种情况下，我们如何停顿至关重要。如果我们只是简单地说“我现在没空谈这个”，对话伙伴只能自行解读我们的行为。他们可能会认为我们不感兴趣、不在乎，或者在回避他们。为了提高我们停顿的成效，我们需要说明我们选择停顿的原因。以下是一些例子：

• “I’d really like to continue our conversation, and I’m not in the best frame of mind to do that right now. Can we take a break and come back to this…[tomorrow, next time]?”

• “我很想继续我们的谈话，但我现在状态不太好。我们能不能休息一下，明天或者下次再聊？”

• “I’d really like to hear what you have to say, and I’m feeling a little overwhelmed, so I don’t think I’ll be able to listen well. Let’s take a break for an hour. Okay?”

• “我很想听听你的想法，但我现在感觉有点不知所措，所以恐怕没法好好听。我们休息一个小时吧，好吗？”

• “I’m committed to figuring this out together, and I don’t quite have the space to think clearly now. I’d like to put this on hold until…Would that be okay?”

• “我决心和你们一起解决这个问题，但我现在实在没有精力冷静思考。我想把这件事暂时搁置一下……可以吗？”

• “I want to finish this conversation, and I don’t think anything else I say right now will be useful. How about we pause here and come back later?”

• “我想结束这次谈话，我觉得我现在再说任何话都没有用了。我们先暂停一下，过会儿再回来吧？”

Look closely at these examples. What do you notice in common?

仔细观察这些例子。你发现了什么共同点？

First, they all begin with our intention to connect (the second step to effective conversation). This preempts any tendency to interpret our break as rejection or avoidance. It lets the other person know we are considering them in our desire to pause. This needs to be genuine. Find your own words to express what’s true.

首先，所有对话都始于我们想要建立联系的意愿（这是有效对话的第二步）。这可以避免对方将我们的暂停解读为拒绝或回避。它让对方知道，我们暂停的初衷是考虑到他们的感受。这种暂停必须是真诚的。用你自己的语言表达你的真实想法。

Second, each statement takes responsibility for our limitations or desires. We’re clear that we’re acting on our own need for space rather than blaming the other person.

其次，每份声明都承认我们自身的局限或欲望。我们明确表示，我们这样做是为了满足自身对空间的需求，而不是指责他人。

Finally, they each end with a request to finish the conversation later, which helps reduce anxiety about what will happen. The more specific we can be about when, the better.

最后，他们都以请求稍后再继续谈话结束，这有助于减轻人们对未来走向的焦虑。我们越能具体说明何时结束谈话，效果就越好。

As we use this tool of pausing, noticing pauses (or their absence) attunes us to the pace of a conversation. This can be a very rich area to explore and a potent way to train in presence. Because speech is created with breath and because our breath is directly tied to our nervous system, the pace of our speaking is often a direct reflection of our internal state. What’s fascinating is that changing our pace of speech can shift our internal state.

当我们运用停顿这一技巧时，留意停顿（或停顿的缺失）能帮助我们更好地把握对话的节奏。这本身就是一个值得深入探索的领域，也是训练临场感的有效方法。由于言语是由呼吸产生的，而呼吸又与神经系统直接相关，因此我们说话的节奏往往直接反映了我们的内在状态。令人着迷的是，改变说话的节奏也能改变我们的内在状态。

PRACTICE : Modulating Pace

练习：调节节奏

Notice when and how your pace varies in conversation. At what pace do you feel most comfortable, confident, and relaxed? When is it slow and steady? When does it quicken or become rapid? Can you choose how quickly or slowly you speak? How does your pace affect the tone of the conversation?

注意你在谈话中语速的变化时间和方式。你觉得什么样的语速最舒适、自信和放松？什么时候语速缓慢而稳定？什么时候语速加快或变得急促？你能控制自己说话的快慢吗？你的语速如何影响谈话的氛围？

Choose an easy, low-stakes conversation with which to experiment. As you speak, vary the pace of your speech. Speed up a little, speaking more rapidly. Notice the effect on your body, your thoughts, your overall energy. Slow down some. What is the effect on your state of mind and body? On the quality of connection in the relationship?

选择一段轻松、无压力的对话进行实验。说话时，尝试改变语速。稍微加快语速，注意身体、思维和整体能量的变化。然后放慢语速。这对你的身心状态有何影响？对你们关系的亲密程度有何影响？

Slowing down even a little bit usually increases our ability to lead with presence. This is especially true in times of conflict, when things tend to speed up. Dialing our pace back in such situations can have a calming effect on our nervous system. 1

哪怕只是稍微放慢节奏，通常也能提升我们展现领导力的能力。在冲突时期尤其如此，因为冲突往往会加速发展。在这种情况下放慢节奏可以起到镇静神经系统的作用。

Speaking at a relaxed pace can also help us claim space in a conversation and makes it easier for the listener to take in what we’re saying. When we’re confident and self-assured, we usually speak at a leisurely rate. There’s no rush; we trust that what we have to say matters and is worth listening to. We breathe naturally and easy, taking our time. In general, our words carry more weight when we speak in this manner, which can draw and hold the attention of our listener.

以轻松的语速说话有助于我们在对话中占据主导地位，也让听者更容易理解我们所说的话。当我们自信从容时，说话通常比较舒缓。我们不急于求成；我们相信自己所说的话很重要，值得倾听。我们呼吸自然流畅，不慌不忙。一般来说，这样说话更有分量，更容易吸引并保持听者的注意力。

It’s important to note that there’s no “right” pace. The ideal pace supports presence and helps create connection, and that can vary a lot depending on the circumstances or culture.

需要注意的是，并没有所谓的“正确”节奏。理想的节奏有助于集中注意力，建立联系，而这会因环境或文化而异。

Maturing in Presence: Mutuality

在彼此陪伴中成长：互惠

Leading with presence is a rich experience that matures over time. As it develops, presence illuminates the existence of the other. The more I sense myself, the more aware I become of you. This observation is so basic we can take it for granted: relationship by definition means there are two of us! To be truly in dialogue means that we see the other person as an autonomous individual, with their own hopes, fears, dreams, desires, joys, and sorrows.

以临在为先是一种丰富的体验，它会随着时间的推移而日臻成熟。随着临在的加深，它会照亮对方的存在。我越是觉察自身，就越能意识到你的存在。这种观察如此基本，以至于我们常常习以为常：关系的定义就是我们两个人！真正的对话意味着我们将对方视为一个独立的个体，拥有自己的希望、恐惧、梦想、渴望、喜悦和悲伤。

In Zulu there is a traditional greeting, Sawubona, “We see you.” Orland Bishop, director of the ShadeTree Multicultural Foundation, explains, “The response is Yabo sawubona, ‘Yes, we see you too.’ When two humans meet in this gesture of Sawubona the acknowledgment is, ‘We see each other.’ That becomes an agreement. It’s an invitation to participate in each other’s life.” 2 Can we bring this simple, profound recognition of another’s presence to our conversations?

在祖鲁语中，有一句传统的问候语“Sawubona”，意思是“我们看到你了”。ShadeTree多元文化基金会主任奥兰·毕晓普解释说：“回应是‘Yabo sawubona’，意思是‘是的，我们也看到你了’。当两个人以‘Sawubona’这个手势相遇时，彼此的确认就是‘我们彼此看见’。这便成为一种共识，一种邀请，邀请彼此参与对方的生活。”我们能否将这种简单而深刻的对他人的认可融入到我们的对话中呢？

We’ve all had experiences of not being seen or of looking right through someone else. It feels as if the other person is talking “at you” rather than “to you” or like you’re talking to a wall. Lack of mutuality is an absence of presence; it turns dialogue into monologue. It’s that distant gaze of the checkout clerk, the flat monotone of a customer service agent.

我们都曾有过这样的经历：感觉自己不被对方看见，或者感觉自己仿佛与人擦肩而过。那种感觉就像对方在“对你说话”，而不是“与你交流”，又或者像是在对着一堵墙自言自语。缺乏互动意味着缺乏临场感，它把对话变成了独白。就像收银员那种疏离的眼神，或是客服人员那种单调乏味的语气。

We lose mutuality for many reasons. It happens when we’re on automatic. It can occur when we are extremely impassioned or when we feel scared, upset, or angry. Tragically, we lose mutuality with the friends and family we see every day. They become so familiar that we stop seeing them.

我们失去彼此间的互动有很多原因。当我们处于机械式的状态时，这种情况就会发生。当我们情绪激动、感到恐惧、沮丧或愤怒时，这种情况也可能发生。更令人悲哀的是，我们甚至会与每天见面的朋友和家人失去互动。他们变得如此熟悉，以至于我们不再关注他们。

Without the mutuality of presence there is a fundamental disconnect. “You” are reduced to an object in relation to “me.” You become a mental representation from the past, a vehicle for getting what I want, or an obstacle in my way. When human beings become objects rather than persons, there is nothing we can’t justify: from ordinary slights to the horrors of slavery, sex trafficking, and genocide.

缺乏彼此在场的互动，就会产生根本性的隔阂。“你”沦为相对于“我”的客体。你变成了来自过去的心理表征，成了我获取欲望的工具，或是挡在我路上的障碍。当人被物化而非人性化时，我们便可以为任何事辩解：从日常的轻视到奴隶制、人口贩卖和种族灭绝的种种暴行。

Presence opens the door to mutuality. When we lead with presence, we enter a field of relationship in which both of us matter simply by virtue of our existence. We shift from seeing the other as an object, to seeing them as a subject. This is the potent, transformative shift in perspective Martin Buber famously described as the I-Thou relationship. “All real living is meeting,” he wrote. 3 For Buber, respect for the innate subjectivity of life was holy.

临在开启了互惠之门。当我们以临在为先导时，我们便进入了一种关系领域，在这个领域中，我们双方的存在本身就具有意义。我们不再将对方视为客体，而是将他们视为主体。这正是马丁·布伯所描述的那种强有力的、具有变革意义的视角转变——“我-你”关系。“一切真正的生活都是相遇，”他写道。对布伯而言，尊重生命与生俱来的主体性是神圣的。

Principle: Leading with presence includes mutuality, seeing the other person as an autonomous individual, and uncertainty, acknowledging and accepting the unknown, both of which create new possibilities in dialogue.

原则：以临在感为主导包括相互尊重，将对方视为自主的个体，以及不确定性，承认并接受未知，这两点都能在对话中创造新的可能性。

To be truly alive is to enter this experience of mutuality, of sensing one another and the mystery of being here. Relational presence is a true encounter in which I see you for who you are rather than what I want or need you to be. This mutuality is the foundation of real dialogue.

真正活着，就是进入这种相互依存的体验，去感知彼此，去体悟存在的奥秘。关系中的临在，是一种真实的相遇，在这种相遇中，我看到的是你本来的样子，而不是我希望或需要你成为的样子。这种相互依存，是真正对话的基础。

Advanced Practice: Relational Awareness

高级实践：关系意识

In conversation we tend to focus all our attention on ourselves or on the other person. Relational awareness is the capacity to include both you and me, the external and the internal, balancing our attention in a dynamic way. It builds on the foundation of embodiment by expanding awareness to include three more reference points: the other person, our connection, and the space around us. This can increase our flexibility and give us more options to handle intensity in dialogue.

在对话中，我们往往会把所有注意力都集中在自己或对方身上。关系觉察力是指能够同时关注你我、外部世界和内在世界，并动态地平衡我们的注意力。它建立在具身认知的基础之上，扩展了觉察力，纳入了三个新的参照点：对方、我们之间的联结以及我们周围的空间。这可以增强我们的灵活性，并让我们在对话中拥有更多应对激烈冲突的选择。

Relational awareness is an advanced practice, yet it flows quite naturally out of the exercises we’ve already been doing. Awareness is like a flashlight with an adjustable beam. One can vary its aperture or direct it to different locations. Try the exercises below to get a feel for shifting awareness between the internal and external.

关系觉察是一种高级练习，但它能很自然地从我们之前做的练习中自然而然地流露出来。觉察就像一个光束可调的手电筒，你可以调整它的光圈，也可以把它照射到不同的位置。尝试以下练习，感受一下如何在内在和外在之间转换觉察。

PRACTICE : Expanding Awareness

练习：扩展意识

Do this practice solo. Sit comfortably, close your eyes, and let your mind and body begin to settle. Ground your attention in one of the four internal reference points we’ve already explored: gravity, the centerline, breathing, or a touch point such as the hands or feet. Take some time here, feeling the steadiness of these tangible sensations.

请独自进行这项练习。舒适地坐下，闭上双眼，让身心逐渐平静下来。将注意力集中在我们之前探讨过的四个内在参照点之一：重力、身体中线、呼吸，或者某个接触点，例如双手或双脚。花些时间，感受这些切实存在的感觉带来的稳定感。

Then let go of the internal reference point and open your eyes. Become aware of sights and sounds around you. Look around if you like. Notice how it feels to have your attention focused outwardly. Close your eyes, and let your awareness settle again with an internal reference point. Explore opening and closing your eyes, shifting your attention back and forth between inside and outside. Can you find a balance, some of your attention connected to your body and some connected to your surroundings?

然后放下内在的参照点，睁开双眼。觉察周围的景象和声音。如果愿意，可以四处看看。感受一下将注意力集中于外部世界的感觉。闭上双眼，让你的意识再次回到内在参照点。尝试睁眼和闭眼，在内在和外在之间切换注意力。你能找到一种平衡吗？一部分注意力与你的身体相连，一部分注意力与周围的环境相连？

Now, with your eyes closed, begin to widen your awareness. Bring attention to your whole body, feeling its various sensations: warmth, heaviness, pulsing, or tingling. Next, bring your attention to the surface of your skin. See if you can feel any sensations there: the touch of your clothing, the temperature of the air.

现在，闭上眼睛，开始扩展你的感知范围。将注意力集中在你的全身，感受它各种不同的感觉：温暖、沉重、脉动或刺痛。接下来，将注意力转移到你的皮肤表面。看看你是否能感觉到那里的任何感觉：衣服的触感、空气的温度。

Widen your awareness further to the space immediately around your body. Can you sense the space just beyond the surface of your skin? To help notice this, imagine that you are in a crowded subway car, bodies pressed against you. Now bring your attention to the space around your body here and now. Can you notice the absence of pressure? The sense of spaciousness?

将你的注意力进一步扩展到你身体周围的空间。你能感觉到皮肤表面之外的空间吗？为了帮助你注意到这一点，想象你身处拥挤的地铁车厢，周围都是紧贴着你的人。现在，将你的注意力集中到此时此刻你身体周围的空间。你能感受到没有压力吗？你能感受到开阔的空间感吗？

Last, expand your awareness even further to include the entire room. You can open your eyes, or notice sounds, to get a feel for this openness. Can you be aware of the space around you?

最后，进一步扩展你的感知范围，将整个房间都纳入其中。你可以睁开眼睛，或者留意周围的声音，来感受这种开放感。你能意识到你周围的空间吗？

To end, bring your attention back into your body, feeling the sensations of sitting.

最后，将注意力重新集中到你的身体上，感受坐着的感觉。

This series of exercises reveals the fluidity of awareness. In the next practice, we’ll further explore balancing internal and external awareness.

这一系列练习揭示了意识的流动性。在接下来的练习中，我们将进一步探索如何平衡内在意识和外在意识。

PRACTICE : Relational Awareness

实践：关系意识

Try these suggestions individually in different settings or sequentially within one conversation. You can do this with a partner, or you can experiment silently in a relaxed social situation.

您可以分别在不同的场合尝试这些建议，也可以在一次对话中按顺序尝试。您可以和伴侣一起尝试，也可以在轻松的社交场合中独自进行尝试。

Use an internal reference point to ground your awareness in your body. Notice how it feels to keep some attention there. Next, let the awareness of your body, feelings, or thoughts be in the background and place your focus on the person before you, giving them 100 percent of your attention. Notice how this feels.

利用一个内在参照点，将你的注意力集中在身体上。留意一下将注意力集中在那里是什么感觉。接下来，让你的身体、感受或想法退居幕后，将注意力完全集中在眼前的人身上，给予他们百分之百的关注。留意一下这种感觉。

As you listen or speak, begin to shift your attention back and forth, between yourself and the other person. Can you balance your awareness between the internal and external, including both?

当你倾听或说话时，试着在自己和对方之间来回转移注意力。你能否平衡地关注内在和外在，并将两者都纳入考量？

As the conversation unfolds, notice any sense of connection. How does it feel to be here with this person? Rather than focusing on “me” or “you,” can you put your attention on “us,” the sense of being here together?

随着谈话的进行，留意彼此之间的联系感。和这个人在一起感觉如何？与其关注“我”或“你”，不如把注意力放在“我们”上，放在我们在一起的感觉上。

Next, expand your awareness to the space between or around both of you. Can you widen your awareness to the space of the room? Noticing ambient sounds, silence, or any gaps in the conversation can help you shift your attention to this wider frame. Notice how this feels.

接下来，将你的注意力扩展到你们两人之间或周围的空间。你能将注意力扩展到整个房间吗？留意周围的声音、寂静，或者谈话中的任何停顿，都能帮助你将注意力转移到这个更广阔的空间。感受一下这种变化。

Finally, explore moving between these reference points: your own embodiment, balanced attention between self and other, the sense of “us” or connection, and the wider space within which the conversation is happening. What qualities do you notice in each?

最后，探索如何在这些参照点之间转换：你自身的身体感受、自我与他人之间平衡的关注点、“我们”或联结感，以及对话发生的更广阔的空间。你注意到每个参照点有哪些特质？

These are advanced practices and require time to develop. Each lends a unique strength and can be useful at different times. Balancing attention between self and other can serve as a resting place through the shifts and changes of a conversation. The sense of “us” can be particularly useful in savoring a sweet moment or accessing compassion in a trying one. The widest frame can be helpful when things get intense, giving you a large container to hold strong emotions.

这些都是高级练习，需要时间培养。每一种练习都有其独特的优势，在不同的情况下都能发挥作用。在对话的转换和变化中，平衡对自身和他人的关注，可以为你提供一个休憩之所。“我们”的意识在品味美好时刻或在困境中唤起同情心时尤为重要。当情况变得紧张时，尽可能宽广的视角会很有帮助，它能为你提供一个容纳强烈情绪的容器。

Uncertainty: Meeting the Unknown

不确定性：迎接未知

Presence also reveals the fundamental uncertainty and mystery of being alive. Human beings are unpredictable. No matter how well I know someone, I can never be sure what they are thinking, how they are feeling, or what they will say. I can’t know how a conversation will evolve. We can plan and strategize all we want, but how often do things unfold the way we imagined?

临在也揭示了生命中根本的不确定性和神秘性。人是不可预测的。无论我多么了解一个人，我永远无法确定他们在想什么、感受如何，或者会说什么。我无法预知一场对话会如何发展。我们可以制定各种计划和策略，但事情又有多少会按照我们想象的方式展开呢？

If we become fixated on a plan, we lose touch with the moment. When that happens, we lose access to wisdom. Our ability to respond appropriately to what’s actually happening becomes clouded by preconceived ideas about what we think should be happening. When we plan, can we recognize our ideas for what they are: a tentative, imagined future?

如果我们过于执着于计划，就会脱离当下。一旦如此，我们就失去了获得智慧的途径。我们对实际发生的事情做出恰当反应的能力，会被我们对应该发生的事情的先入为主的观念所蒙蔽。当我们制定计划时，我们能否认清自己的想法本质：它们不过是一种暂时的、想象中的未来？

There is a saying in Zen: “Not knowing is most intimate.” True presence always entails a tremble of uncertainty. This is healthy; it means we are in touch with reality. When we first begin to experience the uncertainty of true presence, we may feel unsettled or vulnerable. Over time, we learn to feel more at ease with not knowing. What was initially uncomfortable gives way to a feeling of aliveness.

禅宗有句谚语：“不知乃至亲。”真正的临在总是伴随着一丝不确定感。这其实是健康的；它意味着我们与现实相连。当我们初次体验到真正临在的不确定感时，或许会感到不安或脆弱。随着时间的推移，我们会逐渐学会坦然面对未知。最初的不适感会逐渐转化为一种鲜活的生命力。

Here we arrive at a fuller sense of what it means to lead with presence. We are aware of what’s happening within and around us in an honest way. We include the other person with mutual respect. We are alert to the inherent uncertainty of the moment, pregnant with possibility. We train ourselves to rest with this poise—flexible, honest, mutual, and uncertain.

在这里，我们对“临在式领导”有了更深刻的理解。我们以诚实的态度觉察自身内外发生的一切。我们以相互尊重的态度接纳他人。我们敏锐地意识到当下固有的不确定性，以及其中蕴藏的无限可能。我们训练自己保持这种沉稳的状态——灵活、诚实、相互尊重，同时又不失不确定性。

As our skill in leading with presence grows, our embodied awareness becomes a resource that is available at any moment: helping us discern how we’re feeling and what we need to say, catching the signals of reactivity and providing the space to handle that energy, and perceiving the wealth of information that’s coming from our interlocutor so that we can guide the conversation toward greater connection and understanding.

随着我们运用临场感领导的能力不断提高，我们的身体意识成为随时可用的资源：帮助我们辨别自己的感受和需要表达的内容，捕捉反应的信号并提供空间来处理这种能量，感知来自对话者的丰富信息，以便我们能够引导对话朝着更深层次的联系和理解的方向发展。

The leading edge of conversation is always mindful presence. The more we see its strengths and benefits, the more we trust it as a core foundation for human relationship.

对话的关键始终在于专注当下。我们越是体会到它的优势和益处，就越会将其视为人际关系的核心基石。

PRINCIPLES

原则

Leading with presence includes mutuality, seeing the other person as an autonomous individual, and uncertainty, acknowledging and accepting the unknown, both of which create new possibilities in dialogue.

以临在感为主导包括相互尊重，将对方视为独立的个体，以及承认和接受未知，这两点都能在对话中创造新的可能性。

KEY POINTS

要点

We can practice presence in conversation with:

我们可以通过以下方式练习在对话中保持专注：

• Choice Points: Notice the choice between listening and speaking.

• 选择点：注意听和说之间的选择。

• Pausing: Experiment with taking micropauses or longer breaks.

• 暂停：尝试进行短暂的暂停或更长时间的休息。

• Pace: Modulate our pace to bring more awareness to speaking.

• 语速：调整语速，提高说话时的专注力。

• Relational Awareness: Develop a balance of inner and outer awareness.

• 关系意识：培养内在意识和外在意识的平衡。

QUESTION & ANSWER

问答

Q: I’m confused. When I try these practices with another person, it seems as if I am less present. Am I doing something wrong?

问：我很困惑。当我尝试用这些方法与其他人一起练习时，我似乎无法全神贯注。我是不是做错了什么？

Remember that there’s a difference between using a practice and the experience of presence. The practices are tools to strengthen our capacity to stay alert and balanced in conversation. At first, they can feel unnatural and even distracting. Like learning anything, it takes time to feel comfortable.

请记住，练习方法和体验临在感是有区别的。练习方法是增强我们在对话中保持警觉和平衡能力的工具。起初，它们可能会让人感觉不自然，甚至分散注意力。就像学习任何东西一样，需要时间才能感到自在。

What’s most important is to choose a tool that feels relatively easeful and stick with it until it becomes second nature. It’s easy to feel present when talking with a friend and all is well. But when things get heated, if we haven’t trained ourselves to lead with presence, we’re more likely to fall back on old habits. Developing a reliable method for cultivating presence increases our chances of remembering to use these tools when we need them the most.

最重要的是选择一种用起来比较顺手的工具，并坚持使用，直到它成为一种本能。和朋友聊天时，很容易保持专注，一切都很顺利。但当气氛变得紧张时，如果我们没有训练自己以专注的态度引导对话，就更容易回到过去的习惯。培养一种可靠的专注力训练方法，可以提高我们在最需要的时候想起使用这些工具的几率。

Q: I get really anxious when I try bringing more presence to conversations. It feels so vulnerable, like I’m totally exposed. Do you have any suggestions?

问：我尝试在谈话中更加投入时，会感到非常焦虑。感觉很脆弱，好像完全暴露在外。您有什么建议吗？

Presence means feeling more vulnerable; that vulnerability is a sign that you are in touch with reality. Part of the anxiety may be not having enough tools. It’s a little bit like a butterfly that’s just come out of a chrysalis; its wings are too tender to fly.

临在意味着感到更加脆弱；这种脆弱恰恰表明你与现实保持着联系。焦虑的部分原因可能是缺乏应对工具。这有点像一只刚刚破茧而出的蝴蝶；它的翅膀太过娇嫩，无法飞翔。

Give the process time, like a butterfly drying its wings in the sun. Do what you can to keep from feeling overwhelmed. When we’re overwhelmed, we stop learning. By contrast, if things are too comfortable, we don’t grow. Aim for the middle, what NVC Trainer Miki Kashtan calls “strategic discomfort.”

给这个过程一些时间，就像蝴蝶在阳光下晾晒翅膀一样。尽量避免感到不知所措。当我们感到不知所措时，就会停止学习。相反，如果一切都太安逸，我们就不会成长。要追求中间状态，也就是非暴力沟通培训师米基·卡什坦所说的“策略性不适”。

We can learn to inhabit that space with ease. Study the feeling of vulnerability. Investigate what’s happening in your body; examine any beliefs or fears in your mind. As your capacity to tolerate the discomfort grows, you can begin to relax and find your bearings. Vulnerability is a doorway to a more fulfilling experience of being alive. It can be a gift rather than a liability.

我们可以学会轻松地适应这种状态。仔细体会脆弱的感觉。探究身体的感受；审视内心的任何信念或恐惧。随着你对不适的承受能力增强，你就能开始放松，找到方向。脆弱是通往更充实人生的大门。它是一种馈赠，而非负担。

Q: How do you actually remember to use these tools? I find myself reacting and arguing before I can do anything. Sometimes I don’t remember until hours afterward!

问：你是怎么记住要用这些工具的？我发现自己总是先做出反应、争辩，然后才来得及采取行动。有时候，我甚至要过好几个小时才会想起来！

It’s humbling, isn’t it? The Tibetan Buddhist teacher Chögyam Trungpa Rinpoche once said, “Spiritual practice is one insult after another.” Communication practice can feel that way too! Take the long view and create a positive feedback loop. What matters most is that we remember, not when we remember. We can capitalize upon that moment by celebrating it rather than beating ourselves up.

这确实令人感到谦卑，不是吗？藏传佛教上师丘扬·创巴仁波切曾说过：“修行之路是一连串的羞辱。”沟通练习有时也会有这种感觉！要着眼长远，建立积极的反馈循环。最重要的是我们是否记得，而不是何时记得。我们可以好好利用那一刻，庆祝它，而不是自责。

The next part is being persistent. It’s entirely possible to develop more presence in our lives; the history of human contemplative traditions is a testament to that. It takes patience, dedication, and a willingness to forget and remember again and again. Over time, the gaps get shorter. Instead of days elapsing, it’s hours; then instead of hours, it’s minutes; and so forth until we’re able to remember in real time, in the midst of a conversation.

接下来是坚持不懈。我们完全有可能在生活中培养更多的临在感；人类冥想传统的历史就是最好的证明。这需要耐心、专注，以及反复遗忘和回忆的意愿。随着时间的推移，间隔会越来越短。不再是几天，而是几个小时；然后不再是几个小时，而是几分钟；如此反复，直到我们能够在实时对话中回忆起一切。

The wonderful thing is that most people welcome a do-over. If you realize you totally bungled a conversation, why not let the other person know? Say, “Hey, I said some things I didn’t mean earlier. Would you be up for rewinding and trying that again with me?”

最棒的是，大多数人都乐意重来一次。如果你意识到自己把谈话搞砸了，为什么不告诉对方呢？你可以说：“嘿，我刚才说了一些我本意并非如此的话。你愿意倒回去再跟我重新说一遍吗？”

# ↩

part two

# ↩

第二部分

the second step

第二步

come from curiosity and care

源于好奇心和关怀

IF WE WANT to speak our truth and listen deeply, leading with presence gets us on the map. Once we’re actually here, the next step is choosing a helpful intention to ensure that we’re pointed in the right direction. This is like checking that the map is oriented correctly. We can put a lot of energy into a conversation, but if our intention is off, we might be heading in the wrong direction.

如果我们想要表达真我并认真倾听，那么以专注的态度引领我们就能找到方向。一旦我们真正做到这一点，下一步就是选择一个有益的意图，以确保我们朝着正确的方向前进。这就像检查地图的方向是否正确。我们可以在对话中投入大量精力，但如果我们的意图不对，我们可能就会走错方向。

The second step of mindful communication is to come from curiosity and care. Our intention can determine the whole tone and trajectory of a dialogue. Intention is where we’re coming from inside. It’s the motivation or inner quality of heart behind our words or actions. You could say it’s the vector that drives what’s happening in one direction or another. Intention is about how and why we speak or listen.

正念沟通的第二步是怀着好奇心和关怀。我们的意图可以决定对话的整体基调和走向。意图源于我们的内心，是我们言语或行为背后的动机或内在品质。你可以说，它是驱动事态发展的向量。意图关乎我们如何说话或倾听，以及为何如此。

A great deal of our communication is nonverbal: body language, facial expressions, gestures, tone of voice. We can say one thing and communicate the complete opposite. In other words, how we say something is equally important—if not more important—than what we say. All of this is shaped by our intention.

我们的大部分沟通都是非语言的：肢体语言、面部表情、手势、语气。我们可能口是心非，表达的意思却截然相反。换句话说，我们说话的方式与我们说话的内容同等重要，甚至更重要。而这一切都源于我们的意图。

If we’re not consciously choosing our intention, we’re on automatic—relying on unconscious, habitual patterns. If that’s what’s happening, it’s pretty hit-or-miss whether we’re going toward our destination.

如果我们没有有意识地选择意图，我们就处于自动状态——依赖于无意识的习惯模式。如果真是这样，我们能否朝着目标前进就完全取决于运气。

So where are we coming from? How are we approaching the conversation? In this section of the book we’ll look at some of our habitual ways of relating to conflict, the shortcomings and limitations of that conditioning, and how we can realign our intentions to have more effective and meaningful conversations.

那么，我们的出发点是什么？我们又是如何展开对话的？在本书的这一部分，我们将探讨一些我们处理冲突的惯常方式，这些方式的不足和局限性，以及我们如何调整自己的意图，从而进行更有效、更有意义的对话。

# ↩

4

the blame game

互相指责

Children learn to speak, though they have no learned teachers.

— UNKNOWN

孩子们在没有受过专业训练的老师的情况下学会说话。——佚名

I DID A lot of backpacking in my early twenties. One winter, a good friend from college and I headed out for a few days of snow camping in New York’s Catskill Mountains. Aaron is a poet, musician, and composer. We’d been close in college, spending many hours together pondering religion, philosophy, and the utter mystery of being alive. Since graduating, I’d wanted to stay in touch more than he had.

我二十出头的时候经常背包旅行。有一年冬天，我和大学时的一个好朋友去纽约州的卡茨基尔山脉进行了几天的雪地露营。亚伦是一位诗人、音乐家和作曲家。大学时我们关系很亲密，经常一起探讨宗教、哲学以及生命存在的奥秘。毕业后，我一直比他更想和他保持联系。

On the trip I decided to try out some of my newfound Nonviolent Communication skills. I felt hurt and angry, and I expressed my desire for more connection and closeness. I asked him why he hadn’t been in touch, inviting him to open up and share more. Aaron was quieter than I was, but I kept pushing. Needless to say, it didn’t go well.

旅途中，我决定尝试一下新学的非暴力沟通技巧。我感到受伤和愤怒，并表达了渴望与他建立更紧密联系的愿望。我问他为什么不联系我，并邀请他敞开心扉，分享更多。亚伦比我沉默寡言，但我坚持不懈地追问。结果可想而知，并不顺利。

Looking back, I can see that I wasn’t leading with presence or coming from curiosity and care. Though I genuinely wanted to connect, I was so focused on my way of doing so that I failed to see him for who he was or get curious about what was going on for him. I wasn’t able to balance my own longing for closeness with care for his needs. I don’t think I even checked if he was willing to have the conversation: “Hey man, I’ve missed you a lot since we graduated. I think we might have different expectations of keeping in touch. Are you up for talking about that?”

回想起来，我意识到我当时并没有以真诚的态度对待他，也没有出于好奇和关心。虽然我真心想和他建立联系，但我却过于关注自己的方式，以至于忽略了他这个人，也没有关心他正在经历什么。我无法平衡自己渴望亲近和关心他的需求。我甚至都没问过他是否愿意谈谈：“嘿，哥们儿，自从我们毕业后，我真的很想你。我觉得我们对保持联系的方式可能不太一样。你愿意聊聊吗？”

In addition, my intention was off. My approach was mixed with subtle layers of blame (I thought to myself: “Why hadn’t he been in touch? Wasn’t that what friends do?”) and manipulation (“What’s so hard about

此外，我的动机也不对。我的做法掺杂着微妙的责备（我心想：“他为什么不联系我？朋友之间不就应该这样做吗？”）和操控（“这有什么难的？”）

sharing feelings? Couldn’t he just say what was on his mind?”) After that trip we drifted further apart. It caused me great pain to lose him as a friend. In spite of many attempts on my part to reach out, we’ve never reconnected.

分享感受？他难道就不能直接说出心里话吗？那次旅行之后，我们渐行渐远。失去他这个朋友让我非常痛苦。尽管我多次尝试联系他，我们却始终未能重新建立联系。

Intention is the motivation or inner quality of heart behind our words and actions.

意图是我们言语和行为背后内在的动机或品质。

This is the power of intention and the risk of not choosing it wisely. Others can feel where we’re coming from inside, regardless of how polished our words are. Perhaps you’ve had the experience of talking to someone who’s taken a communication workshop and now has fancier words to run the same old trips? We can make “I statements” and “active listen” all we want; if we’re not genuine in our intention to connect, it’s unlikely to bring us closer.

这就是意图的力量，也是选择不当的风险。无论我们的言辞多么华丽，别人都能感受到我们内心的真实想法。或许你曾遇到过这样的人：他们参加过沟通技巧培训，现在只会用更华丽的辞藻来重复老生常谈？我们可以尽情地使用“我陈述句”和“积极倾听”，但如果我们没有真诚的沟通意图，就很难拉近彼此的距离。

Our Unconscious Training

我们的无意识训练

What’s our default when we’re on automatic? To transform our intentions in conversation, we need to examine how we are looking at things.

当我们处于自动状态时，我们的默认行为是什么？为了改变我们在对话中的意图，我们需要审视我们看待事物的方式。

Let’s take a fairly common situation between housemates. Have you ever lived with someone who didn’t like things as tidy as you? You leave the kitchen neat while they let things pile up. When they do clean, it’s not up to your standards. If this is familiar, you’ve probably found yourself feeling exasperated, saying, “What’s wrong with you? Why are you so messy? Is it that hard to…?” Maybe you even called them a slob!

我们来看一个室友之间很常见的情况。你有没有和不太爱干净的人合住过？你总是把厨房收拾得干干净净，而他们却任由东西堆积。就算他们打扫了，也达不到你的标准。如果你也有过这样的经历，你可能经常会感到恼火，忍不住抱怨：“你怎么这么邋遢？就不能好好收拾一下吗……？”说不定你还骂过他们邋遢呢！

Yet if you’ve ever been in the other role, your response probably went something like this: “Why are you such a neat freak? Can’t you just relax?”

但如果你曾经扮演过另一个角色，你的回应可能是这样的：“你为什么这么有洁癖？你就不能放松点吗？”

In professional situations, depending on how we relate to the details, the other person is either “disorganized and unprofessional” or “anal and micromanaging.” In romantic relationships, the person who wants more closeness and affection sees their partner as “aloof” or “distant,” while their partner may see them as “needy and dependent.”

在职业场合，根据我们对细节的关注程度，对方要么被贴上“缺乏条理且不专业”的标签，要么被贴上“吹毛求疵且事无巨细地管控”的标签。在恋爱关系中，渴望更多亲密和关爱的一方会觉得伴侣“冷漠疏离”，而伴侣则可能觉得他们“黏人且依赖性强”。

Do you see the underlying pattern? Whatever is happening with me, regardless of which side of the equation I’m on, becomes about you. If I want something different than you do, it’s somehow your fault. When our needs aren’t met, we play the blame game.

你看出其中的规律了吗？无论我身处何种境地，最终都会归咎于你。如果我想要的东西和你想要的不一样，那似乎都是你的错。当我们的需求得不到满足时，我们就会互相指责。

Step back and consider the logic here. If I want you to change your behavior, how useful is it for me to tell you what’s wrong with you? What a backward strategy for inspiring change! I was astounded the first time I heard Marshall Rosenberg name this blatantly obvious pattern. When approached with blame and criticism people usually defend themselves, which makes it harder to communicate. A more extreme example is yelling to feel heard. How does that usually work out? When we’re on automatic, we end up employing strategies that have little chance of working or that backfire.

退一步想想这其中的逻辑。如果我想让你改变行为，指出你的错误对你有什么帮助呢？这简直是本末倒置，根本不是激励改变的方法！我第一次听到马歇尔·卢森堡指出这种显而易见的模式时，感到非常震惊。当人们被指责和批评时，通常会为自己辩护，这反而使沟通更加困难。一个更极端的例子是，为了获得关注而大声喊叫。但这样做通常效果如何呢？当我们处于自动反应状态时，最终会采用一些几乎不可能奏效甚至适得其反的策略。

The pattern also gets inverted. We inflict that critical eye inward and blame ourselves. “It’s my fault. I’m always…I’ll never…” It’s still the same game, just turned in the other direction: unmet needs equals someone’s fault.

这种模式也会反转。我们会用批判的眼光审视自己，责怪自己。“都是我的错。我总是……我永远也……”本质上还是同样的套路，只是方向相反：需求未得到满足就等于别人的错。

The Deeper Roots of Our Training

我们培训的更深层次根源

To understand how we approach conflict, we have to look deeper than intentions of blame or defensiveness. The roots of the blame game are in how we’ve learned to perceive difference.

要理解我们如何处理冲突，就必须深入探究，而不能仅仅关注指责或辩解的意图。互相指责的根源在于我们如何看待差异。

Long before we learn about gravity in school, we know that if we let go of something at a height it will fall to the ground. This understanding is ingrained in our bodies through lived experience. In the same way, we learn much more than our mother tongue from our parents and society. As NVC trainer Miki Kashtan explains in her book, Spinning Threads of Radical Aliveness, we also learn a worldview.

早在学校学习重力之前，我们就知道如果从高处松手，物体就会落到地上。这种理解通过生活经验深深地烙印在我们的身体里。同样，我们从父母和社会中学到的远不止母语。正如非暴力沟通（NVC）培训师米基·卡什坦（Miki Kashtan）在她的著作《编织激进生命的丝线》（Spinning Threads of Radical Aliveness）中所阐述的那样，我们也在学习一种世界观。

Through repeated experience we form basic stories about who we are, how the world works, and what’s possible in life. Depending on where and when we grew up, our class and social location, we learn certain things about what it means to have a male or female body; to have light-or dark-colored skin; to be part of a certain community, religion, or group; and so on. Perceptions of difference become as ingrained as the feeling of gravity, in spite of the fact that they’re socially constructed.

通过反复的经历，我们逐渐形成关于自身、世界运行规律以及人生可能性的基本认知。根据我们成长的地点和时间、阶级和社会地位，我们会学习到关于男性或女性身体、肤色深浅、所属社群、宗教或群体等方面的特定概念。尽管差异是社会建构的产物，但这些认知却像重力一样根深蒂固。

Beneath all these layers lie ideas about human relationship that have been passed on by our family, culture, and society. We all learn a basic story that forms the underlying template for how we view difference and conflict. For most of us, it goes something like this: we are separate and there’s not enough, so people tend to be selfish to meet their needs. When we examine this orientation to human relationship and its results on our personal lives and social institutions, the implications are staggering. Scarcity and separation are essentially a recipe for war. 1

在所有这些层面之下，隐藏着我们从家庭、文化和社会中传承下来的关于人际关系的观念。我们都学习过一个基本的故事，它构成了我们看待差异和冲突的根本模板。对我们大多数人来说，这个故事大致是这样的：我们彼此分离，资源匮乏，所以人们倾向于自私地满足自身需求。当我们审视这种人际关系取向及其对个人生活和社会制度的影响时，其后果令人震惊。匮乏和分离本质上就是战争的根源。

This is part of our unconscious communication training. It’s unconscious because we didn’t choose it. We absorbed it from the environment around us. We studied it very closely growing up—learning as much as possible about how our family system works, then how school works, and eventually how society functions. What are the rules? How do I take care of myself? How do I survive and find safety for my person, family, and community?

这是我们无意识沟通训练的一部分。之所以说是无意识的，是因为我们并非有意选择它。我们从周围环境中吸收了它。成长过程中，我们对此进行了深入研究——尽可能多地了解家庭系统的运作方式，然后是学校的运作方式，最终是社会的运作方式。规则是什么？我该如何照顾自己？我该如何生存，如何为自身、家庭和社区找到安全保障？

It’s also unconscious because it generally wasn’t intentionally chosen by those from whom we learned it. Just as no one chooses their mother tongue, no one chooses their conditioned worldviews. In most cases, our parents simply passed along their way of understanding the world—based on the society in which they lived and their social location—without questioning it.

这种观念也是无意识的，因为它通常并非我们学习它的人的有意选择。正如没有人会选择自己的母语一样，也没有人会选择自己后天习得的世界观。在大多数情况下，我们的父母只是将他们理解世界的方式——基于他们所处的社会环境和自身社会地位——传承下来，而没有对此进行质疑。
