We learn these lessons early in life. When our needs as children didn’t align with the expectations of adults around us, what was the outcome? Usually someone got what they wanted, and someone didn’t. Every time this happened, regardless of the outcome, we implicitly learned three things: (1) difference usually means someone wins and someone loses, (2) those with more power get their needs met more often, and (3) conflict is inherently dangerous because we can lose that which is important to us.

我们很小的时候就学会了这些道理。小时候，当我们的需求与周围成年人的期望不一致时，结果会怎样呢？通常情况下，有人如愿以偿，有人则落空。每次发生这种情况，无论结果如何，我们都潜移默化地学到了三件事：（1）差异通常意味着有人赢有人输；（2）权力越大，需求越容易得到满足；（3）冲突本质上是危险的，因为我们可能会失去对我们重要的东西。

We see this play out every day in our public and private lives. Adults regularly use force with children when safety is not at stake, using their power to get children to behave in ways that are socially acceptable or convenient. “Couches aren’t for jumping.” “We have to leave now.” This is how we internalize our default patterns. Instead of teaching children how to consider their own needs in relation to the needs of those around them (which is possible at ages much, much younger than we think, even with toddlers), we force children to do what we want because it seems more efficient, or because we lack the energy or skill to do it differently. As best we know how, we train our children to function in a society that is not centered around meeting human needs, often passing along the very mechanisms that create and perpetuate separation and competition.

我们每天都能在公共和私人生活中看到这种情况。即使安全并未受到威胁，成年人也经常对孩子使用武力，利用权力迫使孩子按照社会认可或方便的方式行事。“沙发不是用来跳的。”“我们现在必须走了。” 这就是我们内化默认行为模式的方式。我们没有教导孩子如何将自身需求与周围人的需求联系起来（这在远比我们想象的要小得多的年纪，甚至幼儿时期就已具备），而是强迫孩子做我们想让他们做的事，因为这样做似乎更有效率，或者因为我们缺乏精力或能力去采取不同的方式。我们尽其所能地训练孩子在一个并非以满足人类需求为中心的社会中生存，常常将制造和延续分离与竞争的机制传递给他们。

Intertwined with these lessons come ideas of right and wrong, good and bad, should and shouldn’t. When there is a disagreement or difference, someone is right and someone is wrong. To protect the well-being of others, we’re taught to rely on external concepts of morality and obligation rather than being guided to recognize our innate ethical sensitivity or to rely on dialogue. As we grow up, these messages are continually reinforced through experience as well as through the media and entertainment industries. 2

这些教训中交织着对错、好坏、应该与不应该等观念。当出现分歧或差异时，总会有人是对的，有人是错的。为了维护他人的福祉，我们被教导要依赖外在的道德和义务概念，而不是被引导去认识我们内在的伦理敏感性或依靠对话。随着我们长大，这些信息会通过经验以及媒体和娱乐产业不断得到强化。

View Determines Intention

观点决定意图

How we view things determines how we relate to them, which shapes our intention. If we view conflict as a dangerous affair, one of scarcity (of time, energy, resources, goodwill, or creativity) in which our only options are to win or lose, we play the blame game; we try to win by going on the offensive, or we try to protect ourselves. When we view things in terms of right and wrong, we are further compelled to judge or defend. If we see other human beings merely as objects in relation to our needs, aiding or blocking us from achieving our goals, we attempt to coerce, manipulate, or control the situation to get our way.

我们如何看待事物决定了我们如何与它们相处，进而塑造了我们的意图。如果我们把冲突视为危险之事，视为一种稀缺（时间、精力、资源、善意或创造力）之事，认为我们唯一的选择只有输赢，那么我们就会互相指责；我们会试图通过进攻来赢得胜利，或者试图保护自己。当我们用对错的眼光看待事物时，我们更会不由自主地去评判或辩护。如果我们仅仅把他人视为满足自身需求的工具，认为他们能够帮助我们或阻碍我们实现目标，那么我们就会试图胁迫、操纵或控制局面以达到自己的目的。

Based on our life experiences we form certain views. Those views engender certain intentions, which tend to reproduce the same experiences. Over time, our experiences and worldviews cocreate and reinforce each other.

基于我们的人生经历，我们会形成某些观点。这些观点会引发某些意图，而这些意图往往会重复相同的经历。随着时间的推移，我们的经历和世界观相互影响、彼此强化。

Principle: Our intentions, views, and experiences reinforce each other: views determine intentions, intentions shape experiences, and experiences confirm our views. Shifting our view therefore can change our intentions and our experience.

原则：我们的意图、观点和经验相互强化：观点决定意图，意图塑造经验，经验印证我们的观点。因此，改变我们的观点可以改变我们的意图和经验。

The table below outlines some of the fundamental, conditioned views we pick up in life and their most likely results.

下表概述了我们在生活中形成的一些基本观念和它们最可能导致的结果。

VIEWS →

浏览量 →

Lead to → INTENTIONS

导致 → 意图

Create → EXPERIENCES

创造 → 体验

Fear, Anxiety

恐惧、焦虑

Win/Lose

胜/负

Attack/Demand

攻击/需求

Anger, Aggression

愤怒，攻击性

Right/Wrong

对/错

Protect/Defend

保护/防御

Shutting down, Freezing

关机，冻结

Protect/Defend

保护/防御

Shutting down, Freezing

关机，冻结

Conflict is dangerous, a problem, something wrong

冲突是危险的，是个问题，是件错事。

Blame/Judge

责备/评判

Judgment, Rejection

评判，拒绝

Others seen as objects in relation to our needs

另一些人则被视为与我们需求相关的客体。

Coerce/Manipulate/Control

胁迫/操纵/控制

Disconnection

断开

Alienation

异化

Four Habitual Ways of Responding to Conflict

应对冲突的四种常见方式

Because of this conditioning, very few people feel at ease in the face of conflict. The word conflict literally means to “strike together.” Its earliest form referred to armed battle! 3 Our internal experience mirrors the meaning. When we believe one person’s needs will be met at the expense of the other’s, conflict is inherently threatening. We each tend to respond to this “striking together” of needs in one of several different ways:

由于这种思维模式，很少有人能在冲突面前感到自在。“冲突”一词的字面意思是“共同攻击”。它最早的形式指的是武装战斗！我们的内在体验也反映了这一含义。当我们认为满足一方的需求会以牺牲另一方的需求为代价时，冲突就具有内在的威胁性。我们每个人面对这种需求的“共同攻击”往往会以以下几种不同的方式做出反应：

1. Conflict Avoidance

1. 避免冲突

2. Competitive Confrontation

2. 竞争对抗

3. Passivity

3.被动性

4. Passive Aggression

4. 被动攻击

Each of these default strategies has its own logic, strengths, and dangers. Remember, these are learned, internalized behaviors; they’re not our fault. They’re deeply rooted patterns based on the painful socialization process and repeated life experiences. We use them because they’ve worked to some extent. The first step to shifting these patterns is to see how they operate in our lives. When we’re more aware of them, we can begin to investigate and transform the underlying beliefs and emotions that hold them in place and start to make different choices.

每一种默认策略都有其自身的逻辑、优势和风险。请记住，这些都是后天习得的、内化的行为模式；这并非我们的错。它们是根深蒂固的模式，源于痛苦的社会化过程和反复的生活经历。我们之所以使用这些模式，是因为它们在某种程度上行之有效。改变这些模式的第一步是了解它们如何在我们的生活中运作。当我们更加意识到它们的存在时，我们就可以开始探究并转变那些维系这些模式的潜在信念和情绪，并开始做出不同的选择。

Principle: Being aware of our habitual conflict styles allows us to transform the underlying beliefs and emotions that hold them in place and to make different choices.

原则：意识到我们习惯性的冲突方式，可以让我们转变维持这些方式的潜在信念和情绪，并做出不同的选择。

PRACTICE : Exploring Conflict Styles

实践：探索冲突风格

As you read the following sections, consider which conflict style(s) you tend toward. What’s your go-to strategy? Do you have different patterns with different people? What’s the common orientation in your family? In your culture? Which strategies do those around you employ most often?

在阅读以下章节时，请思考你倾向于哪种冲突处理方式。你最常用的策略是什么？你与不同的人相处时是否会有不同的模式？你的家庭和文化中普遍的冲突处理方式是什么？你周围的人最常使用哪些策略？

Conflict Avoidance

避免冲突

The default stance of conflict avoidance can be summed up in two words: anything but. This approach aims to circumvent or avoid addressing a conflict, sometimes at very high costs. We might change the subject, focus on positive things, ignore a problem, or flat out pretend it’s not happening.

默认的冲突回避策略可以用两个字概括：避而不谈。这种方法旨在绕过或避免处理冲突，有时代价非常高昂。我们可能会转移话题、关注积极的事情、忽视问题，或者干脆假装问题不存在。

Conflict avoidance is at play when we decide to live with things the way they are to avoid the stress of a difficult conversation. It’s the strategy of a family member who refuses to discuss another’s addiction. It’s operating when a colleague sidesteps our request by changing the subject or won’t tell us that they disagree with our choices on a project.

当我们为了避免艰难对话带来的压力而选择维持现状时，冲突回避策略就发挥作用了。例如，家庭成员拒绝讨论他人的成瘾问题，就是这种策略。当同事回避我们的请求，转移话题，或者不愿直言不讳地表达他们对我们在项目上的选择的不同意见时，冲突回避策略也同样适用。

The aim and hope of conflict avoidance is usually to keep the peace. One or more of the following unexamined beliefs often lie beneath avoiding conflict:

避免冲突的目的和希望通常是为了维护和平。避免冲突背后往往隐藏着以下一种或多种未经审视的信念：

• Conflict is dangerous.

冲突是危险的。

• Others will be offended if I bring up this conflict or discuss our differences.

• 如果我提起这场冲突或讨论我们之间的分歧，其他人会感到被冒犯。

• More harm will be caused by my trying to address this than letting it be.

• 如果我试图处理这件事，造成的危害会比放任不管更大。

• If I don’t deal with it, it will go away or resolve itself.

• 如果我不去处理，它就会消失或者自行解决。

Underneath this strategy are often needs for connection, safety, or belonging. Avoiding (or postponing) conflict can maintain harmony and temporarily preserve relationships. This strategy often comes with an ability to sense the needs of others but a failure to honor our own needs. It’s usually supported by noticing and celebrating what’s going well and a certain flexibility in adapting to difficult situations or sidestepping them, sometimes minimizing contact with the person with whom we have the conflict.

这种策略背后往往隐藏着对联结、安全感或归属感的需求。回避（或推迟）冲突可以维持和谐，暂时维系关系。这种策略通常伴随着感知他人需求的能力，却忽略了自身的需求。它通常伴随着对进展顺利之事的关注和庆祝，以及在应对困境或规避困境时展现出的灵活性，有时甚至会尽量减少与冲突对象的接触。

When employed unconsciously, this strategy can be dangerous. Chronically avoiding confrontation breeds resentment and can destroy relationships from the inside out. It can lead to feelings of mistrust, confusion, and even self-doubt, where we sense something is awry but it’s not being named. Over time, forcing ourselves to ignore and suppress our feelings and needs can engender a kind of emotional deadness.

无意识地运用这种策略可能很危险。长期回避冲突会滋生怨恨，并从内部瓦解人际关系。它会导致不信任、困惑，甚至自我怀疑，让我们感觉哪里不对劲，却又说不清道不明。久而久之，强迫自己忽视和压抑感受与需求，会造成一种情感麻木。

In situations that are emotionally or physically abusive, conflict avoidance can be self-protective or can enable continued harm, depending on the circumstances. In these situations, the fear and uncertainty of change can prevent us from addressing the abuse. Instead, we choose the security of what’s familiar. When what’s familiar is abuse, the consequences can be tragic. 4

在遭受情感或身体虐待的情况下，回避冲突可能是一种自我保护，但也可能助长伤害的持续，这取决于具体情况。在这种情况下，对改变的恐惧和不确定性会阻止我们直面虐待。相反，我们会选择熟悉的舒适区。然而，当熟悉的舒适区本身就是虐待时，后果可能是悲剧性的。

Competitive Confrontation

竞争对抗

Another common response to conflict is competitive confrontation. Here, we are forceful and push for what we want, sometimes driving so hard that we’re unable to see the other person’s point of view. This approach is often characterized by a quality of aggression and an exclusive focus on our own needs. We might raise our voice, blame, judge, demand we get our way, coerce, or even threaten others.

另一种常见的冲突应对方式是竞争性对抗。在这种方式中，我们强势行事，力求得到自己想要的东西，有时甚至咄咄逼人，以至于无法理解对方的观点。这种方式通常带有攻击性，并且只关注自身的需求。我们可能会提高音量、指责、评判、强求、胁迫甚至威胁他人。

This strategy is plastered all over the Internet, entertainment, and social media. It’s presented as the strong, dominant, male energy. This approach drove my conversations with Aaron on that winter camping trip. It’s at play when one family member directly coerces another to attend an event. It’s there when a coworker demands we do things their way or responds to our request by pointing out our shortcomings. Politicians use this strategy regularly, denouncing their opponents with personal attacks rather than considered analysis of the issues. It also occurs when conflict avoidance reaches a limit and we flip to other side.

这种策略充斥着互联网、娱乐和社交媒体。它被包装成一种强势、支配性的男性力量。在那个冬季露营之旅中，我和亚伦的对话也深受这种策略的影响。当一个家庭成员直接强迫另一个家庭成员参加某个活动时，这种策略就体现出来了。当同事要求我们按照他们的方式做事，或者对我们的请求做出回应时，这种策略也同样存在。政客们经常使用这种策略，他们用人身攻击来抨击对手，而不是对问题进行深思熟虑的分析。当回避冲突的策略达到极限，我们转而站在对手一边时，这种策略也同样适用。

The goal of this approach is to ensure our needs are met at any cost; the method is control or domination. Underlying beliefs leading to a confrontational approach can include:

这种方法的目的是不惜一切代价满足我们的需求；其手段是控制或支配。导致对抗性做法的潜在信念可能包括：

• I’m on my own; it’s “every man for himself.”

• 我孤身一人；一切都“各人自扫门前雪”。

• If I don’t stand up and fight, I’ll lose my power or be destroyed.

• 如果我不站起来反抗，我就会失去力量或者被毁灭。

• Vulnerability is weakness; any empathy I show will be used against me.

• 脆弱就是弱点；我表现出的任何同情心都会被用来对付我。

• I’m right; they’re wrong.

• 我是对的，他们是错的。

The strengths inherent in the competitive approach are assertiveness, directness, and often a clarity about certain aspects of our experience. While we can appear strong and courageous when working this approach, we often feel great fear and protectiveness beneath the surface. Unconscious use of this strategy frequently means being out of touch with more vulnerable feelings and relational needs. Confrontation is usually connected with needs for autonomy, agency, safety, and knowing that we matter.

竞争型策略的优势在于自信、直接，以及对自身某些经历的清晰认知。虽然运用这种策略时我们可能显得坚强勇敢，但内心深处往往充满恐惧和自我保护的本能。无意识地使用这种策略常常意味着我们与自身更脆弱的情感和人际关系需求脱节。对抗通常与自主、能动、安全感以及被认可的需求密切相关。

This kind of confrontation is distinct from a direct, openhearted engagement with conflict that includes care for both people’s needs. Instead, it’s limited by its rigidity and can be dangerous in its disconnection from empathy. The costs of this approach are high. We may get what we want but compromise others’ trust or lose relationships entirely. People may avoid us or refrain from being honest for fear of an argument. The lack of collaboration can result in a loss of creativity; the absence of honest feedback can develop into loss of intimacy. Competition also comes at a cost to our own well-being, leading to feelings of isolation, alienation, and ignorance of our own needs for connection and compassion.

这种对抗方式与坦诚相待、兼顾双方需求的直接冲突处理方式截然不同。相反，它僵化刻板，缺乏同理心，因此可能造成危险。这种方式代价高昂。我们或许能如愿以偿，但却会损害他人的信任，甚至彻底失去关系。人们可能会因为害怕争吵而疏远我们，或者不敢坦诚相待。缺乏合作会导致创造力的丧失；缺乏真诚的反馈会导致亲密关系的疏离。竞争也会损害我们自身的幸福感，导致孤独、疏离，以及对自身联结和关怀需求的忽视。

Passivity

被动性

Passivity is the opposite of confrontation. Here, we give up what we want and acquiesce to whatever requests, needs, or demands are presented by those around us. Some people do this so automatically that they offer to give up their needs preemptively, at the slightest suggestion that someone else may have a different preference.

被动与对抗截然相反。在这种状态下，我们放弃自己的意愿，顺从周围人提出的任何要求、需求或诉求。有些人甚至对此习以为常，只要有人稍稍暗示他们可能有不同的偏好，他们就会主动放弃自己的需求。

When using this approach, others may perceive us as easygoing, accommodating, and conciliatory or as a pushover. We might say things such as “It doesn’t matter…whatever you want.” Passivity can be coupled with a tendency to blame ourselves to avoid conflict: “You’re right…I’m sorry, it’s my fault. I should have…” A roommate using this strategy accepts others’ preferences in their house. In a romantic relationship, a passive response shows up as one person regularly deferring to the other’s wishes. The coworker being passive will say yes even when they disagree.

使用这种方法时，别人可能会觉得我们随和、包容、善于调解，或者觉得我们软弱可欺。我们可能会说“没关系……随你便”。被动往往伴随着一种自责的倾向，以此来避免冲突：“你说得对……对不起，是我的错。我应该……” 室友如果采用这种策略，就会接受别人在家里的喜好。在恋爱关系中，被动的回应表现为一方经常顺从另一方的意愿。即使不同意，被动的同事也会说“是”。

Passivity is different from conflict avoidance, as the aim is to defuse any potential conflict by abandoning our own needs or preferences. Some of the core beliefs that may be present with passive behavior are:

被动与回避冲突不同，被动的目的是通过放弃自身的需求或偏好来化解任何潜在的冲突。被动行为可能包含的一些核心信念包括：

• If I go along with this, everything will be okay.

• 如果我同意这样做，一切都会好起来的。

• My needs don’t matter. I don’t deserve to be happy.

• 我的需求无关紧要。我不配拥有幸福。

• If I give others what they want, they’ll like me.

• 如果我给别人他们想要的东西，他们就会喜欢我。

• I’ve done something wrong.

• 我做错了事。

Being passive is often an attempt to meet needs for belonging, harmony, safety, and connection. Its close cousin, appeasing, impels us to shape ourselves to please others. Those who default to appeasing are often highly attuned to the needs of others and skilled at adapting to difficult situations. Both passivity and appeasing require great internal strength (it takes a lot of energy to suppress one’s needs), yet those employing these strategies often feel weak inside.

被动往往是为了满足归属感、和谐感、安全感和联结感的需求。与之密切相关的“讨好型人格”则驱使我们塑造自身以取悦他人。那些习惯于讨好他人的人通常对别人的需求非常敏感，并且善于适应困境。被动和讨好都需要强大的内在力量（压抑自身需求需要耗费大量精力），然而，采用这些策略的人往往内心感到脆弱。

The limits of passivity are that we have fewer options for meeting our needs, beyond the spontaneous goodwill of others. Over time, repeatedly giving in to others can breed resentment. It can lead us to become so disconnected from our own feelings, needs, and desires that we forget how to discern what’s authentic.

被动的局限性在于，除了他人的善意之外，我们满足自身需求的选择余地会减少。久而久之，一味地迁就他人会滋生怨恨。它会导致我们与自身的感受、需求和渴望脱节，以至于忘记如何分辨真假。

The passive approach to conflict, though it aims to enhance a relationship by smoothing things out, can diminish connection and beget dullness over time. Intimacy depends on being able to know one another. When we refuse to share our true feelings and desires for fear of conflict or rejection, we deny those around us the opportunity to get to know us more deeply.

被动地处理冲突，虽然旨在通过缓和矛盾来增进关系，但随着时间的推移，却会削弱彼此的联系，最终导致关系的冷淡。亲密关系建立在彼此了解的基础上。当我们因为害怕冲突或被拒绝而拒绝分享自己的真实感受和愿望时，我们就剥夺了身边人深入了解我们的机会。

Passive Aggression

被动攻击

This strategy is an indirect form of confrontation, masquerading as passivity. When employing this approach, we express our displeasure about a situation in a roundabout way, often with some degree of veiled hostility while verbally maintaining that all is well. It can look like conflict avoidance, but we are actually taking actions to express our anger or dissatisfaction.

这种策略是一种间接的对抗形式，伪装成被动。采用这种方式时，我们会拐弯抹角地表达对某种情况的不满，往往带有某种隐晦的敌意，同时口头上却说一切安好。这看起来像是在回避冲突，但实际上我们是在采取行动来表达愤怒或不满。

When we’re being passive aggressive, we might clean everything in the kitchen except our roommate’s dishes, in effect saying, “Clean up after yourself!” In a romantic relationship, a partner being passive aggressive may agree to do something and then silently sulk or seethe to show their displeasure. We might agree to do a chore and either “forget” to follow through or do it so poorly that the other person is unlikely to ask again. In a professional situation, we might procrastinate, deliberately avoid certain aspects of our job, or do them in such a way that it creates problems and more work for someone else.

当我们采取被动攻击的方式时，我们可能会把厨房里除了室友的碗碟以外的所有东西都收拾干净，实际上是在说：“你自己收拾！”在恋爱关系中，采取被动攻击方式的一方可能会答应做某事，然后默默生闷气或怒气冲冲地表达不满。我们可能会答应做家务，然后“忘记”去做，或者做得一塌糊涂，让对方以后不太可能再让我们做。在工作中，我们可能会拖延，故意逃避工作的某些方面，或者以某种方式处理这些工作，从而给别人制造麻烦，增加工作量。

The aim of passive aggression is usually to find some way to meet our needs when we don’t believe that engaging directly will help. Beliefs beneath this behavior include:

被动攻击的目的通常是在我们认为直接沟通无济于事时，找到某种方式来满足自身需求。这种行为背后的信念包括：

• I don’t have a choice.

• 我别无选择。

• My needs don’t matter.

• 我的需求无关紧要。

• There’s no space for me.

• 没有我的位置。

• No one else cares about what I want.

• 没有人关心我的想法。

• Speaking up won’t make a difference; it could make things worse.

• 发声并不会改变什么；反而可能会让事情变得更糟。

The strengths of passive aggressive behavior can be a sharp and intuitive understanding of relationship dynamics, an ability to stay connected to our own feelings and needs in situations that may not support our autonomy, and a certain creativity in finding alternate ways of self-expression.

被动攻击行为的优势在于：对人际关系动态有敏锐而直觉的理解，能够在不利于我们自主的情况下保持与自身感受和需求的联系，以及在寻找替代自我表达方式方面具有一定的创造力。

Beneath this pattern is often a feeling of helplessness. Faced with the choice of abandoning our needs entirely or expressing them indirectly, we choose the latter, often with thinly disguised contempt rooted in our sense of disempowerment. Some of the needs that may be at the root of this behavior are having autonomy and choice, being seen or knowing that we matter.

这种模式背后往往隐藏着一种无助感。面对彻底放弃自身需求或间接表达需求的选择，我们往往选择后者，这种选择常常伴随着隐晦的轻蔑，而这种轻蔑源于我们内心的无力感。这种行为的根源可能在于拥有自主权和选择权，渴望被关注或感受到自身的重要性。

The short-term gains of this approach also come at a cost. Passive aggression can erode trust in relationships, create enemies, and eat away at our sense of well-being. Ironically, the more we use passive aggressive behavior instead of engaging directly, the less empowered we feel to advocate for ourselves.

这种方法虽然能带来短期收益，但也会带来代价。被动攻击会侵蚀人际关系中的信任，树立敌人，并蚕食我们的幸福感。讽刺的是，我们越是使用被动攻击而非直接沟通，就越会感到无力维护自身权益。

Loosening the Grip of Habit

摆脱习惯的束缚

When we are stuck in habitual, conditioned views of conflict, our attention becomes narrowly focused on a way of seeing that is rooted in negative experiences from our past. Our whole nervous system enters a familiar pattern, based on our ingrained views and corresponding intentions. We feel anxious, aggressive, or frozen. We may go on the offensive, backpedal, or zone out and pretend nothing is happening. We easily lose touch with our deeper values, the importance of a relationship, or our capacity to see things from multiple perspectives. The humanity of the other person can become obscured by our thoughts, beliefs, or emotions.

当我们陷入习惯性的、条件反射式的冲突观时，我们的注意力就会狭隘地集中在一种源于过往负面经历的视角上。我们的整个神经系统会进入一种基于根深蒂固的观点和相应意图的熟悉模式。我们会感到焦虑、愤怒或麻木。我们可能会采取进攻姿态，也可能退缩退让，或者神游物外，假装什么都没发生。我们很容易与自己更深层的价值观、人际关系的重要性以及从多个角度看待问题的能力失去联系。我们的想法、信念或情绪可能会蒙蔽我们对他人人性的感知。

We each know the frustration of feeling locked into these habitual modes. (If you weren’t at least a little tired of the blame game, you probably wouldn’t be reading this book.) Yet we rely on our habitual strategies because they serve us. If they didn’t work to some extent, we wouldn’t use them. To shed these patterns, we need alternatives. Before we’ll give them up, we need to develop other approaches that work at least as well.

我们每个人都体会过被困在这些习惯模式中的挫败感。（如果你对互相指责的游戏没有丝毫厌倦，你可能就不会读这本书了。）然而，我们依赖这些习惯性策略，因为它们对我们有益。如果它们没有一定效果，我们就不会使用它们。为了摆脱这些模式，我们需要其他选择。在我们放弃它们之前，我们需要发展出至少同样有效的其他方法。

Mindfulness can loosen the grip of our habits and create the possibility of choosing a different course. As soon as we become aware of what’s happening, we can reorient the map (our views), call forth different intentions, and guide our energy in a different direction.

正念可以松开我们习以为常的束缚，让我们有机会选择不同的道路。一旦我们意识到正在发生的事情，我们就可以重新调整方向（我们的视角），唤起不同的意图，并将我们的能量引导到不同的方向。

Handling these habits—in ourselves and in others—takes care, skill, and persistence. In the next chapter, we’ll explore how to step out of the blame game with another approach to conflict: collaboration. When we can engage in true dialogue, balancing our own needs with openness and care for another’s needs, we move beyond the framework of either/or, of separation and scarcity, and new possibilities emerge.

处理这些习惯——无论是我们自身还是他人的——都需要细致、技巧和坚持。在下一章中，我们将探讨如何摆脱互相指责的局面，转而采用另一种冲突处理方式：合作。当我们能够进行真正的对话，在满足自身需求的同时，也以开放和关怀的态度对待他人的需求时，我们就能超越非此即彼、分离和匮乏的思维框架，新的可能性便会涌现。

PRINCIPLES

原则

Our intentions, views, and experiences reinforce each other: views determine intentions, intentions shape experiences, and experiences confirm our views. Shifting our view therefore can change our intentions and our experience.

我们的意图、观点和经历相互强化：观点决定意图，意图塑造经历，经历印证我们的观点。因此，改变我们的观点可以改变我们的意图和经历。

Being aware of our habitual conflict styles allows us to transform the underlying beliefs and emotions that hold them in place and to make different choices.

意识到我们习惯性的冲突处理方式，可以帮助我们转变维持这些方式的潜在信念和情绪，并做出不同的选择。

KEY POINTS

要点

Habitual views of conflict lead to default intentions of blame and self-protection, which constellate in four habitual patterns:

习惯性的冲突观会导致默认的指责和自我保护的意图，这些意图体现在以下四种习惯性模式中：

1. Conflict Avoidance: attempting to avoid addressing conflict

1. 回避冲突：试图避免解决冲突

2. Competitive Confrontation: engaging directly with aggression or force

2. 对抗性冲突：直接诉诸侵略或武力。

3. Passivity: yielding to conflict by acquiescing, giving up our own needs, or appeasing

3. 被动：通过默许、放弃自身需求或安抚来向冲突屈服

4. Passive Aggression: engaging indirectly by expressing displeasure or hostility while pretending that all is well

4. 被动攻击：通过表达不满或敌意来间接进行攻击，同时假装一切安好。

QUESTION & ANSWER

问答

Q: How can I stop being so defensive? I like the idea of being more curious and open-minded, but in practice I find it really hard to do.

问：我怎样才能克服这种防御心理？我喜欢变得更好奇、更开放包容的想法，但实际上我发现这很难做到。

The most important step, which it sounds like you’re already taking, is to become aware of what’s happening—to notice the default patterns. Try to view these habits with a kindly eye. Remember, they’ve protected and helped us for years. If you’re out at sea and the only thing you have to stay afloat is a log, you’re not going to let go until something better comes along. The concepts and practices in this book are like a stabler, nimbler raft.

最重要的一步，听起来你已经在做了，就是意识到正在发生的事情——注意到那些默认的模式。试着用友善的眼光看待这些习惯。记住，它们多年来一直在保护和帮助我们。如果你身处茫茫大海，唯一能让你保持漂浮的东西是一根木头，你肯定不会轻易放手，直到找到更好的东西。这本书中的理念和实践就像一艘更稳定、更灵活的木筏。

Once you see the pattern, investigate its benefits and its limits. Seeing this clearly will increase your motivation to try the new tools. The trick is to start small. In strength training, you start with five or ten pounds, not one hundred. The more you have small successes, the more your nervous system will trust and remember there’s a new way of doing this.

一旦你发现了其中的规律，就要探究它的好处和局限性。清楚地认识到这一点会增强你尝试新方法的动力。诀窍在于从小处着手。力量训练时，你应该从五磅或十磅开始，而不是一百磅。你取得的小成功越多，你的神经系统就越会信任并记住这种新的训练方法。

Q: My pattern isn’t to blame or attack others, it’s to blame myself. How can I work with this?

问：我的习惯不是责怪或攻击他人，而是责怪自己。我该如何克服这个问题？

We can be so, so hard on ourselves! I certainly got a good dose of that conditioning.

我们对自己真的太苛刻了！我肯定深受其害。

There are two basic ways of working with this painful habit. The first is to build up internal resources to counter the harshness of self-criticism. Cultivate positive practices such as gratitude and self-empathy ( chapter 9 ), as well as other methods such as self-compassion and loving-kindness meditation. These practices strengthen resilience. It’s like stepping out of a burning house to breathe fresh air.

应对这种痛苦习惯有两种基本方法。第一种是建立内在资源来对抗自我批评的苛刻。培养积极的习惯，例如感恩和自我同理心（第九章），以及其他方法，例如自我关怀和慈心禅修。这些练习可以增强韧性。这就像从燃烧的房子里走出来呼吸新鲜空气一样。

The second aspect involves putting out the fire, which means transforming the pattern itself. Learn to develop a relationship of empathy, clarity, and firmness with that critical voice. Translate self-judgments to hear the messages behind them ( chapter 10 ). What feelings and needs are that voice expressing? We can use mindfulness to investigate the beliefs upon which the pattern may be resting. Often such habits have roots in early childhood, so it can be helpful to get support from another person to disentangle and heal some of those places. It’s equally important to find ways to simply say no to the critical voice. When the blame is strong, compassion might mean cutting off the pattern. Interrupt it and redirect your attention in whatever ways you can to break the cycle.

第二个方面是扑灭火焰，也就是改变模式本身。学会与那个批判的声音建立一种同理心、清晰的认知和坚定的态度。解读自我评判，聆听其背后的信息（第十章）。那个声音表达了哪些感受和需求？我们可以运用正念来探究支撑这种模式的信念。通常，这类习惯根植于童年早期，因此寻求他人的支持来解开和疗愈这些创伤会很有帮助。同样重要的是，要找到方法对批判的声音说“不”。当责备感强烈时，慈悲可能意味着切断这种模式。打断它，并尽你所能地转移注意力，打破恶性循环。

# ↩

5

where are you coming from?

你来自哪里？

I developed NVC as a way to train my attention—to shine the light of consciousness—on places that have the potential to yield what I am seeking. What I want in my life is compassion, a flow between myself and others based on a mutual giving of the heart.

— DR . MARSHALL B . ROSENBERG

我发展出非暴力沟通（NVC）的方法，是为了训练我的注意力——将意识之光照射到那些可能带来我所寻求之物的领域。我生命中渴望的是慈悲，是建立在我与他人之间基于彼此真诚付出的和谐关系之上。——马歇尔·B·罗森伯格博士

HAVE YOU EVER persevered through a challenging situation with a friend and come out the other side with more respect for one another? Or worked out a disagreement with a loved one, finding that you feel even closer, with more care and affection?

你是否曾经和朋友一起克服过困难，最终彼此更加尊重？或者和爱人化解过分歧，发现彼此更加亲近，更加关心彼此？

Intimacy is born in conflict. Difference can bring us together and help us know one another. Friction can be creative and synergistic, leading to new ideas and perspectives. These kinds of conversations are characterized by very different intentions than our unconscious communication behavior.

亲密关系诞生于冲突之中。差异可以让我们走到一起，帮助我们彼此了解。摩擦可以激发创造力，产生协同效应，带来新的想法和视角。这类对话的意图与我们无意识的沟通行为截然不同。

What if there were a way to identify and support the conditions that lead to this kind of experience? A way to shift out of our habitual responses to conflict to a more helpful approach? This is one of the central questions behind Marshall Rosenberg’s development of Nonviolent Communication. In the beginning of his seminal book, he writes:

如果有一种方法可以识别并支持那些导致此类体验的条件呢？如果有一种方法可以让我们摆脱应对冲突的惯性反应，转而采取更有效的方式呢？这正是马歇尔·卢森堡发展非暴力沟通理论的核心问题之一。在他那本开创性著作的开篇，他写道：

Believing that it is our nature to enjoy giving and receiving in a compassionate manner, I have been preoccupied most of my life with two questions. What happens to disconnect us from our compassionate nature, leading us to behave violently and exploitatively? And conversely, what allows some people to stay connected to their compassionate nature under even the most trying circumstances? 1

我相信，以慈悲之心给予和接受是我们的天性，因此我一生都在思考两个问题：是什么让我们与这种慈悲的天性脱节，导致我们做出暴力和剥削的行为？反过来，又是什么让一些人即使在最艰难的处境下也能保持慈悲之心？

Rosenberg grew up in Detroit in the 1940s. During that time, he witnessed the race riots in which dozens of people lost their lives. These events, and his experiences of anti-Semitism as a youngster, seeded in him a passion for understanding the roots of violence. He discovered that our thoughts and speech play a huge role in our ability to stay connected to compassion. His method of NVC comprises a systematic training of our attention—relearning how to think, speak, and listen in ways that are more conducive to peace and harmony.

罗森伯格在20世纪40年代的底特律长大。那时，他亲眼目睹了种族骚乱，数十人丧生。这些事件，以及他童年时期遭受的反犹主义经历，在他心中埋下了探究暴力根源的种子。他发现，我们的思想和言语在维系慈悲心方面起着至关重要的作用。他的非暴力沟通方法（NVC）包含一套系统的注意力训练——重新学习如何以更有利于和平与和谐的方式思考、说话和倾听。

Instead of getting caught in habitual narratives of blame and judgment, in NVC we learn to identify the specific observations we want to discuss, our feelings about those events, the deeper human needs from which those feelings arise, and our requests for how to move forward together. We learn to listen in the same way, sensing what’s beneath others’ words. The entire system rests upon one core theme: creating a quality of connection sufficient to meet needs. 2

非暴力沟通（NVC）让我们不再陷入习惯性的指责和评判，而是学会识别我们想要讨论的具体观察结果、我们对这些事件的感受、这些感受背后更深层次的人类需求，以及我们希望如何共同前进。我们学习以同样的方式倾听，感知他人言语背后的含义。整个体系的核心在于：建立足以满足需求的联结。

This isn’t about what we say but rather where we’re coming from. It’s about our intention.

这无关乎我们说了什么，而是关乎我们的出发点。这关乎我们的意图。

When Daryl Davis Met the KKK

当达里尔·戴维斯遇到三K党

Daryl Davis is an African American musician and author who spent the first years of his life abroad. It wasn’t until age ten, in 1968, that he discovered people could hate him for his skin color. While marching with his all-white Cub Scout troop in Massachusetts, people threw rocks and bottles at him. The incident sparked a lifelong curiosity about human attitudes. “How can you hate me when you don’t know me?” he wondered.

达里尔·戴维斯是一位非裔美国音乐家和作家，他的童年早期在国外度过。直到1968年，10岁的他才意识到人们会因为他的肤色而憎恨他。当时，他正和一群白人童子军在马萨诸塞州游行，有人向他扔石头和瓶子。这件事激发了他对人类态度的终生好奇。“你们根本不了解我，怎么会恨我呢？”他不禁疑惑。

Years later, after playing a gig in an all-white bar in Maryland, Davis was approached by a white man who said it was the first time he’d “heard a black man play as well as Jerry Lee Lewis.” Davis shared that Jerry Lee Lewis was a friend of his and that Lewis had learned to play from black musicians. The two continued their conversation and over time became friends. The man eventually shared the names of local KKK leaders, whom Davis contacted and interviewed for a book he was writing.

多年后，戴维斯在马里兰州一家全是白人的酒吧演出后，一位白人男子走过来对他说，这是他第一次听到“一个黑人演奏得像杰瑞·李·刘易斯一样好”。戴维斯告诉他，杰瑞·李·刘易斯是他的朋友，刘易斯的演奏技艺是从黑人音乐家那里学来的。两人继续交谈，并逐渐成为朋友。后来，这位男子透露了当地三K党领导人的姓名，戴维斯联系了他们并进行了采访，以便为他正在撰写的一本书做准备。

Davis asked them about their views on various subjects and listened. At first, the Klansmen never asked Davis for his thoughts, believing he was “inferior.” However, with patient, friendly conversation and through Davis’s continual effort to create a real connection, they gradually became interested in his side of things. It was as if Davis’s own warmth and respect slowly drew forth those very qualities in them.

戴维斯询问他们对各种问题的看法，并认真倾听。起初，三K党成员从未征求过戴维斯的意见，认为他“低人一等”。然而，通过耐心友好的交谈，以及戴维斯不断努力建立真诚的联系，他们逐渐开始对他的观点产生兴趣。仿佛戴维斯自身的温暖和尊重，慢慢地激发了他们身上同样的品质。

In the end, he formed friendships with many Klansmen whose beliefs shifted after getting to know Davis. Many left the Klan and even gave Davis their robes and hoods. Over the course of his work, Davis has convinced—through dialogue and friendship—more than two hundred members of the KKK to leave the organization. 3 Daryl Davis may have never taken an NVC class, but he understands the power of intention. When we create genuine human connection, radical transformation is possible.

最终，他与许多三K党成员建立了友谊，这些人在认识戴维斯后改变了信仰。许多人离开了三K党，甚至把他们的长袍和头罩送给了戴维斯。在他的工作中，戴维斯通过对话和友谊，说服了两百多名三K党成员退出该组织。达里尔·戴维斯或许从未上过非暴力沟通课程，但他深谙意念的力量。当我们建立起真诚的人际关系时，彻底的改变便有可能发生。

Enlightened Self-Interest

开明的利己主义

Intention is the single most powerful and transformative ingredient in dialogue. It shapes our verbal and nonverbal communication, directing the course of a conversation. If you take nothing else from this whole book, I hope you will take with you the importance the intention to understand, to come from curiosity and care, has in your interactions.

意图是对话中最强大、最具变革性的要素。它塑造着我们的语言和非语言沟通，引导着对话的走向。即便你从这本书中只能记住一点，我也希望你能记住：出于好奇和关怀而产生的理解意图，在你的互动中至关重要。

This intention to understand represents a fundamental, radical shift at the basis of our orientation to a dialogue. It involves weeding from our consciousness any blame, defensiveness, control, or manipulation and instead focusing on creating a quality of connection that is conducive to collaboration. Everything I share with you in this book is designed toward this end: creating more connection and understanding.

这种理解的意愿代表着我们对话方式的根本性转变。它意味着从我们的意识中摒弃一切指责、防御、控制或操纵，转而专注于建立一种有利于合作的联结。我在本书中与你分享的一切都旨在实现这一目标：增进联结，加深理解。

To make this shift, we need to see the limits of our habitual responses and the value of the intention to understand—its potential for transformation, creativity, and wholeness. There are two key principles that support this. The first runs through this entire book: the less blame and criticism in our words, the easier it will be for others to hear us. When someone trusts that we’re actually interested in understanding them—that we’re not manipulating things to get our way, that we’re not trying to win or prove them wrong—they can stop defending themselves and just hear what we’re saying.

为了实现这种转变，我们需要认识到自身习惯性反应的局限性，以及理解意愿的价值——它蕴含着变革、创造力和完整性的潜力。有两个关键原则支撑着这一点。第一个原则贯穿全书：我们言语中指责和批评越少，别人就越容易倾听我们。当别人相信我们是真心想了解他们——我们并非为了达到目的而操纵局面，并非试图取胜或证明他们错了——他们就能停止自我辩解，认真倾听我们所说的话。

Principle: The less blame and criticism, the easier it is for others to hear us.

原则：指责和批评越少，别人就越容易听我们说话。

From this perspective, it’s in our best interest to come from curiosity and care. If we’re rooted in this intention, our verbal and nonverbal communication sends the message that we’re genuinely interested, which ultimately helps create the space to hear each other and work together.

从这个角度来看，出于好奇和关怀才是最符合我们利益的做法。如果我们秉持这种意愿，我们的言语和非言语沟通就会传递出我们真诚感兴趣的信息，这最终有助于创造彼此倾听和合作的空间。

This leads to the next principle: the more mutual understanding, the easier it is to work together and find creative solutions. This seems self-evident, yet we often lose sight of this simple fact. When we comprehend the deeper reasons behind what each of us wants, we can start to collaborate.

这就引出了下一个原则：相互理解越多，就越容易合作并找到创造性的解决方案。这看似不言而喻，但我们却常常忽略这个简单的道理。当我们理解彼此需求背后的深层原因时，我们才能开始合作。

Principle: The more mutual understanding, the easier it is to work together and find creative solutions.

原则：相互了解越多，就越容易合作并找到创造性的解决方案。

We’re wired to feel joy when we give and to feel empathy in the face of suffering. Contributing to others is one of the most rewarding experiences we can have. This natural impulse is like an inexhaustible well of goodwill deep within the human spirit.

我们天生乐于付出，也善于体谅他人的苦难。帮助他人是我们所能拥有的最有意义的体验之一。这种与生俱来的冲动，就像人类精神深处一口取之不尽的善意之井。

Because we feel joy in giving and compassion with suffering, when we fully understand one another we want to help instinctively. If I truly understand what’s in your heart, why you want what you want, I am moved to find a way to work together. When I can help you see why something is important to me, priorities shift and there’s more space and willingness to collaborate. (Just think of a time when you initially said no to a request, only to agree later when you better understood the situation.)

因为我们乐于付出，同情苦难，所以当我们真正了解彼此时，就会本能地想要帮助对方。如果我真正理解你的内心，明白你为什么想要你所想要的，我就会想要找到合作的方式。当我能帮助你理解某件事对我的重要性时，彼此的优先事项就会发生转变，合作的空间和意愿也会随之增加。（想想你最初拒绝某个请求，但后来在更好地了解情况后同意的情形。）

This approach to conflict is at the heart of nonviolent resistance. We have more power and integrity when appealing to the humanity of our fellow beings. This was the principle underlying Gandhi’s work, the civil rights movement, and why Rosenberg named his method Nonviolent Communication. Taking this approach doesn’t mean that we are passive, that we don’t assert ourselves or take a stand for what we believe in. Cultivating the intention to understand makes us more effective by leveraging our connection to one another’s humanity. 4

这种处理冲突的方式是非暴力抵抗的核心。当我们诉诸于他人的人性时，我们便拥有更大的力量和更坚定的信念。这正是甘地著作、民权运动的根本原则，也是罗森伯格将其方法命名为“非暴力沟通”的原因。采取这种方式并不意味着我们消极被动，不去维护自身权益或捍卫信仰。培养理解的意愿，能够让我们通过与他人人性的联结，更加有效地应对冲突。

A Different Way of Seeing

不同的视角

Davis’s story, and the stories of many others who meet hatred, racism, and bigotry with love, points to a different way of viewing the world. It’s a view that Rosenberg was seeking when he asked questions about the nature of compassion and violence. It depends on our ability to look for the humanity in each other, to see beyond our disagreements to something more essential.

戴维斯的故事，以及许多其他以爱对抗仇恨、种族主义和偏见的人们的故事，指向了一种不同的世界观。这正是罗森伯格在探讨同情与暴力的本质时所寻求的观点。它取决于我们能否在彼此身上发现人性，能否超越分歧，看到更深层次的东西。

All human actions are attempts to meet fundamental needs. Beneath our behaviors, preferences, beliefs, and desires are certain longings for physical, relational, or spiritual needs. We all have needs for safety, belonging, connection, and empathy. We have needs for meaning, contribution, creativity, or peace. (We’ll explore this concept in greater depth in chapter 7 .)

人类的一切行为都是为了满足基本需求。在我们行为、偏好、信仰和欲望的背后，都隐藏着对生理、人际关系或精神需求的渴望。我们都需要安全感、归属感、联结感和同理心。我们也需要意义感、贡献感、创造力和内心的平静。（我们将在第七章更深入地探讨这个概念。）

One finds this idea across many religious, spiritual, and contemplative traditions, as well as in the behavioral and social sciences. In Buddhism, it’s put succinctly: “All beings want to be happy.” It’s the kind of wisdom that struck me as being right intuitively the first time I heard it. What happiness looks like differs from person to person, even from day to day, but at the root is an attempt to meet our needs.

这种理念在许多宗教、灵修和冥想传统中都有体现，在行为科学和社会科学领域也同样如此。佛教对此的表述简洁明了：“一切众生皆欲享乐。” 我第一次听到这种智慧时，就觉得它发人深省，仿佛冥冥之中自有安排。幸福的定义因人而异，甚至每天都在变化，但其根源在于满足我们自身的需求。

Principle: Everything we do, we do to meet a need.

原则：我们所做的一切，都是为了满足某种需求。

Remembering this perspective is one key to being able to come from curiosity and care. The view calls forth the intention. Whatever is happening, we can get curious about the deeper human needs and values beneath our words or actions. When we understand each other at the level of our needs, our similarities outweigh our differences. This, in turn, creates a generative, positive cycle of views, intentions, and experiences.

记住这种视角是保持好奇心和关怀的关键之一。这种视角会激发我们的意图。无论发生什么，我们都可以对言行背后更深层次的人类需求和价值观产生好奇。当我们从需求层面理解彼此时，我们的相似之处就会大于差异。反过来，这会形成一个积极向上、富有成效的观点、意图和体验循环。

The great strength of this approach is that it’s not limited to our intimate relationships. Whether we want to enjoy time with a friend, collaborate with a coworker, or build a diverse coalition, our genuine intention to understand has the power to create or enhance connection (for its own sake and in service of meeting needs).

这种方法的最大优势在于它不仅限于亲密关系。无论我们想与朋友共度时光、与同事合作，还是建立一个多元化的联盟，我们真诚的理解意愿都有能力创造或加强彼此之间的联系（既是为了建立联系本身，也是为了满足彼此的需求）。

To employ this in conversation requires a few things. First, we need to build our capacity to come from curiosity and care. We need to really home in on what it feels like to have a genuine intention to understand so that we can bring our mind back there at will. Next, we need to train ourselves to notice when we’re operating from our habitual tendencies. Last, we learn how to find our way back to curiosity and care.

要在对话中运用这种方法，需要做到以下几点。首先，我们需要培养好奇心和关怀的能力。我们需要真正体会到真心想要理解的感觉，这样才能随时将注意力拉回到这种状态。其次，我们需要训练自己觉察何时受到习惯性思维的影响。最后，我们要学会如何重新找回好奇心和关怀。

VIEWS →

浏览量 →

Lead to → INTENTIONS

导致 → 意图

Create → EXPERIENCES

创造 → 体验

Win/Win

双赢

Conflict is natural,
a ground for learning

冲突是自然的，也是学习的土壤。

We share universal needs

我们拥有共同的需求

Others have inherent value,
independent of our
own needs

其他事物则具有内在价值，独立于我们自身的需求。

To inquire/listen

询问/倾听

To care

照顾

To collaborate

合作

To connect

连接

Intimacy, safety

亲密感，安全感

Belonging

归属感

Understanding & mutual respect

理解与相互尊重

Creativity, synergy

创造力，协同作用

Coming from Curiosity and Care

源于好奇心和关爱

Every child is born with a natural desire to understand their world. Just as we have the innate capacity to be aware, we all have the capacity to be interested. Just as we can train ourselves in presence, we can cultivate the intention to understand.

每个孩子天生都渴望了解世界。正如我们拥有与生俱来的感知能力一样，我们也都拥有产生兴趣的能力。正如我们可以训练自己保持专注一样，我们也可以培养理解的意愿。

To genuinely understand something requires curiosity and care. Curiosity means that we are interested in learning. Learning requires humility; we must be willing to not know. To understand means “to stand beneath.” To comprehend anything, we need to put aside our preconceived ideas and be open to new ways of seeing.

真正理解事物需要好奇心和关怀。好奇心意味着我们对学习感兴趣。学习需要谦逊；我们必须愿意承认自己的未知。理解意味着“站在其下方”。要理解任何事物，我们需要放下先入为主的观念，并以开放的心态接受新的视角。

Curiosity also requires patience. Conservationist and researcher Cynthia Moss shared that it took her twenty years of observing elephants, closely studying their habits and movements, before she began to realize how complex they were. 5 Such enduring patience can only arise when there is true curiosity, a deep intention to understand.

好奇心也需要耐心。自然保护主义者和研究员辛西娅·莫斯分享说，她花了二十年时间观察大象，仔细研究它们的习性和活动，才开始意识到它们有多么复杂。这种持久的耐心只有在真正好奇、渴望了解的情况下才会产生。

In order to be interested in something, to give attention, we also need to care. We don’t pay attention to things we don’t care about, and we don’t care about things we don’t pay attention to. This caring can be about many things. We might care about integrity, staying true to our values. We might care about peace and well-being. We might care about broadening our perspective. We might care about resolving conflict in our own lives in order to nourish hope that we can do better as a society. We might care about transforming the systems and institutions within which we live.

要想对某件事感兴趣，投入注意力，我们也需要关心它。我们不会关注我们不关心的事，也不会关心我们不关注的事。这种关心可以体现在很多方面。我们可能关心正直，坚守自己的价值观。我们可能关心和平与福祉。我们可能关心拓展视野。我们可能关心解决自身生活中的冲突，从而滋养希望，相信我们作为一个社会可以做得更好。我们可能关心改变我们身处的制度和机构。

What’s essential is the quality of care itself, goodwill connected to the empathic sense. It includes warmth, vulnerability, and flexibility. Care means that we are open to being affected by what we learn, that we are committed to seeing the other person’s humanity, and that we are willing to include their needs in the situation rather than be rigidly fixated on getting what we want in exactly the way we want it. All of this is possible with practice.

真正重要的是关怀本身的质量，是与同理心相连的善意。它包含温暖、脆弱和灵活。关怀意味着我们愿意接受所学到的东西，致力于看到他人的人性，并且愿意将他们的需求纳入考量，而不是固执地执着于以我们想要的方式得到我们想要的东西。所有这些都可以通过实践来实现。

PRACTICE : Coming from Curiosity and Care

实践：源于好奇心和关怀

Explore cultivating curiosity and care in conversation. Beforehand, reflect on your intention. How do you want to approach things? Where do you want to come from inside? See if you can find a genuine intention to understand the other person—their thoughts, views, feelings, or needs. How does it feel to be genuinely interested?

探索如何在对话中培养好奇心和关怀。事先思考一下你的意图。你想如何切入问题？你想从内心深处出发？看看你是否能找到一种真诚的意图去理解对方——他们的想法、观点、感受或需求。真正感兴趣的感觉如何？

Try recalling this perspective when you are in conversation. What matters to this person? What do they long for or need? What is the effect when you are able to come from curiosity and care? As always, try this out in low-stakes situations at first.

在与人交谈时，试着从这个角度思考。这个人最看重的是什么？他们渴望什么，需要什么？当你带着好奇和关心去倾听时，会产生怎样的效果？和往常一样，先在无关紧要的场合尝试一下。

Mindfulness and the Intention to Understand

正念与理解的意图

Our ordinary relationship to experience is to judge and control it. Sit down and observe your own mind for a few minutes and you’ll notice these tendencies firsthand. We react to experience by moving toward what’s pleasant and away from what’s unpleasant, judging the pleasant as good and the unpleasant as bad.

我们通常对待经验的方式是评判和控制它。花几分钟时间静下心来观察一下自己的内心，你就会亲身感受到这些倾向。我们对经验的反应是趋向愉悦，远离不愉悦，并将愉悦的判断为好，不愉悦的判断为坏。

Through mindfulness practice we find that this habit is not only futile but also stressful and exhausting. We waste a great deal of our energy chasing pleasure and resisting pain, trying to control things beyond our sphere of influence. The basic shift we make over and over again in formal meditation is to cultivate the intention to understand experience rather than judge or control it. The more we explore this in mindfulness practice, the more readily we can make this shift in our conversations and day-to-day lives.

通过正念练习，我们发现这种习惯不仅徒劳无功，而且令人倍感压力和疲惫。我们浪费大量精力去追逐快乐、抗拒痛苦，试图控制那些超出我们掌控范围的事情。在正规的冥想练习中，我们反复进行的根本转变是培养理解体验而非评判或控制体验的意图。我们在正念练习中越深入地探索这一点，就越容易在日常对话和生活中做出这种转变。

PRACTICE : Observing with the Intention to Understand

练习：以理解为目的的观察

Take ten minutes or more for seated mindfulness practice. Do whatever helps you to arrive: orient; take some slow, deep breaths; relax into your sitting posture.

花十分钟或更长时间进行静坐冥想练习。做任何能帮助你进入状态的事情：辨别方向；做几次缓慢深呼吸；放松地进入坐姿。

Let your attention settle with the sensations of breathing in and breathing out, allowing your breath to be natural. Whenever you notice your mind has wandered, gently let go and bring your attention back to breathing.

让注意力集中在吸气和呼气的感觉上，让呼吸自然而然地进行。每当你发现自己的思绪游离时，轻轻地放下它，将注意力重新集中到呼吸上。

Pay particular attention to when your mind reacts to experience, liking or disliking what happens. When you feel something unpleasant, do you resist it, pulling away? When you feel something pleasant, do you try to hold on to it? When thoughts come, do you grow frustrated or berate yourself? Notice how your mind judges and tries to control the flow of experience.

特别留意你的思维对经历的反应，无论是喜欢还是不喜欢。当你感到不愉快时，你会抗拒它，试图逃避吗？当你感到愉快时，你会试图抓住它吗？当思绪涌现时，你会感到沮丧还是责备自己？注意你的思维是如何评判并试图控制经历的流动。

Each time you notice this reactivity, cultivate an intention to understand rather than to judge. Whatever is happening, can you bring some curiosity and care to the experience? Try to notice the difference between when your mind is interested in the present moment and when it is reacting—pushing or pulling, leaning forward or manipulating. Which happens automatically? Which is more peaceful?

每次你注意到这种反应时，试着培养一种理解而非评判的意图。无论发生了什么，你能否带着好奇和关怀去体验？试着留意你的心思专注于当下和做出反应——推拉、前倾或操控——之间的区别。哪种是自动发生的？哪种更平和？

There are many ways to cultivate the intention to understand in the midst of conversation. For me, one of the primary ways of strengthening curiosity and care has been to integrate these qualities into my daily life. Try it out for a period of time—a day, a week, or more. Anything that occurs—an email, a conversation—simply aim to understand. “What matters here—to me, to them? What can I learn from this?” The more we remember this way of looking at things and feel a sincere interest in learning, the easier it becomes to approach dialogue in this way.

在对话中培养理解的意愿有很多方法。对我而言，增强好奇心和关怀的主要方法之一就是将这些品质融入我的日常生活。不妨尝试一段时间——一天、一周甚至更久。无论发生什么——一封邮件、一次对话——都以理解为目标。“对我来说，对他们来说，什么才是重要的？我能从中学习到什么？”我们越是记住这种看待事物的方式，越是真心实意地想要学习，就越容易以这种方式进行对话。

A Mindfulness Bell

正念之铃

One of my first communication teachers, Sandra Boston, has a great shorthand for remembering to use these tools: “Just say ‘Oh!’ ” Whenever we find ourselves slipping back into our old patterns, we can use the friction we feel as a kind of mindfulness bell, “Oh—I have some tools here! I can handle this.” We recall our training and bring up a perspective conducive to curiosity and care.

我的第一位沟通老师桑德拉·波士顿（Sandra Boston）有一个很棒的速记方法，可以帮助我们记住如何使用这些工具：“只要说‘哦！’”每当我们发现自己又回到了旧有的模式时，我们可以把这种摩擦感当作一种正念警示：“哦——我这里有一些工具！我可以应对。”我们回忆起之前接受的训练，并以一种有助于保持好奇心和关怀的视角来看待问题。

The first step is to be able to identify when we’re on autopilot. We learn to recognize the attributes of being caught in our old habits and use those very signs as reminders to wake up out of their trance. Returning to presence, we find some inner ground. Then we get curious—first and foremost about our own experience. “What’s happening here? Let me try to just understand this.” Try this next practice whenever you find yourself defaulting to unconscious communication habits.

第一步是能够识别我们何时处于自动驾驶模式。我们要学会辨别陷入旧习惯的特征，并利用这些迹象提醒自己从这种恍惚状态中醒来。回归当下，我们就能找到内心的平静。然后，我们会产生好奇心——首先也是最重要的，是对我们自身体验的好奇心。“这里发生了什么？让我试着理解一下。”每当你发现自己不自觉地陷入无意识的沟通习惯时，不妨试试这个方法。

PRACTICE : Just Say “Oh!”

练习：只需说“哦！”

As you get more familiar with your default conflict styles, begin to study their signature in your body, heart, and mind. What lets you know you’re on automatic? Here are a few common signs:

随着你越来越熟悉自己默认的冲突应对方式，开始观察它们在你身体、内心和思想中的体现。哪些迹象表明你正处于自动应对模式？以下是一些常见的迹象：

Physical

身体的

• Tightness in your jaw

• 下巴紧绷

• Tension in your limbs or body

• 四肢或身体紧张

• Shallow or rapid breathing

• 呼吸浅快或急促

• Flushes of heat, sweating, or cold

• 一阵阵发热、出汗或发冷

• Feeling disembodied, ungrounded, or “up in your head”

• 感觉脱离身体、不踏实，或者“心不在焉”

Emotional

情绪

• Fear, anxiety, or a feeling of wanting to run away

• 恐惧、焦虑或想要逃跑的感觉

• Irritation, anger, annoyance, or a feeling of aggression

• 烦躁、愤怒、恼怒或攻击性情绪

• An urge to protect, explain, or defend yourself

• 想要保护、解释或为自己辩护的冲动

• Feeling frozen, overwhelmed, or stuck

感到茫然、不知所措或停滞不前

Mental

精神的

• Thoughts or images of anger, hate, or negativity

• 愤怒、仇恨或消极的想法或画面

• Thoughts or images of hopelessness or despair

• 绝望或悲观的想法或画面

• Thoughts or images of worst-case scenarios

• 最坏情况的想法或画面

Verbal

口头

• An increase in the pace, pitch, or volume of speech

• 语速、音调或音量加快

• Reluctance to speak or respond; withdrawing verbally

• 不愿说话或回应；口头上退缩

• “But…that’s not what I meant…”

“但是……我不是那个意思……”

• “You don’t understand…You’re not listening…”

• “你不明白……你根本没在听……”

• “Should…never…always…right…wrong…”

• “应该……永远……总是……对……错……”

When you notice any of these signs, pause internally. Silently name what you feel and try to relax any tension or tightness. Recall that you have a choice about how to proceed. Use whatever method helps you lead with presence (finding gravity, the centerline, breathing, touch points). Then use one of the suggestions below to bring forth some curiosity and care.

当你注意到这些迹象时，请在内心稍作停顿。默默地描述你的感受，并尝试放松任何紧张或僵硬的情绪。记住，你可以选择如何继续。使用任何能帮助你保持觉察的方法（例如，找到重心、找到中心线、调整呼吸、寻找接触点）。然后，运用以下建议之一，培养一些好奇心和关怀。

These patterns aren’t the enemy. In fact, noticing them can become the cue to return to presence. They also can be important signposts to investigate and uncover what’s driving our own reactivity, which in turn brings more space and balance to engage in dialogue.

这些模式并非敌人。事实上，觉察到它们可以成为回归当下的契机。它们也可以成为重要的路标，帮助我们探究和揭示自身反应背后的驱动因素，从而为我们创造更多空间和平衡，以便进行对话。

PRACTICE : Recalling Your Intention

练习：回忆你的意图

To whatever degree possible, find a genuine intention to understand. You can silently ask yourself a question to seed curiosity and care. Here are a few suggestions:

尽可能地，怀着真诚的理解意愿。你可以默默地问自己一个问题，以此来激发好奇心和关怀。以下是一些建议：

• “What’s happening here? How can I relax and find some balance?”

• “这里发生了什么？我该如何放松身心，找到平衡？”

• “What if there were something to learn here?”

• “如果这里有什么值得学习的地方呢？”

• “What if we figured this out and became closer?”

• “如果我们能弄清楚这件事，关系会不会变得更亲密呢？”

• “How can we start to understand each other more?”

• “我们如何才能更好地了解彼此？”

• “What might work for both of us?”

• “什么方法对我们双方都有利？”

• “Regardless of the outcome, how do I want to handle myself here?”

• “无论结果如何，我该如何应对？”

• “What’s most important to me? What are my needs?”

• “对我来说最重要的是什么？我的需求是什么？”

• “What matters to them? What do they need?”

• “他们最看重什么？他们需要什么？”

Let that simple intention guide what you say or do next, perhaps even expressing it explicitly: “I’d really like to understand what’s been happening for you.”

让这个简单的意图指导你接下来的言行，甚至可以明确地表达出来：“我真的很想了解你最近发生了什么事。”

At first, putting down our old habits and finding sincere curiosity take time. With practice, we can learn to notice what’s happening and shift our intention in a matter of moments.

起初，放下旧习惯、培养真诚的好奇心需要时间。但通过练习，我们就能学会觉察正在发生的事情，并在瞬间转变我们的意图。

A couple of years ago, my girlfriend and I spent New Year’s Eve moving out of our apartment. We’d spent the weekend packing and had been carrying boxes and furniture down two flights of stairs for a couple of hours. It was getting late, we were both tired, and my back hurt—a perfect storm for losing presence and the intention to understand.

几年前，我和女友在新年夜搬出了我们的公寓。我们花了整个周末打包，又花了几个小时把箱子和家具搬下两层楼。当时天色已晚，我们俩都很累，我的背也疼——各种状况叠加在一起，让我们完全无法集中注意力，也无法集中精力去理解周围的一切。

In typical male fashion, I took charge of loading the van, telling Evan what to bring down next or instructing her where to leave things, all with mounting irritation due to my exhaustion. At a certain point, responding to my tone of stress, Evan declared with frustration, “I feel like everything you say is criticizing me, telling me I’m doing something wrong!”

像所有男人一样，我负责装车，告诉埃文接下来该搬什么，或者指示她把东西放在哪里，但疲惫让我越来越烦躁。到了某个时候，埃文听出了我的焦虑，沮丧地说道：“我觉得你说的每句话都在批评我，说我做错了什么！”

I immediately felt defensive. Everything inside wanted to snap at her, “I’m just trying to get this done!” Instead, I closed my eyes and just stood there breathing hard. I could sense she was in pain, and I didn’t want to add more. I felt a wave of anger rise through my body, everything burning. I didn’t want to act from that place and knew there would be time to share my side of things after I made some space for her. I kept breathing and put my attention in my lower body to ground myself. I felt my feet on the floor and the wave passed. I exhaled, and my breathing slowed as my fists unclenched.

我立刻感到一阵强烈的防御心理。内心深处，我几乎要冲她吼道：“我只是想把事情做完！” 但我没有，而是闭上眼睛，站在那里，大口喘着气。我能感觉到她很痛苦，我不想让她更难过。一股怒火涌遍全身，仿佛烈火焚身。我不想在这种情绪下行事，我知道等我给她一些空间之后，会有时间跟她解释我的想法。我继续深呼吸，将注意力集中在下半身，让自己稳住。我感觉到双脚踩在地上，那股怒火渐渐消散。我呼出一口气，呼吸也渐渐平缓下来，紧握的拳头也松开了。

“I hear you,” I said, looking at her. “I’m sorry my words have had that impact on you.” I paused, waiting to see how this landed. “Thank you,” she said, still huffing a bit but softening. In one or two more short exchanges we understood each other, let go, and went back to loading the van—feeling more at ease and aligned.

“我明白了，”我看着她说，“很抱歉我的话对你造成了这样的影响。”我停顿了一下，等着看她的反应。“谢谢，”她说，语气里还带着一丝不悦，但已经缓和下来。又过了一两次简短的交流，我们彼此理解，释怀了，然后继续往货车上装东西——感觉轻松多了，也更合拍了。

I don’t always catch the wave. But that time my training allowed me to notice the impulse to defend, return to presence, and come from a different place inside. Had I missed those signals and acted out of habit, I can imagine the argument that might have ensued.

我并非总能把握住时机。但那次，我的训练让我能够察觉到那种想要防御的冲动，重新回到现实，并从内心深处做出反应。如果我错过了这些信号，只是出于习惯行事，我可以想象接下来可能会引发怎样的争吵。

Two Questions

两个问题

Resisting the force of our old habits can be hard. We might see what’s happening but lack the restraint to keep from acting it out or the energy to shift our intention. Maybe we’re having trouble trusting that a new approach will work. In these cases, investigating our expectations and recalling our values can help.

抵制旧习惯的力量并非易事。我们或许明明看到了正在发生的事情，却缺乏克制力来避免付诸行动，或者缺乏改变意图的精力。也许我们难以相信新的方法会奏效。在这种情况下，审视我们的预期并重温我们的价值观会有所帮助。

Rosenberg had a succinct way of doing this. He encouraged people to ask two questions: First, “What do I want the other person to do?” Second, “What do I want their reasons to be for doing it?”

罗森伯格用一种简洁的方式阐述了这一点。他鼓励人们问自己两个问题：第一，“我希望对方做什么？”第二，“我希望他们这样做的理由是什么？”

If we only ask the first question, we might use any strategy we can to get our needs met. We may blame them. We may manipulate, coerce, or even threaten in some way. (That New Year’s Eve, I might have snapped, “Will you stop being so sensitive—I’m just trying to get things done.”) While these strategies may produce results in the short term, they come at a cost in the quality of the relationship. We lose some of the other person’s trust and goodwill.

如果我们只问第一个问题，我们可能会不择手段地满足自己的需求。我们可能会责怪对方，可能会操纵、胁迫，甚至以某种方式威胁对方。（那年除夕夜，我可能就脱口而出：“你能不能别这么敏感——我只是想把事情做好。”）虽然这些策略短期内或许能奏效，但却会损害彼此的关系。我们会失去对方的一些信任和好感。

If we ask ourselves the second question, we’re much less likely to resort to these strategies. Do we want the person to change their behavior because they fear punishment or retaliation? Or do we want them to do something out of an intrinsic motivation, because they understand its value or why it’s important to us?

如果我们问自己第二个问题，我们就不太可能诉诸这些策略。我们是希望对方因为害怕惩罚或报复而改变行为吗？还是希望他们出于内在动机去做某件事，因为他们理解这件事的价值或它对我们的重要性？

These questions prime us to come from a very different place inside, to strive to create more connection. Our whole angle becomes, “Let’s see if we can understand each other.” In my situation with Evan, I wanted her to stay focused on packing because she understood what was happening for me, not because I’d won an argument or proved her wrong. Once we understood each other, moving forward was easy.

这些问题促使我们从截然不同的内心出发，努力建立更深层次的联系。我们整个过程的出发点变成了：“看看我们能否互相理解。” 就我和埃文的情况而言，我希望她能专注于收拾行李，因为她理解我的处境，而不是因为我赢了争论或者证明了她错了。一旦我们彼此理解，接下来的事情就顺理成章了。

PRACTICE : Inquiry

实践：探究

Use this exercise to prepare for conversations. Reflect on the questions below to help you get clear on your intentions and strengthen your ability to stay connected to curiosity and care. With practice you may find that you’re able to use these questions to shift your intention in the midst of conversation.

利用这个练习为对话做好准备。思考以下问题，帮助你明确自己的意图，并增强保持好奇心和关怀的能力。通过练习，你可能会发现，你可以在对话过程中运用这些问题来调整你的意图。

QUESTION 1: What do you want the other person to do? Do you have more than one idea that might work for you? Try to be as creative and open-minded as possible.

问题1：你希望对方做什么？你是否有不止一个可行的想法？尽量发挥你的创造力，保持开放的心态。

QUESTION 2: What do you want their reasons to be for doing this? Why do you want them to do it? What is it you’d like them to know or understand?

问题 2：你希望他们这样做的理由是什么？你为什么希望他们这样做？你希望他们知道或理解什么？

CONSIDER : Knowing this, how would you like to approach the conversation?

思考：了解了这一点，你希望如何展开对话？

When we fall back on our habitual patterns, it’s easy to make assumptions about another’s intentions. A friend running late or a partner forgetting an agreement can take on much larger significance, implying that we don’t matter. “If you knew how much this mattered you would…” or “If you loved me, you would…” Having the intention to understand opens new ways of seeing what’s happening and may create alternative ideas for addressing the situation.

当我们习惯于既有的思维模式时，很容易对他人的意图妄加揣测。朋友迟到或伴侣忘记约定，都可能被无限放大，仿佛我们无关紧要。“如果你知道这件事有多重要，你就会……”或者“如果你爱我，你就会……”。然而，如果我们真心想要理解，就能以全新的视角看待问题，并可能找到解决问题的其他方法。

Using Force to Protect

使用武力保护

There are situations in life where an immediate result is more important than collaboration and dialogue—mostly when safety is involved. When our primary objective is to protect our own or another’s well-being, we employ what Rosenberg calls the protective use of force. If a child is running into the street, we shout or grab them, doing whatever it takes to keep them safe.

生活中有些情况下，立竿见影的效果比合作和对话更为重要——尤其是在涉及安全问题时。当我们首要目标是保护自身或他人的福祉时，我们会采取罗森伯格所说的“保护性武力使用”。如果一个孩子跑到街上，我们会大声呵斥或抓住他，竭尽所能确保他的安全。

This is complicated terrain philosophically. Does the end ever justify the means, and if so, when? Who has the authority to determine that? As soon as we decide it’s okay to use unilateral force “for their own good” or “for the greater good,” we run the risk of abusing power and causing harm. For the sake of our exploration, I want to point out a few key differences between Rosenberg’s protective use of force and relying on our default habits. First, in Rosenberg’s definition, we use force consciously rather than fall back on it unconsciously out of desperation or habit. Second, we use force without any malice, with the wish to protect rather than to harm. Third, it is a temporary, time-limited strategy. Last, we remain connected to the other person’s humanity instead of seeing them as a problem or enemy.

从哲学角度来看，这是一个复杂的问题。目的是否能证明手段的正当性？如果可以，又该在什么情况下才算正当？谁有权做出这样的判断？一旦我们认为单方面使用武力“为了他们好”或“为了更大的利益”是合理的，我们就面临着滥用权力、造成伤害的风险。为了便于探讨，我想指出罗森伯格的保护性武力使用与我们依赖惯性思维之间的几个关键区别。首先，在罗森伯格的定义中，我们有意识地使用武力，而不是出于绝望或习惯而无意识地诉诸武力。其次，我们使用武力时没有任何恶意，目的是为了保护而非伤害。第三，这是一种暂时的、有时限的策略。最后，我们始终将对方的人性放在首位，而不是将他们视为问题或敌人。

Once all are safe, we can return to a more relational approach. Systems of restorative justice (as opposed to retributive criminal justice) are based on these principles. Once the immediate danger is removed, we can work to build understanding, creating the conditions for repair and more safety in the future.

一旦所有人都安全了，我们就可以回归到更注重关系的模式。修复性司法体系（而非报复性刑事司法）正是基于这些原则。一旦直接危险消除，我们就可以努力增进彼此的理解，为未来的修复和更安全创造条件。

The Power of Curiosity and Care: Aikido in Action

好奇心与关怀的力量：合气道的实践

Aikido teacher Terry Dobson tells one of my favorite stories about embodying curiosity and care. Dobson is an ex-marine who’d been studying the martial art of aikido in Japan with its founder. Though his teacher stressed that aikido is a way of peace and reconciliation, Dobson was eager to test his training in combat.

合气道老师特里·多布森讲述了一个我最喜欢的关于如何体现好奇心和关怀的故事。多布森曾是一名海军陆战队员，在日本跟随合气道创始人学习这门武术。尽管他的老师强调合气道是一种和平与和解之道，但多布森却渴望在实战中检验自己的训练成果。

One afternoon in Tokyo, a large, drunk day laborer stumbled into the subway, cursing angrily. He lunged at a woman and her baby, nearly hitting them. Dobson stood up and called out to the laborer, ready to defend the passengers. The man began hurling insults at Dobson, who provoked him further by blowing a kiss in his direction. Just then, from the other side of the train, a sharp voice called out, “Hey! Come here and talk to me.”

东京的一个下午，一个身材魁梧、醉醺醺的临时工踉踉跄跄地走进地铁，嘴里不停地咒骂。他猛地扑向一位妇女和她的婴儿，差点撞到她们。多布森站起身来，冲着那名临时工喊话，准备保护乘客。那人开始辱骂多布森，多布森反而朝他飞吻，进一步激怒了他。就在这时，从车厢另一侧传来一个尖锐的声音：“嘿！过来跟我说话！”

A little old man sat on the other side of the car. The laborer turned and yelled, “Why should I talk to you?”

车子另一边坐着一位老先生。工人转过身，大声喊道：“我为什么要跟你说话？”

“What’chya been drinking?” the old man asked.

“你喝的是什么？”老人问道。

“I been drinking sake, and its none of your goddamn business!”

“我喝的是清酒，这跟你他妈的有什么关系！”

“Oh, that’s wonderful,” the old man said with delight. “Absolutely wonderful! I love sake too. Every night, me and my wife—she’s seventy-six, you know—we warm up a little bottle of sake and take it out into the garden, and we sit on the old wooden bench that my grandfather’s first student made for him. We watch the sun go down, and we look to see how our persimmon tree is doing…”

“哦，那太好了，”老人欣喜地说，“真是太好了！我也喜欢清酒。每天晚上，我和我妻子——你知道，她已经七十六岁了——都会温一小瓶清酒，然后拿到花园里，坐在我祖父的第一个学生为他做的那张旧木凳上。我们看着夕阳西下，看看我们的柿子树长得怎么样了……”

As the old man spoke, the drunk man’s expression began to soften. “Yeah, I love persimmons…”

老人说话间，醉汉的表情渐渐柔和下来。“是啊，我也喜欢柿子……”

The old man asked, “I’m sure you have a lovely wife too?”

老人问道：“我相信你也有一位贤惠的妻子吧？”

Tears began to stream down the laborer’s face, who shared that his wife had died. He began to sob, “I don’t got no wife, I don’t got no home, no job, no money, nowhere to go. I’m so ashamed.”

工人的眼泪夺眶而出，他告诉大家妻子去世了。他开始抽泣：“我没有妻子，没有房子，没有工作，没有钱，无处可去。我太羞愧了。”

Soon the laborer was sitting beside the old man, his head in his lap, allowing his matted hair to be gently stroked. Dobson concludes, “What I had wanted to do with muscle and meanness had been accomplished with a few kind words. I had seen aikido tried in combat and the essence of it was love….I would have to practice the art with an entirely different spirit. It would be a long time before I could speak about the resolution of conflict.” 6

很快，那工人便坐在老人身旁，头枕在老人的腿上，任由老人轻轻抚摸他蓬乱的头发。多布森总结道：“我原本想用蛮力和凶狠来解决的问题，几句善言就解决了。我曾亲眼目睹合气道在实战中的运用，它的精髓在于爱……我必须以截然不同的精神来练习这门技艺。我还需要很长时间才能谈论如何化解冲突。”

This is the transformative power of coming from curiosity and care, of staying connected to each other’s humanity in the face of aggression. Creating this kind of connection is a skill that takes practice. Leading with presence is the prerequisite and primary foundation. Having a genuine intention to understand is the compass that points us in the right direction.

这就是源于好奇和关怀的变革力量，在面对侵略时，依然能够与彼此的人性保持联结。建立这种联结需要练习。以临在为先是前提和根本。真诚地想要理解，就像指南针一样，指引我们走向正确的方向。

PRINCIPLES

原则

The less blame and criticism, the easier it is for others to hear us.

指责和批评越少，别人就越容易听进去我们的话。

The more mutual understanding, the easier it is to work together and find creative solutions.

相互了解越多，就越容易合作并找到创造性的解决方案。

Everything we do, we do to meet a need.

我们所做的一切，都是为了满足某种需求。

KEY POINTS

要点

Intention shapes our verbal and nonverbal communication and directs the course of a conversation. The intention to understand includes curiosity and care:

意图塑造了我们的语言和非语言沟通，并引导着对话的走向。理解的意图包含着好奇心和关怀：

• Curiosity means that we are interested in learning and recognize what we don’t know.

• 好奇心意味着我们对学习感兴趣，并且认识到我们不知道的事情。

• Care is goodwill. It depends on our willingness to pay attention and our commitment to seeing one another’s humanity.

关怀是一种善意。它取决于我们是否愿意关注彼此，以及我们是否愿意看到彼此的人性。

Mindfulness practice helps us cultivate the intention to understand rather than to judge. We can train ourselves to notice habitual tendencies to blame and shift to the intention to understand with these practices:

正念练习帮助我们培养理解而非评判的意图。我们可以通过以下练习训练自己觉察到习惯性的指责倾向，并转向理解的意图：

• Consider inwardly, “What matters to this person?”

• 认真思考一下，“对这个人来说，什么最重要？”

• Just say “Oh!” Notice any habitual intentions and get curious.

• 只需说“哦！” 注意任何习惯性意图并感到好奇。

• Recall your intention.

• 回想一下你的意图。

• Ask yourself two questions: “What do I want the other person to do? What do I want their reasons to be for doing it?”

• 问问自己两个问题：“我希望对方做什么？我希望他们这样做的理由是什么？”

QUESTION & ANSWER

问答

Q: How do you come from curiosity and care when you believe the other person doesn’t have good intentions, when they’re deliberately doing something to upset you or make things difficult?

问：当你认为对方没有善意，故意做一些让你不高兴或使事情变得困难的事情时，你如何才能保持好奇和关心的态度？

It’s not easy, especially if it’s a contentious situation with little mutual trust. First, you need to find a way to handle your own experience with curiosity and care: get empathy from a friend, use self-empathy to relieve any distress, and get clear about your own needs. I also encourage you to hold your interpretation about their intentions lightly. We long to make sense of their actions, but our assumptions aren’t always correct.

这并不容易，尤其是在双方缺乏信任、充满争议的情况下。首先，你需要找到一种方法，以好奇和关怀的态度来处理自己的经历：从朋友那里获得共情，运用自我同理心来缓解任何不适，并明确自己的需求。我也鼓励你不要过分执着于对他们意图的解读。我们渴望理解他们的行为，但我们的假设并不总是正确的。

All of this frees up space inside to inquire, “What could they be longing for?” Remember, everything we do, we do to meet a need. Try to shift your perspective. Can you see their actions as strategies to meet deeper, more universal needs? This attempt to stretch your heart and imagine their experience can be transformative.

这一切都腾出了内心的空间，让我们去思考：“他们究竟渴望什么？”记住，我们所做的一切，都是为了满足某种需求。试着转换视角。你能否将他们的行为视为满足更深层次、更普遍需求的策略？这种敞开心扉、设身处地地感受他们经历的尝试，或许能带来意想不到的改变。

The last piece is to try to cultivate some compassion for the other person, which will ease your heart from any bitterness and open more possibilities in the relationship. As the saying goes, “Hurt people hurt people.” I encourage you to try to see their vulnerability, pain, or insecurity that may be connected to their actions.

最后一点是，试着对对方培养一些同情心，这能抚平你心中的苦涩，并为你们的关系开启更多可能性。正如俗语所说，“受伤的人会伤害别人”。我鼓励你试着去理解他们的脆弱、痛苦或不安全感，这些或许与他们的行为有关。

Q: I tried coming from curiosity and care and it didn’t work. The other person wasn’t interested in what matters for me. It seems like this stuff only works if both people are using it.

问：我尝试过出于好奇和关心去了解对方，但没成功。对方对我在乎的事情并不感兴趣。看来只有双方都用心去做，这种方法才有效。

It certainly makes it easier! But it only takes one person to change the dynamics of a relationship or shift a dialogue. If one person changes their stance, it affects the shape and flow of the process.

这当然会方便很多！但只需要一个人就能改变关系的动态或转变对话走向。如果一个人的立场发生改变，就会影响整个过程的走向和发展。

There are many factors at play here. We may start out curious but lose touch with that genuine intention when under pressure. It requires practice and skill to stay grounded in challenging situations. We may repeatedly need to meet intense blame or anger with balance, hearing their deeper needs, defusing aggression, and sharing our point of view in a timely and helpful way. Finally, it’s important to examine our expectations of what success looks like. If we’re only interested in getting our way, then we’re not really open to dialogue. We have to be willing to shift, to discover creative possibilities.

这里有很多因素在起作用。我们或许一开始充满好奇，但在压力之下却会失去这份初心。在充满挑战的环境中保持冷静需要练习和技巧。我们可能需要反复地用平衡的心态来应对强烈的指责或愤怒，倾听他们深层的需求，化解攻击性，并及时有效地表达自己的观点。最后，审视我们对成功的预期至关重要。如果我们只想着如何达到目的，那么我们就无法真正敞开心扉地进行对话。我们必须愿意转变思维方式，去发现创造性的可能性。

A colleague tells the story of two groups of women in Boston—a pro-choice group and pro-life group—who met regularly to discuss their conflicting views on abortion. In the end, none of them changed their views, but they built meaningful relationships of mutual respect. When the pro-life group heard through their network about plans for someone to bomb an abortion clinic, they sent a clear message that such actions were not welcome in their community. To me, that’s success. Their views hadn’t changed, but they were not willing to use violence as a strategy to meet their needs because they had learned to see the humanity of the other side.

一位同事讲述了波士顿两组女性的故事——一组支持堕胎权，一组反对堕胎——她们定期聚会，讨论她们在堕胎问题上的分歧。最终，她们的观点都没有改变，但却建立了彼此尊重、意义深远的友谊。当反对堕胎的那组女性通过她们的社交网络得知有人计划炸毁一家堕胎诊所时，她们明确表示，这种行为在她们的社区是不受欢迎的。在我看来，这就是成功。她们的观点没有改变，但她们不再愿意诉诸暴力来满足自身的需求，因为她们学会了理解对方的人性。

Q: What about situations where you know your needs aren’t going to get met? It’s just not going to happen. How do you handle that?

问：如果你知道自己的需求无法得到满足，这种情况该怎么办？你该如何应对？

It can be so difficult, so painful when our needs aren’t met. A big part of using these tools is to find ways to handle those times in life by mourning our unmet needs. It can be very healing to allow ourselves to feel both the sadness and the longing. Finding tenderness with those feelings helps us learn to be at peace with our unmet needs, which brings more freedom to our lives.

当我们的需求得不到满足时，会感到非常艰难和痛苦。运用这些工具的关键在于找到应对人生低谷的方法，比如坦然面对那些未被满足的需求。允许自己感受悲伤和渴望，本身就是一种疗愈。温柔地对待这些感受，能帮助我们学会与未被满足的需求和平共处，从而为我们的生活带来更多自由。

Part of this process is differentiating between our needs and any fixation we have on a specific strategy. A lot of the time, this mourning is about the loss we feel over a particular strategy not being possible. One of the benefits of identifying our needs is that it gives us more choice. It gives us access to more creative options.

这个过程的一部分在于区分我们的需求和我们对特定策略的执着。很多时候，这种遗憾源于我们对某种特定策略无法实现的失落感。明确自身需求的好处之一在于，它能让我们拥有更多选择，接触到更多富有创意的方案。

I also would encourage you to be fully conscious of the difference between what’s actually happening and your predictions or beliefs. Sometimes when we tell ourselves, “There is no way so-and-so would…” we are trying to protect ourselves from the disappointment or pain of rejection. See if it changes anything for you to frame it this way: “I’m having trouble imagining a way in which they would say yes to what I want.” This can feel more empowering and might lead to a different choice about how you engage. Or it might lead to a different internal experience, one based on clarity about the other needs you are choosing to meet by not making a request.

我也想鼓励你充分意识到实际情况与你的预测或信念之间的差异。有时，当我们告诉自己“某某绝对不会……”时，我们其实是在试图保护自己免受被拒绝的失望或痛苦。不妨换个角度思考：“我很难想象他们会答应我的请求。”这样或许会让你感觉更有力量，并可能促使你选择不同的应对方式。或者，它可能会带来不同的内心体验，让你更清楚地认识到，你选择不提出请求，是为了满足其他方面的需求。

# ↩

6

don’t let the call drop

别让通话中断。

Listening with ears is less fine than listening with the heart.

— HSU - T ’ ANG CHIH - YU

用耳朵听不如用心听好。——徐唐志宇

LISTENING IS A cornerstone of dialogue and a powerful metaphor for spiritual practice. When we come from curiosity and care, we’re willing and able to listen. We’re opening a conduit that allows connection and understanding to happen.

倾听是对话的基石，也是灵性修行中一个强有力的隐喻。当我们怀着好奇和关怀之心时，我们便愿意且能够倾听。我们打开了一条通道，让联结和理解得以发生。

There are so many ways to listen. We can listen to the content of what someone says, to how they’re feeling, to what’s important beneath their words. We can listen halfheartedly or wholeheartedly.

倾听的方式有很多种。我们可以倾听别人话语的内容，感受他们的感受，以及话语背后真正重要的东西。我们可以漫不经心地倾听，也可以全心全意地倾听。

To truly listen depends on a kind of inner silence. It requires that we empty ourselves and make space to receive something new. I had a powerful reminder of this a few years ago when I had a disagreement with Jeremy, an old friend from high school.

真正倾听需要一种内心的平静。它要求我们清空自己，腾出空间去接受新的事物。几年前，我和高中老朋友杰里米发生争执，这件事让我对此有了深刻的体会。

“Bro—you’re not listening!” he exclaimed.

“兄弟——你根本没在听！”他喊道。

We were standing in his kitchen and he was passionately upset. Though I no longer remember the details, I remember that I was only half-listening. I was waiting for him to finish so I could explain my perspective. Even though I was completely silent, making eye contact, and hearing every word, he could sense that I wasn’t really taking it in. I was building my case, preparing to defend myself.

我们当时站在他家的厨房里，他情绪激动，非常生气。虽然我已经记不清细节了，但我记得我当时只是心不在焉地听着。我等着他说完，好让我有机会解释我的看法。尽管我全程沉默，眼神交流，也听清了他说的每一个字，但他还是能感觉到我并没有真正听进去。我当时正在整理思路，准备为自己辩护。

I took a deep breath. Closing my eyes, I let go of my interpretation, my desire to explain. There would be time for that later. I put all of that down for the moment and just relaxed into listening and trying to understand. I felt my feet on the ground and opened my eyes.

我深吸一口气。闭上眼睛，我放下自己的解读，放下想要解释的念头。以后有的是时间。我暂时把这一切都抛在脑后，放松下来，静静聆听，努力理解。我感觉双脚踩在地上，然后睁开了眼睛。

“Okay,” I said. “Go on.” As soon as I released my agenda to defend myself, the whole tone of the conversation shifted.

“好的，”我说，“继续。”我刚一亮出我的论点为自己辩护，整个谈话的气氛就变了。

“Thank you,” Jeremy sighed as he continued, sensing that I now was actually willing and available to listen. He went on to explain how he was feeling and why. I listened, really heard him, and acknowledged the truth of his experience independent of my own feelings or views: “Yeah, I get that’s how you felt. I can see why you’d be upset.”

“谢谢，”杰里米叹了口气，继续说道，他感觉到我现在真的愿意倾听了。他接着解释了自己的感受和原因。我认真地听着，真正理解了他的话，并且不带任何个人感受或观点地承认他经历的真实性：“是啊，我明白你的感受。我能理解你为什么会难过。”

Offering some words of understanding, things settled. I may have shared my side—I can’t recall, and it didn’t even matter much anymore. The vital shift had been letting go enough to hear him with genuine curiosity and care.

我说了几句表示理解的话，事情就平静下来了。我可能也说了自己的版本——我记不清了，而且现在说这些也无关紧要了。关键的转变在于，我终于能够放下成见，用真诚的好奇和关怀去倾听他。

Learning How to Listen

学习如何倾听

To listen entails a fundamental letting go of self-centeredness. We have to be willing to put down our own thoughts, views, and feelings temporarily to truly listen. It’s a wholehearted, embodied receptivity that lies at the core of both communication and contemplative practice.

倾听意味着从根本上放下自我中心。我们必须愿意暂时放下自己的想法、观点和感受，才能真正倾听。这是一种全心全意、身心合一的接纳，也是沟通和冥想实践的核心。

Every conversation requires silence. Without it we can’t listen, and no real communication happens. The silence of listening isn’t forced or strained. It’s a natural quiet that arises from interest. When you want to smell a flower, what do you do? You close your eyes, get close, and inhale slowly. Your mind grows still as you find the aroma. This is perhaps the most powerful way to listen: with full presence. As the poet and teacher Mark Nepo writes, “To listen is to lean in softly with a willingness to be changed by what we hear.” 1

每一次对话都需要沉默。没有沉默，我们就无法倾听，也无法进行真正的交流。倾听的沉默并非强迫或勉强，而是一种源于兴趣的自然宁静。当你想要闻一朵花的香气时，你会怎么做？你会闭上眼睛，靠近它，然后慢慢地吸气。随着香气的散发，你的思绪也渐渐平静下来。这或许是倾听最有力的方式：全然地投入。正如诗人兼教师马克·尼波所写：“倾听就是轻轻地靠近，并愿意被我们所听到的内容所改变。”

The wilderness has taught me a lot about how to listen. The ancient steadiness of an old-growth redwood, the stillness of a high mountain lake, or the vibrant music of a stream—all have the power to quiet the mind and still the heart. In the face of such wonders, our mental chatter falls away. What remains is a state of pure listening.

荒野教会了我很多关于聆听的道理。古老红杉的沉稳、高山湖泊的静谧、溪流的潺潺——所有这些都拥有抚慰心灵、平复心情的力量。面对如此美景，我们纷乱的思绪烟消云散，剩下的只有纯粹的聆听。

We learn this kind of deep listening in meditation, discovering the stillness of awareness. With practice we can access it in the midst of conversation. The more we learn how to listen, the more available we become for others and for our life in general.

我们在冥想中学习这种深度聆听，体验觉知的宁静。通过练习，我们可以在交谈中也能做到这一点。我们越学会聆听，就越能更好地关爱他人，也越能更好地享受生活。

This is just as important for the wonderful moments as it is for the difficult ones. True listening allows us to appreciate the presence of a loved one or to let kindness touch us. When sharing affection or a hug, Evan and I will often gently invite one another to be present in this way, asking, “Are you letting it in?” This kind of receptive listening can nourish the spirit.

无论是在美好的时刻还是在艰难的时刻，这一点都同样重要。真正的倾听让我们能够珍惜爱人的陪伴，或感受善意的触动。当我和埃文分享爱意或拥抱时，我们常常会轻轻地邀请彼此以这种方式去感受，问：“你感受到了吗？”这种接纳式的倾听能够滋养心灵。

PRACTICE : Listening Wholeheartedly

练习：全心全意地倾听

All listening begins with presence. When in conversation, see if you can bring your heart’s full attention to listening. Notice any tendencies to interpret, comment, or plan what you’ll say next. Can you return to the simplicity of presence over and over again and just listen, letting go of these tendencies when they arise?

倾听始于专注。在交谈中，试着将全部注意力集中在倾听上。注意自己是否有解读、评论或计划接下来要说什么的倾向。你能否一次又一次地回归专注的本质，只是倾听，并在这些倾向出现时放下它们？

Don’t Let the Call Drop

别让通话中断。

One of our primary aims in dialogue is to make a connection (to the degree necessary to handle the matter at hand) and then to do our best to maintain it. If we lose that connection, communication wanes or ceases altogether.

对话的主要目标之一是建立联系（达到处理当前问题所需的程度），然后尽力维持这种联系。如果我们失去了这种联系，沟通就会减弱甚至完全停止。

This is most apparent in heated arguments, when all attempts to acknowledge or understand one another can disappear. Instead, we end up layering one charged statement on top of another, never slowing down to check if we’re actually hearing one another. The call dropped long ago but we’re both still talking.

这一点在激烈的争吵中最为明显，此时彼此理解和回应的尝试都会消失殆尽。取而代之的是，我们不断地抛出充满攻击性的言论，却从未停下来确认自己是否真的听懂了对方。通话早已中断，但我们仍在喋喋不休。

Much of the time, we maintain connection nonverbally, through culturally appropriate body language: facial expressions, eye contact, tone of voice, and so forth. We nod or say, “Mm hmm.” We may tip our head to the side, narrow our eyes, or furrow our brow to indicate that we’re losing the thread or to ask for clarification. A speaker may even insert simple yes/no questions: “Are you still with me? Does that make sense? You know what I mean?”

很多时候，我们通过非语言方式，运用符合文化习俗的肢体语言来维系联系：面部表情、眼神交流、语调等等。我们会点头或说“嗯哼”。我们可能会歪着头、眯起眼睛或皱起眉头，表示我们跟不上思路或需要澄清。说话者甚至可能会插入一些简单的是非问句：“你明白我的意思吗？我这么说你懂吗？你明白我的意思吗？”

This can create a lovely call-and-response rhythm that strengthens the connection by confirming that listening and understanding are occurring. In this way, we use presence and intention to keep checking that we’re connected with one another, that the call hasn’t dropped. It’s like keeping one hand on the wheel while driving to ensure that we don’t drift out of our lane. Most of us do this intuitively and automatically; we can enhance our capacities in this area by bringing conscious attention to this process.

这可以营造一种美妙的呼应节奏，通过确认彼此的倾听和理解，从而加强联系。这样，我们就能运用专注和意图，不断确认彼此的连接是否畅通，通话是否中断。这就像开车时一只手始终放在方向盘上，以确保不偏离车道。我们大多数人都是凭直觉和自动完成这项操作的；但我们可以通过有意识地关注这个过程来提升这方面的能力。

PRACTICE : Staying Connected

实践：保持联系

The next time you are in conversation, track the connection. Use the first two steps—leading with presence and coming from curiosity and care—to make a connection with the other person. Then listen and use body language, facial expression, tone of voice, or short verbal inquiries to check periodically if you’re still connected. Anytime the call drops—if you sense a disconnect or misunderstanding—slow down and see if you can reestablish the connection.

下次与人交谈时，注意保持联系。首先，运用前两步——展现专注和好奇心，并表达关心——与对方建立联系。然后，倾听并运用肢体语言、面部表情、语调或简短的询问来定期确认联系是否依然牢固。如果通话中断——或者你感觉到沟通出现断断续续或误解——请放慢节奏，尝试重新建立联系。

Completing the Cycle

完成循环

Checking informally through voice and body language helps us assess the general connection in a conversation, yet it relies on an unspoken assumption. If I ask, “Do you understand?” and you say, “Yes,” all I really know is that you think you understand. As the saying goes, the single biggest problem with communication is the illusion that it has taken place.
