通过语音和肢体语言进行非正式的确认有助于我们评估对话中的整体沟通情况，但这依赖于一个未言明的假设。如果我问“你明白吗？”，你回答“明白”，我真正知道的只是你认为自己明白了。正如俗语所说，沟通最大的问题在于人们常常误以为沟通已经完成。

To make sure the call hasn’t dropped, we need a more reliable method, an authentic, lightweight way to confirm that we’re actually hearing one another. When listening, we want to know that we’ve heard correctly, and when speaking, we want to know if we’ve been understood. In difficult situations, the need is even greater.

为了确保通话没有中断，我们需要一种更可靠的方法，一种真实、便捷的方式来确认我们是否真的听到了对方的声音。在倾听时，我们希望确认自己听得是否正确；在说话时，我们希望确认自己是否被对方理解。在棘手的情况下，这种需求就更加迫切了。

“You’re not listening! You don’t understand!” How many times have you said (or heard) this in the midst of an argument? Just because we’re speaking the same language doesn’t mean we understand each other. We say one thing, they hear something else. They say one thing and mean something else. It’s amazing how quickly we can get entangled!

“你根本没在听！你听不懂！” 你是不是经常在争吵中说（或听到）这句话？就算我们说的是同一种语言，也不代表我们就能互相理解。我们说一套，他们听的却是另一套；他们说一套，心里想的却是另一套。我们竟然这么容易就陷入争论的漩涡，真是不可思议！

When someone says, “You’re not listening,” part of what they mean is “I don’t feel heard right now.” It’s often a plea for empathy and a sign that we’ve lost connection. To get back on track we first need to reconnect. Let’s look at two examples of how this might play out in a conversation.

当有人说“你根本没在听”时，他们话里有几分是“我现在感觉自己没被理解”。这通常是在寻求共情，也是我们之间失去了联系的信号。要想重回正轨，首先需要重新建立联系。让我们来看两个例子，看看这种情况在对话中是如何发生的。

PERSON A : “You’re not listening!”

PERSON B : “Yes, I am! I heard everything you said.”

PERSON A : “You’re not listening!”

PERSON B : “It sounds like you’re not feeling heard. I’m really trying to listen but let me try again.”

OR, PERSON B : “Okay—I’d really like to understand more. What could I do or say that would help you to feel heard?”

A：“你根本没在听！” B：“我在听！你说的我都听到了。” A：“你根本没在听！” B：“听起来你好像没被我听进去。我真的在努力听，但让我再试一次。” 或者，B：“好的——我真的很想更了解你。我该怎么做或说什么才能让你觉得被我听进去呢？”

Which conversation is more likely to move toward resolution? In the first instance, each person may feel less understood, which usually spurs us to assert our position more forcefully. This leads to less connection, more assertions, and so on. Most of us know how awful it feels to be caught in this kind of a vortex, how quickly things devolve and how painfully they can end.

哪种对话更有可能朝着解决问题的方向发展？首先，双方都可能感到不被理解，这通常会促使我们更加强硬地表达自己的立场。这会导致沟通减少、争吵增多，如此循环往复。我们大多数人都知道陷入这种恶性循环有多糟糕，事情恶化得有多快，结局又有多痛苦。

Notice the difference in the second example, when we find some willingness to listen with empathy. Here, the speaker acknowledges the other person’s experience and tries to reconnect. Doing this depends on our ability to lead with presence and come from curiosity and care rather than fall back into our default modes of defending or blaming.

注意第二个例子中的不同之处，那时我们能感受到对方愿意倾听并感同身受。说话者认可对方的经历，并试图重新建立联系。做到这一点取决于我们能否以专注的态度引导，并以好奇和关怀为出发点，而不是退回到惯常的辩解或指责模式。

The main tool here is using a verbal reflection to “complete a cycle” of communication. We listen, then get confirmation at key moments that what one person hears matches what the other person meant, that message sent equals message received.

这里的主要工具是运用口头反馈来“完成”沟通的“循环”。我们先倾听，然后在关键时刻确认对方听到的内容与自己想表达的意思一致，确保发出的信息与接收到的信息完全一致。

A reflection is a restatement of or inquiry about what’s been said to confirm understanding.

反思是对已说过的内容的重述或询问，以确认理解。

If you’re ordering takeout, the restaurant employee repeats your order back to you to check that they have it correctly. In conversation, know when to reflect what you hear before you respond. If you say something important, ask the other person for a reflection so you know if they heard what you intended.

如果你点外卖，餐厅员工会复述你的订单，以确认无误。在交谈中，要懂得在回应之前复述对方的话。如果你说了重要的话，请对方复述一遍，这样你才能知道他们是否理解了你的意思。

Reflecting before we respond is a fundamental building block of communication. It can make the difference between an effective conversation and an argument. When we complete a cycle, it feels good. It’s satisfying to get confirmation and know we’re hearing each other. There’s often a sense of settling, relief, or a spontaneous outbreath. And when we feel heard, we have more space inside to listen to someone else. In this way, offering empathy and listening to someone else is in our best interest.

在回应之前进行反思是沟通的基石。它能决定对话是有效还是争吵。当我们完成一个反思循环时，会感觉很好。得到对方的确认，知道彼此都在倾听，这种感觉令人满足。通常会有一种平静、释然，或者不由自主地长舒一口气的感觉。当我们感到被倾听时，内心就会有更多空间去倾听他人。因此，给予同理心并倾听他人，对我们自己也是有益的。

Principle: People are more likely to be willing to listen when they feel heard. To build understanding, reflect before you respond.

原则：当人们感到被倾听时，他们更愿意倾听。为了增进理解，请在回应之前先思考。

Evan and I often rely on this tool to work through difficulties. I remember one time, early in our relationship, we sat on the couch discussing our different expectations around frequency of communication.

我和埃文经常用这个工具来解决难题。我记得有一次，在我们刚开始交往的时候，我们坐在沙发上讨论我们对沟通频率的不同期望。

EVAN : “I feel trapped, like you’ll get angry if I don’t respond immediately.”

OREN : “Sounds like you’re feeling frustrated because you’d like more time to respond to text messages when you’re at work?”

EVAN : “Yeah, it’s just not reasonable to expect me to reply right away.”

OREN : “And you want some understanding for the fact that you have other responsibilities that may be more important than replying to my text messages?”

埃文：“我感觉被困住了，好像如果我不马上回复你，你会生气似的。” 奥伦：“听起来你是因为想在上班的时候有更多时间回复短信而感到沮丧？” 埃文：“是啊，指望我马上回复确实不合理。” 奥伦：“你是不是也希望我能理解，你还有其他更重要的事情要做，而不是回复我的短信？”

Evan majored in environmental engineering and enjoys the clarity of science. At one point, after we’d settled into a rhythm of completing each cycle before moving on to a new piece of content, she exclaimed, “Wow! I never knew communication could be like math!” When we have the tools and the patience to hear one another and work something out, it can be exhilarating.

埃文大学主修环境工程，她很喜欢科学的清晰性。有一次，在我们逐渐形成一种节奏，完成一个周期后再进行下一个内容时，她惊呼：“哇！我以前从不知道沟通也可以像数学一样！” 当我们拥有沟通的工具和耐心去倾听彼此、解决问题时，那真是令人兴奋。

In addition to providing the relief of feeling heard, reflecting before we respond slows things down. It helps create understanding one step at a time—speaking, listening, reflecting—and gives each person time to integrate what’s been said.

除了让人感到被倾听之外，在回应之前进行反思还能放慢节奏。它有助于我们一步一步地建立理解——说话、倾听、反思——并让每个人都有时间消化对方所说的话。

We may need to reflect many times in a given conversation before responding. It can take several cycles of empathic reflection before there is sufficient connection, particularly when someone is emotionally activated. If we stick with it, this kind of persistent empathy can have dramatic results.

在回应之前，我们可能需要在对话中反复思考。尤其是在对方情绪激动时，可能需要多次同理心的反思才能建立足够的联系。如果我们坚持下去，这种持续的同理心可以带来显著的效果。

PRACTICE : Reflect Before You Respond

实践：三思而后行

Experiment with reflecting before you respond in a low-stakes conversation. After the other person shares something important, offer a reflection of what you heard to check that you understand. Do this when nonverbal confirmation is insufficient, when there is a lot of content, or when strong emotions are present.

在不太重要的对话中，尝试在回应之前先进行反思。当对方分享了一些重要信息后，复述一下你听到的内容，以确认自己是否理解。当非语言确认不足、信息量很大或存在强烈情绪时，这样做尤为重要。

Pointers

指针

• Offer your understanding of what the other person has said in words they can easily relate to.

• 用对方容易理解的语言表达你对对方所说内容的理解。

• Phrase your reflection as a question rather than a statement. You’re checking to ensure you understand rather than telling someone what they said.

• 将你的反思以问题的形式表达，而不是陈述。你是在确认自己是否理解，而不是告诉别人他们说了什么。

• Stay connected to genuine curiosity and care.

• 保持真诚的好奇心和关怀。

• Keep your language as natural and authentic as possible.

• 尽量使用自然地道的语言。

• Try this with celebrations and successes as well as difficult news.

• 尝试用这种方法来应对庆祝活动和成功，以及令人沮丧的消息。

Watch for signs of completing a cycle: a verbal affirmation, an outbreath, or some settling. Even if your reflection is not 100 percent accurate, it often leads to more connection because it gives the other person the chance to clarify or explain further what they mean.

注意观察对话循环完成的迹象：口头肯定、呼气或情绪平静下来。即使你的反馈并非百分之百准确，也往往能增进彼此的联系，因为它给了对方机会进一步澄清或解释他们的意思。

Examples

示例

STATEMENT : “I just can’t believe she would say that. After all we went through…”

REFLECTION : “You’re really stunned that she said that, huh?”

OR : “It sounds like you’re really upset, trying to figure out what would motivate her to say that?”

STATEMENT : “I’m sick and tired of being the only one around here who does anything!”

REFLECTION : “Wow—you’re totally fed up. You feel like you’re the only one doing anything?”

OR : “You’re really sick of this, huh? Are you wanting more teamwork or balance in the chores?”

陈述：“我简直不敢相信她会这么说。我们经历了那么多……” 反思：“你真的很震惊她会这么说，是吗？” 或者：“听起来你很生气，想弄明白她为什么会这么说？” 陈述：“我受够了，这里只有我一个人干活！” 反思：“哇——你真是受够了。你觉得自己是唯一一个在干活的人吗？” 或者：“你真的厌倦了，是吗？你是想要更多的团队合作，还是想要家务分配更均衡一些？”

Keeping It Real

保持真实

What I’m encouraging here is different from what’s often called “active listening.” Many people learn to do this with stock phrases such as “So what I hear you saying is…” When we use a technique without being genuine, our speech sounds formulaic, which reduces connection. And we can miss the point. We get so focused on the technique that we forget to really listen.

我在这里提倡的，与通常所说的“积极倾听”有所不同。许多人学会用一些固定的短语来表达“所以，我理解你的意思是……”。当我们不真诚地使用技巧时，我们的表达听起来就会很生硬，这会削弱彼此的联系。而且，我们可能会错过重点。我们过于关注技巧本身，反而忘记了真正地倾听。

It’s essential right from the beginning to not lose sight of the principle beneath the training. Reflecting before you respond is a tool to build enough connection and understanding to collaborate. It’s not a dogma: “Thou shalt always reflect before you respond.”

从一开始就牢记培训背后的原则至关重要。在回应之前进行反思是建立足够联系和理解以进行合作的工具。这并非教条：“你必须在回应之前始终进行反思。”

Communication practice is not about what we say. It’s about where we’re coming from and how we say it. Let the sincerity of your intention guide your listening and your words. What would you say if you genuinely wanted the other person to feel heard? How would you check that you understood? How would you ask, if you genuinely wanted to feel heard?

沟通的真谛不在于我们说了什么，而在于我们的出发点和表达方式。让你的真诚意图指引你的倾听和言辞。如果你真心希望对方感到被倾听，你会怎么说？你会如何确认自己理解了对方的意思？如果你真心希望被倾听，你会如何提问？

It’s also important to note that no matter how hard we try to be natural, there’s often a period of awkwardness in learning anything. It takes time to find our voice and get comfortable with a new way of communicating.

同样重要的是，无论我们多么努力地想要表现得自然，学习任何东西都常常会经历一段尴尬期。我们需要时间来找到自己的表达方式，并适应新的沟通方式。

The Roots of Empathy

同理心的根源

At the heart of verbal reflection is empathy: an intuitive reaching to understand another’s experience on its own terms. Without empathy, the reflection will feel empty.

语言反思的核心在于同理心：一种直觉式的、试图从他人的角度去理解其经历的能力。缺乏同理心，反思就会显得空洞无物。

Spend time with a giggling toddler or a puppy and something inside softens. Stand near someone who is angry or panicked and we feel it! This is the phenomenon known as emotional contagion. Babies begin to cry when they hear other babies crying. When we see that toddler or puppy hurting, something inside us quivers. We feel a compassionate impulse to reach out.

和咯咯笑着的幼儿或小狗待在一起，我们内心深处的情感就会被触动。站在愤怒或惊慌失措的人身边，我们也能感受到他们的情绪！这就是所谓的情绪传染。婴儿听到其他婴儿的哭声也会跟着哭。当我们看到幼儿或小狗受伤时，我们内心深处也会感到一阵悸动。我们会不由自主地想要伸出援手，给予他们关爱。

Today we are learning more about the neurological and evolutionary bases of empathy. Infants need empathic connection for their brains to develop properly. One of the most groundbreaking findings for the neurobiology of empathy was the discovery of mirror neurons, which provide an immediate kind of somatic empathy. Mirror neurons fire when we see another being perform an action. Part of our brain is silently enacting the movements of those around us as if we were doing them ourselves. This includes facial expressions. Our brains inwardly mimic the emotional expressions of others; they’re wired for empathy.

今天，我们将深入了解同理心的神经学和进化基础。婴儿需要同理心的联结才能使大脑正常发育。同理心神经生物学领域最突破性的发现之一是镜像神经元的发现，它提供了一种即时的躯体同理心。当我们看到他人做出某个动作时，镜像神经元就会被激活。我们大脑的一部分会默默地模仿周围人的动作，仿佛我们自己也在做一样。这包括面部表情。我们的大脑会在内心模仿他人的情绪表达；它们天生就具备同理心。

Empathy is at the heart of listening. When I closed my eyes and took the time to really hear Jeremy, I was shifting gears to empathy. Empathy plays many functions: it can create healing and build resilience; it can stimulate healthy bonding; it can de-escalate strong emotions, facilitate understanding, and help resolve differences.

同理心是倾听的核心。当我闭上眼睛，认真倾听杰里米的讲述时，我便进入了同理心的状态。同理心具有多种功能：它可以疗愈创伤，增强心理韧性；它可以促进健康的亲密关系；它可以缓和强烈的情绪，增进理解，并帮助化解分歧。

Empathy is the capacity to understand or feel what another person is experiencing from their point of view.

同理心是指能够从他人的角度理解或感受他人经历的能力。

Empathy literally means to “feel into.” While it can be expressed in many ways (silent listening, verbal reflection, touch, action), empathy is primarily a quality of presence in the heart. It’s a receptive attunement to felt experience, our own and others’. We could say that empathy is a union of presence and the intention to understand. It’s a genuine, caring interest that allows us to reach into another’s world and understand their experience. Carl Rogers, one of the founders of humanistic psychology, described empathy in this way:

同理心字面意思是“感受”。虽然它可以以多种方式表达（例如默默倾听、言语回应、触摸、行动），但同理心本质上是一种发自内心的临在感。它是一种对自身和他人的感受的敏锐感知。我们可以说，同理心是临在感与理解意愿的结合。它是一种真诚的、关怀的兴趣，使我们能够走进他人的世界，理解他们的经历。人本主义心理学的创始人之一卡尔·罗杰斯曾这样描述同理心：

Empathy is a complex, demanding, strong, yet subtle and gentle way of being…it means entering the private perceptual world of the other and becoming thoroughly at home in it. It involves being sensitive moment to moment to the changing felt meanings which flow in this other person. 2

同理心是一种复杂、要求高、强大而又微妙温柔的存在方式……它意味着进入他人的私密感知世界，并完全融入其中。它需要对他人内心不断变化的情感保持敏锐。

This resonant, receptive faculty of empathy is one of the primary qualities that makes us human. 3 Given adequate safety, sustenance, and other basic needs, the natural tendency of the human being is toward empathy and compassion—to feel with another.

这种共鸣的、接受性的同理心能力是使我们成为人类的主要品质之一。 3 在获得足够的安全保障、食物和其他基本需求的情况下，人类的自然倾向是同情和怜悯——与他人感同身受。

Roadblocks to Empathy

同理心的障碍

While empathy is innate, all sorts of conditions can hinder it. Most broadly, we learn not to be empathic through the socialization process. We are taught (by our family, culture, society) to fear or hate those different from us. We shut off our empathic capacity in order to fit in, to protect ourselves, or to get by in a world that is not structured to meet our needs.

虽然同理心是与生俱来的，但各种各样的因素都会阻碍它的发展。最普遍的情况是，我们在社会化过程中学会了缺乏同理心。我们的家庭、文化和社会教导我们恐惧或憎恨与我们不同的人。为了融入群体、保护自己，或者为了在一个无法满足我们需求的世界中生存下去，我们关闭了自己的同理心。

Being disconnected from empathy comes at a high cost, as Miki Kashtan explains in Spinning Threads of Radical Aliveness:

正如米基·卡什坦在《编织激进活力的线索》一书中解释的那样，缺乏同理心会付出沉重的代价：

To say, as I believe, that we are “hard-wired” for mutual recognition and empathy does not necessarily mean that we will always act in caring, compassionate ways. Rather, it means that to the extent that we ignore care and empathy and cultivate other emotional postures, we pay enormous prices: depression, apathy, nightmares, victimization, and anger on an individual level, and crime, neglect, and isolation on a societal level. 4

我认为，我们天生就具备相互理解和同理心，但这并不意味着我们总是会以关爱和同情的方式行事。相反，这意味着，如果我们忽视关爱和同理心，转而培养其他的情感态度，我们将付出巨大的代价：个人层面的抑郁、冷漠、噩梦、受害感和愤怒，以及社会层面的犯罪、忽视和孤立。

Reclaiming our capacity for empathy is essential for well-being, for healthy relationships, and for effective dialogue. Many of the same things that disconnect us from presence will reduce access to empathy: being tired, stressed, or hungry; feeling emotionally activated, angry, or helpless; wanting something intensely or being attached to a specific outcome. Empathy can be blocked by strong views, fear, anticipation of pain, or burnout. There is even new research that suggests the more time we spend on electronic devices, the less empathy we feel. 5

重拾同理心对于身心健康、良好的人际关系和有效的对话至关重要。许多让我们无法专注于当下的因素也会削弱我们的同理心：疲惫、压力过大或饥饿；情绪激动、愤怒或无助；强烈渴望某样东西或执着于某个特定结果。强烈的个人观点、恐惧、对痛苦的预期或职业倦怠都会阻碍同理心的产生。甚至有新的研究表明，我们花在电子设备上的时间越多，我们感受到的同理心就越少。

When we don’t receive the empathy we want from others and don’t realize (or forget) that there are things that can block empathy, we can make up stories to try to explain what’s happening. We may assume there’s something wrong with us, or with the other person, or that they don’t care. Instead of believing these stories, we can recognize that the conditions for empathy to emerge might not be present. This leaves more room to come from curiosity and care, to identify those conditions and address them creatively. 6

当我们得不到他人想要的同理心，并且没有意识到（或忘记）有些因素会阻碍同理心时，我们可能会编造故事来试图解释正在发生的事情。我们可能会假设是自己或对方出了问题，或者对方根本不在乎。与其相信这些故事，不如认识到同理心产生的条件可能并不具备。这样，我们就可以更多地运用好奇心和关怀，去发现这些条件，并以创造性的方式去解决它们。

There are some fairly common ways we respond when we aren’t feeling empathy. The psychologist Thomas Gordon calls them “communication roadblocks” because they hinder connection and understanding. 7

当我们缺乏同理心时，有一些相当常见的反应方式。心理学家托马斯·戈登称之为“沟通障碍”，因为它们阻碍了彼此的联系和理解。

PRACTICE : Identifying Roadblocks to Empathy

练习：识别同理心的障碍

Take a moment to think about a time you felt frustrated or stuck. It can be something difficult (a relationship breakup) or mundane (getting the runaround at the DMV). Imagine telling a friend about it, then read the responses below.

请花点时间想想你感到沮丧或束手无策的时刻。它可以是件难事（比如分手），也可以是件琐事（比如在车管所被敷衍）。想象一下你跟朋友倾诉这件事，然后阅读下面的回复。

BLAMING, JUDGING, OR CRITICIZING : “It’s probably your fault. You always mess things up.”

指责、评判或批评：“这可能是你的错。你总是把事情搞砸。”

LECTURING, TEACHING : “You need to learn how to advocate for yourself. You should have spoken up…”

训诫、教导：“你需要学会如何维护自己的权益。你应该早点开口……”

GIVING ADVICE : “What you need to do is…I know a great therapist…”

给出建议：“你需要做的是……我认识一位很棒的心理咨询师……”

WARNING, THREATENING : “You better take care of this soon or…How many times have I told you…”

警告、威胁：“你最好尽快处理这件事，否则……我跟你说过多少遍了……”

ORDERING, DIRECTING : “Get over it. It’s time to move on.”

命令、指导：“别再纠结了。是时候向前看了。”

ANALYZING, DIAGNOSING : “The problem is…I think there’s a pattern here that may have to do with your childhood…”

分析、诊断：“问题是……我认为这里存在某种模式，可能与你的童年经历有关……”

COMPARING , “ ONE - UPPING ”: “You think that’s bad? This one time…”

比较，“胜过”：“你觉得那很糟糕？那这一次……”

DISTRACTING, SARCASM, HUMORING : “So, what are you going to do with your free time? Have you seen that new film?”

分散注意力、讽刺、幽默：“那么，你打算怎么打发空闲时间？你看过那部新电影了吗？”

QUESTIONING : “Where were you? Why did you get involved with this?”

质问：“你当时在哪里？你为什么会卷入这件事？”

PRAISING, AGREEING : “You are the most generous, kind person I know…You’re right…”

赞扬、赞同：“你是我认识的最慷慨、最善良的人……你说得对……”

SYMPATHIZING, REASSURING : “Oh, you poor thing…You did the best you could. It’ll be okay.”

表示同情和安慰：“哦，你真可怜……你已经尽力了。一切都会好起来的。”

How does it feel to not be received with empathy? Which of these types of responses do others in your life employ? On which do you rely habitually?

不被他人理解和同情是什么感觉？你生活中其他人会采用哪些类型的回应？你又习惯性地依赖哪些回应？

The difference between empathy and some of these responses can be subtle. Sympathy, generally regarded as positive, can contain a quality of pity that is marked by separation and a reluctance to encounter another’s pain. Questioning can derail the speaker’s train of thought. Praising and agreeing, while validating, may ignore another’s emotions. Even reassurance can fail to offer adequate space to feel what’s true and is often motivated by our own discomfort.

同理心与某些回应之间的区别可能很微妙。同情心通常被认为是积极的，但其中可能包含怜悯的成分，这种怜悯的特点是疏离感和不愿直面他人的痛苦。提问可能会打断说话者的思路。赞扬和赞同虽然能起到肯定作用，但可能会忽略他人的情绪。即使是安慰，也可能无法提供足够的空间去感受真实的感受，而且往往是出于我们自身的不适。

While some of these responses may be useful at the appropriate time, they are usually habitual and automatic, taking the place of genuine empathy. What would it be like, instead, to feel into the other person’s experience? Maintaining presence, how might you respond from natural empathy?

虽然有些回应在适当的时候可能有用，但它们通常是习惯性的、自动的，取代了真正的同理心。那么，如果能够设身处地地感受对方的体验，又会是怎样一番景象呢？保持专注，你会如何以自然的同理心做出回应呢？

With empathy, we join another in what they feel. It’s often expressed more through our tone than specific words. We can say “I’m so sorry” with cool distance or with sincere concern. At its core, empathy seeks to know experience directly, on its own terms, without trying to fix it, change it, or explain it. This willingness to be with experience is the key to empathy.

同理心让我们感同身受，体会他人的感受。它往往更多地体现在语气而非具体的言辞上。我们可以冷淡地说“我很抱歉”，也可以真诚地表达关切。同理心的核心在于直接地、客观地理解他人的体验，而不是试图去改变、修正或解释它。这种与体验同在的意愿是同理心的关键。

Three Dimensions of Empathy

同理心的三个维度

Maya Angelou once said, “If I had the power, I would make everybody an African American at least for one week; know what it’s like.” 8 What would be the effect if everyone in the United States knew from the inside the daily experience of living with brown skin in America? That kind of empathy could begin to heal the legacy of slavery and racism in this country.

玛雅·安杰卢曾说过：“如果我有能力，我会让每个人至少体验一周非裔美国人的生活；让他们知道那是什么滋味。”如果美国每个人都能从内部了解在美国拥有棕色皮肤的日常生活，那会产生怎样的影响？这种同理心或许能够开始治愈这个国家奴隶制和种族主义遗留的创伤。

True empathy is three-dimensional; it is at once cognitive, affective, and somatic. Cognitive empathy is about taking the other’s perspective. It’s the ability to put ourselves in another’s shoes and understand intellectually how a person feels. Affective (emotional) empathy means being able to feel along with the other person. It goes beyond a cognitive grasp of another’s internal world to an emotional experience of it. Just as a stringed instrument vibrates with harmonic resonance, so too our heart can tremble in resonance with the suffering or delight of another.

真正的同理心是三维的，它同时包含认知、情感和身体层面。认知同理心是指设身处地地站在他人的角度思考问题，也就是能够设身处地地理解他人的感受。情感同理心则意味着能够与他人感同身受，它超越了对他人内心世界的认知理解，而是一种情感上的体验。正如弦乐器会因和谐的共鸣而颤动，我们的心也会因他人的痛苦或喜悦而颤抖。

The third kind of empathy is somatic empathy, which is the ability to sense another’s experience in an embodied way. 9 This is a visceral, gut-level understanding. In his renowned book Between the World and Me, the African American writer Ta-Nehisi Coates describes a powerful somatic empathy in a letter to his teenage son:

第三种同理心是躯体同理心，它是一种能够以身体感受的方式感知他人经历的能力。这是一种发自内心的、本能的理解。非裔美国作家塔-内西·科茨在他著名的著作《在世界与我之间》中，在一封写给他十几岁儿子的信里，描述了一种强烈的躯体同理心：

But all our phrasing—race relations, racial chasm, racial justice, racial profiling, white privilege, even white supremacy—serves to obscure that racism is a visceral experience, that it dislodges brains, blocks airways, rips muscle, extracts organs, cracks bones, breaks teeth. You must never look away from this. You must always remember that [it lands]…with great violence, upon the body. 10

但我们所有的措辞——种族关系、种族鸿沟、种族正义、种族歧视、白人特权，甚至白人至上主义——都掩盖了种族主义是一种切肤之痛的体验，它会摧毁大脑、阻塞呼吸道、撕裂肌肉、摘除器官、折断骨骼、打碎牙齿。你绝不能对此视而不见。你必须始终牢记，它会以极大的暴力冲击你的身体。

Deepening empathy is not merely a cognitive or intellectual exercise, though it begins there. It is an endeavor to inhabit both an emotional and an embodied understanding of another’s experience. Without these complementary dimensions, our empathy will be incomplete. When cognitive empathy is divorced from affective empathy, it can be used to manipulate or harm others, even to make torture more effective. True empathy is the integration of all three of these domains. It can bring healing, resilience, and transformation.

加深同理心并非仅仅是认知或智力上的练习，尽管它始于此。它是一种努力，旨在从情感和切身层面去理解他人的经历。缺少这些互补的维度，我们的同理心便是不完整的。当认知同理心与情感同理心分离时，它可能被用来操纵或伤害他人，甚至使酷刑更加有效。真正的同理心是这三个维度的融合。它能够带来疗愈、韧性和转变。

Empathy challenges the view that we are separate and invites us to reach for our shared humanity with others. The first step is connecting more deeply with our own experience through mindfulness. Self-awareness is the basis for empathic connection. As we experience the inner landscape of our life with more detail and richness, so grows our ability to understand the inner lives of others. 11

同理心挑战了我们彼此分离的观点，并引导我们与他人建立共同的人性。第一步是通过正念更深入地体验自身经历。自我觉察是建立同理心的基础。当我们更细致、更丰富地体验自身内在世界时，我们理解他人内心世界的能力也会随之增强。

We then need to put down our own story, to step outside of our frame of reference. In describing the role of empathy in his craft, Broadway actor Okieriete Onaodowan put it quite eloquently: “To walk a mile in my shoes, you must first take off your own.” 12 We stretch our heart and mind beyond our own views, opinions, and feelings to envision the inner world of another. We use imagination, creativity, and intuition to sense what it might be like to live inside their skin.

接下来，我们需要放下自己的故事，跳出固有的认知框架。百老汇演员奥基里特·奥纳多万（Okieriete Onaodowan）在描述同理心在其表演艺术中的作用时，曾精辟地指出：“要想感同身受，首先要脱下自己的鞋子。” 12 我们敞开心扉，超越自身的视角、观点和感受，去设身处地地去想象他人的内心世界。我们运用想象力、创造力和直觉，去体会生活在他人的视角之下会是怎样的感受。

Listening with empathy is a primary way of coming from curiosity and care and a building block of dialogue. Here are three ways you can begin to practice bringing more empathy into your life that synthesize what you’ve learned in this chapter.

用同理心倾听是出于好奇和关怀的主要方式，也是对话的基石。以下三种方法可以帮助你开始在生活中练习培养更多同理心，它们综合了你在本章中所学到的知识。

PRACTICE : Empathy

练习：同理心

Try practicing this in conversations that aren’t about you. It’s often easier to access empathy when you’re not under fire. Remember that empathy is not in the words; it’s a quality of presence in your heart. Aim to understand the other person’s experience and let the words flow naturally.

试着在与你无关的对话中练习这种方法。当你没有受到攻击时，往往更容易产生同理心。记住，同理心不在于言语，而在于你内心深处的感受。努力理解对方的经历，让话语自然流露。

SILENT EMPATHIC PRESENCE : Practice listening completely, with the heartfelt intention to understand and “feel into” what the other person is saying. How is this for them?

无声的同理心：练习全神贯注地倾听，用心去理解和“感受”对方所说的话。这对他们来说感觉如何？

PARAPHRASE : After listening, summarize the gist of what you’ve heard. What are the key features of what they’ve said? Sometimes simply repeating one or two key words can be enough.

复述：听完后，总结一下你听到的内容要点。他们说的话有哪些关键点？有时候，只需重复一两个关键词就足够了。

EMPATHIC REFLECTION : After listening, check that you understand by reflecting what you hear is most important to them. This may include how they feel and/or what they need. What matters most to this person, beneath the story? How can you help them feel heard? Remember to phrase your reflections as questions, checking to ensure you’ve got it right.

同理心反馈：倾听之后，通过反馈来确认你是否理解对方的诉求，并指出对他们而言最重要的是什么。这可能包括他们的感受和/或需求。在故事的背后，对这个人来说最重要的是什么？你如何才能让他们感到被倾听？记住，要以提问的形式表达你的反馈，并反复确认你是否理解正确。

There are many other ways to show empathy. We may express empathy through a kind word, with loving touch, or by sharing how we feel in response to what we hear. At times, we can show empathy by expressing interest with open-ended invitations, “Tell me more…” or “What else?”

表达同理心的方式还有很多。我们可以通过一句温暖的话语、充满爱意的抚摸，或者分享我们对所听到内容的感受来表达同理心。有时，我们也可以通过提出开放式的邀请来表达兴趣，比如“跟我说说更多……”或者“还有什么想说的吗？”

My student Susan teaches high school art and told me the following story. Avery, a freshman who is usually cheerful and bubbly, began showing up early to class. Susan struck up a conversation and realized how much Avery was struggling. They agreed to meet later that day to talk, when Susan had more time.

我的学生苏珊教高中美术，她跟我讲了下面这个故事。艾弗里是个高一新生，平时活泼开朗，但最近开始经常提前到教室。苏珊主动和她攀谈起来，发现艾弗里学习很吃力。她们约好当天晚些时候见面详谈，等苏珊有空的时候再聊。

“I don’t want to go to this school anymore,” Avery said. She was thinking about dropping out. Susan noticed the impulse to go into problem-solving mode, an old habit of hers. Having just finished our week’s lesson on empathy, she paused and decided to try listening instead. “Tell me more. What’s going on?”

“我不想再去这所学校了，”艾弗里说。她正在考虑退学。苏珊注意到她又开始像以前那样，下意识地进入解决问题的模式。苏珊刚刚结束了我们这周关于同理心的课程，她停顿了一下，决定试着倾听。“跟我说说吧。到底发生了什么事？”

Avery began to open up. She was being bullied. She felt sad, alone, and depressed. Every time Susan noticed the urge to fix or solve, she attended to feeling the weight of her body and her feet on the floor, and resisted the temptation to offer solutions. Susan focused her attention on what Avery was feeling and reflected what she was hearing. Avery began to cry, oscillating between speaking, sobbing, and awkwardly making eye contact as if to check whether all of this was okay. There were a lot of tears, tissues, and long moments in which Susan simply held Avery’s gaze.

艾弗里开始敞开心扉。她被欺负了。她感到悲伤、孤独和沮丧。每当苏珊察觉到想要帮她解决问题的冲动时，她都会专注于感受艾弗里身体的重量和双脚踩在地板上的感觉，并克制住想要提供解决方案的冲动。苏珊将注意力集中在艾弗里的感受上，并回应她所听到的。艾弗里开始哭泣，时而说话，时而抽泣，时而笨拙地与苏珊对视，仿佛在确认这一切是否正常。泪水、纸巾，还有苏珊长时间凝视着艾弗里的双眼。

Avery spoke more about her feelings of sadness, loneliness, and not feeling valued. “I’ve felt like this since first grade,” Avery mentioned. “Was that the first time you felt so sad and alone?” Susan inquired. No, it started when she was three, when her dad left. They looked at each other, realizing they’d hit the root of her pain. Eventually they explored what Avery might need at school. They came up with some strategies to address the bullying. Avery decided to stay in school and to make a public art piece for the classroom about depression.

艾弗里更多地谈起了她的悲伤、孤独和不被重视的感觉。“我从一年级就开始这样了，”艾弗里说。“那是你第一次感到如此悲伤和孤独吗？”苏珊问道。不，这一切始于她三岁的时候，那时她爸爸离开了。她们彼此对视，意识到她们找到了她痛苦的根源。最终，她们探讨了艾弗里在学校可能需要什么。她们想出了一些应对校园霸凌的策略。艾弗里决定留在学校，并为教室创作一件关于抑郁症的公共艺术作品。

This is the power of empathy. We can receive each word expressed, each emotion revealed, with a listening heart. When we come from curiosity and care instead of our default, habitual communication strategies, healing and transformation are possible.

这就是同理心的力量。我们可以用一颗聆听的心去接纳每一个字句，每一份情感流露。当我们以好奇和关怀而非惯常的沟通方式去对待他人时，疗愈和转变便成为可能。

PRINCIPLES

原则

People are more likely to be willing to listen when they feel heard. To build understanding, reflect before you respond.

人们在感到被倾听时更愿意倾听。为了增进理解，请在回应前先思考。

KEY POINTS

要点

The intention to understand is often expressed through listening, which involves temporarily putting aside our own thoughts, feelings, views, and opinions. We can listen in many ways:

理解的意图通常通过倾听来表达，这需要我们暂时放下自己的想法、感受、观点和意见。我们可以通过多种方式倾听：

• With complete, wholehearted presence

• 全心全意地投入

• To the content of what someone says

• 指某人所说的话的内容

• To the feelings and needs beneath the content

• 触及内容背后的情感和需求

Staying connected in conversation helps us build understanding and collaborate:

保持沟通交流有助于我们增进理解和开展合作：

DON ’ T LET THE CALL DROP : Seek to establish and maintain connection in conversation.

不要让通话中断：努力在对话中建立和保持联系。

REFLECT BEFORE YOU RESPOND : Confirm that you’re hearing each other accurately before moving on. This “completes a cycle” of communication.

回应前请三思：在继续之前，请确认你们都准确理解了对方的意思。这样才能完成一个完整的沟通循环。

At the heart of listening is empathy, which includes:

倾听的核心是同理心，其中包括：

• Cognitive empathy: seeing things from another’s perspective

认知同理心：从他人的角度看待事物

• Affective empathy: feeling another’s emotions

• 情感共情：感受他人的情绪

• Somatic empathy: sensing another’s embodied experience

• 躯体同理心：感知他人的身体体验

QUESTION & ANSWER

问答

Q: What if someone wants advice? Is that ever okay?

问：如果有人想寻求建议呢？这样做可以吗？

Of course. When someone asks for advice, you might try offering empathy first. I’ll often say, “I’m happy to share some of my ideas, but first I just want to take in what you’ve said.” I’ll follow that with an empathic reflection of what I’m hearing and check if I’ve understood. This can help the other person process their experience and clarify what matters. I then circle back to inquire if they still want advice; sometimes it’s no longer relevant.

当然。当有人寻求建议时，你可以先尝试表达同理心。我通常会说：“我很乐意分享一些我的想法，但首先我想先听听您说了些什么。” 之后，我会以同理心回应我听到的内容，并确认我是否理解正确。这可以帮助对方梳理自己的经历，理清哪些事情才是最重要的。然后，我会再次询问他们是否仍然需要建议；有时，建议可能已经不再适用。

If the tables are turned and you want to give someone advice, check first. Let them know: “I have an idea that I think might be helpful. Are you open to some advice?” This honors their autonomy, minimizes the chances that your input will be disempowering, and guards against giving advice as a way of soothing your own anxiety.

如果角色互换，你想给别人提建议，最好先征求对方的意见。你可以这样说：“我有个想法，或许对你有帮助。你愿意听听我的意见吗？” 这样既尊重了对方的自主权，又能最大限度地降低你的建议会让他们感到无力的可能性，还能避免你为了缓解自己的焦虑而给出建议。

Q: I’ve been exploring these empathy tools with close friends and family and my new approach creates a lot of awkwardness. What do you do when others expect you to communicate in a certain way?

问：我一直在和亲朋好友一起探索这些同理心技巧，但我的新方法却造成了很多尴尬。当别人期望你以某种特定方式沟通时，你会怎么做？

It can be confusing when our attempts to create more connection backfire. Part of what you’re experiencing is the relational dimension of communication habits. They occur in a dynamic, so when we shift it affects others. It also may simply be the learning curve; it takes time to find an authentic voice with these tools.

当我们试图建立更多联系却适得其反时，难免会感到困惑。你所经历的部分原因在于沟通习惯的关系层面。沟通习惯是一个动态的过程，因此当我们改变沟通方式时，也会影响到他人。当然，这也可能仅仅是学习的过程；运用这些工具找到真正属于自己的表达方式需要时间。

Let go of the form and focus on your genuine intention to connect. What would help this person to feel heard? If someone is used to us showing care by asking questions or agreeing and we respond by reflecting their needs, that may throw them off. Try to tune in to what they want. When all else fails, let people know that you’re trying something new that you hope will bring you closer. Ask them to humor you while you learn.

放下形式，专注于你真诚的沟通意图。怎样才能让对方感到被倾听？如果对方习惯于我们通过提问或附和来表达关心，而我们却以回应他们的需求的方式来回应，这可能会让他们感到不自在。试着去理解他们想要什么。如果所有方法都无效，那就告诉对方你正在尝试一种新的沟通方式，希望能够拉近彼此的距离。请他们在你学习的过程中给予一些理解和包容。

# ↩

part three

# ↩

第三部分

the third step

第三步

focus on what matters

专注于重要的事情

THE FIRST TWO steps we’ve covered in this book set the stage for effective conversation: leading with presence makes everything possible; coming from curiosity and care points us in the right direction and guides the conversation. The third step, focusing on what matters, determines where we actually go.

本书前两步为有效对话奠定了基础：以临场感引领，一切皆有可能；怀着好奇心和关怀，指引我们走向正确的方向，并引导对话。第三步，聚焦于真正重要的事情，决定了我们最终的对话方向。

This third step is about training where we put our attention. There are so many elements to a conversation. How do we sort out what’s relevant from what’s not? How do we determine what to address first? Training our attention is an invaluable resource in navigating these complexities.

第三步是关于训练我们如何集中注意力。对话中包含诸多要素。我们如何区分哪些是相关的，哪些是不相关的？我们如何决定首先讨论什么？训练我们的注意力是应对这些复杂情况的宝贵资源。

I’d like to invite you to do a short experiment. First, place your attention in your hands and feel any sensations you notice there: warm or cool, heavy or light, dry or moist. Now put your attention in your feet and feel any sensations there: temperature, weight, texture.

我想邀请你做一个小实验。首先，请将注意力集中在你的双手上，感受一下它们的感觉：温暖或凉爽、沉重或轻盈、干燥或湿润。现在，请将注意力集中在你的双脚上，感受一下它们的感觉：温度、重量、质地。

Moving your attention from your hands to your feet illustrates a fundamental aspect of the mind: we can have conscious choice over where we place our attention. We use our hands and feet all day long, so we can put our attention there at will. This capacity to train our attention is the basis for the third step to effective conversation.

将注意力从手部转移到脚部，体现了思维的一个基本方面：我们可以有意识地选择将注意力放在哪里。我们整天都在使用手脚，因此可以随意将注意力集中在那里。这种训练注意力的能力是有效对话第三步的基础。

Marshall Rosenberg points out four key aspects of experience that, when clearly identified, help us stay connected to our humanity and support collaboration. Rather than being limited by blame, reactive judgment, and narrow interpretations, we learn to parse the actual observations that are most relevant to a situation, the emotions associated with those events, the deeper concerns and needs from which those feelings arise, and the specific requests that might move a conversation forward. In other words: What happened? How do you feel about it? Why? And where do we go from here?

马歇尔·卢森堡指出，清晰地识别经验的四个关键方面，有助于我们保持人性联结，并促进合作。我们不再受制于指责、反应式的评判和狭隘的解读，而是学会分析与情境最相关的实际观察结果、与这些事件相关的情绪、这些情绪背后更深层次的关切和需求，以及能够推动对话发展的具体请求。换句话说：发生了什么？你对此有何感受？为什么？我们接下来该怎么做？

In part three , we’ll train our attention to discern and weave together these four components—observations, emotions, needs, and requests. As we grow familiar with these aspects of experience, we learn how they fit together like steps of a dance. We can use them to express ourselves more clearly and hear one another more easily.

在第三部分，我们将训练自己去辨别和整合这四个要素——观察、情绪、需求和请求。随着我们对这些体验层面的熟悉程度加深，我们会逐渐明白它们如何像舞蹈的舞步一样完美契合。我们可以运用它们来更清晰地表达自己，也更容易地倾听彼此。

Within this rich domain, the third step to effective conversation is extraordinarily flexible. Focusing on what matters can be a broad view of things or a narrow treatment of one aspect. We hone our attention to keep identifying what matters most in any given moment. This kind of skill gives us great freedom and flexibility in our communication, setting aside what’s extraneous for what’s essential. When we stay focused on what matters, we can say what we mean and build an effective conversation one step at a time.

在这个丰富的领域中，有效对话的第三步具有极大的灵活性。关注重点可以是宏观的视角，也可以是微观的层面。我们需要不断磨练自己的注意力，才能在任何特定时刻识别出最重要的事情。这种能力赋予我们极大的沟通自由和灵活性，让我们能够舍弃无关紧要的内容，专注于本质。当我们始终专注于重要的事情时，就能准确表达自己的想法，并一步步构建有效的对话。

# ↩

7

getting down to what matters

回到正题

Now here is my secret. It is very simple. It is only with one’s heart that one can see clearly. What is essential is invisible to the eye.

—ANTOINE DE SAINT-EXUPÉRY

这就是我的秘密。它很简单。只有用心才能看得更清楚。真正重要的东西，用眼睛是看不见的。——安托万·德·圣埃克苏佩里

IMAGINE WHAT IT would be like if, no matter what anyone said or did, you were able to hear the deeper concerns beneath their words and actions. What would it be like to see into their heart and sense what they were truly longing for, to feel natural empathy for that person? Or to know intuitively what was most important to you in any given situation?

想象一下，无论别人说什么做什么，你都能听出他们言行背后更深层次的担忧，那会是怎样一番景象？能够看透他们的内心，感受到他们真正渴望的是什么，并自然而然地对他们产生同理心，那又会是怎样一番体验？或者，能够凭直觉知道在任何情况下什么对你来说最重要，那又会是怎样一番感受？

This is possible. It’s the result of training our attention to identify human needs and values. It is a practice that is at once transformative, powerful, and liberating. It can take time and a certain discipline of attention to learn to see in this way, but it’s entirely within our grasp and the results are profound.

这是可能的。这源于我们训练自己去识别人类的需求和价值观。这种练习既具有变革性，又充满力量，更能解放人心。学会以这种方式观察需要时间和一定的专注力，但这完全在我们能力范围之内，而且其结果意义深远。

In chapter 5 we explored one of the fundamental views at the heart of communication practice: everything we do, we do to meet a need. This is so core that I want to delve deeper into the implications of this perspective and the training of attention that supports it. To realize the transformative power of this view, we need to learn about needs and values. Being skilled at identifying needs and relating to them wisely brings more insight, freedom, and choice, allowing us to navigate even the most difficult relationships.

在第五章中，我们探讨了沟通实践的核心观点之一：我们所做的一切，都是为了满足某种需求。这一点至关重要，因此我想更深入地探讨这一视角及其背后的意义，以及支撑这一视角的注意力训练。为了充分发挥这一观点的变革力量，我们需要了解需求和价值观。善于识别需求并明智地与之互动，能够带来更深刻的洞察力、更大的自由度和更多的选择，使我们能够驾驭最棘手的人际关系。

When I was first introduced to the concept of needs at a communication workshop in my early twenties, I was astounded. I’d been going through a fairly rough period: feeling lonely, struggling to find my place in the world, getting into conflicts with coworkers and family. Learning that there were real reasons behind my emotions was a revelation and a relief. I had found a new tool to understand behavior that made sense intuitively: we are each just doing our best to meet our needs.

二十出头的时候，我在一次沟通工作坊上第一次接触到“需求”这个概念，当时我震惊不已。那段时间我过得相当艰难：感到孤独，难以找到自己的人生方向，还和同事、家人都产生了冲突。了解到我的情绪背后有着真实的原因，对我来说既是一种顿悟，也是一种解脱。我找到了一种理解行为的新方法，而且这种方法也符合直觉：我们每个人都在尽力满足自己的需求。

In Nonviolent Communication and the work of many psychologists and social theorists, the term need refers to something very specific, different from ordinary usages. Colloquially we might say “I need you to listen to me” or “I need you to be on time.” These are strategies —ideas about how to meet our needs. Needs are what matter beneath our strategies. 1 They are fundamental values that drive our actions. If I want you to listen to me, I may need understanding. A desire for more punctuality may be about valuing respect, teamwork, or efficiency.

在非暴力沟通以及众多心理学家和社会理论家的研究中，“需求”一词指的是非常具体的东西，与日常用法有所不同。在口语中，我们可能会说“我需要你听我说”或“我需要你准时”。这些都是策略——满足我们需求的策略。需求才是我们策略背后真正重要的东西。它们是驱动我们行动的基本价值观。如果我希望你听我说，我可能需要的是理解。渴望你更加守时，可能源于对尊重、团队合作或效率的重视。

Needs are the core values that motivate our actions. They’re what matter most, the root reasons for why we want what we want. *1

需求是驱动我们行动的核心价值观。它们至关重要，是我们想要某些东西的根本原因。

We can think of needs as facets of our humanity. They are universal, positive qualities that animate a flourishing human life. We all share the same needs, though we feel them with varying degrees of intensity and have different strategies to meet them. 2 Anything that’s tied to a specific person, place, time, object, or action is a strategy. Some strategies succeed, some do not. Some are wise, some are unwise. Any action can be understood as an attempt to meet many needs. We take a walk for health, relaxation, or to clear our head. Similarly, there are many strategies to meet a given need: we might relax by talking to a friend, going out, or doing yoga.

我们可以将需求视为人性的各个方面。它们是普遍存在的积极品质，赋予人类生活活力。我们都拥有相同的需求，尽管我们对这些需求的感受强度各不相同，满足需求的方式也各有差异。任何与特定人物、地点、时间、物品或行为相关的事物都是一种策略。有些策略成功，有些则失败。有些策略明智，有些则不明智。任何行为都可以被理解为满足多种需求的尝试。我们散步是为了健康、放松或清醒头脑。同样，满足特定需求也有许多策略：我们可以通过与朋友聊天、外出或练习瑜伽来放松身心。

A Constellation of Needs

一系列需求

Abraham Maslow was one of the primary figures to introduce the concept of human needs in the modern era. In his formative theory of psychological health, he proposed a “hierarchy of needs,” sometimes depicted as a pyramid, with our most basic, physiological needs at the base; relational needs such as community, belonging, and respect in the middle; and higher needs such as meaning, fulfillment, and peace toward the top. 3 Maslow’s work was further developed by fellow humanistic psychologist Carl Rogers, who went on to mentor Marshall Rosenberg.

亚伯拉罕·马斯洛是现代引入人类需求概念的主要人物之一。在他开创性的心理健康理论中，他提出了“需求层次理论”，有时被描绘成金字塔：最基本的生理需求位于底部；关系需求，例如社群、归属感和尊重，位于中间；更高层次的需求，例如意义、成就感和内心的平静，位于顶部。马斯洛的理论后来由人本主义心理学家卡尔·罗杰斯进一步发展，罗杰斯后来又指导了马歇尔·卢森堡。

The concept of a hierarchy of needs points to the fact that, in many situations, it becomes difficult to attend to higher needs when more basic ones aren’t met. If we’re stressed and tired, it may be harder to access empathy. Creativity may take a back seat if we don’t have access to clean water, medicine, or physical safety.

需求层次理论指出，在许多情况下，当基本需求得不到满足时，就很难顾及更高层次的需求。如果我们压力过大、疲惫不堪，就很难产生同理心。如果我们无法获得清洁的水源、药品或人身安全保障，创造力也可能受到抑制。

Yet there is no absolute hierarchy of needs. There are countless ways in which we rise to the occasion above our basic needs. We may find patience to bear with a difficult conversation when we’re stressed; parents and partners make daily acts of self-sacrifice for children and lovers; throughout history and to this day individuals find strength, compassion, and forgiveness in terrible situations of violence and poverty.

然而，需求并不存在绝对的等级之分。我们总能以无数种方式超越基本需求，满足更高层次的需求。例如，当我们压力巨大时，或许能耐心应对棘手的谈话；父母和伴侣每天都会为了孩子和爱人做出自我牺牲；纵观历史，直至今日，人们在暴力和贫困的困境中依然能够找到力量、同情和宽恕。

I am often moved when I think of people such as Nelson Mandela who, after twenty-seven harsh years in prison, unable to attend the funerals of his own mother and son, famously said, “As I walked out the door toward the gate that would lead to my freedom, I knew if I didn’t leave my bitterness and hatred behind, I’d still be in prison.” 4 Or I think of Etty Hillesum, a Jewish woman whose diaries and letters tell of her extraordinary inner transformation during WWII in occupied Amsterdam and later in a camp prior to being sent to Auschwitz. She dropped a note from the train en route to Auschwitz, where she died, which read, “We left the camp singing.” Those five words speak volumes about the strength of the human spirit to rise above circumstances.

我常常被纳尔逊·曼德拉这样的人所感动。他在狱中度过了二十七年的艰难岁月，甚至无法参加母亲和儿子的葬礼。他曾说过一句名言：“当我走出牢房，走向通往自由的大门时，我知道，如果我不放下心中的苦涩和仇恨，我仍然身陷囹圄。” 我也常常想起埃蒂·希勒苏姆，这位犹太女性的日记和信件记录了她在二战期间，在被占领的阿姆斯特丹以及后来被送往奥斯维辛集中营前的集中营里，经历的非凡的内心转变。在前往奥斯维辛的火车上，她留下了一张纸条，上面写着：“我们歌唱着离开了集中营。” 这五个字，无比展现了人类精神超越逆境的强大力量。

There is a deep well of resilience in human beings. We are not and can never be entirely self-sufficient, but we can develop our inner capacities of self-reliance to a tremendous degree. 5 Needs are fluid. There is no set hierarchy, universally or within the individual. Rather, our needs are a constellation of interrelated qualities within each of us. The ones we value most at any particular time are determined by a myriad of changing factors.

人类拥有深厚的韧性。我们并非也永远无法完全自给自足，但我们可以极大地发展自身的自立能力。需求是流动的，不存在固定的等级制度，无论是普遍意义上的还是个体内部的。相反，我们的需求是我们每个人内在相互关联的一系列特质。我们在任何特定时刻最看重的需求，都受到诸多变化因素的影响。

And yet, all of our needs matter. Human beings can survive for a few minutes without air; for a few days without water; and for a few weeks without food. When our relational and higher needs are not met, there is also real damage—it is just further delayed in time. Infants will die without loving touch. Children raised without sufficient care and empathy may struggle to form healthy relationships in life. Many of us must work hard to heal sufficiently from the absence of such core relational needs early in life. Adults can go only so long without human warmth and meaning before the mind becomes twisted and the spirit breaks.

然而，我们所有的需求都至关重要。人类可以几分钟不呼吸，几天不喝水，几周不吃饭。当我们的人际关系需求和更高层次的需求得不到满足时，也会造成真正的伤害——只不过这种伤害会延迟出现。婴儿如果没有爱的抚触就会夭折。缺乏足够关爱和同理心的孩子，在生活中可能难以建立健康的人际关系。我们中的许多人必须努力疗愈，才能从早年缺失这些核心人际关系需求的创伤中恢复过来。成年人如果长期缺乏人与人之间的温暖和意义，他们的心智就会扭曲，精神也会崩溃。

The List of Human Needs in the following practice isn’t intended to be complete. It indicates the range of needs we have as humans, any of which may be present at any time. NVC trainers have shared a version of this needs list with people all over the world, from all cultures and walks of life, asking, “Do you need these to thrive?” With small nuances, the answer is always yes.

以下练习中的“人类需求清单”并非完整清单。它仅列出了我们作为人类所拥有的各种需求，这些需求可能随时出现。非暴力沟通（NVC）培训师曾与世界各地、来自不同文化背景和各行各业的人们分享过这份需求清单，并询问他们：“你需要这些才能茁壮成长吗？”答案虽略有不同，但通常都是肯定的。

PRACTICE : Reflecting on Human Needs

实践：反思人类需求

Below is a partial list of human needs. Notice how it feels as you read each word. Which ones bring a sense of openness, joy, or relief? Are there any words that evoke discomfort or anxiety? Which needs are most important to you in your life? Does this differ in various roles—at home, at work, with friends?

以下是人类需求的部分列表。阅读每个词语时，请注意你的感受。哪些词语让你感到轻松、快乐或释然？有没有哪些词语让你感到不适或焦虑？在你的生活中，哪些需求对你最重要？这些需求在不同的场合——在家、在工作场所、与朋友相处时——是否有所不同？
