Cultural Myths: Independence, Self-Sufficiency, and Needs

文化迷思：独立、自给自足和需求

We can feel great reluctance to acknowledge our own and others’ needs. We may have many associations with the word need: weakness, dependence, selfishness, being “needy.” I’ve inquired what someone needed only to be met with a flat and defensive shrug: “I don’t need anything. I’m fine.” I’ve heard those same words issue from my own lips as I struggled to protect myself from emotional pain or to maintain a facade of independence.

我们往往很不愿意承认自己和他人的需求。对于“需求”这个词，我们可能有很多联想：软弱、依赖、自私、“需要人照顾”。我曾询问过别人需要什么，得到的却只是冷漠而防御性的耸肩：“我什么都不需要，我很好。” 我也曾说过类似的话，当时我正努力保护自己免受情感伤害，或努力维持独立自主的假象。

When we encounter others’ needs, we may experience feelings of obligation, resentment, suffocation, or indifference. Depending on how we’ve been socialized, we may be highly attuned to others’ needs and feel compelled to meet them (often at the expense of our own autonomy, freedom, or well-being), or we may be more focused on our own needs and feel threatened by others’ requests (often at the expense of our sensitivity, connection, or intimacy). Almost all of us exhibit some complicated mixture of socially conditioned responses that vary depending on the context. Whatever one’s particular style, it’s tragically common for this kind of cultural training to result in feeling inauthentic, stifled or powerless in our lives.

当我们遇到他人的需求时，可能会感到义务感、怨恨、窒息感或冷漠。根据我们成长过程中受到的社会化方式，我们可能对别人的需求高度敏感，并感到有义务去满足他们（这往往会牺牲我们自身的自主性、自由或幸福感）；或者，我们可能更关注自身的需求，并感到他人的要求对我们构成威胁（这往往会损害我们的敏感度、联结感或亲密感）。几乎每个人都会表现出一些复杂的、受社会制约的反应，这些反应会根据不同的情境而变化。无论一个人的具体反应方式如何，这种文化熏陶常常会导致我们在生活中感到不真实、压抑或无力，这令人遗憾。

Gender is a huge area in which this social conditioning occurs: our needs become limited by the reification of gender roles. For me, this was mostly the contemporary Western myths of masculine self-sufficiency (“I don’t need anything”), meritocracy (“Anyone who works hard enough can succeed”), and hyperindividualism (“Decide alone and do it on your own”). From an early age, these stories shaped my experiences and expectations.

性别是这种社会制约发生的重要领域：我们的需求因性别角色的固化而受到限制。对我而言，这主要体现在当代西方关于男性自给自足（“我什么都不需要”）、精英主义（“只要足够努力就能成功”）和极端个人主义（“自己做决定，自己行动”）的神话中。从很小的时候起，这些观念就塑造了我的经历和期望。

As a man conditioned by our culture’s norms, I felt hesitant at times to acknowledge my needs for affection, intimacy and support. I also struggled for many years with feeling overwhelmed whenever I needed help. Unspoken assumptions at school and images in TV shows, movies, and comic books all presented an ideal of the independent hero conquering trials through his own strength. When things got hard, I held my emotions inside and tried to manage on my own. It took great patience (and countless reminders from those who loved me) to understand that we all need support sometimes, and that I could actually ask for help.

作为一个深受文化规范影响的男人，我有时难以启齿自己对关爱、亲密和支持的需求。多年来，每当需要帮助时，我都会感到不知所措。学校里那些不言而喻的假设，以及电视节目、电影和漫画中的形象，都塑造了一种独立英雄凭借自身力量战胜一切的理想形象。每当遇到困难，我都会把情绪压抑在心底，试图独自应对。我花了极大的耐心（以及无数来自爱我的人的提醒）才明白，我们都需要支持，而我其实也可以寻求帮助。

At some point I recognized that I can’t do everything by myself. And perhaps more importantly, why would I want to? I saw that the illusion of independence, the fantasy of being a perfect masculine hero, separated me from others, while acknowledging my limits and asking for help connected us. It gave others the opportunity to see me and to contribute in meaningful ways.

我渐渐意识到，我不可能事事亲力亲为。或许更重要的是，我为什么要这么做呢？我发现，那种独立的幻觉，那种成为完美男性英雄的幻想，反而让我与他人疏离；而正视自己的局限并寻求帮助，却能将我们联系在一起。它让别人有机会看到我，并以有意义的方式为我做出贡献。

For many of the women I am close to in my life, the messages they received growing up were more along the lines of caretaking (“Life’s meaning is found in nurturing others”) and self-sacrifice (“Giving is the highest good”). Many of them were socialized to ignore or negate their personal needs; they were taught to believe their needs didn’t matter. (This was even more true for my grandmothers, who had less access to education and opportunity and gave up their entire lives for their husbands and families.) Female friends and colleagues have had to work hard to counter this social conditioning. The balance for them has often been in embracing their needs for autonomy, honoring the truth of their own experience, and trusting their ability to be assertive. 6

在我生命中，许多与我亲近的女性从小接受的教育更侧重于照顾他人（“人生的意义在于关爱他人”）和自我牺牲（“给予是至善”）。她们中的许多人被社会化地教导要忽略或否定自己的个人需求；她们被灌输了一种观念：自己的需求无关紧要。（我的祖母们更是如此，她们受教育的机会和资源都比较匮乏，为了丈夫和家庭放弃了自己的一切。）我的女性朋友和同事们不得不努力对抗这种社会制约。她们往往需要找到平衡点，既要拥抱自身对自主的需求，又要尊重自身经历的真实感受，还要相信自己有能力坚持己见。

Based on our culture and role in society, certain needs can become viewed as liabilities rather than as natural expressions of our humanity or innate values that animate our life. Many of the beliefs and stories we learn about our needs—though deeply ingrained and firmly held—are simply not true. They are at odds with the reality of our human existence. They’re myths. Complete self-sufficiency isn’t possible; complete self-sacrifice is rarely healthy when performed as a role.

基于我们的文化和社会角色，某些需求可能被视为负担，而非我们人性的自然流露或赋予我们生命活力的内在价值。我们所了解的许多关于自身需求的信念和故事——尽管根深蒂固、难以动摇——却并非事实。它们与我们人类生存的现实背道而驰，是谬论。完全的自给自足是不可能的；而将完全的自我牺牲作为一种角色扮演，也鲜少有益于身心健康。

As mammals, we are born physiologically dependent on those around us. All through childhood and adolescence, our nervous system is forming through relational bonds with adults. We are social creatures, and for millennia we have depended on the strength of close communities for our mental, emotional, and spiritual well-being, not to mention on the environment for sustenance. Every day—more so now than ever before in human history—we depend on thousands for our most basic necessities, from food and clothing to power and transportation. The use of money masks the vast interconnected web of relations upon which our lives depend, while at the same time revealing the depth and breadth of this web.

作为哺乳动物，我们生来就对周围的人有着生理上的依赖。在整个童年和青少年时期，我们的神经系统都是通过与成年人的关系纽带而形成的。我们是社会性动物，千百年来，我们一直依赖紧密社群的力量来维持心理、情感和精神的健康，更不用说依赖环境来获取生存所需了。如今，我们每天——在人类历史上比以往任何时候都更加如此——都依赖成千上万的人来满足我们最基本的生活需求，从食物和衣物到能源和交通。金钱的使用掩盖了我们生活所依赖的庞大而相互关联的关系网络，同时也揭示了这张网络的深度和广度。

Similarly, the story of our great meritocracy in the United States—intricately tied to the myths of self-sufficiency and individualism—fails to account for the gross imbalance in access to resources and opportunities based on skin color, class, gender, sexual orientation, and physical ability, among others, as well as implicit biases for or against our success based on these factors.

同样，美国伟大的精英制度的故事——与自给自足和个人主义的神话紧密相连——未能解释基于肤色、阶级、性别、性取向和身体能力等因素在获取资源和机会方面存在的巨大不平衡，以及基于这些因素对我们成功或失败的隐性偏见。

The effects on our person, our families, and our society of operating under these myths are devastating. When we find ourselves struggling, when we feel depressed or lonely, where do we look for answers? Do we include in our malaise the devaluing of core needs such as connection and belonging? Are we cognizant of the spiritual poverty of modern culture? Do we include the disintegration of community and the incessant barrage of messages equating happiness with consumption and material success? Or do we blame ourselves and consider it a personal failing, wondering, “What’s wrong with me?”

受这些谬论影响，对我们个人、家庭和社会都造成了毁灭性的影响。当我们感到挣扎、沮丧或孤独时，我们该从何处寻求答案？我们是否将人际关系和归属感等核心需求的贬低纳入考量？我们是否意识到现代文化的精神贫瘠？我们是否将社群的瓦解以及将幸福等同于消费和物质成功的铺天盖地的信息也纳入考量？还是我们会责怪自己，将其视为个人的失败，并疑惑：“我到底哪里出了问题？”

In place of recognizing our interconnectedness as humans—in place of the healing truth that we are inseparable from the rest of life, that we depend on one another and this planet for each breath, each sip of water, each morsel of food or love—we struggle to get by, thinking of ourselves as separate.

我们不愿认识到人类之间的相互联系——不愿接受我们与生命其他部分密不可分、我们彼此依赖、依赖地球才能呼吸、喝水、吃东西或获得爱的治愈真理——我们却挣扎求生，认为自己是分离的。

Learning to identify and be aware of our deeper human needs means coming to terms with all of this. It includes mourning the losses we as individuals and as societies have suffered and perhaps feeling anger at ways our institutions, culture, and the media perpetuate a widespread disconnect from our awareness of human needs. I wept when I realized how hard I’d been driving myself to “do it all” on my own, how unquestioned beliefs had prevented me from seeking support for so many years.

学会识别并觉察我们更深层次的人类需求，意味着要正视这一切。这包括哀悼我们作为个体和社会所遭受的损失，或许还会对我们的制度、文化和媒体如何加剧我们对自身需求的认知脱节而感到愤怒。当我意识到自己多年来是如何苦苦挣扎，试图独自“包揽一切”，以及那些未经质疑的信念是如何阻碍我寻求帮助时，我不禁潸然泪下。

This process is about reclaiming our humanity. We are interdependent. However we have been conditioned, our needs matter. It is often our relationships that bring us the most joy and meaning, as well as the most pain and heartbreak. Thus, aspects of healing and wholeness often come through relationship. On a larger scale, we see that it is only by acknowledging our shared needs and collaborating that we will be able to solve the dire problems of our time. There are no individual solutions to structural problems.

这个过程关乎重拾我们的人性。我们彼此依存。无论我们受到何种环境影响，我们的需求都至关重要。人际关系往往带给我们最大的快乐和意义，也带来最大的痛苦和心碎。因此，疗愈和完整往往源于人际关系。从更宏观的角度来看，只有承认我们共同的需求并携手合作，我们才能解决当今时代的严峻问题。结构性问题没有个人能够解决的方案。

This process of healing our hearts, reclaiming our needs, and working together to create a more just and equitable society begins with our ability to identify needs. We can use mindfulness and the intention to understand to inquire what matters most to us in any situation. The following practice builds this core capacity. 7

疗愈心灵、重拾需求、携手共建更加公正平等的社会，这一过程始于我们识别自身需求的能力。我们可以运用正念和理解的意愿，在任何情况下探寻对我们而言最重要的东西。以下练习旨在培养这种核心能力。

PRACTICE : Sensing Your Needs

练习：感知你的需求

Think of something that happened recently that did not meet your needs. Remember to choose something that’s not too difficult or it will be hard to learn the skill.

想想最近发生的哪些事情没有满足你的需求。记住，选择一些不太难的事情，否则学习起来会很困难。

1. Identify what you do want, a specific strategy. What could have happened, what could have been said or done that would have pleased you?

1. 明确你想要什么，制定具体的策略。原本可能发生什么，说了什么或做了什么会让你满意？

2. Inquire: Why is that important? What matters about that to me? Or: If I had that, then what would I have? This is a way of investigating your needs. Don’t think too much or try to figure it out cognitively. Listen inwardly.

2. 询问：为什么这件事很重要？它对我来说有什么意义？或者：如果我拥有了它，我还会拥有什么？这是一种探索自身需求的方法。不要想太多，也不要试图用理性去理解。倾听内心的声音。

3. Whatever response comes, ask one of the questions again. Continue asking that question and listening until you arrive at something that feels like a core value or need. You may feel settled or clear inside when you identify what matters most to you.

3. 无论得到什么回应，都再次提出其中一个问题。反复追问并倾听，直到找到你内心深处的核心价值观或需求。当你明确什么对你最重要时，你可能会感到内心平静或清明。

4. Shift your attention to this need itself, as a universal facet of being human, independent of the situation. Where in your body do you know that this is something important, something you want not just for yourself but for everyone? Can you appreciate the beauty and dignity of this need? Can you sense its innate value? What’s that feel like?

4. 将注意力转移到这种需求本身，将其视为人类普遍存在的一个方面，它独立于具体情境。你身体的哪个部位让你意识到这是很重要的，是你不仅希望自己拥有，也希望每个人都拥有的？你能欣赏到这种需求的美好和尊严吗？你能感受到它内在的价值吗？那是一种怎样的感觉？

You may find it easy to identify what you need, or things may feel quite opaque. It takes time to develop this skill. Be patient with the different thoughts and feelings that arise. What’s important is the inquiry itself, learning how to listen for what matters with curiosity and care.

你或许能轻易辨别自己的需求，也或许会感到迷茫。培养这种能力需要时间。耐心对待涌现的各种想法和感受。重要的是探寻本身，学习如何带着好奇和关怀去倾听那些真正重要的东西。

When we become aware of needs at this root level, something shifts inside. We are more directly in touch with a driving force in our life, and that will have an effect on the felt sense of our body. When we identify a core value or need, we may experience a somatic feeling of being settled, grounded, or clear. We can have a feeling of open spaciousness, an inner alignment, or a sense of energy and vitality.

当我们意识到自身最根本的需求时，内在会发生一些转变。我们会更直接地与生命中的驱动力建立联系，而这会对我们的身体感受产生影响。当我们识别出核心价值观或需求时，可能会体验到一种安定、踏实或清明的身体感受。我们可能会感受到开阔的空间感、内在的和谐，或者充满活力和朝气。

Part of the trick in getting to this level is learning to be conscious of our needs in the positive rather than the negative. They’re about what we do want rather than what we don’t want. To gain proficiency with this skill we must work against the negativity bias—our evolutionary tendency to look for threats and focus on what isn’t working. To create change—in our life, our relationships, our society—we need to imagine and identify new possibilities. Gandhi spoke of the “constructive program.” Martin Luther King Jr. envisioned the “Beloved Community.”

达到这种境界的关键之一在于学会以积极而非消极的视角看待自身需求。这关乎我们真正想要的是什么，而非我们不想要的是什么。为了熟练掌握这项技能，我们必须克服消极偏见——这种源于进化的倾向让我们倾向于寻找威胁，并关注那些不如意的事情。为了创造改变——无论是在我们的生活、人际关系还是社会中——我们需要想象并发现新的可能性。甘地曾提出“建设性方案”，马丁·路德·金则构想了“理想社区”。

Training our attention to identify needs (our own and others’) involves developing several different capacities. First, as we’ve already begun to explore, we expand our vocabulary for needs. The more familiar we are with these succinct words for needs, the more we notice them in our lives. Second, we train our attention to see life through the “lens of needs,” from the point of view that all actions are attempts to meet needs. We practice shifting our perspective from strategies to needs again and again, until it becomes as easy as moving our attention from our hands to our feet.

训练我们识别需求（包括我们自己的和他人的需求）需要培养多种能力。首先，正如我们已经开始探索的，我们需要扩展关于需求的词汇量。我们越熟悉这些简洁明了的需求词汇，就越能在生活中注意到它们。其次，我们需要训练自己从“需求视角”看待生活，即所有行为都是为了满足需求。我们需要反复练习将视角从策略转移到需求，直到这种转变像将注意力从手转移到脚一样自然流畅。

The more we are able to differentiate between our strategies and needs, the more clarity and choice we have. Following a short NVC training in Israel, one participant reported a dramatic shift. He reached for a cigarette in the car and, having just learned that all actions are attempts to meet needs, paused to contemplate his choice. “If that’s true, what am I actually needing in this moment?” He wanted to relax and take his mind off things. In that moment, he saw clearly many options to meet those needs that didn’t compromise his health. He stopped smoking that day.

我们越能区分策略和需求，就越能拥有清晰的思路和更多的选择。一位学员在以色列参加了一次简短的非暴力沟通（NVC）培训后，报告说他的人生发生了戏剧性的转变。他在车里伸手去拿烟，但刚刚了解到所有行为都是为了满足需求，于是他停下来思考自己的选择。“如果真是这样，我此刻真正需要的是什么？”他想放松一下，暂时忘却烦恼。那一刻，他清晰地看到有很多既能满足这些需求又不会损害健康的选择。那天，他就戒烟了。

After a retreat I taught, a woman shared how her newfound understanding of needs transformed a difficult situation with her adult daughter. Her daughter was home for the holidays, had very little money for gifts, and sorely needed a few things herself. She felt ashamed and uncomfortable at the prospect of receiving more than she could give. They talked, and the daughter realized how joyful it would be for her parents to help. She saw how her needs for self-respect and autonomy were not mutually exclusive with her parents longing to contribute. The shame dissipated, and she was able to give and receive with more freedom.

在我主持的一次静修活动之后，一位女士分享了她如何通过对需求的全新理解，化解了与成年女儿之间棘手的局面。她的女儿回家过节，囊中羞涩，买不起礼物，自己也急需一些东西。想到自己可能要付出比接受更多的东西，她感到羞愧和不自在。她们交谈之后，女儿意识到父母的帮助会让她多么开心。她明白，自己对自尊和自主的需求与父母渴望付出并不矛盾。羞愧感消散了，她能够更加自由地给予和接受。

Principle: The more we are able to differentiate between our strategies and needs, the more clarity and choice we have.

原则：我们越能区分我们的战略和需求，我们就越能清晰地了解情况并做出选择。

We always have choice. Even when external options are limited, we have a choice about how we respond to life internally. Things we tell ourselves that we “have to do” are choices to meet our needs. We may stay in a job we loathe because we value having a place to live or need to feed our children. We choose a strategy we don’t like because it meets more profound needs. Becoming conscious of our needs can bring renewed energy and vitality, or it may prompt us to reevaluate our actions and make different choices.

我们永远都有选择。即使外部选择有限，我们仍然可以选择如何从内心深处应对生活。那些我们告诉自己“不得不做”的事情，其实是为了满足自身需求而做出的选择。我们或许会继续做一份自己厌恶的工作，因为我们珍视住所，或是需要养家糊口。我们或许会选择一种自己并不喜欢的策略，因为它满足了我们更深层次的需求。意识到自身的需求可以带来新的活力和能量，也可能促使我们重新审视自己的行为，做出不同的选择。

PRACTICE : Seeing Life through the Lens of Needs

实践：从需求的角度看待生活

To familiarize yourself with this way of paying attention, dedicate a period of time—an hour, a day, or more—to practice viewing yourself and others through the lens of human needs. As your day unfolds, consider what needs you are trying to meet with your choices. As you observe others, consider: What matters to this person? What might be motivating them? Someone getting on a bus, agitated on a phone call, waving goodbye—what needs are they trying to meet?

为了熟悉这种关注方式，不妨抽出一段时间——一小时、一天甚至更久——练习用人类需求的视角来看待自己和他人。在日常生活中，思考你的选择是为了满足哪些需求。观察他人时，思考：对这个人来说，什么最重要？是什么在驱使着他们？比如，有人上了公交车，有人焦躁地打电话，有人挥手告别——他们试图满足哪些需求？

Extend this inquiry to conversations you overhear, coworkers chatting, the news, and so on. Behind each statement, what matters? What might this person need? When is it easiest to identify possible needs? When is it more challenging? Notice the effect of attending to your own and others’ experience in this way.

将这种探究方式扩展到你无意中听到的对话、同事间的闲聊、新闻等等。每句话背后，真正重要的是什么？这个人可能需要什么？什么时候最容易发现潜在需求？什么时候又更难？留意一下以这种方式关注自己和他人的经历会产生怎样的影响。

When we begin to see life through the lens of needs, something unexpected can happen. We may start to see how our commonalities outweigh our differences. Seeing needs is a doorway to compassion. We can understand the stories of blame and judgment we tell, words of anger and defensiveness from others, as expressions of unmet needs. Even extreme acts of violence can be seen as reaching for deeper needs—autonomy, freedom, empathy—however confused or distorted the strategy. As Rosenberg often said, “All violence is a tragic expression of unmet needs.”

当我们开始从需求的角度看待生活时，意想不到的事情就会发生。我们或许会开始意识到，彼此的共同点远大于分歧。理解需求是通往同情心的大门。我们可以将自己讲述的指责和评判的故事，以及他人愤怒和防御的言语，理解为未被满足的需求的表达。即使是极端暴力行为，也可以被视为对更深层次需求的渴求——自主、自由、同理心——无论其策略多么混乱或扭曲。正如罗森伯格常说的：“一切暴力都是未被满足的需求的悲剧性表达。”

Awareness of needs is transformative. The internal mechanism that expresses our unmet needs as blame and judgment (of self or others) is based on our unconscious conditioning. Knowing which needs are at play, we shift into a wider field of awareness where new forms of understanding and creativity become possible. If I’m about to call someone “selfish,” I can pause and inquire what I need. Instead of projecting my dissatisfaction outward as blame, I may recognize that I want consideration or more support.

对自身需求的觉察具有变革性的力量。我们未被满足的需求会转化为责备和评判（无论是对自己还是对他人），这种内在机制源于我们无意识的制约。当我们意识到哪些需求正在发挥作用时，我们的觉察力就会扩展到更广阔的领域，从而产生新的理解和创造力。如果我正要指责某人“自私”，我可以停下来，问问自己需要什么。与其将不满投射到他人身上，指责他人，我或许会意识到自己只是想要得到体谅或更多的支持。

The Power of Vulnerability

脆弱的力量

It’s common to feel vulnerable or awkward discussing our needs. We can expand our capacity for authenticity while recognizing that the conditions to discuss all of our needs may not be present in every relationship. We can take care with what we share, with whom, and when. For example, sensing that someone lacks the capacity to meet our needs for empathy, we may seek empathy from others.

谈论自身需求时感到脆弱或尴尬是很常见的。我们可以提升表达真诚的能力，同时也要意识到，并非每段关系都具备讨论所有需求的条件。我们可以谨慎选择分享的内容、分享对象和分享时间。例如，当我们感觉到某人缺乏满足我们同理心需求的能力时，我们可能会寻求其他人的同理心。

There are a few ways to develop discernment about sharing our vulnerability. First, it’s essential to build close relationships of trust and mutual respect, in which we feel safe enough to explore needs. In a world that often does not acknowledge human needs, even one such connection is invaluable. For me, meeting a couple of folks in my early twenties who could see my pain and offer empathy was tremendously nourishing. It created enough space inside for me to break the cycle of isolation and start to open up to others.

培养辨别力，学会坦诚分享脆弱的一面，有几种方法。首先，建立亲密的、充满信任和相互尊重的关系至关重要，在这种关系中，我们感到足够安全，可以坦诚地表达自己的需求。在这个常常忽视人类需求的世界里，哪怕只有一次这样的联结也弥足珍贵。对我而言，二十出头时遇到几个能够理解我的痛苦并给予我同理心的朋友，对我来说是莫大的滋养。这为我创造了足够的内心空间，让我得以打破孤立的恶性循环，开始向他人敞开心扉。

Second, we can grow proficient at attuning to the level of vulnerability that supports understanding and collaboration, depending on the context. Evan spent time working at one hospital that lacked a culture of appreciation. She worked hard many hours a day, filling in when they were short-staffed and working holidays. Not being seen for her contributions brought up painful fears of inadequacy and distrust in her own value. At home, we could discuss her longing to be seen and to know that she mattered. At work, Evan chose to be less vulnerable. She framed the situation in terms of recognizing each person’s contribution as a way to enhance motivation and teamwork. Instead of discussing her deeper psychological needs, she articulated shared values in the department for contribution, meaning, and teamwork in a way her manager was more likely to hear.

其次，我们可以根据具体情况，逐渐掌握如何调整自身脆弱程度，从而促进理解和协作。埃文曾在一家缺乏认可文化的医院工作过一段时间。她每天辛勤工作好几个小时，人手不足时顶班，节假日也不例外。由于她的贡献不被认可，她感到痛苦，觉得自己能力不足，对自己价值缺乏信任。在家里，我们可以和她讨论她渴望被关注、渴望知道自己很重要的感受。但在工作中，埃文选择减少脆弱感。她把这种情况理解为认可每个人的贡献可以增强积极性和团队合作精神。她没有谈论自己更深层次的心理需求，而是用一种更容易被经理接受的方式，阐述了部门里关于贡献、意义和团队合作的共同价值观。

Third, we can transform our relationship to the experience of vulnerability itself, honoring it as a source of strength rather than a liability. To feel our vulnerability is to be in touch with reality. When we move beyond the discomfort, we find clarity and dignity. It is a great gift to be able to open one’s heart and lovingly speak the truth.

第三，我们可以转变对脆弱体验本身的看法，将其视为力量的源泉而非负担。感受脆弱，就是与现实相连。当我们超越不适感，便能找到清晰的认知和尊严。能够敞开心扉，用爱心说出真相，是一份莫大的恩赐。

Before I was born, my father fought in two wars, losing his younger brother in the second. Later in life, the trauma of these events and the pain of his divorce caught up with him. He grew obese, sedentary, and depressed. My mother, brother, and I each tried our best to offer support, empathy, encouragement, diet plans—you name it. Regardless of the intervention, he would always slide back into the same habits.

在我出生之前，父亲参加过两场战争，并在第二场战争中失去了他的弟弟。后来，这些战争带来的创伤以及离婚的痛苦让他不堪重负。他变得肥胖、缺乏运动，并且抑郁。我和母亲、弟弟都尽力给予他支持、理解和鼓励，制定饮食计划——我们能想到的都试过了。然而，无论我们采取什么措施，他总是会重蹈覆辙，回到以前的坏习惯中。

Out of options, I tried a different approach. During one visit back home, we sat at the dining room table as we usually did. I spoke from my heart, sharing the complete vulnerability of my feelings. “Dad, you know how much I love you. I want you to be here, to be in my life for a long, long time. And when I see the way you’re living, I feel so scared. I’m angry, and worried, and helpless. I want you to take better care of yourself, and I’ve tried everything I know to do to help you and none of it has worked. I don’t know what else to do, so I’m telling you this. What’s it like for you to hear all of this?”

走投无路之下，我尝试了另一种方法。有一次回家探亲，我们像往常一样坐在餐桌旁。我敞开心扉，毫无保留地倾诉了自己的感受。“爸爸，你知道我有多爱你。我希望你永远在我身边，永远陪伴我。可是，看到你现在的生活状态，我感到非常害怕。我既愤怒又担忧，还感到无助。我希望你能好好照顾自己，我已经尽我所能地想办法帮助你，但都无济于事。我不知道还能怎么办，所以才跟你说这些。你听了这些话，感觉如何？”

He looked at me and took my hand in his. He said that he understood, and that he didn’t know what to say. We both shed a few tears. My words did not heal his depression nor his obesity, but it did bring us closer together. The anger and pain in my heart began to dissipate. We enjoy a warm and loving relationship to this day. When one speaks authentically, vulnerability carries tremendous power.

他看着我，握住了我的手。他说他明白，却不知该说什么。我们都流下了眼泪。我的话语并没有治愈他的抑郁症，也没有治好他的肥胖，但却拉近了我们之间的距离。我心中的愤怒和痛苦也开始消散。直到今天，我们依然保持着温暖而充满爱的关系。当一个人真诚地表达自己时，脆弱蕴藏着巨大的力量。

The Beauty of Needs

需求之美

Over time, our relationship with needs matures. In the beginning we often think of them in a personal way. Needs belong to someone (me or you), and we measure them based on the extent to which they are satisfied. Evolution impels part of our mind to continually evaluate: Is my need met? How much? In this mode, our well-being is determined primarily by need satisfaction.

随着时间的推移，我们与需求的关系日趋成熟。起初，我们往往从个人角度看待需求。需求属于某个人（我或你），我们根据需求的满足程度来衡量它们。进化促使我们的一部分思维不断地评估：我的需求是否得到满足？满足程度如何？在这种模式下，我们的幸福感主要取决于需求的满足程度。

This approach limits our ability to navigate dialogue and constrains our inner life. It keeps us narrowly focused on ourselves and perpetually at the whim of circumstance. Regardless of our skill in communicating, much of life is beyond our control. Sometimes our needs are met; sometimes they aren’t. Inner freedom doesn’t come from being able to control outcomes; it comes from knowing our values, developing the inner resources to meet life with balance, and letting go.

这种方式限制了我们进行对话的能力，也束缚了我们的内心世界。它让我们过于关注自身，永远受制于环境。无论我们的沟通技巧如何，生活中很多事情都超出了我们的掌控。有时我们的需求得到满足，有时则不然。内心的自由并非源于掌控结果，而是源于了解自身的价值观，培养平衡应对生活的内在资源，并学会放手。

This process of maturation begins with developing the capacity to be at peace with unmet needs. When life doesn’t offer what we long for, we learn to mourn. We feel the pain of loss, great and small, with tenderness. This may include healing certain core wounds related to chronically unmet needs, often from childhood. When a need has gone unmet for many years, we may develop a quality of desperation around it. Being stranded in a desert, one becomes obsessed with water. At the first signs of moisture, we hold on for dear life! Even after arriving at an oasis, we may not trust there will be enough. Thirsty for love and affection, I suffered through the disintegration of many romantic relationships as I latched on to partner after partner with disproportionate intensity.

这种成熟的过程始于培养与未被满足的需求和平相处的能力。当生活无法提供我们渴望的东西时，我们会学会哀悼。我们会温柔地感受失去的痛苦，无论大小。这可能包括疗愈与长期未被满足的需求相关的某些核心创伤，这些创伤往往源于童年时期。当某种需求多年未被满足时，我们可能会对其产生一种绝望感。就像身处沙漠，我们会对水产生强烈的渴望。一旦发现一丝水源，我们就会紧紧抓住不放！即使抵达绿洲，我们也可能仍然不相信水源充足。我渴望爱与关怀，因此在一段又一段的恋爱关系中饱受痛苦，因为我过分执着地依附于不同的伴侣。

Turning inward opens the door to a new way of seeing. Our willingness to consciously experience an unmet need with awareness is transformative. After bringing empathy and compassion to the pain, we can learn to widen our perspective. Instead of focusing on the need’s satisfaction, we can shift our attention to the need itself, independent of any conditions.

向内探索开启了一扇通往全新视角的大门。我们愿意有意识地觉察未被满足的需求，这本身就具有变革的力量。当我们对痛苦抱有同理心和同情心之后，便能学会拓宽视野。我们不再执着于满足需求，而是将注意力转移到需求本身，使其独立于任何条件之外。

Needs have the fascinating property of being both personal and universal. They are personal in that we feel them intimately and experience directly the results of their satisfaction or lack thereof. Needs are universal to the degree that they are shared by every human. They partake of what it is to be human.

需求具有一种奇妙的特质，它既是个人化的，又是普遍的。说它是个人化的，是因为我们能切身感受到它，并直接体验到它得到满足或未得到满足所带来的后果。说它是普遍的，是因为它为所有人所共有。它是人性的一部分。

Every need also exists as a value that we carry within us, independent of whether or not it is satisfied. When we are in touch with our inner life in this way, a need’s gratification is less salient than our awareness and appreciation of it as a value. 8 Each need, in the very fact of its existence, contains a beauty and a fullness in and of itself as an aspect of our humanity. 9 The need for peace is especially alive in times of war; a vision of equity and love is felt deeply in the midst of violent oppression.

每一种需求都以价值的形式存在于我们内心，无论它是否得到满足。当我们以这种方式与内心世界相连时，需求的满足就显得不那么重要了，重要的是我们意识到并欣赏它的价值。每一种需求，就其存在本身而言，都蕴含着一种美和圆满，是我们人性的一个方面。在战争时期，对和平的需求尤为强烈；在暴力压迫之中，人们深切感受到公平与爱的愿景。

This is an advanced level of awareness, yet when we touch this more universal dimension of our needs, we encounter great freedom. Whether or not our needs are met, we can still “meet” them—we can greet them face-to-face. When I directly encounter my need for peace—when I experience it as an ancient part of my humanity—I can feel it as a value within me whether or not it is fulfilled. This, paradoxically, allows me to advocate energetically for peace without burning out if I do not achieve a desired result, for my actions come from a place of integrity and inner alignment rather than a fixation on the outcome.

这是一种更高层次的觉知，然而当我们触及自身需求的更普遍维度时，我们便会体验到极大的自由。无论我们的需求是否得到满足，我们依然可以“遇见”它们——我们可以直面它们。当我直接面对自己对和平的需求——当我体验到它是我人性中古老的一部分——无论它是否得到满足，我都能感受到它在我内心深处的价值。矛盾的是，这使我能够积极倡导和平，而不会因为未能达成预期结果而精疲力竭，因为我的行动源于正直和内在的和谐，而非执着于结果。

The question is not whether or not we have needs—needs are a fact of our existence—but rather how we relate to them. When our only perspective is a personal view of need gratification (“my needs” or “your needs” being satisfied), we tend to relate to them with a quality of grasping. Depending on our conditioning, we may overlook the reality of others’ needs or erase the importance of our own. We may narrow our primary aim to gratifying certain needs and ignoring others, which often leads to conflict and tension. When we widen our view to a more universal perspective, to appreciating needs in and of themselves, we can remain fully committed to meeting both our own and others’ needs, without being defined by the outcome. Letting go doesn’t mean that we give up on our values, stop caring, or cease working for change. 10 It means that we recognize that the outcome of our efforts is not completely in our hands because in many ways we don’t control the context.

问题不在于我们是否有需求——需求是我们存在的必然事实——而在于我们如何看待这些需求。当我们的视角仅限于满足个人需求（“我的需求”或“你的需求”得到满足）时，我们往往会以一种执着的态度看待它们。根据我们受到的影响，我们可能会忽视他人需求的现实，或者忽略自身需求的重要性。我们可能会将主要目标局限于满足某些需求而忽略其他需求，这往往会导致冲突和紧张。当我们拓宽视野，以更普世的视角去欣赏需求本身时，我们就能全身心地致力于满足自身和他人的需求，而不会被结果所定义。放手并不意味着放弃价值观、停止关心他人或停止为改变而努力。它意味着我们认识到，我们努力的结果并非完全由我们掌控，因为在很多方面，我们无法控制环境。

We can explore developing this advanced awareness with more peripheral needs. For example, if others at work are too busy to offer appreciation for a presentation you gave, can you feel okay inside knowing that you worked hard, sensing your value for appreciation without needing it to be met? Try experimenting with the instructions below to shift your attention from the personal to the universal aspect of a need, from satisfying a need to experiencing its innate value and beauty. 11

我们可以探索如何从更边缘化的需求中培养这种高级意识。例如，如果同事们忙于工作而无暇对你做的演示表示赞赏，你是否能够坦然接受自己付出的努力，感受到自身的价值，而无需刻意追求认可？尝试按照以下说明，将注意力从个人层面转移到需求的普遍层面，从满足需求本身转移到体验需求的内在价值和美感。

PRACTICE : Letting Go and Meeting Your Needs

练习：学会放手并满足自身需求

Think of a situation in the last few weeks in which a need wasn’t met. For this exercise, it’s essential that you choose something that is low on the scale of difficulty in order to learn the skill of shifting your attention between the personal and universal aspects of a need. If you choose something that is too hard (think “water in the desert”), the emotional pain will likely hinder your learning.

想想过去几周里，你遇到过哪些需求没有得到满足的情况。为了练习这项技能，你必须选择难度较低的情况，以便学习如何在需求的个人层面和普遍层面之间切换注意力。如果你选择太难的情况（比如“沙漠中的水”），情绪上的痛苦很可能会阻碍你的学习。

Identify a key need in the situation. Inquire, “What matters about this to me? What do I want?” Listen inwardly, and then ask again, “If I had that, then what would I have?” Keep asking until you feel a settled clarity about the need or value for which you long.

找出问题的关键需求。问问自己：“这件事对我来说有什么重要意义？我想要什么？” 倾听内心的声音，然后再次提问：“如果我拥有了它，我又会拥有什么？” 反复追问，直到你对自己渴望的需求或价值有了清晰的认识。

Place your attention on the personal aspect of this need: the fact that it hasn’t been met. You can say silently to yourself, “My need for _________ wasn’t met.” Notice how it feels to experience the need as a lack, something personal and unfulfilled.

将注意力集中在这种需求的个人层面：它尚未得到满足。你可以默默地对自己说：“我对____的需求没有得到满足。” 注意这种将需求体验为匮乏、个人层面且未被满足的感觉。

Next, let go of the situation, the circumstances, and see if you can shift your attention to the need itself. Focus on the inherent value of this need as a universal aspect of being human. You can say silently to yourself, “I deeply value _________” or, “Just as I long for _________, so do all people need _________.” Can you sense the beauty and dignity of this need? Can you experience its fullness, independent of whether or not it is satisfied?

接下来，放下眼前的境况和环境，试着将注意力转移到需求本身。专注于这种需求作为人类普遍存在的内在价值。你可以默默地对自己说：“我非常珍视____”或者“正如我渴望____一样，所有人都需要____”。你能感受到这种需求的美好和尊严吗？你能体验到它的圆满，而无论它是否得到满足吗？

If you have trouble sensing the universal aspect of the need, try to remember (or imagine) a time when the need was met. Remember how it feels to have the need fulfilled. Then try to shift your attention to the universal aspect of this need as something you would want for all people.

如果你难以感受到这种需求的普遍性，试着回忆（或想象）一次这种需求得到满足的经历。回想一下需求得到满足时的感受。然后，试着将注意力转移到这种需求的普遍性上，把它想象成你希望所有人都能拥有的东西。

Needs in Dialogue

对话中的需求

Identifying our own needs and developing a balanced relationship with them form the groundwork for being able to express ourselves and engage effectively in dialogue. When we understand what matters most, we can de-escalate tension, nurture empathy, and support collaboration. The more we know our own needs and trust our ability to meet them, the more space we have to hear others. At the same time, identifying others’ needs allows us to make heartfelt connections across differences. We gain the ability to sense the deeper values behind positions quite different from our own. Views that may seem incomprehensible on the surface become expressions of our shared humanity.

认清自身需求并与之建立平衡关系，是表达自我和有效对话的基础。当我们明白什么才是最重要的，就能缓和紧张气氛，培养同理心，促进合作。我们越了解自身需求，越相信自己有能力满足这些需求，就越能倾听他人。同时，认清他人需求，也能让我们跨越差异，建立真挚的联结。我们得以感知与自身立场截然不同的深层价值观。那些表面上看似难以理解的观点，最终会成为我们共同人性的体现。

Conflict occurs at the level of our strategies. Understanding what’s at stake can take us out of the strategy-based framework of the conflict, our polarized approach of either/or and win/lose, and generate more space to use our imagination and think creatively together.

冲突发生在我们的战略层面。理解利害关系可以让我们跳出以战略为基础的冲突框架，摆脱非此即彼、输赢两极分化的思维模式，从而腾出更多空间，让我们能够运用想象力，共同进行创造性思考。

On a recent communication retreat, Kristin recounted a recurring situation in which her mother corrected her parenting style, gesturing and making comments, in front of her son. Kristin felt angry and hurt. Past conversations had devolved into screaming matches about who was right. Exploring her needs, we identified that she wanted respect and support for her choices as a parent, and she also wanted her son to have a relationship with his grandmother. Contemplating her mother’s actions, we surmised that she wanted to contribute to her grandson’s learning and growth. Articulating these needs revealed new possibilities for engaging in a dialogue. Instead of arguing about their beliefs, she could imagine discussing parenting strategies and making agreements about what was non-negotiable and where she was willing to flex.

在最近一次沟通交流研讨会上，克里斯汀讲述了一个反复出现的情况：她的母亲当着儿子的面，一边做手势一边评论，纠正她的育儿方式。克里斯汀感到愤怒和受伤。过去，她们的对话总是演变成争吵，争论谁对谁错。通过了解她的需求，我们发现她希望自己的育儿选择得到尊重和支持，也希望儿子能和祖母建立亲密的关系。思考她母亲的行为，我们推测她希望为孙子的学习和成长贡献一份力量。明确这些需求后，我们发现了与母亲进行对话的新可能性。与其争论彼此的信念，她可以设想与母亲讨论育儿策略，并就哪些是不可妥协的原则以及哪些方面可以做出让步达成共识。

Focusing on needs in conversation relies upon the very simple principle we’ve already seen: the more we understand one another, the easier it is to find solutions. When discussing any issue, it’s helpful to keep this principle in mind. Our aim is to get all needs out on the table. Then we examine the situation together, from all angles.

在对话中关注需求，依据的是我们之前已经提到的一个非常简单的原则：我们越了解彼此，就越容易找到解决方案。在讨论任何问题时，牢记这一原则都很有帮助。我们的目标是把所有需求都摆到桌面上来。然后，我们从各个角度一起审视情况。

Principle: The more we understand one another, the easier it is to find solutions that work for everyone. Therefore, establish as much mutual understanding as possible before problem solving.

原则：我们越了解彼此，就越容易找到对大家都适用的解决方案。因此，在解决问题之前，应尽可能建立相互理解。

Such mutual understanding has the power to shift our position in a dialogue. When we understand one another’s inner life, our priorities often reorganize. Contacting the universal quality of needs, the sense of identification with “my needs” or “your needs” can soften, and we experience the situation from a different perspective. All of the needs present matter, regardless of which person they happen to be located in. Out of this deeper connection, our need for compassion may rise to the surface and create the space for a different outcome.

这种相互理解能够改变我们在对话中的立场。当我们理解彼此的内心世界时，我们的优先事项往往会重新调整。当我们触及需求的普遍性时，对“我的需求”或“你的需求”的认同感就会减弱，我们会从不同的角度看待问题。所有存在的需求都至关重要，无论它们存在于谁身上。在这种更深层次的联结中，我们对同情的需求可能会浮现出来，并为不同的结果创造空间。

Laura found herself overwhelmed and incensed at Thanksgiving one year when—in addition to cooking and hosting the dinner—she was volunteered by her husband to care for his elderly grandmother both the night before and the night of the holiday. In discussing the situation with him, she learned that he had struggled to find a way to make everyone happy and felt awful about “assigning” her this extra responsibility. His grandmother felt uncomfortable having a man look after her at night, and he couldn’t figure out another way to get the family together. Seeing his inner conflict, Laura’s anger shifted. They made some agreements about how to work together in the future and how to share the responsibilities for the holiday.

有一年感恩节，劳拉发现自己既不知所措又怒不可遏。除了准备和招待晚餐，她丈夫还自告奋勇地让她在感恩节前夜和当晚照顾年迈的祖母。在与丈夫商量后，她了解到他一直在努力想办法让每个人都满意，并且对“指派”她这项额外的责任感到很愧疚。他的祖母觉得晚上由男人照顾自己不太自在，而他也想不出其他办法让全家人团聚。看到他内心的挣扎，劳拉的怒气消散了。他们就未来如何合作以及如何分担节日责任达成了一些协议。

This outcome was possible because of a fundamental shift in Laura’s approach to the dialogue from habitual conflict strategies to the intention to understand. Having done some training with me, Laura was able to check her assumptions and her impulse to blame and instead approach the conversation with curiosity. A key to this shift is valuing all of the needs present and letting the other person know that we are interested in finding a solution that works for both of us. When the other person trusts that we are genuinely interested in understanding what they want (not just getting our own way), we can begin to collaborate. The dynamic transforms from opposing forces to curiously examining a puzzle together, side by side.

这一结果的实现，源于劳拉对话方式的根本转变：她从惯常的冲突策略转向了理解的意图。经过我的培训，劳拉能够审视自己的假设和指责的冲动，转而以好奇心参与对话。这种转变的关键在于重视对方的所有需求，并让对方知道我们真心希望找到一个对双方都有利的解决方案。当对方相信我们是真心想了解他们的想法（而不仅仅是为了满足自己的私欲）时，我们才能开始合作。双方的互动模式也从对立转变为携手探索，共同寻找答案。

Principle: Conflict generally occurs at the level of our strategies— what we want. The more deeply we are able to identify our needs— why we want what we want—the less conflict there is.

原则：冲突通常发生在我们的策略层面——也就是我们想要什么。我们越能深入地了解自身需求——我们为什么想要这些——冲突就越少。

Another student of mine, Noga, likes to meditate in the morning. Her roommate is often up early getting ready for work. Noga felt caught. Asserting her own need for quiet left little room for dialogue; not addressing the situation left her at the mercy of his schedule. A shift came when she realized that she genuinely valued both of their needs. She wanted some quiet and respect for her space, but she also wanted him to be able to get ready with ease, without feeling anxious or tiptoeing around the house. Knowing that she wanted to find a solution that honored both of their needs, it became much easier to have the conversation in an open and curious manner.

我的另一个学生诺加喜欢早上冥想。她的室友经常早起准备上班。诺加感到左右为难。如果她坚持自己需要安静的环境，就很难和室友沟通；如果不解决这个问题，她就只能任由室友的作息安排摆布。后来，她意识到自己真心重视他们双方的需求，情况才有所转变。她想要安静的空间，也希望室友能够轻松地准备上班，不用焦虑不安，也不用在屋里蹑手蹑脚。当她意识到自己想要找到一个能兼顾双方需求的解决方案时，她就能以开放和好奇的态度与室友进行沟通了。

Making this shift rests upon our ability to identify others’ needs. In the next exercise, we’ll refine the practice of empathy we’ve already learned by focusing our attention externally on what matters most for someone else.

这种转变的关键在于我们能否识别他人的需求。在接下来的练习中，我们将把注意力转移到对他人最重要的事情上，从而进一步提升我们已经学到的同理心。

PRACTICE : Listening for Needs

练习：倾听需求

This practice contains three parts that develop our capacity to identify others’ needs. Try this out in low-stakes conversations with friends.

这项练习包含三个部分，旨在培养我们识别他人需求的能力。不妨在与朋友的轻松对话中尝试一下。

1. Ground yourself in presence and the intention to understand. Find some genuine curiosity and care.

1. 专注于当下，并怀着理解的意愿。找到真正的好奇心和关怀。

2. As you listen, focus your attention on what they might need. You might ask yourself silently, “What matters here? What’s most important to them about this?”

2. 倾听时，将注意力集中在他们的需求上。你可以默默地问自己：“这里什么最重要？对他们来说，这件事最重要的是什么？”

3. At times, practice completing a cycle of communication by reflecting before you respond. Inquire in a natural way, “Is this what matters to you?” Remember, the intention of this question is to check that you understand rather than to analyze or tell them what they feel.

3. 有时，在回应之前先进行反思，以此来完成一个完整的沟通循环。自然地询问：“这是你关心的事情吗？”记住，这个问题的目的是确认你是否理解对方的意思，而不是分析或替他们表达感受。

Notice how it feels to listen in this way. What does it feel like to check if you understand? Does it lead to more connection? What happens if your guess isn’t totally accurate?

注意一下这种聆听方式的感受。确认自己是否理解是什么感觉？这是否能增进彼此的联系？如果你的猜测并不完全准确，会发生什么？

Focusing our attention on needs can feel awkward at first. Sometimes it’s easiest to listen wholeheartedly and then consider what matters after the other person has finished.

一开始，把注意力集中在需求上可能会感觉很别扭。有时候，最简单的办法是先全神贯注地倾听，等对方说完后再去思考什么才是最重要的。

Many people find that they feel more connected when listening this way. Offering an empathic reflection can produce visible relief. Similar to the somatic shift we feel when we recognize our own needs, another person may spontaneously exhale, sigh, or offer verbal affirmation—“Exactly!” At the same time, guessing what matters isn’t about getting it right. It’s not a performance test. It’s about our genuine intention to understand. If we haven’t understood correctly, the other person will clarify. Even when our guess is not accurate, it can still lead to greater understanding and may even reveal new layers of meaning that the speaker hadn’t sensed.

许多人发现，以这种方式倾听能让他们感到与对方更加亲近。给予同理心的回应可以带来明显的缓解。就像我们意识到自身需求时身体会感受到的变化一样，对方可能会自发地呼气、叹息，或者口头上肯定地说：“正是如此！” 同时，猜测对方的诉求并非在于能否猜对。这并非一场表演测试，而是关乎我们真诚的理解意愿。如果我们理解有误，对方会进行澄清。即使我们的猜测并不准确，它仍然能够加深理解，甚至可能揭示说话者尚未察觉的新含义。

Empathic listening is a gift we can offer in all situations. It can enhance the quality of any relationship, creating more trust and closeness in friendships, family, and intimate bonds. It’s also essential when things get tense. Remembering to listen for needs in a conflict is like gaining a window into another’s world. Negative images of the other person begin to crumble as we see their humanity: “Oh, they want…respect, support, ease… just like me. ”

在任何情况下，同理心倾听都是我们可以给予他人的礼物。它能提升任何关系的质量，在友谊、亲情和亲密关系中建立更多的信任和亲近感。当气氛紧张时，同理心倾听也至关重要。在冲突中倾听对方的需求，就像打开了一扇通往他人世界的窗口。当我们看到对方的人性时，对对方的负面印象便开始瓦解：“哦，他们也想要……尊重、支持、舒适……就像我一样。”

When we become aware of another’s needs, our heart opens; something softens inside as we understand intuitively what matters to someone else. This is a very important point. If we can’t support what we’ve identified in the other party, then we aren’t connecting at the level of needs. If you can’t get behind it and say “Yes, I want that for them,” it’s not a need. Needs are universal; they connect us. They are by definition something that we want for everyone, something to which we can internally say yes.

当我们意识到他人的需求时，我们的心扉便会敞开；当我们凭直觉理解他人真正重视的是什么时，内心深处便会涌起一股暖流。这一点至关重要。如果我们无法支持我们所发现的对方的需求，那么我们就无法在需求层面建立联系。如果你无法真正理解并认同“是的，我希望他们拥有这些”，那么这就不算是真正的需求。需求是普遍存在的；它们将我们彼此连接。从定义上讲，需求是我们希望每个人都拥有的东西，是我们内心能够由衷认同的东西。

Authenticity and Needs

真实性和需求

As our awareness of needs grows, we learn to find an authentic way to discuss this aspect of human experience. In conversation, stating needs in the positive, in a colloquial manner, can make it easier to establish connection and hear one another. Consider the examples in the chart below. What differences do you feel reading the statements?

随着我们对自身需求的认知不断加深，我们学会了用真诚的方式探讨人类经验的这一方面。在对话中，以积极、口语化的方式表达需求，有助于建立联系，让彼此更容易倾听。请参考下表中的示例。阅读这些陈述，你感受到了哪些不同之处？

Needs in the Negative

负面需求

Needs in the Positive

积极方面的需求

“I can’t stand it when things are messy and chaotic.”

“我最讨厌混乱无序的情况。”

“I enjoy it when things are clean and tidy.”

“我喜欢干净整洁的环境。”

“I don’t want to be trapped in our relationship.”

“我不想被困在我们的关系里。”

“I want a sense of space and flexibility in our relationship.”

“我希望我们的关系中能有空间和灵活性。”

“I don’t want to be controlled or told what to do.”

“我不想被控制，也不想被告知该做什么。”

“Having some autonomy and freedom are so important to me.”

“对我来说，拥有一定的自主权和自由非常重要。”

“I don’t want to feel sick or tired anymore.”

“我不想再感到生病或疲惫了。”

“I long to feel healthy and well.”

“我渴望拥有健康的身体。”

Notice how the negative constructions often imply a sense of blame, which can get in the way of being heard. The examples are also more colloquial, forgoing the word need. Below are some additional tips for how to refer to needs colloquially. As you experiment with these tools, try to find your own way of talking about needs and values.

注意，否定句式往往带有指责的意味，这可能会阻碍人们表达自己的想法。这些例子也更口语化，省略了“需要”这个词。以下是一些关于如何用口语表达需求的技巧。在尝试这些方法的过程中，试着找到你自己表达需求和价值观的方式。

Drop the Word Need

去掉“需要”这个词

Because of our cultural associations, the word need may not be useful. Instead, try more natural phrases.

由于文化背景的限制，“需要”这个词可能不太合适。不妨尝试使用更自然流畅的表达方式。

EXAMPLE : Instead of “Do you need more respect?” you might say, “Sounds like you really value respect?” or “You were wanting more respect. Is that right?”

例如：与其问“你需要更多尊重吗？”，不如说“听起来你很重视尊重？”或者“你想要更多尊重，是这样吗？”

ADDITIONAL PHRASES : “I/you love…value…really enjoy…long for…would be nourished by…thrive on…” “X matters to me/you…is important to me/you…is fun for me/you…is meaningful to me/you…”

其他短语：“我/你喜欢……重视……非常享受……渴望……会从中受益……如鱼得水……”“X 对我/你很重要……对我/你很有意义……让我/你觉得有趣……对我/你很有意义……”

Describe the Need with a Phrase

用一句话描述需求

One-word needs are helpful for training our attention to get at the heart of the matter. To acknowledge the context and be more concrete, describe the need with a phrase.

用一个词概括需求有助于我们集中注意力，抓住问题的核心。为了更好地理解语境并使其更加具体，可以用短语来描述需求。

EXAMPLE : Instead of “Sounds like you need more order?” you might say, “You really like knowing that everything is in its place, yes?”

例如：与其问“听起来你需要更有序的环境？”，不如说“你真的很喜欢一切都井然有序，对吗？”

State the Need in the Positive

以积极的方式陈述需求。

Needs are about what we do want rather than what we don’t want. Stating needs in the positive can be empowering and affirming and can move us toward creative solutions. Restate what matters in terms of what someone longs for.

需求关乎我们想要什么，而非我们不想要什么。以积极的方式表达需求可以增强自信，并能引导我们找到创造性的解决方案。用人们渴望的词语来重新表述重要的事情。

EXAMPLE : Instead of “I hear how much you dislike getting mixed messages, huh?” try saying, “I hear how much you want clarity and directness, knowing you can take what’s said at face value. Is that right?”

例如：与其说“我听说你很讨厌收到模棱两可的信息，是吗？”，不如说“我听说你很想要清晰明了、直截了当的信息，并且知道你可以完全相信对方所说的话。是这样吗？”

Ask, Don’t Tell

问，别说

Few people like being told what they are feeling, which can sound patronizing. When listening for what matters, pose reflections as questions—checking that you’ve understood—rather than tell the person what they said.

很少有人喜欢被告知自己的感受，那样听起来可能很居高临下。在倾听真正重要的信息时，与其直接告诉对方他们说了什么，不如以提问的形式提出反馈——确认你是否理解。

EXAMPLE : Instead of “You want to feel more engaged at work,” make it a question: “Do you want to feel more engaged at work?” Or follow the reflection with an inquiry such as, “Is that right?”

例如：与其说“你想在工作中更有投入感”，不如把它变成一个问题：“你想在工作中更有投入感吗？”或者在反思之后提出一个疑问，例如：“是这样吗？”

Over time you will develop more facility with talking about needs in a natural, unforced manner. The foundation is learning to focus your attention on needs and values, what matters most to oneself or another.

随着时间的推移，你会越来越擅长以自然、不做作的方式谈论需求。关键在于学会将注意力集中在需求和价值观上，也就是对自己或他人而言最重要的事。

Rosenberg teaches that, as we grow in skill and awareness, we can learn to hear every statement as saying “Please” or “Thank you.” In some respect, we can boil the essence of any communication down to one of these two messages: “Please, meet my need” or “Thank you, you’ve met my need.” Are we not always saying one or the other?

罗森伯格认为，随着我们技能和意识的增长，我们可以学会将每句话都理解为“请”或“谢谢”。在某种程度上，我们可以将任何沟通的本质归结为以下两种信息之一：“请满足我的需求”或“谢谢，你满足了我的需求”。我们难道不是一直在表达其中之一吗？

When we hear one another in this way, our heart responds with two profound emotions. “Please” gives rise to compassion, and “thank you” to gratitude. In these moments we experience our needs as fundamental expressions of our relatedness. Instead of being trapped alone to fend for ourselves, our lives have something to do with one another. Needs point to our interconnectedness with each other, the environment, and life.

当我们以这种方式倾听彼此时，我们的内心会涌现出两种深刻的情感。“请”会引发同情，“谢谢”会引发感激。在这些时刻，我们体验到自身的需求是彼此关联的基本体现。我们不再孤立无援地自谋生路，而是与彼此息息相关。需求指向我们与彼此、与环境、与生命的紧密联系。

PRINCIPLES

原则

The more we are able to differentiate between our strategies and needs, the more clarity and choice we have.

我们越能区分我们的战略和需求，我们就越能清晰地了解情况并做出选择。

The more we understand one another, the easier it is to find solutions that work for everyone. Therefore, establish as much mutual understanding as possible before problem solving.

我们越了解彼此，就越容易找到对大家都适用的解决方案。因此，在解决问题之前，尽可能地建立相互理解。

Conflict generally occurs at the level of our strategies— what we want. The more deeply we are able to identify our needs— why we want what we want—the less conflict there is.

冲突通常发生在我们的策略层面——也就是我们想要什么。我们越能深入地了解自身需求——我们为什么想要这些——冲突就越少。

KEY POINTS

要点

Needs are the fundamental, root reasons for why we want what we want. When we can identify our needs, we can:

需求是我们想要某样东西的根本原因。当我们能够识别自己的需求时，我们就能：

• Connect: We all share the same needs, though we feel them with varying degrees of intensity and have different strategies to meet them.

• 连接：我们都拥有相同的需求，尽管我们感受到这些需求的强度不同，并且满足这些需求的策略也不同。

• Choose: Becoming conscious of our needs can bring renewed energy and vitality and may prompt us to reevaluate our actions and make different choices.

• 选择：意识到自己的需求可以带来新的能量和活力，并可能促使我们重新评估自己的行为并做出不同的选择。

• Transform Patterns of Blame and Judgment: Knowing which needs are at play, we shift into a wider field of awareness where new forms of understanding and creativity become possible.

• 转变责备和评判的模式：了解哪些需求在起作用，我们就能进入更广阔的意识领域，从而产生新的理解和创造力。

• Collaborate: Work together to find creative solutions to as many needs as possible.

• 协作：共同努力，寻找创造性的解决方案来满足尽可能多的需求。

Training our attention to identify needs (our own and others’) involves:

训练我们关注自身需求（包括自身和他人的需求）的能力包括：

• Expanding our vocabulary for needs

• 扩展我们的词汇量以满足需求

• Training our attention to see life through the “lens of needs”

• 训练我们用“需求视角”看待生活

• Building close relationships of trust and mutual respect, in which we feel safe enough to explore needs

• 建立紧密的信任和相互尊重的关系，让我们感到足够安全，可以探讨需求

• Attuning to the level of vulnerability that supports understanding and collaboration, depending on the context

• 根据具体情况，调整脆弱程度，以促进理解和协作。

• Learning to be at peace with unmet needs

• 学会坦然接受未被满足的需求

• Developing the ability to shift our attention from the personal to the universal aspect of needs, from a narrow focus on satisfying our needs to a broader appreciation for the beauty of human needs

• 培养将注意力从个人需求层面转移到普遍需求层面的能力，从狭隘地关注满足自身需求转向更广泛地欣赏人类需求之美。

QUESTION & ANSWER

问答

Q: When I try to figure out what I need, I get lost, blaming the other person, feeling upset, planning what to say. Do you have any tips for this?

问：当我试图弄清楚自己需要什么时，我反而会迷失方向，责怪对方，感到沮丧，并反复思考该如何开口。您有什么建议吗？

We’re working with decades of conditioning. If we’re emotionally activated, the force of those patterns is even stronger. Give yourself time. Basic mindfulness practice, which steadies our attention, is a huge support here.

我们受到几十年来形成的固有思维模式的影响。如果我们情绪激动，这些模式的力量会更强。给自己一些时间。基本的正念练习，可以帮助我们集中注意力，在这方面能起到很大的帮助。

As you learn the associated skills of noticing feelings and making observations, you’ll have more tools to disentangle things. The basic form of Nonviolent Communication—observations, feelings, needs, requests—provides a kind of road map to connect with our internal experience. The more you practice walking your attention through those steps, the more easily you’ll be able to do it in real time.

当你学会觉察感受和进行观察的相关技巧后，你将拥有更多工具来理清思绪。非暴力沟通的基本形式——观察、感受、需求、请求——为我们与内在体验建立联系提供了一张路线图。你越是练习引导注意力经历这些步骤，就越能在现实生活中轻松做到这一点。

Grounding all of this in your body is also very important. There is a conceptual component to needs, but they are also felt in our body as a gut-level knowing. Keep listening inwardly.

将这一切与你的身体连接起来也非常重要。需求既包含概念层面，也体现在我们身体的本能感受中。要持续倾听内心的声音。

Last, I can’t emphasize enough the importance of getting help from others. We learned to think and speak in relationship, and those patterns are best transformed in relationship.

最后，我必须强调寻求他人帮助的重要性。我们是在人际关系中学会思考和说话的，而这些模式也最好在人际关系中得到转变。

Q: You talk a lot about collaborating to meet all of the needs present, but what about when the needs are in conflict? Or if there isn’t a way to meet all of the needs?

问：您经常谈到要通过合作来满足所有需求，但是当这些需求相互冲突时该怎么办？或者如果根本无法满足所有需求该怎么办？

Examine if it is actually the needs themselves or the strategies to meet them that are in conflict. More often than not, it is the latter. When our needs are in conflict—say, one partner wants closeness and connection, the other wants space and autonomy—then we work to deepen mutual understanding. To truly and wholly understand one another can bring transformation. Either person (or both) may shift because at that depth of understanding, one’s need for compassion and contribution can outweigh the original need for space or connection.

仔细审视究竟是需求本身存在冲突，还是满足需求的方式存在冲突。通常情况下，是后者。当我们的需求发生冲突时——例如，一方渴望亲密和联结，另一方则渴望空间和自主——我们就需要努力加深彼此的理解。真正全面地理解对方能够带来改变。双方（或其中一方）都可能做出转变，因为在这种深度的理解下，对同情和贡献的需求可能会超越最初对空间或联结的需求。

In some situations, it’s not possible to meet all the needs on the table. We can still find togetherness in valuing one another’s needs and work together to meet as many as possible. When we’re unable to think creatively enough to find a strategy that meets more needs, we can mourn that together. There can be a sense of connection and care in the experience of not finding an adequate solution.

在某些情况下，我们无法满足所有人的需求。但我们仍然可以通过尊重彼此的需求，并共同努力满足尽可能多的需求，从而建立起团结。当我们无法创造性地找到满足更多需求的策略时，我们可以共同为此感到遗憾。即使找不到合适的解决方案，这种经历也能让我们感受到彼此的联结和关怀。

Q: Can you say more about letting go of needs? I feel like I get stuck there.

问：您能详细说说如何放下需求吗？我觉得自己在这方面总是卡住。

“Letting go” of needs doesn’t mean denying, rejecting, or getting rid of them in some way. It means transforming our relationship to needs from one of contraction and demand to one of receptivity and openness.

“放下”需求并不意味着否认、拒绝或以某种方式摆脱它们。它意味着转变我们与需求的关系，从一种收缩和索取的关系转变为一种接纳和开放的关系。

The first step is simply to know what your needs are. Then begin to examine your relationship with specific needs, one at a time. Are you grasping inside, needing a need to be met in a certain way? Are you pushing it away or rejecting it? Or do you have a sense of space around that need? Letting go of needs means that we accept our needs and aren’t damaged if they aren’t satisfied. We may feel sad or disappointed, but we have enough resilience to handle that. There’s space inside to feel those emotions and mourn the absence of the object of our longing.

第一步很简单，就是了解自己的需求。然后，逐一审视你与具体需求的关系。你是否紧紧抓住不放，非要以某种特定方式满足某种需求？你是否在抗拒或排斥它？或者，你是否对这种需求保持着一定的包容度？放下需求意味着我们接纳自己的需求，即使它们得不到满足，我们也不会受到伤害。我们可能会感到悲伤或失望，但我们有足够的韧性去应对。我们的内心有足够的空间去感受这些情绪，去哀悼我们渴望之物的缺席。

This shift happens slowly and comes from finding the balance and compassion inside to be with the tension and discomfort of grasping. If we’re fixated and attached, start there. It feels awful to be gripped with desperation. If we can breathe gently with that experience, finding ways to calm and soothe the ache, it will begin to release and soften on its own. Again, with a lot of these areas, it’s helpful (and sometimes necessary) to receive support from others. Get empathy for the pain of the longing. Brainstorm together other ways to begin to meet those needs and ease out of the narrow, tight space of clinging.

这种转变是缓慢发生的，源于在内心找到平衡和慈悲，去接纳执着带来的紧张和不适。如果我们执着于某件事，那就从这里开始。被绝望紧紧抓住的感觉糟透了。如果我们能温柔地呼吸，与这种体验共处，找到方法来平静和抚慰痛苦，它就会开始自行释放和软化。同样，在很多情况下，获得他人的支持是有帮助的（有时甚至是必要的）。对渴望带来的痛苦感同身受。一起集思广益，寻找其他方法来满足这些需求，并逐渐走出执着带来的狭隘和压抑。

*1 Throughout this chapter I use the terms need, value, and what matters interchangeably to refer to this root aspect of human experience. While there are philosophical distinctions between a need and a value, here I am more interested in providing different ways of referring colloquially to the range of qualities that motivate us.

*1 在本章中，我交替使用“需要”、“价值”和“重要之事”这几个术语来指代人类经验的这一根本方面。虽然在哲学上，“需要”和“价值”之间存在区别，但在这里，我更感兴趣的是提供一些通俗易懂的方式来指代那些激励我们的各种特质。

# ↩

8

emotional agility

情绪敏捷性

Feeling emotions is what makes life rich.

—DANIEL GOLEMAN

感受情感使生活丰富多彩。——丹尼尔·戈尔曼

HUMAN LIFE IS a tapestry of changing emotions.

人生就像一幅由不断变化的情感交织而成的锦绣画卷。

Our ability to relate wisely to this flow of emotions is among the most important skills we can develop. When understood, emotions give us valuable information about our own and others’ needs, key input about our environment, and robust guidance for navigating conversations. Our emotions are our mind and body’s age-old way of sending immediate, tangible messages to us about our relationship with the world.

我们能否明智地应对情绪的流动，是我们能够培养的最重要的技能之一。理解情绪，就能让我们了解自身和他人的需求，获得关于环境的关键信息，并为有效沟通提供有力指导。情绪是我们身心古老的一种方式，它能直接、切实地向我们传递关于自身与世界关系的信息。

How we handle emotions—our own and others’—can make or break a relationship. The intensity of our feelings can push us to say or do things that we later regret. Strong emotions can inhibit us from speaking the truth or sharing the things for which we long. Even our idioms point to the power emotions have to drive our behavior: we become “blind with rage,” “choked up,” “weak in the knees,” “bent out of shape.”

我们如何处理自己的和他人的情绪，会直接影响一段关系的成败。强烈的情绪会驱使我们说出或做出事后后悔的事情。强烈的情绪也会让我们难以说出真相，或难以分享内心渴望的事物。甚至连我们的一些习语也体现了情绪对行为的强大影响：我们会“怒不可遏”、“哽咽难言”、“腿软”、“心烦意乱”。

In a single day, how many emotions course through us? Though we have little choice over what we feel, we can have choice over how we handle our emotions. In this chapter, we’ll explore emotions: where they come from, their role in dialogue, and how to develop emotional agility so we don’t get slammed when the emotional volume gets turned up.

一天之中，我们究竟会经历多少种情绪？虽然我们无法控制自己的感受，但我们可以选择如何处理这些情绪。本章我们将探讨情绪：它们的来源、它们在人际交往中的作用，以及如何培养情绪灵活性，从而避免在情绪高涨时被情绪淹没。

A Lesson of the Heart

心灵的教训

In my midthirties, feeling unfulfilled by work and life in general, I had the privilege to step out of my routine and focus more intensively on my spiritual practice. I went to the monastery, and after a few months decided to take temporary ordination as an anagarika, the first step of Buddhist monastic training. 1

三十五岁左右，我感到工作和生活都缺乏成就感，于是我有幸跳出日常生活的窠臼，更加专注于灵修。我去了寺院，几个月后决定接受临时戒律，成为一名阿那伽利迦（anagarika），这是佛教僧侣训练的第一步。

When I told my Jewish mother about my decision, things didn’t go well. The thought of her son “renouncing the world” with shaved head and white robes was more than she could handle. At one of the most important moments of my life she was aghast, bereft with anger and mourning.

当我把我的决定告诉犹太裔母亲时，事情进展并不顺利。一想到儿子要剃光头、穿白袍“遁世隐居”，她就难以接受。在我人生最重要的时刻之一，她震惊不已，悲痛欲绝，愤怒交织。

We both felt deeply hurt. To her, I seemed to be rejecting everything she believed and had raised me to value: ethical action to make the world a better place. For me, her rejection cut to the core. I desperately wanted her to see the true intentions behind my choice. I tried my best to hear her, but the pain between us was too much to bear. She withdrew completely, refusing to speak with me for almost an entire year. Ouch.

我们俩都深受伤害。在她看来，我似乎否定了她所信仰的一切，以及她从小教导我珍视的一切：用合乎道德的方式让世界变得更美好。而对我来说，她的拒绝如同利刃般刺痛了我的心。我迫切地希望她能明白我选择背后的真正用心。我努力倾听她的心声，但我们之间的痛苦实在难以承受。她彻底疏远了我，将近一年都没跟我说过话。唉。

I was ordained for two and a half years, during which I had plenty of time to contemplate our relationship: to cry, to forgive, and to heal. My mother and I eventually reconciled. We were able to talk about our views and feelings. Over time, she saw how my Buddhist training enabled me to help others in the world. In the end, we grew even closer. The process called forth powerful qualities in both of us: courage, honest vulnerability, patience, and humility. It taught me a lot about the willingness to feel and the gifts that wait on the other side.

我接受了两年半的僧侣戒律，这期间我有充足的时间反思我们之间的关系：哭泣、宽恕、疗愈。我和母亲最终和解了。我们能够坦诚地交流彼此的观点和感受。随着时间的推移，她逐渐明白我的佛法修行如何帮助我更好地服务他人。最终，我们的关系更加亲密。这个过程唤醒了我们彼此身上强大的品质：勇气、坦诚的脆弱、耐心和谦逊。它教会了我很多关于感受的真谛，以及感受之后等待着我的种种馈赠。

The Middle Way

中道

Emotions are rich and complex phenomena. They occur in our bodies and often include a mental or psychological component. As we’ll see, the ability to distinguish the felt sensations of an emotion from our thoughts and interpretations is key in being able to handle and express emotions skillfully. For our purposes (and keeping with Rosenberg’s language of NVC), I will use the two terms emotions and feelings interchangeably. 2

情绪是丰富而复杂的现象。它们发生在我们的身体中，并且通常包含心理或精神成分。正如我们将看到的，区分情绪的实际感受与我们的想法和解读的能力，是熟练处理和表达情绪的关键。为了便于讨论（并遵循罗森伯格的非暴力沟通理论），我将交替使用“情绪”和“感受”这两个术语。

Emotions are multifaceted, affective experiences felt in the body.

情绪是身体感受到的多方面情感体验。

How we relate to our emotions falls on a spectrum. At one extreme, a tide rushes in and floods us. We get swept up and speak impulsively. In a flash of anger, fear, or pain, we can find ourselves lashing out, often harming the ones we love. We may be on the receiving end of harsh words, stabbed by “verbal daggers,” as the Buddha once said. The cost of expressing our emotions reactively can be excruciatingly high. It can take weeks, months, or years to repair something that took seconds to say. Sometimes we never mend the rift. Less intense emotions can also take over a conversation, reducing our capacity to choose how we respond or making it harder to hear one another.

我们如何对待自己的情绪是一个连续谱。在一端，情绪如同潮水般涌来，将我们淹没。我们被情绪裹挟，冲动地脱口而出。在愤怒、恐惧或痛苦的瞬间，我们可能会情绪失控，攻击他人，常常伤害到我们所爱的人。我们可能会成为恶语相向的受害者，被佛陀所说的“言语之刃”刺伤。情绪冲动的代价可能极其沉重。修复一句几秒钟就能说出口的话，可能需要数周、数月甚至数年。有时，我们甚至永远无法弥合裂痕。不那么强烈的情绪也可能主导对话，削弱我们选择如何回应的能力，或者使彼此难以倾听。

Seeing all of this, we may swing to the other extreme, suppressing emotions. Afraid they’ll overwhelm us, damage a relationship, or complicate dialogue, we may try to ignore or avoid them. We pretend they’re not happening or try to work around them. We may try to keep things bottled up until we snap or allow emotions to stay repressed indefinitely. Yet in spite of our efforts, emotions have a way of seeping into conversation, often in unproductive ways.

看到这一切，我们可能会走向另一个极端，压抑自己的情绪。害怕情绪会让我们不知所措、破坏人际关系或使对话复杂化，我们可能会试图忽略或逃避它们。我们假装它们不存在，或者试图绕过它们。我们可能会把所有事情都憋在心里，直到情绪爆发，或者任由情绪无限期地被压抑下去。然而，尽管我们努力尝试，情绪总会以某种方式渗入对话，而且往往是以无益的方式。

Unacknowledged emotions can make it harder to hear another person, leading to confusion or mistrust. Our body language, facial expressions, and tone belie deeper feelings. Emotions show up in our choice of words, in the quickness of a retort, even in our silences. We can create an entire story about someone else, their motives or views, all to try to make sense of an emotion that’s under the surface.

未被察觉的情绪会让我们难以倾听他人，导致困惑或不信任。我们的肢体语言、面部表情和语气都隐藏着更深层次的感受。情绪会体现在我们选择的措辞、回应的速度，甚至沉默之中。我们可能会臆造出关于他人、其动机或观点的完整故事，试图理解隐藏在表面之下的某种情绪。

Taking a cue from Buddhist teachings, the path through this murky terrain is the middle way between reactive expression and habitual suppression. Developing emotional agility involves three capacities: identifying emotions, finding balance with our internal experience of them, and expressing them openly without blame or judgment. The tools of mindfulness and the framework of NVC help us handle the intensity of emotions, to better understand them, and to channel their powerful energy toward more useful ends.

借鉴佛教教义，穿越这片迷雾重重的领域，关键在于找到一条中庸之道，既非反应式的情绪表达，也非习惯性的压抑。培养情绪敏捷性包含三种能力：识别情绪、与内在的情绪体验找到平衡，以及坦诚地表达情绪而不加责备或评判。正念的工具和非暴力沟通的框架能够帮助我们应对强烈的情绪，更好地理解它们，并将它们强大的能量引导到更有益的方向。

A Mythology of Emotions

情感神话

In exploring this terrain, it can be helpful to examine how we’ve learned to relate to emotions. We each receive a kind of emotional inheritance. Wherever we’re born, we inherit generations of ideas, beliefs, and behaviors from our family, culture, religion, and society. Through the socialization process, we are given certain messages over and over again about what emotions we are allowed to feel and express based on aspects of our social location such as our gender, age, class, or race.

在探索这一领域时，审视我们如何习得与情绪的关系或许有所助益。我们每个人都继承了一种情感遗产。无论出生在何处，我们都从家庭、文化、宗教和社会中继承了数代人的观念、信仰和行为。在社会化过程中，我们不断被灌输某些信息，这些信息基于我们的社会地位，例如性别、年龄、阶级或种族，告诉我们应该感受和表达哪些情绪。

The fundamental template for understanding our emotions in the West began over two thousand years ago. Since the time of the Greek philosophers and the early Gnostics, aspects of Western philosophy and religion have posited a split between reason and emotion. The “passions” of the heart are seen as irrational and “base.” They drive us to do harmful things and threaten the fabric of the social order, so they must be subdued, tamed, and controlled by reason. 3 Today, emotions are often associated with vulnerability, the feminine, weakness, and danger or with manipulation and subtle coercion.

西方理解情感的基本框架始于两千多年前。自古希腊哲学家和早期诺斯替教徒时代起，西方哲学和宗教的某些方面就假定理性与情感之间存在着割裂。“激情”被视为非理性的、“低级的”。它们驱使我们做出有害的事情，威胁社会秩序，因此必须用理性来压制、驯服和控制。如今，情感常常与脆弱、女性特质、软弱和危险联系在一起，或者与操纵和隐蔽的胁迫联系在一起。

This dichotomy set the stage for most of the ideas I was exposed to in public education. School is where we learn to reason. Emotions are generally unwelcome and rarely discussed, let alone integrated. As a child, how often did your teachers ask how you felt?

这种二元对立奠定了我接受公立教育的大部分观念的基础。学校是学习推理的地方。情感通常不受欢迎，很少被讨论，更不用说融入其中了。小时候，你的老师多久会问你一次你的感受呢？

I grew up Jewish in the suburbs of New Jersey. At home I learned that it was natural to express a colorful range of emotions. At school I learned hard lessons about what was and wasn’t socially acceptable. Sent out of class for raising my voice and cursing, I understood that it’s risky to express anger. Shamed by a teacher and ridiculed by other boys for crying, I learned it’s not safe to cry in public, especially not around other men. Although we each receive different messages based on our sociocultural location, almost all of us as children imbibe certain social rules about emotions based on our perceived gender: “Don’t cry.” “Grow up. Be a man.” “Big girls don’t cry.”

我在新泽西州郊区长大，是个犹太人。在家里，我学会了自然地表达各种各样的情绪。在学校，我却深刻地体会到了哪些行为在社会上是被接受的，哪些是不被接受的。因为大声说话和说脏话而被赶出教室，我明白了表达愤怒是有风险的。因为哭泣而被老师羞辱，被其他男孩嘲笑，我明白了在公共场合哭泣是不安全的，尤其是在其他男性面前。虽然我们每个人由于所处的社会文化环境而接收到的信息各不相同，但几乎所有人在孩童时期都会根据自身性别认同而接受一些关于情绪的社会规则：“别哭。”“长大点，像个男人。”“大女孩不哭。”

We have been systematically trained to avoid and suppress our emotions. These rules are not merely theoretical. Their impact on us as individuals can be felt every day through a deadening of our vitality; in the shame, depression, and anxiety that are so prevalent in modern society; and in our inability to manage emotions in relationships.

我们被系统性地训练去回避和压抑自己的情绪。这些规则并非仅仅是理论。它们对我们每个人的影响每天都能体现出来：活力的丧失；现代社会普遍存在的羞耻感、抑郁和焦虑；以及我们在人际关系中无法妥善处理情绪。

In spite of these experiences, I was able to internalize the message that it was important to feel. My mother laid important groundwork by making regular efforts to encourage my sensitivity and emotional intelligence. The loneliness of being a sensitive, heterosexual man became an important motivator to understand and transform the emotional roles I inherited from society.

尽管有过这些经历，我还是领悟到了感受的重要性。母亲一直以来都努力培养我的敏感度和情商，这为我奠定了重要的基础。作为一个敏感的异性恋男性，我所感受到的孤独感，成为了我理解并转变从社会继承而来的情感角色的重要动力。

PRACTICE : Seeking Myths

实践：探寻神话

Part of developing a wise relationship with our emotions is becoming aware of the notions we carry about them. Take some time to reflect on what you believe about feelings. What messages did you receive from your family, culture, religion, or society? What messages do you receive today through the media or your community? Which are explicit (“Don’t cry”) and which are implicit (through example or behavior)?

与情绪建立明智的关系，一部分在于觉察我们对情绪的固有观念。花些时间反思一下你对情绪的看法。你从家庭、文化、宗教或社会中接收到哪些信息？如今，你又从媒体或社区接收到哪些信息？哪些是明确的（例如“别哭”），哪些是隐含的（例如通过言行举止）？

Make a list of the views and beliefs you notice. Are there certain emotions that feel more acceptable than others? As you move through your day, notice any fear of feeling your emotions or of others expressing emotions.

列出你注意到的一些观点和信念。是否存在某些情绪比其他情绪更容易被接受？在日常生活中，留意你是否害怕感受自己的情绪，或者害怕别人表达情绪。

Reclaiming Our Right to Feel

重拾我们感受的权利

These mythologies of culture, history, and religion would have us believe that our emotions are signs of a flawed nature; that they are abnormal occurrences that can be ignored, overcome, or explained away. Yet there is something deeper in us. We each receive an inheritance that is older, greater, and far more powerful than what our family, culture, or society bestows.

这些关于文化、历史和宗教的神话让我们相信，我们的情感是人性缺陷的体现；它们是异常的现象，可以被忽视、克服或轻易解释。然而，我们内心深处蕴藏着更深层次的东西。我们每个人都继承了一份比家庭、文化或社会赋予的更为古老、更为伟大、也更为强大的遗产。

Our emotions are immutable expressions of our biology. They’re as natural and essential to our life as our body’s own immune system. Far from being irrational, we feel things for a reason. If there’s emotion, something matters. Emotions are primary ways the body-mind sends signals about our needs. When our needs are met, we feel pleasant emotions. When our needs are not met, we feel unpleasant emotions.

我们的情绪是生物本能的必然表达。它们如同我们身体的免疫系统一样，自然而然地存在于我们的生命之中。情绪并非非理性，而是有其原因的。只要有情绪存在，就意味着某些事情很重要。情绪是身心传递需求信号的主要方式。当我们的需求得到满足时，我们会感到愉悦；当我们的需求没有得到满足时，我们会感到不愉悦。

Our feelings constitute their own unique form of experience and system of information. Any emotion is no more of a “problem” than the smoke detector in our house. When the smoke alarm goes off, we understand the signal and set about seeking its source. In the same way, we can learn to experience and understand our emotions as feedback signals about life. What are these signals telling us? Rather than taking them as imperatives to action, we can see them as information.

我们的感受构成了一种独特的体验形式和信息系统。任何情绪都不像家里的烟雾报警器那样是个“问题”。当烟雾报警器响起时，我们能理解它发出的信号，并着手寻找其来源。同样，我们也可以学会体验和理解我们的情绪，将它们视为关于生活的反馈信号。这些信号在告诉我们什么？与其将它们视为行动的指令，不如将它们视为信息。

Of course, the feedback loops of memory, thought, and social conditioning can complicate the way we experience our emotions. Sometimes there’s fire, sometimes there isn’t. But we don’t throw away the smoke detector just because the battery needs to be changed! We can learn to hear the wisdom in emotion.

当然，记忆、思维和社会制约的反馈回路会使我们体验情绪的方式变得复杂。有时候会有火灾，有时候则没有。但我们不会仅仅因为电池没电就把烟雾报警器扔掉！我们可以学会倾听情绪中的智慧。

From this perspective, all emotions are okay to feel. It’s how we respond, what we do with them, that matters. When we’re not aware of our emotions, or when we become flooded and allow them to take over, they can cause harm. What’s problematic is not the emotion itself but rather our reactive expression of a feeling or our habitual suppression of it. When reactively expressed, the immediate harm is outward. When reflexively suppressed, the damage turns inward, with potential harm to others over time.

从这个角度来看，所有情绪都是可以接受的。重要的是我们如何回应，如何处理它们。当我们意识不到自己的情绪，或者被情绪淹没并任其支配时，它们就会造成伤害。问题不在于情绪本身，而在于我们对情绪的反应性表达，或是我们习惯性的压抑。当情绪被反应性地表达出来时，直接的伤害是向外的。而当情绪被本能地压抑时，伤害会转向内心，随着时间的推移，甚至可能对他人造成伤害。

Our capacity to feel emotions emerges from millions of years of evolution and is deeply rooted in our neurobiology. 4 We are sensitive creatures built to feel things, touched both literally and figuratively by the world around us. The nerves that run throughout our body and viscera ensure precise and immediate feedback from our environment—sensory, mental, and emotional.

我们感受情绪的能力源于数百万年的进化，并深深植根于我们的神经生物学之中。我们是敏感的生物，天生就能感受事物，从字面意义和象征意义上都被周围的世界所触动。遍布我们身体和内脏的神经确保我们能够从环境中获得精准而即时的反馈——包括感官、心理和情感方面的反馈。

Volumes of research today illustrate the inherent value and intelligence of our emotional life. 5 From the cascade of hormones released to support healthy bonding between caregiver and child to the boiling of anger or the tremble of fear in response to a threat, the affective domain is an essential part of being human. When we understand emotions’ natural purpose as a source of information, we can cut through the mythology we’ve internalized and allow ourselves to be aware of them and feel them more fully.

如今大量的研究表明，我们的情感生活蕴含着巨大的价值和智慧。从促进照护者与孩子之间健康联结的激素级联反应，到面对威胁时怒火中烧或恐惧颤抖，情感领域是人类不可或缺的一部分。当我们理解情绪作为信息来源的自然功能时，我们就能打破内化的种种迷思，更充分地觉察和感受它们。

A Palette of Emotion

情感的调色板

Mindfulness is the primary tool to develop our capacity to identify emotions (emotional recognition) and to feel them with balance (emotion regulation). Emotion recognition begins with noticing and naming what we’re feeling—this is sometimes called affect labeling. At first, our vocabulary for emotions may be rudimentary. We may find we have just a handful of words to describe our feelings: happy, sad, mad, confused. It’s like trying to paint with only a few colors.

正念是培养我们识别情绪（情绪识别）和平衡感受情绪（情绪调节）能力的主要工具。情绪识别始于觉察并命名我们的感受——这有时被称为情感标签。起初，我们描述情绪的词汇可能非常有限。我们可能发现自己只有寥寥几个词来描述自己的感受：快乐、悲伤、愤怒、困惑。这就像试图只用几种颜色作画一样。

PRACTICE : Reflecting on Feelings

练习：反思感受

Below is a partial list of feelings we experience when our needs are or are not met. Take some time to read it over and consider: Which feelings are most familiar? Which are least familiar? As you move through your day, what feelings do you notice in your own or other’s experience? Name them silently. In particular, notice how your own emotions change over the course of one day, coming and going.

以下列举了一些当我们的需求得到满足或未得到满足时会经历的感受。请花些时间阅读并思考：哪些感受你最熟悉？哪些感受你最不熟悉？在日常生活中，你注意到自己或他人有哪些感受？请在心中默默地将它们说出来。尤其要注意，你的情绪在一天中是如何变化的，来来去去。
