These limits are often not just conceptual; they’re also sensory—meaning our capacity to feel the nuances of our emotional life may be attenuated or atrophied. Years of shutting off or avoiding emotions can mute things. 6 This is completely workable. We begin by bringing awareness to our experience just as it is, wherever we are.

这些限制往往不仅仅是概念上的，也包括感官上的——这意味着我们感受情感生活细微差别的能力可能会减弱或退化。多年来封闭或逃避情感会让我们变得麻木。但这完全可以解决。我们首先要做的，就是觉察当下的体验，无论身处何地。

We all have a different relationship to emotions. It’s common to not know how we feel, even to feel numb at times. Sometimes we may feel things quite intensely. There’s no “right” way to be. What we’re aiming for is the ability to identify how we feel in the moment, to clear the mental and sensory channels so that we receive the feedback from our surroundings and relationships.

我们每个人与情绪的关系都不同。有时不知道自己感受如何，甚至感到麻木，这很常见。有时我们也会感受到非常强烈的情绪。没有所谓的“正确”状态。我们追求的是能够识别当下的感受，清理思绪和感官通道，从而接收来自周围环境和人际关系的反馈。

Naming our emotions is a necessary foundation for mindful communication and the first component of emotion recognition. We refine this ability by feeling them in our body.

为自己的情绪命名是进行有效沟通的必要基础，也是情绪识别的第一步。我们通过感受身体中的情绪来提升这种能力。

Have you ever stopped to examine an emotion directly? What is this surge of energy that can race through us like a hurricane? If you look closely, you’ll discover that every emotion is a dynamic interplay of body, heart, and mind, a blend of sensations fed by thoughts and meanings.

你是否曾停下来直接审视过某种情绪？这股如同飓风般席卷我们全身的能量究竟是什么？如果你仔细观察，就会发现每一种情绪都是身、心、灵之间动态互动的结果，是各种感觉与思想和意义交织而成的产物。

A word such as sadness or joy refers to a rich world of inner experience. Sensation is a primary component of an emotion. Sadness may include pressure in our chest, a hardness in our throat, or heaviness in our eyes. Joy feels expansive, spacious, warm, or light.

悲伤或喜悦这样的词语，都指向丰富的内心体验。感觉是情绪的主要组成部分。悲伤可能包括胸闷、喉咙哽咽或眼眶沉重。喜悦则让人感到开阔、舒畅、温暖或轻松。

Emotions also have embodied shape. Sadness lowers our head and droops our shoulders. Anger clenches our jaw and fists. Confidence lifts our chin. It works in the reverse too: assuming the bodily posture of an emotion stimulates its associated neurochemistry. Articulating the facial muscles into a smile can raise our spirits and standing tall can induce strength.

情绪也有其具体的形态。悲伤会让我们低下头，耸起肩膀；愤怒会让我们紧咬牙关，握紧拳头；自信则会让我们昂首挺胸。反过来也是如此：摆出某种情绪对应的身体姿态，就能刺激与之相关的神经化学物质。微笑可以振奋精神，挺拔的身姿可以增强力量。

The more clearly we begin to sense the somatic experience of our emotions, the more alert and skilled we become at identifying what we are feeling. Over time, through patient mindful attention, our palette begins to expand. We go from just four colors to ten, then twenty, and eventually to a rich display. Like a painter with different tones of blue, lavender, and gray to paint the sky, we can learn to identify and feel the full range of our emotions.

我们越能清晰地感知自身情绪的身体体验，就越能敏锐地识别自己的感受。随着时间的推移，通过耐心专注的觉察，我们的情绪调色板开始扩展。我们从最初的四种颜色扩展到十种，再到二十种，最终呈现出丰富多彩的景象。就像画家运用不同色调的蓝色、淡紫色和灰色来描绘天空一样，我们也能学会识别和感受自身情绪的全部范围。

Yet just because our palette is growing doesn’t mean we know how to paint. We can be aware of what we’re feeling and still be driven or oppressed by our emotions. Their intensity can transfix our attention and spin us around.

然而，即便我们的感官体验日益丰富，也不意味着我们懂得如何作画。我们或许能够意识到自己的感受，却仍然会被情绪所驱使或压制。情绪的强烈程度足以让我们目不转睛，甚至迷失方向。

The next phase of practicing emotional agility is to learn how to manage them: to experience them in a nonreactive way. This is sometimes called emotion regulation, and it has more to do with internal balance than control. To return to the analogy, if emotion recognition expands our palette, emotion regulation teaches us to hold the brush properly.

练习情绪敏捷的下一阶段是学习如何管理情绪：以非反应性的方式体验情绪。这有时被称为情绪调节，它更多地与内在平衡而非控制有关。回到之前的比喻，如果说情绪识别拓宽了我们的调色板，那么情绪调节则教会我们如何正确地握笔。

Every emotion has a tone, a kind of primary “flavor” of pleasant, unpleasant, or neutral. This underlying agreeable or disagreeable tone is often what gets us going. It’s what we crave, what we try to avoid, or what we resist feeling. Emotions can also have an energetic component, a sensory experience that spreads throughout the body. Anger often has a roiling, rushing feeling. Loving care can have a soothing, soft, or warm quality. Excitement and joy may be bubbly. Anxiety can feel brittle or jangled.

每一种情绪都有其基调，一种基本的“味道”，可以是愉悦的、不愉悦的，或是中性的。这种潜在的愉悦或不愉悦的基调往往是我们行动的动力。它决定了我们渴望什么、试图避免什么，或是抗拒感受什么。情绪也可能包含能量成分，一种扩散至全身的感官体验。愤怒常常带来翻腾、奔涌的感觉。关爱则可能带来舒缓、柔和或温暖的特质。兴奋和喜悦可能充满活力。焦虑则可能让人感到脆弱或焦虑不安。

The tonality and energy of emotions tend to pull us in and push us around. It’s our inability to tolerate the intensity of an unpleasant tone that sparks our reactivity. We can use mindfulness to notice this aspect of our feelings and stabilize our attention there, instead of being dragged along by the thoughts and stories that feed them. Rather than clamping down or cutting ourselves off from our emotions, emotion regulation invites us to feel them fully. 7 We develop the patience, strength, and spaciousness to let these waves of tone and energy wash through us without getting toppled by them. 8

情绪的基调和能量往往会拉扯我们，左右我们。正是我们无法忍受不愉快情绪的强度，才引发了我们的反应。我们可以运用正念来觉察自身感受的这一方面，并将注意力集中于此，而不是被滋养这些情绪的想法和故事牵着鼻子走。情绪调节并非压制或切断我们与情绪的联系，而是引导我们充分地感受它们。我们培养耐心、力量和包容心，让这些情绪和能量的浪潮流淌过我们，而不被它们击垮。

Our emotions almost always come with a story. While we may feel joyful or sad for no apparent reason, more often than not we are responding to something specific in our internal or external environment. This last dimension of emotions is the most complex: the thoughts, stories, and meanings associated with them.

我们的情绪几乎总是伴随着一个故事。虽然我们有时会毫无缘由地感到快乐或悲伤，但更多时候，我们都在对内在或外在环境中的某些特定因素做出反应。情绪的最后一个维度最为复杂：它包含了与之相关的想法、故事和意义。

The interplay between our thoughts and emotions is fascinating to explore. They often feed one another: thoughts and stories provide fuel for emotion, which in turn sparks further thinking and rumination. 9 Sifting through layers of thought, we usually find at the core of an emotion some meaning or belief that is connected to our deeper needs. Focusing on what matters means getting at the crux of this juncture, to any meaning and associated needs. Within sadness we may find the perception “I’m all alone” and a longing for companionship, friendship, or community. At the heart of shame may be the belief “I’m not good enough” and needs for self-acceptance, dignity, or recognition.

探索我们的思想和情感之间的相互作用非常有趣。它们常常相互滋养：思想和故事为情感提供燃料，而情感反过来又会激发进一步的思考和反省。 9 层层剖析思绪，我们通常会在情感的核心发现某种意义或信念，它与我们更深层次的需求息息相关。关注真正重要的事情意味着抓住这一关键点，探寻其意义和相关的需求。在悲伤中，我们可能感受到“我孤身一人”，并渴望陪伴、友谊或归属感。羞耻的核心可能是“我不够好”的信念，以及对自我接纳、尊严或认可的需求。

When I told my mother I was ordaining as a Buddhist monastic, storms of all these components—meaning, tone, energy, and sensation—tore through our hearts. To handle our emotions, we must develop the ability to notice these elements and feel them fully, to attune to all dimensions of an emotion without getting thrown by any of them. The more balanced we are internally, the easier it becomes to talk about our own and others’ emotions.

当我告诉母亲我要出家成为佛教僧侣时，所有这些要素——意义、语气、能量和感受——如同风暴般席卷了我们的心房。为了驾驭自己的情绪，我们必须培养觉察这些要素并充分感受它们的能力，能够感知情绪的各个层面而不被任何一方面所左右。我们内心越平衡，就越容易谈论自己和他人的情绪。

Principle: Being aware of our emotions supports our ability to choose consciously how we participate in a conversation.

原则：意识到自己的情绪有助于我们有意识地选择如何参与对话。

PRACTICE : Feeling Emotions

练习：感受情绪

Take some time to practice mindfulness and thoroughly explore the different components of an emotion. Begin by grounding your attention in your body. Steady your awareness with breathing and let things settle to whatever degree possible. Then call to mind a situation that brought up some feelings (nothing too difficult). Let it become clear in your mind. Use the steps below to explore any emotions present, one at a time:

花些时间练习正念，深入探索情绪的不同组成部分。首先，将注意力集中在身体上。通过呼吸稳定意识，尽可能地让情绪平静下来。然后，回想一个引发你某些感受的情境（不必太过复杂）。让它在你的脑海中清晰呈现。按照以下步骤，一次探索一种情绪：

EMOTION : Name the emotion. How do you feel?

情绪：说出你的情绪。你感觉如何？

LOCATION : Where do you feel it? Is it in your face, your chest, your back? Somewhere else?

位置：你感觉疼痛的部位在哪里？是在脸上、胸口、背部，还是其他地方？

SENSATION : What does it feel like there? What are the actual sensations you experience associated with the emotion? Is there pressure, tightness, aching, heaviness? Warmth, openness, lightness, flowing?

感觉：那里是什么感觉？你与这种情绪相关的实际感觉是什么？有压力、紧绷、疼痛、沉重感吗？还是温暖、舒展、轻盈、流动感？

TONALITY : What’s the overall flavor or tone of the emotion? Is it pleasant or unpleasant? Can you relax there, softening and widening your attention?

语调：这种情绪的整体感觉或语调是什么？是令人愉悦的还是令人不快的？你能否放松下来，柔化并扩大你的注意力？

MEANING : Are there any thoughts, stories, or meanings associated with the emotion? If you had to boil it down to one word, what would it be?

含义：这种情绪是否与某些想法、故事或意义相关联？如果必须用一个词来概括，你会选择哪个词？

NEEDS : To what needs is this emotion connected? What matters to you here?

需求：这种情绪与哪些需求相关？对你而言，什么最重要？

Naming our emotions and identifying their components can help us self-regulate. 10 Using mindfulness to identify what’s happening creates perspective. As soon as we name something, we’re no longer completely identified with it; we have a relationship with it. With the space that’s created by that perspective, the emotion can begin to settle.

命名我们的情绪并识别其组成部分有助于我们进行自我调节。运用正念来识别正在发生的事情可以让我们获得更全面的视角。一旦我们命名了某件事，我们就不再完全认同它；我们与它建立了一种联系。在这种视角所创造的空间里，情绪可以开始平静下来。

Sometimes emotions are so powerful that we can’t differentiate any of the above components, let alone tolerate them. Our mind and body flood with a surge of intensity. This can happen with pleasant emotions such as love or exuberance as much as with unpleasant emotions such as anger or disgust.

有时，情绪如此强烈，以至于我们无法区分上述任何组成部分，更遑论承受它们。我们的身心会被一股强烈的情绪所淹没。这种情况既可能发生在爱或热情等愉悦的情绪中，也可能发生在愤怒或厌恶等不愉悦的情绪中。

Here we can use mindfulness of breathing to soothe the intensity of strong emotions, fully appreciating the experience of the pleasant ones and bringing balance to the unpleasant ones. Just as we used a reference point in the body to anchor our attention for presence, we can use the breath or the body to steady our awareness amid the storms of strong emotions.

在这里，我们可以运用呼吸正念来舒缓强烈的情绪，充分体验愉悦的感受，并平衡不愉快的情绪。正如我们利用身体上的参照点来锚定注意力，从而保持觉知当下一样，我们也可以利用呼吸或身体来稳定意识，抵御强烈情绪的冲击。

PRACTICE : Soothing Strong Emotions

练习：安抚强烈的情绪

The next time you feel a surge of strong emotion, try using your breath to calm and soothe your mind and body. Take a few slow, deep breaths. Feel the air filling your belly and chest as you breathe in. Purse your lips gently and breathe out long and slow, releasing your breath in a thin stream of air. Notice how your body feels, paying extra attention to any amount of settling or calming.

下次当你感到强烈的情绪涌上心头时，试着用呼吸来平静身心。做几次缓慢而深长的呼吸。吸气时，感受空气充满你的腹部和胸腔。轻轻抿起嘴唇，缓慢而悠长地呼气，让气息像细流一样缓缓流出。留意身体的感觉，特别注意任何平静或安抚的迹象。

All emotions simply want our attention. They long to be known, felt, and released. As we observe our emotions, feeling them fully, we begin to see a deep truth: they are fleeting. Even as they send us important signals, they are like weather systems that come and go. The Latin roots of the word emotion literally mean “to move out.” When we allow ourselves to consciously feel our emotions, they can do their job of helping take care of us. They inform our choices about how to respond to things and move on their way.

所有情绪都渴望得到我们的关注。它们渴望被了解、被感受、被释放。当我们观察自己的情绪，全然地感受它们时，我们便开始领悟一个深刻的真理：它们是转瞬即逝的。即便它们传递着重要的信号，它们也如同天气系统一般，来去无常。“情绪”（emotion）一词的拉丁语词根字面意思是“向外移动”。当我们允许自己有意识地感受情绪时，它们便能发挥其作用，帮助我们更好地应对各种情况。它们指引我们如何选择回应事物，然后继续前行。

Hacking the Blame Game: Radical Responsibility

打破互相指责的局面：彻底的责任

As we find more internal balance and stability with emotions, our ability to engage relationally grows as well. With a full palette and proper brush control, we’re ready to paint. The last phase of emotional agility is to develop the capacity to hear and express them without blame. This is as much about how we think as it is about what we say.

随着我们内心情绪的平衡与稳定，我们处理人际关系的能力也会随之提升。有了丰富的经验和精准的掌控力，我们便能尽情挥洒情感。情绪敏捷性的最后一个阶段是培养倾听和表达情绪而不加指责的能力。这不仅关乎我们的言语，也关乎我们的思考方式。

One of the most pervasive and unquestioned myths about emotions is that they are someone else’s fault. This notion is reinforced daily by the media and entertainment industries. “I’m angry because you …” This is our unconscious communication training at work, miring us in the blame game. I throw some blame and you toss it back, arguing and defending.

关于情绪，最普遍也最容易被忽视的误区之一就是认为情绪都是别人的错。媒体和娱乐行业每天都在强化这种观念。“我生气是因为你……”这是我们在工作中无意识的沟通训练，让我们深陷于互相指责的泥潭。我指责别人，你反驳回来，争辩辩解。

Our thoughts and words have the power to shape our experience. Taking responsibility for our feelings and extricating ourselves from blame involves keen attention to the very mechanisms of perception in our mind that generate and reinforce the blame game. The diagram below illustrates the logic behind the game. A friend is fifteen minutes late to meet you, and you say, “I’m so annoyed that you’re late.” Is this actually a direct cause-and-effect relationship, in which their actions cause your emotions?

我们的思想和言语能够塑造我们的体验。要为自己的感受负责，并摆脱责备，就需要我们敏锐地关注大脑中那些产生并强化“责备游戏”的感知机制。下图展示了这种游戏背后的逻辑。假设朋友迟到了十五分钟，你说：“你迟到真让我生气。”这真的是一种直接的因果关系吗？是他们的行为导致了你的情绪吗？

On a different day you might have a different reaction. You might feel hurt, worried, or—if you’ve had a busy day—relieved to have a few minutes to yourself!

换一天你可能会有不同的反应。你可能会感到受伤、担忧，或者——如果你忙碌了一天——会因为能有几分钟独处时间而感到轻松！

Our feelings are never caused directly by other people or their actions. There is a relationship, but it is an indirect one. The outward event is the stimulus for our feelings; it is a necessary but insufficient condition for our emotional response. The most direct root cause is how we relate to the event: our needs and values, represented by point B in the diagram below. This includes the context—our day, cultural conditioning, personal and social history, and expectations, as well as the stories we tell ourselves and meanings we fashion from the situation. All these factors are tied to our needs.

我们的感受并非直接由他人或其行为引起。二者之间存在关联，但这种关联是间接的。外在事件是引发我们感受的刺激因素；它是我们产生情绪反应的必要条件，但并非充分条件。最直接的根本原因在于我们如何看待该事件：我们的需求和价值观，如下图中的B点所示。这包括情境——我们的日常经历、文化熏陶、个人和社会背景、期望，以及我们讲述给自己的故事和我们从情境中构建的意义。所有这些因素都与我们的需求息息相关。

The blame game tries to hold someone else responsible for our emotional reactions, entangling us in argument. Can anyone make you feel something? How can you be responsible for my reaction? And vice versa, how can I possibly be responsible for your reaction?

互相指责试图将我们情绪反应的责任推卸给别人，使我们陷入争论。任何人都能让你产生某种感觉吗？你怎么能为我的反应负责？反过来，我又怎么可能为你的反应负责呢？

We are each responsible for our actions and our reactions. Remember that our feelings are a function of our needs. To take responsibility for my reactions means training my mind to trace emotions back to the needs from which they arise. Every time my attention goes outward to blame someone, I can pause and investigate: Is this person solely responsible for my reaction? What meaning am I making about this event? What do I need? How is the broader context of my life, or my social location, structuring my experience?

我们每个人都应该为自己的行为和反应负责。记住，我们的感受源于我们的需求。要对自己的反应负责，就意味着训练自己去追溯情绪的根源，找到它们产生的原因。每当我把注意力转向外部，试图责怪他人时，我都可以停下来反思：这个人真的应该为我的反应负全部责任吗？我对这件事的理解是什么？我需要什么？我的生活背景或社会地位是如何影响我的体验的？

When we step out of the blame game and take radical responsibility for our feelings, we carve the channels of our own freedom. If you are the cause of my emotions, you have power and I remain helpless. When we understand feelings as a function of needs rather than the direct result of another’s actions, we reclaim our autonomy and agency. This is how humans facing brutal treatment, torture, or other horrors can feel compassion instead of hatred toward their oppressors. Our emotional life becomes an extension of our own values and a barometer for our needs rather than a liability or weakness we need to protect.

当我们不再互相指责，而是真正为自己的感受承担责任时，我们就开辟了通往自由的道路。如果你是我的情绪的根源，你就拥有了权力，而我则无能为力。当我们理解感受是需求的体现，而非他人行为的直接结果时，我们就重获自主权和能动性。这就是为什么面对残酷对待、酷刑或其他恐怖经历的人们，能够对压迫者产生同情而非仇恨。我们的情感生活不再是需要保护的负担或弱点，而是我们自身价值观的延伸，成为我们需求的晴雨表。

The Grammar of Inner Freedom

内在自由的语法

Have you ever tried to pull up grass to plant a garden? If you have, you know why activists call their work “grassroots” organizing. Our conditioning to blame others for our feelings is just as tenacious; it’s a way of seeing that is deeply embedded in our minds.

你试过拔掉杂草种菜吗？如果你试过，你就会明白为什么活动家们称他们的工作为“草根”组织。我们习惯性地把自己的感受归咎于他人，这种观念同样根深蒂固；它是一种深深植根于我们思想中的视角。

There are a few telltale signs that you’re playing the blame game, and a clear way to short-circuit it. First and foremost, watch for how our language

如果你在玩推卸责任的游戏，有一些明显的迹象可以表明你在玩这个游戏，而且也很容易避免这种情况。首先，也是最重要的一点，要注意我们的语言。

constructs a narrative of blame. If you find yourself placing the cause of your feelings outside, thinking or saying, “I feel __________ because you (they) …,” turn it around and connect to your needs. As Rosenberg taught, use the following structure to locate the source of your feelings internally:

构建一种归咎于他人的叙事。如果你发现自己将感受的根源归咎于外部因素，比如想着或说着“我感到____是因为你（他们）……”，那就转变思路，与自身的需求建立联系。正如罗森伯格所教导的，运用以下结构来找到你内在感受的根源：

I feel __________ because I need / want / value __________.

You feel __________ because you need / want / value __________.

我感到____，因为我需要/想要/重视____。你感到____，因为你需要/想要/重视____。

Note the parallel consistency of subjects: my feelings linked to my needs, your feelings linked to yours. Practice repeating this over and over again, until it becomes the default view of emotions in your mind. This will undercut the foundation of the blame game, making it easier to express yourself and to hear others.

注意主语之间的平行关系：我的感受与我的需求相关，你的感受与你的需求相关。反复练习，直到它成为你脑海中处理情绪的默认方式。这将削弱互相指责的根基，让你更容易表达自己和倾听他人。

Another way the blame game shows up in our language is by disguising thoughts as feelings:

在我们的语言中，另一种推卸责任的方式是将想法伪装成感受：

I feel like you don’t love me.

I feel that this whole thing is ridiculous.

I feel as if you’re not listening.

我觉得你不爱我。我觉得这一切都太荒谬了。我觉得你根本没在听我说话。

Following the verb feel with like, that, or as will express a thought rather than a feeling —frequently blame, judgment, or interpretation. Similarly, following I feel with a pronoun or name will usually take us up into our head with analysis and evaluation:

在动词 feel 后面接 like、that 或 as，表达的是一种想法而非感觉——通常是责备、判断或解释。同样，在 I feel 后面接代词或名称，通常会让我们进行分析和评估：

I feel I’m no good at this.

I feel they keep putting things off intentionally.

I feel Amy isn’t qualified.

我觉得自己不擅长这个。我觉得他们一直在故意拖延。我觉得艾米不胜任。

These are indirect, alienated expressions of our emotions. They hinder our ability to be fully aware of our feelings, to express ourselves, or to hear others in ways that build understanding.

这些都是间接的、疏离的情感表达方式。它们阻碍了我们充分觉察自身感受、表达自我或以增进理解的方式倾听他人的能力。

The last trick of the blame game is even more surreptitious. There are a variety of words in English that colloquially refer to emotions but instead express blame, attributing intention to another person. “I feel attacked” tells a story about what is happening: you are attacking me. What’s more, it leaves out essential information about how I actually feel, which might be anything from afraid to hurt, angry, or confused. If we have the thought that someone is attacking us, here are a few examples of other ways we might express ourselves:

指责游戏的最后一招更加隐蔽。英语中有很多词语在口语中用来指代情绪，但实际上却表达了指责，将意图归咎于他人。“我感觉受到了攻击”这句话描述了正在发生的事情：你在攻击我。更重要的是，它忽略了我真实的感受，而这种感受可能是害怕、受伤、愤怒或困惑等等。如果我们觉得有人在攻击我们，以下是一些我们可以表达自己的其他方式：

“I’m feeling overwhelmed and confused, and would like to talk about this in a way that’s easier for me take in. Could we slow down a bit?”

“我感到不知所措，也很困惑，我想用一种我更容易理解的方式来谈谈这件事。我们能放慢速度吗？”

“I’m a little taken aback and kind of stunned because I had no idea any of this was going on. Are you saying that…[empathy guess]?”

“我有点吃惊，也有点懵，因为我完全不知道发生了这些事。你是说……（感同身受的猜测）？”

“Ouch; that hurts. I really want to be seen for how hard I’ve worked on this. Can we take a few steps back and first review what’s gone well?”

“哎哟，真让人难过。我真的很想让大家看到我为此付出的努力。我们能不能先退后几步，回顾一下哪些方面做得好？”

Each of these statements expresses our needs colloquially, adding context and authenticity, and ends with a request (something we’ll explore in chapter 11 ).

这些陈述都以口语化的方式表达了我们的需求，增加了语境和真实性，并以一个请求结尾（我们将在第 11 章中探讨这一点）。

PRACTICE : Noticing False Feelings

练习：觉察虚假感受

There are a range of words that fall into this category of “false feelings,” that is, referring to an emotion by blaming the other person. In the list that follows, which of these do you find yourself using to express emotions? When you use that word, how do you feel on the inside?

有很多词语都属于“虚假感受”的范畴，也就是说，它们通过指责他人来表达某种情绪。在下面的列表中，你发现自己会用哪些词语来表达情绪？当你使用这些词语时，你内心是什么感受？

False-Feeling Words

虚假的情感之语

Abandoned

弃

Abused

受虐

Attacked

遭到攻击

Betrayed

背叛

Bullied

被欺凌

作弊

胁迫

走投无路

减少

不尊重

中断

感到害怕

Let down

辜负

Manipulated

操纵

Misunderstood

被误解

Neglected

受惠

压力

放下

Taken advantage of

利用

Taken for granted

被视为理所当然

受到不公平对待

受到威胁

PRACTICE : Translating Feelings—“How Do I Feel on the Inside?”

练习：翻译感受——“我内心感觉如何？”

As you move through your day, pay attention to how you think and speak about your emotions. Be on the lookout for signs of the blame game: “because you,” feeling “like or that,” and false-feeling words. (Also watch out for the tendency to blame yourself for blaming!)

在日常生活中，注意你如何思考和表达自己的情绪。留意是否存在“责备游戏”的迹象，例如“因为你”、“感觉像那样”以及虚假的感受。（还要注意不要因为责备别人而自责！）

When you notice any of these, pause and ask yourself, “When I tell myself this, how do I feel on the inside?” Keep asking that question until you discern the actual emotions you are experiencing. Then try to connect your feelings to what matters. What do you value or need?

当你注意到这些情况时，停下来问问自己：“当我这样告诉自己时，我内心感觉如何？” 反复问自己这个问题，直到你辨别出自己真正感受到的情绪。然后试着将你的感受与真正重要的事情联系起来。你珍视什么？你需要什么？

Listen to others in this way. Try to identify what they’re feeling and, with a genuine intention to understand, consider what matters to them. What do they need that connects to these feelings? Try this silently at first, training your attention to identify feelings and needs.

用这种方式倾听他人。试着去理解他们的感受，并真诚地想要了解什么对他们来说最重要。他们需要什么才能与这些感受联系起来？一开始可以默默地尝试，训练自己去识别他人的感受和需求。

If you find yourself caught in blaming perceptions, remember that they too are just another form of information, a particular way we’ve learned to become conscious of our needs. Shift your attention to the emotions beneath the words. Tune in to your feelings, and then listen for the needs to which they are connected. What matters to you?

如果你发现自己陷入了对感知的责备之中，请记住，它们也只是另一种信息形式，是我们用来感知自身需求的一种特定方式。将注意力转移到文字背后的情绪上。倾听你的感受，然后找出与这些感受相关的需求。什么对你来说最重要？

Expressing Feelings

表达感受

Speaking about his show, Mr. Rogers’ Neighborhood, Fred Rogers once said to a US Senate committee that his aim was to “make it clear that feelings are mentionable and manageable.” 11 This perspective lays the groundwork for being able to have successful, productive conversations about the things that matter, including our emotions.

弗雷德·罗杰斯在谈到他的节目《罗杰斯先生的邻居》时，曾对美国参议院委员会说，他的目标是“明确表明，情感是可以表达和可以管理的。” 11 这种观点为我们能够就重要的事情（包括我们的情感）进行成功、富有成效的对话奠定了基础。

When we’ve trained our mind in this way, we have a powerful technology to translate blame and judgment into the feelings and needs that move in the heart. Beneath “You’re being cold,” we hear the pain of longing for more affection or intimacy. Within the expression “Stop being so sensitive,” we intuit frustration, perhaps a desire for more ease and flexibility. We learn to have empathy for others, regardless of how they’re expressing themselves, and to share our own feelings openly in a way that others are more likely to understand.

当我们以这种方式训练自己的思维时，我们就拥有了一种强大的能力，可以将责备和评判转化为内心深处的感受和需求。在“你太冷漠了”这句话背后，我们能感受到渴望更多关爱或亲密关系的痛苦。在“别这么敏感”这句话中，我们能体会到挫败感，或许是渴望更多轻松和灵活。我们学会了对他人的同理心，无论他们如何表达自己，并以一种更容易被他人理解的方式坦诚地分享自己的感受。

Sharing our feelings and needs in this way can carry a lot of weight. Recently, my friend Sarah’s mother died suddenly in the hospital. Lacking a clear diagnosis, her family made the difficult decision to conduct an autopsy. In handling the arrangements, Sarah had a challenging phone call with the funeral director, who scoffed at their choices and left out key scheduling information.

以这种方式分享我们的感受和需求意义重大。最近，我的朋友莎拉的母亲在医院突然去世。由于没有明确的诊断，她的家人艰难地决定进行尸检。在安排后事的过程中，莎拉与殡仪馆负责人进行了一次艰难的通话，对方对他们的选择嗤之以鼻，并且遗漏了一些重要的日程安排信息。

Disturbed by his lack of empathy, she asked to meet with the director in person. Sarah spoke openly and sincerely, in a nonblaming manner. “I am frustrated with the interaction we had yesterday,” she said. “The loss of my mom has been incredibly challenging for my family, and it’s really important to have as much clarity and ease as possible around these logistics.” She explained that the decision to do an autopsy was very emotional for them. “For all of these reasons, I felt disappointed and frustrated by your responses to our questions.” She encouraged him to respect the wishes of families and to interact with them with more compassion. By the end of the conversation, her clear, steady tone and openheartedness had its effect. The funeral director apologized, saying he understood and would try to communicate with more compassion in the future.

她对殡仪馆负责人缺乏同理心感到不满，于是要求与他当面会面。莎拉坦诚而真挚地表达了自己的想法，语气中没有丝毫责备。“我对昨天的沟通感到非常失望，”她说，“母亲的离世对我的家人来说是巨大的打击，因此，在处理这些事宜时，我们能够尽可能地清晰明了、轻松自在地安排好一切，真的非常重要。”她解释说，决定进行尸检对他们来说是一个极其痛苦的决定。“正因如此，我对您回答我们问题的方式感到失望和沮丧。”她鼓励他尊重家属的意愿，并以更富同情心的态度与他们沟通。谈话结束时，她清晰而沉稳的语气和坦诚的态度最终打动了对方。殡仪馆负责人向她道歉，表示理解，并承诺今后会更加体贴地与她沟通。

Principle: The more we take responsibility for our feelings, connecting them to our needs rather than to others’ actions, the easier it is for others to hear us.

原则：我们越是对自己感受负责，并将感受与我们的需求联系起来，而不是与他人的行为联系起来，别人就越容易理解我们。

Principle: The more we hear others’ feelings as a reflection of their needs, the easier it is to understand them without hearing blame, needing to agree, or feeling responsible for their emotions.

原则：我们越能将他人的感受视为他们需求的反映，就越容易理解他们，而不会感到被责备、需要同意或对他们的情绪负有责任。

Just as with needs, talking about emotions can feel vulnerable. It’s important to use wisdom in choosing when, where, and how to discuss them. This can vary widely depending on the context and culture. There’s generally more bandwidth for talking about emotions in our personal life, intimate relationships, and friendships than in most professional settings. Yet when feelings are present, it’s important to find a way to acknowledge and include them, regardless of the context. Otherwise they can start running the show beneath the surface.

就像谈论需求一样，谈论情绪也会让人感到脆弱。因此，选择何时、何地以及如何谈论情绪至关重要。这会因情境和文化的不同而有很大差异。通常来说，在个人生活、亲密关系和友谊中，我们比在大多数职业场合更容易谈论情绪。然而，当情绪出现时，无论在何种情境下，找到一种承认和接纳它们的方式都非常重要。否则，它们可能会在暗中主导一切。

When circumstances don’t support discussing feelings openly, we can include them in conversation by understating them. To acknowledge anger without inviting too much vulnerability, try choosing words that reflect a lighter emotion or minimizing it with phrases such as “a little” or “kind of.” For example, “Are you angry because you wanted things to go more smoothly?” becomes “Sounds like it’s a little frustrating because you wanted things to go more smoothly?”

当环境不适宜公开讨论感受时，我们可以通过轻描淡写的方式将其融入对话中。为了在不暴露过多脆弱的情况下表达愤怒，可以尝试选择一些反映较轻情绪的词语，或者用“有点”、“算是”之类的短语来弱化它。例如，“你是不是因为希望事情进展得更顺利而生气？”可以改成“听起来好像有点令人沮丧，因为你希望事情进展得更顺利？”

PRACTICE : Hearing and Expressing Emotions

练习：倾听和表达情绪

Try acknowledging feelings in low-stakes situations. As you listen, reflect any emotions you hear in a natural, authentic way. You might simply remark, “Wow, sounds frustrating,” or make an empathy guess, “Are you (feeling)…?” When possible, connect the emotions you sense to needs, guessing at what matters.

试着在无关紧要的情境中觉察他人的感受。倾听时，以自然真诚的方式回应你听到的任何情绪。你可以简单地说：“哇，听起来真让人沮丧”，或者做出一些同理心的猜测：“你（感觉）……？” 如果可能，将你感受到的情绪与需求联系起来，猜测哪些需求对你来说至关重要。

When you feel emotions, ground awareness in your body. Give yourself some time to sense what’s happening. Experiment with sharing your feelings and linking them with what matters to you. Can you be aware of your feelings as a reflection of your needs? Can you find ways to express them openly and honestly without blame, linking them to what you do want rather than what you don’t want?

当你感受到情绪时，将注意力集中在你的身体上。给自己一些时间去感受正在发生的事情。尝试分享你的感受，并将它们与对你重要的事情联系起来。你能否意识到你的感受反映了你的需求？你能否找到坦诚开放、不带指责地表达它们的方式，并将它们与你想要的东西联系起来，而不是与你不想要的东西联系起来？

Being aware of our feelings and needs gives us more choice about how to respond to life. When our needs are met, we may savor, celebrate, or express gratitude. When our needs are not met, we can let someone know how their words or actions affected us, linking our emotions back to our own needs. When others express praise or blame, we can tune in to the feelings and needs they’re experiencing.

觉察自身的感受和需求，能让我们在应对生活时拥有更多选择。当需求得到满足时，我们可以细细品味、庆祝或表达感激之情。当需求未得到满足时，我们可以让对方知道他们的言行对我们产生了怎样的影响，从而将自身的情绪与自身的需求联系起来。当他人表达赞扬或批评时，我们也能体会到他们正在经历的感受和需求。

When my mother and I finally reconciled, we were able to share how we felt and why. She wanted me to be happy, to live a life that she could understand and that was aligned with her values. I wanted to be seen, for her to have trust in my integrity and support for finding my own way. This understanding brought us so much closer.

当我和母亲最终和解时，我们能够坦诚地分享彼此的感受和原因。她希望我快乐，过上她能够理解、符合她价值观的生活。而我则渴望被她看见，渴望她信任我的人格，支持我寻找属于自己的道路。这种理解让我们之间的关系更加紧密。

In some circumstances, we may need to make a change or even end a relationship that is not serving us. Whatever course of action we take, we can choose to respond consciously rather than reactively, based on a clear discernment of our needs and an openness to dialogue.

在某些情况下，我们可能需要做出改变，甚至结束一段对我们无益的关系。无论我们采取何种行动，我们都可以选择理性而非冲动地应对，这基于对自身需求的清晰认知以及开放的对话态度。

We don’t need to fear our emotions. We can learn to handle them with agility, listen to their signals, and find balance within their intensity. When we move beyond the binary options of avoiding and suppressing them or identifying with and acting them out, we allow emotions to flow through us as an integral part of being human. We can receive the information they offer about our heart, the deeper needs and values that trace the lines of our life.

我们无需惧怕自己的情绪。我们可以学会灵活应对，倾听它们的信号，并在它们的强烈程度中找到平衡。当我们不再局限于逃避和压抑情绪，或者认同和付诸行动的二元选择时，我们就允许情绪自然地流淌，成为人类不可或缺的一部分。我们可以从中接收关于内心深处的信息，那些构成我们生命轨迹的深层需求和价值观。

PRINCIPLES

原则

Being aware of our emotions supports our ability to choose consciously how we participate in a conversation.

了解自己的情绪有助于我们有意识地选择如何参与对话。

The more we take responsibility for our feelings, connecting them to our needs rather than to others’ actions, the easier it is for others to hear us.

我们越是为自己的感受负责，并将感受与自身需求而非他人行为联系起来，就越容易让别人理解我们。

The more we hear others’ feelings as a reflection of their needs, the easier it is to understand them without hearing blame, needing to agree, or feeling responsible for their emotions.

我们越能将他人的感受视为他们需求的反映，就越容易理解他们，而不会感到被责备、需要认同或为他们的情绪负责。

KEY POINTS

要点

We tend to relate to our emotions by suppressing them or getting entangled with them, yet emotions are a natural part of being human that gives us important information about our needs. Mindfulness is the primary tool to develop our capacity to:

我们往往通过压抑或沉溺于情绪来应对它们，然而情绪是人类与生俱来的自然组成部分，它能为我们提供关于自身需求的重要信息。正念是培养我们以下能力的主要工具：

• Identify emotions (emotional recognition), noticing and naming what we’re feeling

• 识别情绪（情绪识别），注意到并说出我们正在感受的情绪。

• Feel emotions with balance (emotion regulation), having the space inside to appreciate the pleasant ones and tolerate the discomfort of unpleasant ones

• 能够平衡地感受情绪（情绪调节），内心有足够的空间去欣赏愉悦的情绪，也能容忍不愉快情绪带来的不适。

• Hear and express emotions without blame (emotion expression), connecting them to underlying needs or values

• 倾听并表达情绪，不加指责（情绪表达），并将情绪与潜在的需求或价值观联系起来。

Taking responsibility for our feelings and extricating ourselves from blame involve keen attention to the mechanisms of perception in our mind that generate and reinforce the blame game. We know we’re playing the blame game when we:

为自己的感受负责，并摆脱责备，需要我们敏锐地觉察到大脑中那些产生并强化“指责游戏”的感知机制。当我们有以下行为时，我们就知道自己正在玩“指责游戏”：

• Construct a narrative of blame, placing the cause of our feelings outside

• 构建一种归咎于他人的叙事，将我们感受的根源置于外部因素之上。

• Directly link our feelings to another’s actions

• 将我们的感受与他人的行为直接联系起来

• Disguise thoughts as feelings

将想法伪装成感觉

• Use false-feeling words, words that refer to emotions but instead express blame, attributing intention to another person

• 使用虚假的情感词汇，即那些指涉情绪但实际上表达的是指责、将意图归咎于他人的词汇

QUESTION & ANSWER

问答

Q: What if I don’t notice any emotions or can’t feel anything in my body?

问：如果我感觉不到任何情绪，或者身体没有任何感觉，该怎么办？

This is quite common. We live in a disembodied society, so it can take time to feel our body and experience emotions. If our emotions weren’t validated growing up, we may have learned to repress or avoid them. Or we may have shut ourselves off to our emotions after a traumatic event. Regardless of the cause, you can reawaken the ability to feel and develop a richer relationship with yourself and with life.

这种情况很常见。我们生活在一个情感淡漠的社会，所以需要时间去感受自己的身体和体验各种情绪。如果我们在成长过程中没有得到情感的认可，我们可能学会了压抑或逃避它们。或者，我们可能在经历创伤事件后封闭了自己的情感。无论原因如何，你都可以重新唤醒感受的能力，并与自己和生活建立更丰富的关系。

Notice that experience of “not feeling anything.” Is it blank, empty, numb? Is it located in any particular area of your body? Stay with it; keep being aware. Movement, yoga, dance, or exercise can help. Speak with friends and ask how they think you might be feeling. Sometimes getting a reflection can help you recognize how you feel.

注意那种“感觉不到任何东西”的体验。它是空白、空虚还是麻木？它位于你身体的哪个特定部位？保持觉察，继续感受它。运动、瑜伽、舞蹈或锻炼或许会有帮助。和朋友聊聊，问问他们觉得你可能是什么感觉。有时，反思能帮助你更好地认识自己的感受。

Last, talk to your heart. It sounds hokey, but it works. Tell your own unconscious that you’re available to feel more. Before sleep or upon rising, say to yourself something to the effect of, “I’m interested in feeling my emotions. I’m here; I’m willing to feel.” This plants a seed inside your psyche that can be the catalyst for opening to your emotions.

最后，倾听你的内心。这听起来有点老套，但真的有效。告诉你的潜意识，你愿意去感受更多。睡前或起床后，对自己说类似这样的话：“我想感受我的情绪。我在这里；我愿意去感受。” 这会在你的内心深处种下一颗种子，它能成为你敞开心扉接纳各种情绪的催化剂。

Q: I have the opposite issue. I feel so much I get overwhelmed easily. How can I work with this?

问：我的情况正好相反。我感觉自己情绪波动很大，很容易感到不知所措。我该如何应对这种情况？

Noticing this pattern is the first step to shifting it. Being able to name what’s happening is huge. Study the underlying dynamics. Are there particular situations that trigger the overwhelm? What helps you to rebalance? Use the practice for soothing strong emotions or the orienting exercise in chapter 3 . Many of our emotional wounds arose in relationships, so it can also be healing to explore these patterns in a safe, supportive context with someone else, be it a friend, a mentor, or a professional counselor.

注意到这种模式是改变它的第一步。能够说出正在发生的事情至关重要。研究其背后的动态。是否存在某些特定情境会引发这种不知所措的感觉？什么能帮助你重新获得平衡？可以尝试第三章中关于舒缓强烈情绪的练习或定向练习。我们许多情感创伤都源于人际关系，因此，在安全、支持性的环境中与他人（无论是朋友、导师还是专业咨询师）一起探索这些模式，也能起到疗愈作用。

Q: We’re not responsible for others’ reactions, but we do affect each other. How do you handle it when you’ve done something that was hurtful without getting entangled in the blame game?

问：我们无需为他人的反应负责，但我们的确会互相影响。当你做了伤害别人的事，又不陷入互相指责的漩涡时，该如何处理？

I want to be able to acknowledge when I’ve done something that doesn’t meet someone else’s needs and to repair any damage to the relationship. There’s a difference between a heartfelt apology and taking on blame. The former acknowledges the impact of my actions and expresses my sincere care or regret. The latter interprets my intentions or makes a character judgment of me as being bad or wrong.

我希望能够承认自己做了未能满足他人需求的事情，并修复由此造成的任何关系损害。真诚的道歉和承担责任之间是有区别的。前者承认我的行为造成的影响，并表达我真诚的关心或遗憾。后者则曲解我的意图，或者对我的人格做出评判，认为我不好或错了。

Q: What about when I really do feel manipulated or betrayed? What’s the role of anger in mindful communication?

问：如果我真的感到被操纵或背叛了呢？愤怒在正念沟通中扮演着什么角色？

Anger is a completely natural emotion. It’s a strong signal that our needs aren’t being met. Evolutionarily it protects us when we perceive a threat in our environment. The destructive effects of anger come from how we handle it, not from the anger itself. When we can differentiate the stories of blame from our unmet needs, we can express ourselves more constructively.

愤怒是一种完全自然的情绪。它强烈地表明我们的需求没有得到满足。从进化角度来看，当我们感知到环境中的威胁时，愤怒能够保护我们。愤怒的破坏性影响来自于我们如何处理它，而不是愤怒本身。当我们能够区分指责和未被满足的需求时，我们就能以更具建设性的方式表达自己。

Feeling “manipulated” or “betrayed” indicates that your emotions are colored by an interpretation about the other person’s intentions. To honor the intensity of your experience without getting entangled in the blame game, see those words as information that points back to your feelings and needs. Investigate what’s in your heart. When you tell yourself, “I’m being manipulated,” how do you feel on the inside? What do you need?

感到“被操纵”或“被背叛”表明你的情绪受到了对对方意图的解读的影响。为了正视你强烈的感受，同时避免陷入互相指责的泥潭，请将这些词语视为指向你自身感受和需求的线索。探究你内心的真实想法。当你告诉自己“我被操纵了”时，你内心的感受是什么？你需要什么？

Once this is clear, work on conveying the depth of your feelings without blame. Express the rawness of your emotions and connect them to what matters to you. If you can’t find other words (and if you think the other person will understand), you could take responsibility for the blame by saying something such as, “I’m telling myself a story that you betrayed me.” This indicates your subjective interpretation while leaving space for the other person’s experience.

一旦明确了这一点，就要努力表达你内心深处的感受，但不要指责对方。坦诚地表达你最真实的情绪，并将它们与你重视的事情联系起来。如果你找不到其他合适的词语（并且你认为对方能够理解），你可以承担起责备的责任，比如可以说：“我感觉你背叛了我。” 这句话既表明了你的主观感受，又为对方的感受留出了空间。

Q: What if I don’t have time to feel my emotions during the day?

问：如果我白天没有时间感受自己的情绪怎么办？

This is where formal mindfulness practice can be really beneficial. Taking time for contemplative practice gives us a chance to sort through the day so we’re not carrying the residue of our emotional responses. It also sharpens our awareness and helps us build capacity. The more we explore strong sensations and challenging emotions “on the cushion,” the more skilled we become at feeling and processing emotions “off the cushion” in our lives. Formal mindfulness practice also creates more space inside to tolerate the discomfort of unpleasant emotions without reacting, which enables us to respond in the moment with more care and thoughtfulness.

这就是正规正念练习真正发挥作用的地方。抽出时间进行冥想练习，让我们有机会梳理一天的经历，避免情绪反应的残留影响我们。它还能提升我们的觉察力，帮助我们增强应对能力。我们在“禅垫”上探索强烈感受和挑战性情绪的次数越多，就越能熟练地在生活中“离开禅垫”后感受和处理情绪。正规的正念练习还能在内心创造更多空间，让我们能够容忍不愉快情绪带来的不适而不做出反应，从而使我们能够以更关怀和更周到的方式应对当下。

# ↩

9

enhancing empathy and inner resilience

增强同理心和内在韧性

Learning to stand in somebody else’s shoes, to see through their eyes, that’s how peace begins….Empathy is a quality of character that can change the world.

—PRESIDENT BARACK OBAMA

学会设身处地为他人着想，从他们的角度看待问题，和平便由此开始……同理心是一种能够改变世界的品格。——巴拉克·奥巴马总统

THE COMMUNICATION WE ’ RE exploring in this book involves a deft shifting of attention from our inner experience to the experience of another. This flexibility confers great skill in dialogue and becomes possible when we’ve trained ourselves in empathy.

本书探讨的沟通技巧在于巧妙地将注意力从自身体验转移到他人体验上。这种灵活性赋予我们高超的对话能力，而当我们训练自己培养同理心时，这种能力便成为可能。

In formal meditation, the rhythmic sensations of breathing in and breathing out offer a reliable method to steady awareness and develop mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. In communication practice (which is its own form of meditative training), awareness of feelings and needs supports our ability to stay present, to express ourselves clearly, and to hear others with empathy.

在正式的冥想中，呼吸的节奏感提供了一种可靠的方法来稳定意识，并培养正念、专注力和智慧。在沟通练习（它本身就是一种冥想训练）中，觉察自身的感受和需求有助于我们保持临在，清晰地表达自己，并以同理心倾听他人。

In the third step to effective conversation, sometimes empathy is what matters most. As we’ve seen, empathic listening is what allows us to actually hear one another. It is a potent source for healing and resilience. It’s such an indispensable aspect of communication that I’d like to explore some additional ways to refine this capacity.

在有效对话的第三步中，同理心有时至关重要。正如我们所见，同理心倾听让我们真正理解彼此。它是疗愈和增强韧性的强大源泉。它如此不可或缺地融入沟通，因此我想探讨一些提升这种能力的方法。

Letting in the Good: Gratitude, Joy, and Celebration

接纳美好：感恩、喜悦与庆祝

When we think of empathy, we often focus on handling pain, conflict, and disagreement. Empathy does apply to handling difficulty, but it is also an essential tool for enhancing goodness: deepening friendships, strengthening bonds, and appreciating the beauty of life. Empathy is the resonant capacity of our heart. And when we turn this capacity to that which is nourishing, our heart rejoices. When I shared the news of my ordination as a Buddhist monastic with my family, I was longing for empathy for my joy—to be joined in my celebration.

当我们想到同理心时，往往会想到它如何帮助我们应对痛苦、冲突和分歧。同理心固然有助于我们处理困境，但它也是增进美好生活的重要工具：加深友谊、巩固情感纽带、欣赏生命的美好。同理心是我们心灵共鸣的能力。当我们把这种能力用于滋养身心的事物时，我们的内心便会充满喜悦。当我向家人分享我剃度成为佛教僧侣的消息时，我渴望得到他们的同理心，渴望他们能与我一同庆祝这份喜悦。

This quality (called mudita, or “appreciative joy,” in Buddhism) enhances our well-being and builds resilience. As I’ve heard it told, the Dalai Lama once said, “When you count others’ happiness as your own, your chances of being happy increase six billion to one.”

这种品质（在佛教中被称为“随喜”，或“感恩之乐”）能够提升我们的幸福感，增强我们的韧性。我曾听人说过，达赖喇嘛曾说过：“当你把别人的幸福当作自己的幸福时，你获得幸福的几率会增加六十亿分之一。”

This ability to nourish the healthy aspects of our lives is an important, often overlooked aspect of healing. It can take courage to slow down enough to enjoy a success, take pleasure in a need met, or feel an affirming sensation. With practice, we can broaden our use of empathy to savor the good, cultivate gratitude for the happiness in our own lives, and celebrate the joy or good fortune of others. 1 Try the practices below anytime.

这种滋养我们生活中健康方面的能力，是疗愈过程中一个重要却常常被忽视的环节。我们需要勇气才能放慢脚步，享受成功，为需求的满足而感到愉悦，或感受某种肯定的情绪。通过练习，我们可以拓展同理心的运用，品味美好，培养对自身幸福的感恩之心，并为他人的喜悦或好运而欢欣鼓舞。 1 随时尝试以下练习。

PRACTICE : Gratitude, Joy, and Celebration

练习：感恩、喜悦和庆祝

Take time to contemplate something that you appreciate in life. Be as specific as possible: a meal you ate, a friend you saw recently. Let this circumstance come alive in your mind’s eye. Notice any feelings of warmth, gratitude, or appreciation that arise. Where do you notice those emotions in your body? What’s it feel like there?

花点时间想想生活中让你感到感激的事情。尽可能具体：比如你吃过的一顿饭，或者最近见过的一位朋友。让这件事在你的脑海中鲜活起来。留意任何涌现的温暖、感激或欣赏之情。你感觉这些情绪在你的身体哪个部位？那里是什么感觉？

Next, consider what needs of yours have been met. What matters about this situation, event, or person? Take time to savor the enjoyment of having your needs met. Like soaking in a bath, let yourself fully absorb this.

接下来，想想你的哪些需求得到了满足。这件事、这个事件或这个人，对你来说意味着什么？花点时间细细品味需求得到满足的喜悦。就像泡澡一样，让自己完全沉浸其中。

Turn this appreciative gaze outward. When you hear good news or spend time with someone who is enjoying happiness or success, tune in to their well-being. Can you celebrate with them? Notice any tendency to compare, contract, or believe that their good fortune somehow reduces the amount of happiness available to you. How would you feel if this person were your child? Can you stretch your empathy to celebrate their happiness?

将这份欣赏的目光转向他人。当你听到好消息，或者与正在享受幸福或成功的人相处时，请关注他们的感受。你能和他们一起庆祝吗？注意你是否会有比较、贬低自己，或者认为他们的好运会减少你所能获得的幸福的倾向。如果这个人是你的孩子，你会作何感想？你能否设身处地地为他们感到高兴？

Self-Empathy: The Strength of Tenderness

自我同理心：温柔的力量

During that difficult period in my early twenties while working at a meditation center in rural Massachusetts, I felt increasingly lonely and isolated. As contemplative practice drew my attention inward, I began to feel trapped in my desire for connection. I yearned for others to ask how I was doing, yet few were able to offer the kind of attunement I needed to feel safe enough to share. Every failure to connect reinforced the isolation and heightened my desperation to be seen. Being caught in this vicious cycle was paralyzing.

二十出头那段艰难的时期，我在马萨诸塞州乡村的一家冥想中心工作，感到越来越孤独和孤立。随着冥想练习将我的注意力引向内心，我开始感到自己被困在对联结的渴望中。我渴望别人关心我的近况，但很少有人能给予我那种让我感到安全、愿意分享的共鸣。每一次联结的失败都加剧了我的孤立感，也让我更加渴望被关注。陷入这种恶性循环让我感到无力。

Pain can block empathy. When we are mired in our own distress, it can be difficult to let empathy touch us, let alone listen to others or offer them empathy. Without ways to handle our own suffering, communication becomes increasingly challenging.

痛苦会阻碍同理心。当我们深陷痛苦之中时，很难感受到同理心，更遑论倾听他人或给予他人同理心。如果无法应对自身的痛苦，沟通就会变得越来越困难。

Eventually I found one or two people who had the capacity to offer empathy in a way that I could receive. This eased the intensity of my longing and catalyzed a shift that continued to unfold for several years.

最终，我找到了一两个人，他们能够以我能接受的方式给予我同理心。这减轻了我强烈的渴望，并促成了一种转变，这种转变持续了数年。

Sometimes, receiving empathy is the balm we need to heal. Through the care of others we learn to develop tenderness toward ourselves. Self-empathy enhances resilience, transforming our relationship with ourselves from harshness and judgment to kindness and self-compassion. It includes handling stress and emotional pain, finding peace with unmet needs, and healing our inner critic.

有时，获得同理心就像一剂疗愈良药。通过他人的关爱，我们学会温柔地对待自己。自我同理心增强了我们的韧性，将我们与自己的关系从苛责和评判转变为善待和自我关怀。它包括应对压力和情感创伤，与未被满足的需求和解，以及疗愈我们内心的批判者。

Not only does this make life more enjoyable, but it also gives us considerably more options in dialogue. Self-empathy strengthens patience. With a moment of mindful self-empathy, we can acknowledge our inner experience, put it aside temporarily, and create the space to hear someone else.

这不仅让生活更加愉悦，也为我们的对话提供了更多选择。自我同理心能增强耐心。通过片刻的正念自我同理，我们可以觉察自己的内心体验，暂时将其放下，从而腾出空间倾听他人。

Principle: Having empathy for ourselves increases our capacity to listen to others, whether or not they have the space to listen to us.

原则：对自己有同理心可以提高我们倾听他人的能力，无论他们是否有时间倾听我们。

PRACTICE : Self-Empathy

练习：自我同理心

Use this meditation regularly to develop your ability to bring the caring attitude of empathy to yourself.

经常进行这种冥想练习，可以培养你对自己产生同理心和关怀的态度。

Begin by settling and establishing presence in whatever way feels authentic and natural for you—grounding in the body or taking some slow, mindful breaths. Next, call to mind a situation or event for which you’d like to develop self-empathy (nothing too painful to start).

首先，以任何你觉得真实自然的方式安顿下来，建立临在感——比如感受身体的扎根，或者进行几次缓慢的、正念的呼吸。接下来，回想一个你想培养自我同理心的情境或事件（一开始不要选择太痛苦的）。

What emotions are present? Feel their sensations in your body. If the emotion is strong, widen your attention to the rest of your body. Can you bring a quality of tenderness to any painful feelings?

你现在有哪些情绪？感受一下它们在你身体里的感觉。如果情绪很强烈，就把注意力扩展到身体的其他部位。你能否用温柔的眼光去对待任何痛苦的感觉？

Next, inquire about your needs and values, listening inwardly for what matters. Ask, “If I had that, then what would I have?” or, “What matters about that to me?” Inquire until you feel clear about your needs. Again, see if you can bring a quality of tenderness to how much you value this. Call forth all the care you can find for yourself and rest your attention with this feeling of kindness.

接下来，探究你的需求和价值观，用心聆听内心的声音，找出真正重要的事。问问自己：“如果我拥有了那个，我还会拥有什么？”或者，“这件事对我来说有什么意义？”反复探究，直到你清晰地了解自己的需求。再次尝试用温柔的语气来表达你对它的珍视。唤起你所能找到的所有关爱，并将注意力集中在这份善意上。

Finally, shift your attention to the universal aspect of the need or value itself as a facet of our shared humanity. Can you connect with any sense of wholeness, beauty, or dignity in this value?

最后，将注意力转移到需求或价值本身的普遍性层面，将其视为我们共同人性的一个方面。你能从这种价值中感受到任何完整、美好或尊严吗？

The Riverbanks of Empathy: Dealing with Empathic Distress

同理心的河岸：应对同理心困扰

There is an empathy spectrum in humans, a range of access to empathy and a range of intensity with which we feel it. 2 At times, empathy can come so easily that we feel overwhelmed or flooded by the depth of feeling. Indeed, one common cause of compassion fatigue is a kind of overidentification with the suffering of another, sometimes referred to as empathic distress. 3

人类的同理心存在一个谱系，我们对同理心的感知能力和感受强度各不相同。有时，同理心会如此轻易地涌现，以至于我们感到不知所措，甚至被强烈的情感所淹没。事实上，同情疲劳的一个常见原因就是过度认同他人的痛苦，有时也被称为同理心困扰。

In these instances, the skill of empathy involves learning to manage our distress and sense our separateness. If we become overwhelmed, we lose the ability to engage skillfully. Out of self-protection, we may react in an attempt to manage our own pain or withdraw in fear of becoming lost in another’s experience.

在这些情况下，同理心的技巧在于学习如何应对自身的痛苦并感知自身的疏离感。如果我们感到不知所措，就会失去有效应对的能力。出于自我保护，我们可能会做出反应，试图控制自己的痛苦，或者因为害怕迷失在他人的经历中而选择退缩。

PRACTICE : Meeting Empathic Distress in the Body

实践：在身体层面应对共情带来的痛苦

The three kinds of empathy (somatic, affective, cognitive) provide a useful framework to build a strong inner container, like having riverbanks that support the flow of empathy. 4

三种类型的同理心（躯体同理心、情感同理心、认知同理心）提供了一个有用的框架，可以构建一个强大的内在容器，就像拥有河岸来支撑同理心的流动一样。

Try the following somatic exercises to regain balance:

尝试以下身体练习来恢复平衡：

• Orient to your surroundings to register physical safety.

• 环顾四周，确认自身人身安全。

• Ground your attention, connecting with gravity or another embodied reference point (your centerline, breathing, or touch points such as your hands or feet).

• 将注意力集中到地面上，与重力或其他身体参照点（你的中心线、呼吸或接触点，如你的手或脚）建立联系。

• Sense the boundaries of your skin. Engage in any activity that stimulates the felt sense of your body, such as exercise, massage, gently squeezing your limbs, or a hot shower.

• 感受你皮肤的边界。进行任何能刺激你身体感觉的活动，例如运动、按摩、轻轻挤压四肢或洗个热水澡。

• Notice the physical space between you and the other person or notice the space around you.

• 注意你和对方之间的物理距离，或者注意你周围的空间。

In the affective domain, do your best to pause further input. For example, many people today suffer from empathic distress due to overexposure to intense worldwide suffering through the news media. Recovering and developing a more balanced relationship with empathy often includes limiting one’s intake of news for a time.

在情感领域，尽量暂停接收更多信息。例如，如今许多人由于过度接触新闻媒体报道的全球苦难，而遭受同理心困扰。恢复并建立更平衡的同理心关系通常需要暂时限制新闻摄入量。

In conversation, if you begin to feel overwhelmed or lose presence, find a way to skillfully pause the dialogue. Affirm your desire to stay connected, then share your need for a break. Here are a few examples:

在交谈中，如果你开始感到不知所措或注意力分散，可以巧妙地暂停对话。先表达你想要保持联系的愿望，然后说明你需要休息一下。以下是一些例子：

• “I think I need a moment to gather my thoughts.”

• “我想我需要一点时间整理一下思绪。”

• “Wow, I’d like some time to take that in. Can we pause here for a moment?”

• “哇，我需要点时间消化一下。我们能在这里暂停一下吗？”

• “I’d really like to continue discussing this, and I’m feeling a little overwhelmed. Could we take a break and continue tomorrow?”

• “我真的很想继续讨论这个问题，但我感觉有点应接不暇。我们能休息一下，明天再继续吗？”

Once you’ve pressed pause, here are a few ways to integrate and digest what’s been stimulated emotionally:

按下暂停键后，以下几种方法可以帮助你整合和消化受到的情绪刺激：

• Receive empathy from a friend or a mentor.

• 从朋友或导师那里获得同情和理解。

• Engage in self-empathy practice.

• 进行自我同理心练习。

• Soothe strong emotions with formal mindfulness practice.

• 通过正规的正念练习来舒缓强烈的情绪。

• Balance your activation with forms of healthy pleasure such as time in nature, art, or music.

• 将你的精力投入与健康的娱乐方式相结合，例如亲近自然、艺术或音乐。

Finally, in the cognitive domain, explore underlying beliefs that contribute to any overidentification with another’s feelings. Talk with a friend and try to uncover any assumptions you have about your role in the situation, what it means to care, or how healing occurs. Here are a few of the common beliefs that may be at play:

最后，在认知层面，探究那些导致你过度认同他人感受的潜在信念。和朋友聊聊，试着找出你对自己在情境中的角色、关心的意义以及疗愈过程的任何假设。以下是一些可能起作用的常见信念：

• You may believe it’s your responsibility to take care of others out of duty, fear, or an inability to handle your own discomfort with their struggle.

• 你可能认为，出于责任、恐惧或无法忍受他人困境带来的不适，你有责任照顾他人。

• You may identify with being a caregiver and feel disoriented by the possibility of stepping out of that role.

• 你可能会认同自己是照顾者的角色，并对退出这个角色的可能性感到迷茫。

• You may believe that caring means suffering, that you can’t genuinely have compassion for someone in pain and still be happy yourself.

• 你可能认为关心他人意味着受苦，你不可能真正同情一个正在遭受痛苦的人，同时自己又感到快乐。

• You may believe that you know what they need better than they do.

• 你可能认为你比他们更了解他们的需求。

• If you sense that the other person doesn’t have sufficient inner or outer resources, you may automatically take on more responsibility instead of supporting their agency or capacity for self-care.

• 如果你感觉到对方缺乏足够的内在或外在资源，你可能会自动承担更多责任，而不是支持他们的自主性或自我照顾能力。

• You may have other conscious or unconscious beliefs that oblige you to take on the other person’s suffering.

• 你可能还有其他有意识或无意识的信念，迫使你承担他人的痛苦。

These beliefs can be deeply rooted, compelling you to “fall in” to another person’s pain out of your desire to help. Investigate what may be driving your own empathic distress. If you step back, you’ll recognize that you have more to offer when you’re balanced and well-resourced.

这些信念可能根深蒂固，驱使你出于助人的愿望而“陷入”他人的痛苦之中。探究一下是什么导致了你自身的共情困境。如果你能冷静下来，就会意识到，当你身心平衡、资源充足时，你才能更好地帮助他人。

True empathy rests upon being centered. It arises from a deep trust in life and the innate intelligence of the mind and body. When we try to fix, change, or resolve another’s pain (believing that we even could), we contribute to their fear and helplessness, effectively saying, “You can’t figure this out, so let me do it for you.”

真正的同理心源于内心的平静。它来自对生活的深切信任，以及对身心固有智慧的尊重。当我们试图去修复、改变或解决他人的痛苦（甚至自认为能够做到）时，我们反而会加剧他们的恐惧和无助，实际上是在说：“你解决不了这个问题，所以让我来帮你吧。”

In contrast, the empathic response allows experience to be just as it is. The acceptance, trust, and genuine care of empathy impart a sense of empowerment and often a healing power. As Carl Rogers wrote:

相反，同理心回应允许体验如实呈现。同理心所包含的接纳、信任和真诚关怀赋予人力量感，并常常具有疗愈作用。正如卡尔·罗杰斯所写：

When someone really hears you without passing judgment on you, without trying to take responsibility for you, without trying to mold you, it feels damn good. When I have been listened to and when I have been heard, I am able to re-perceive my world in a new way and to go on. It is astonishing how elements which seem insoluble become soluble when someone listens. How confusions which seem irremediable turn into relatively clear flowing streams when one is heard. 5

当有人真正倾听你，不评判你，不试图为你承担责任，也不试图改变你时，那种感觉真是太棒了。当我被倾听，当我被理解时，我能够以全新的视角重新看待我的世界，并继续前行。令人惊叹的是，那些看似无法解决的问题，在有人倾听之后竟变得可以化解；那些看似无法弥合的困惑，在被倾听之后竟变得清晰明了。

The key to this sort of balance is being able to maintain perspective. We recall certain fundamental truths. Being alive is inherently vulnerable; we all suffer and feel pain. Life is a series of ups and downs, with inevitable challenges and losses. We’re ultimately not in control—we can neither prevent nor remove another’s hardships. This is the wisdom of an elder. It lends equanimity and tenderness in the face of difficulty.

这种平衡的关键在于保持清醒的头脑。我们谨记一些基本真理。活着本身就意味着脆弱；我们都会经历苦难和痛苦。人生起伏跌宕，充满挑战和失去。我们最终无法掌控一切——我们既无法阻止也无法消除他人的苦难。这就是长者的智慧。它让我们在困境面前保持平静和温柔。

When our capacity for empathy is integrated in all three domains—when cognitive empathy is imbued with wisdom, when affective empathy is balanced with resource, and when somatic empathy is grounded in presence—the result is a resilience and poise in relation to pain and suffering. Our heart can resonate with the joys and sorrows of others without being overwhelmed.

当我们的同理心在认知、情感和身体三个层面都得到整合——认知同理心融入智慧，情感同理心与资源相平衡，身体同理心扎根于临在——我们便能拥有面对痛苦和磨难的韧性和沉着。我们的心能够与他人的喜怒哀乐产生共鸣，而不被其所淹没。

Empathy without Agreement

无需认同的同理心

When we disagree, we may resist opening our heart to someone else out of concern that having empathy means agreeing with their views or that it would be interpreted as such. Yet showing that we understand how someone feels or what matters to them is not the same as agreeing with their ideas or supporting actions that don’t align with our values.

当我们意见相左时，我们可能会因为担心同理心意味着认同对方的观点，或者担心别人会这样解读，而抗拒向他人敞开心扉。然而，表达我们对他人感受或价值观的理解，并不等同于认同他们的想法或支持与我们价值观相悖的行为。

This is one of the great strengths of empathy: the possibility of finding connection without agreement. When we focus our attention on another’s feelings and needs, it helps us tune in to their experience and connect with empathy. Try the following exercise to strengthen your capacity for empathy and enhance your ability to shift back and forth from your own experience to another’s.

这就是同理心的一大优势：无需认同也能建立联结。当我们关注他人的感受和需求时，就能更好地体会他们的体验，并产生同理心。不妨尝试以下练习，增强你的同理心，提升你在自身体验和他人体验之间切换的能力。

PRACTICE : Empathy Map

练习：同理心地图

Use this reflection to explore a disagreement or prepare for a conversation. Begin with simpler, less emotionally charged situations, working up to more difficult ones. Draw four quadrants on a piece of paper as in the diagram below.

利用这种反思方法来探究分歧或为对话做准备。先从较简单、情绪不那么激烈的情境入手，逐步过渡到更复杂的情境。在一张纸上画出四个象限，如下图所示。

1. Explore your feelings and enter those in the upper left quadrant.

1. 探索你的感受，并将这些感受填入左上象限。

2. To what needs is each of those feelings connected? What matters most to you? Explore your needs sufficiently until you feel a sense of settling. Enter those needs in the lower left quadrant.

2. 这些感受分别与哪些需求相关？对你来说最重要的是什么？充分探索你的需求，直到你感到安心为止。将这些需求填入左下象限。

3. Shift your attention to the other person and explore their feelings. Imagine what emotions they might be feeling. Enter those in the upper right quadrant.

3. 将注意力转移到对方身上，探索他们的感受。想象一下他们可能正在经历哪些情绪。将这些情绪填入右上象限。

4. Stretch your heart and consider their needs. What matters to this person? To what needs might their feelings be connected? If you don’t feel support for their needs, then you haven’t gotten to the level of their real needs. Inquire, “If they had that, then what would they have?” Enter those needs into the lower right quadrant.

4. 敞开心扉，体会他们的需求。对这个人来说，什么最重要？他们的感受可能与哪些需求相关？如果你感觉不到对他们需求的支持，那就说明你还没有真正理解他们的需求。问问自己：“如果他们得到了这些，他们还会拥有什么？”把这些需求填入右下象限。

5. Compare the two sides. Does anything shift for you? How might you approach the situation having done this exercise?

5. 对比双方观点。你的看法是否有所改变？完成这项练习后，你会如何处理这种情况？

Empathy Map

同理心地图

Refining Empathy: Beyond You or Me

提升同理心：超越你我

In this chapter we’ve explored several methods to navigate the interpersonal terrain of empathy: building an inner well of resources through joy, gratitude, and self-empathy; supporting empathy with strong riverbanks; and stretching our capacity to connect when we disagree. At the center of these techniques lies a fundamental willingness to be affected. Empathy challenges our notions of separateness. To open my heart to the joy or pain of another means that I am willing to feel, willing to be moved.

在本章中，我们探讨了几种在人际交往中运用同理心的方法：通过喜悦、感恩和自我同理心来构建内在资源；用坚实的后盾来支撑同理心；以及在意见相左时拓展我们与他人联结的能力。这些技巧的核心在于一种根本的、愿意被影响的意愿。同理心挑战了我们对分离的认知。敞开心扉去感受他人的喜悦或痛苦，意味着我愿意去感受，愿意被感动。

When I ended my time as a Buddhist monastic after two and a half years and returned to lay life, things got hard fast. In the space of one week, I contracted Lyme disease, left the monastery, and admitted my father to the hospital for systemic sepsis. My own health complications from the Lyme extended from weeks into months. At one point, when sharing my profound exhaustion with a good friend, she looked at me and simply said about the Lyme, “I’m so, so sorry that happened.”

结束两年半的僧侣生活，重返世俗生活后，一切急转直下。短短一周之内，我感染了莱姆病，离开了寺院，父亲也因全身性败血症被送进了医院。莱姆病引发的并发症持续了数周，最终演变成数月。有一次，我向一位好友倾诉自己精疲力竭的感受，她看着我，只是简单地说：“我很抱歉你得了莱姆病。”

It was a moment of true empathy, of sincere and palpable caring. She was not “reflecting feelings and needs.” She was not making an empathic guess or checking if she understood. Having allowed herself to feel my struggle, to sense my pain directly, she authentically expressed the truth in her own heart. In that instance I was no longer alone.

那一刻，她展现了真正的同理心，真挚而真切的关怀。她并非在“反映我的感受和需求”，也并非在进行同情式的猜测或确认自己是否理解。她允许自己去感受我的挣扎，直接体会我的痛苦，并真诚地表达了她内心的真实感受。那一刻，我不再孤单。

In the fields of counseling, psychology, and interpersonal communication we sometimes speak of “giving” and “receiving” empathy. As long as there is a concept of a giver and a receiver, a fixed sense of me and you, we are not inhabiting the full potential of empathy. True empathy transcends the duality between speaker and listener. Instead of engaging in an exchange, we enter a field of empathic presence—one of awareness, warmth, and care—in which all experience, regardless of its local identity as mine or yours, is known and felt. We enter that space by using whatever tools support our ability to open our heart to another’s experience.

在咨询、心理学和人际沟通领域，我们有时会谈到“给予”和“接受”同理心。只要存在给予者和接受者的概念，存在“我”和“你”的固定对立，我们就无法充分发挥同理心的潜能。真正的同理心超越了说话者和倾听者之间的二元对立。我们不再进行简单的交流，而是进入一个充满同理心的场域——一个充满觉察、温暖和关怀的场域——在这个场域中，所有的经历，无论其被定义为“我的”还是“你的”，都能被感知和理解。我们通过运用各种工具，敞开心扉去感受他人的经历，从而进入这个场域。

I believe our society and world today have a vast need for this kind of true, deep empathy. From our individual hunger for connection and healing to the urgent need to bridge political, class, and racial divides; from a growing global refugee crisis to the dangerous effects of climate change—empathy can extend our sense of identity beyond traditional borders, even beyond the human family to include other species and the biosphere as a whole. Fritz Perls, the psychiatrist who founded gestalt therapy, once said, “Contact is curative.” Our ability to develop empathy and genuinely contact each other holds an essential key to our evolution as a species and survival as a civilization.

我相信，当今社会和世界迫切需要这种真正深刻的同理心。从我们个人对联结和疗愈的渴望，到弥合政治、阶级和种族鸿沟的迫切需要；从日益严重的全球难民危机，到气候变化带来的危险影响——同理心能够将我们的身份认同感延伸到传统边界之外，甚至超越人类大家庭，涵盖其他物种和整个生物圈。格式塔疗法的创始人、精神病学家弗里茨·珀尔斯曾说过：“接触具有疗愈作用。”我们培养同理心并真诚地与他人沟通的能力，是我们作为物种进化和作为文明生存的关键所在。

PRACTICE : Ways of Empathy

练习：同理心的表达方式

Below is a review of empathy practices. Experiment with these methods to access, share, and express empathy:

以下是一些培养同理心的方法。尝试运用这些方法来培养、分享和表达同理心：

SILENT EMPATHIC PRESENCE : Offer your wholehearted, undivided attention to another.

无声的同理心陪伴：全心全意地关注他人。

PARAPHRASING : Offer your understanding of the gist of what the other person has said, summarizing their story or its key details.

释义：表达你对对方所说内容的理解，总结他们的故事或其关键细节。

EMPATHIC REFLECTION : Complete the cycle by reflecting before you respond, focusing on what’s most salient in the moment. If feelings are what’s strongest, offer an empathic guess of the other person’s feelings. If their passion seems connected to what matters, guess at their needs. Practice the grammar of inner freedom by connecting their feelings to their needs. Do this as naturally as possible, being sure to phrase your guess as a question. You’re checking that you understand rather than telling the other person their experience.

同理心反思：在回应之前，先进行反思，专注于当下最突出的感受，从而完成整个循环。如果对方最强烈的感受是情绪，那就尝试用同理心去猜测他们的感受。如果他们的热情似乎与重要的事情相关，那就猜测他们的需求。通过将他们的感受与需求联系起来，练习内在自由的语法。尽可能自然地进行，确保将你的猜测表述为一个问题。你是在确认自己是否理解，而不是在替对方讲述他们的经历。

EMPATHIC EXPRESSION : Respond honestly and authentically from your heart. Let yourself take in what’s been shared. How do their words affect you?

同理心表达：真诚地、发自内心地回应。让自己去体会对方分享的内容。他们的话语对你有什么影响？

EMPATHIC / COMPASSIONATE ACTION : Allow yourself to respond with action. This could be touch, inquiring if they have any specific requests, or checking to see if the other person would welcome your support in other ways.

同理心/同情心行动：允许自己以实际行动回应。这可以是触摸对方，询问他们是否有任何具体要求，或者询问对方是否需要其他方式的帮助。

PRINCIPLES

原则

Having empathy for ourselves increases our capacity to listen to others, whether or not they have the space to listen to us.

对自己有同理心，就能提高我们倾听他人的能力，无论他们是否有时间倾听我们。

KEY POINTS

要点

Empathy challenges our notions of separateness. To open our heart to the joy or pain of another means we must be willing to feel. To enhance our access to empathy, we can:

同理心挑战了我们对分离的固有观念。要敞开心扉感受他人的喜悦或痛苦，我们必须愿意去感受。为了增强我们的同理心，我们可以：

• Build an inner well of resilience through joy, gratitude, and self-empathy

• 通过快乐、感恩和自我关怀来建立内在的韧性。

• Manage any distress, potential for overwhelm, or sense of separateness by integrating all three kinds of empathy: somatic, affective, and cognitive

• 通过整合躯体同理心、情感同理心和认知同理心这三种同理心，来应对任何痛苦、潜在的不知所措感或疏离感。

• Stretch our capacity to connect when we disagree by focusing our attention on another’s feelings and needs

• 当我们意见不一致时，通过关注对方的感受和需求，可以提升我们沟通的能力。

We can further balance empathic distress by:

我们还可以通过以下方式进一步平衡共情带来的痛苦：

• Taking a break from the conversation

• 暂停一下谈话

• Getting empathy or practicing self-empathy

• 培养同理心或练习自我同理心

• Self-soothing through healthy pleasure (exercise, music, art)

• 通过健康的娱乐方式（运动、音乐、艺术）进行自我舒缓

• Exploring any beliefs that create obligation, entanglement, or distortion of responsibility with regards to another’s pain

• 探究任何可能导致对他人痛苦产生义务感、纠缠感或责任扭曲的信念

QUESTION & ANSWER

问答

Q: When I empathize, am I just projecting my own experience onto someone?

问：当我表达同理心时，我是否只是将自己的经历投射到别人身上？

This is the paradox of empathy, which asks one to be fully present, rooted in oneself, and simultaneously transcend one’s own experience—to step outside of it and imagine another’s inner world. In some ways, we’re always referencing our own subjective experience to understand one another. Each of our experiences is unique, yet we have words for emotions and needs because there is a universal nature to them. While I can never know exactly how it is for you to feel sad, I can approximate because I’ve felt sad.

这就是同理心的悖论：它要求我们全然临在，扎根于自身，同时又要超越自身的经验——跳出自身局限，设身处地地想象他人的内心世界。在某种程度上，我们总是借助自身的主观经验来理解彼此。每个人的经历都是独一无二的，但我们却拥有描述情感和需求的词汇，因为它们具有某种普遍性。虽然我永远无法确切地知道你感到悲伤是什么滋味，但我可以大致体会，因为我也曾感受过悲伤。

There’s a kind of humility in true empathy. The absence of this quality says, “I know exactly how you feel.” The presence of humility says, “I can’t know exactly how you feel, but I care about what’s happening for you and I will try to understand.” This humility contains within it a deep respect and honor for another’s experience.

真正的同理心蕴含着一种谦逊。缺乏这种品质，就等于在说：“我完全了解你的感受。”而谦逊则意味着：“我无法完全了解你的感受，但我关心你的遭遇，我会努力去理解。”这种谦逊中饱含着对他人经历的深深尊重和敬意。

Q: What’s the difference between empathy and compassion?

问：同理心和同情心有什么区别？

The way I use these terms, empathy is broader and refers to the resonant capacity of the heart. It’s a receptive quality that can attune to the full range of human experience, pleasant or unpleasant, joy as well as sadness. Compassion is a subset of empathy, referring specifically to care for suffering and pain. The receptive aspect of compassion is empathic attunement to the suffering. The active component of compassion is a readiness to respond in order to alleviate suffering. Both empathy and compassion depend on equanimity; we need balance and wisdom to be aware of another’s inner experience without becoming overidentified with it.

我使用这些术语的方式是，同理心的含义更广泛，指的是心灵的共鸣能力。它是一种接纳的品质，能够感知人类体验的方方面面，无论是愉悦还是痛苦，喜悦还是悲伤。慈悲是同理心的一个子集，特指对苦难和痛苦的关怀。慈悲的接纳层面是对苦难的同理心式的感知。慈悲的主动层面则是随时准备回应以减轻痛苦。同理心和慈悲都依赖于内心的平静；我们需要平衡和智慧，才能觉察他人的内心体验而不至于过度认同其中。

Q: I keep trying to empathize with my teenage daughter, but it doesn’t seem to help. I’ll say, “I hear how much you really want to go out tonight, but I need to finish this work so I can’t take you.” She just gets angry or says that I don’t really care.

问：我一直试图理解我十几岁的女儿，但似乎没什么用。我会说：“我知道你今晚很想出去玩，但我得先把工作做完，所以不能带你去。”她要么生气，要么说我根本不在乎。

I’m glad you’re making an effort to use these tools with your family. I have more hope for our world when I think about children learning these skills.

很高兴你努力和家人一起使用这些工具。想到孩子们能够学习这些技能，我就对我们的世界充满希望。

I see a couple of things in your approach that indicate why your daughter might not feel seen or heard. You seem to have already come to the conclusion that there isn’t a way to meet both your needs and her needs. Having a fixed outcome in mind leaves less room to connect and collaborate. This shows up in how quickly you move from empathy to your own needs.

我从你的做法中看出几点，这些可能解释了为什么你女儿会觉得不被重视或倾听。你似乎已经认定无法同时满足你和她的需求。心中预设了结果，就意味着你们之间缺乏沟通和协作的空间。这一点在你迅速从同情转向满足自身需求上体现得淋漓尽致。

Separate offering your daughter empathy from expressing your needs. Give her your full and complete attention, reflecting her feelings and/or needs until she feels heard. Then share your side of things and propose brainstorming to find something that works for both of you. Maybe she helps you and then you take her? Could she take a cab and work later to pay you back? Even if you can’t find a way to meet all of the needs, listening and being open to collaborating will likely strengthen the relationship.

将表达对女儿的同理心与表达自己的需求区分开来。全神贯注地倾听她，回应她的感受和/或需求，直到她感到被理解。然后分享你的想法，并提议一起集思广益，找到一个对双方都合适的解决方案。也许她可以帮你，然后你再送她？或者她可以打车，之后再去工作挣钱还你？即使你无法满足她所有的需求，倾听和开放的合作态度也很有可能增进你们之间的关系。

# ↩

10

how to raise an issue without starting a fight

如何在不引发争吵的情况下提出问题

The ability to observe without evaluating is the highest form of human intelligence.

—JIDDU KRISHNAMURTI

不加评判地观察是人类智慧的最高形式。——吉杜·克里希那穆提

WE ’ VE EXPLORED THE process of listening at some length—using presence and intention to meet others with a balanced and open mind, identifying emotions, sensing needs, and developing empathy. These practices enhance our ability to listen, and they form the basis for speaking.

我们已经深入探讨了倾听的过程——运用专注和意图，以平衡开放的心态与他人交流，识别情绪，感知需求，并培养同理心。这些练习能够提升我们的倾听能力，也是我们表达的基础。

Whenever I teach mindful communication, I generally introduce tools for listening before speaking for a few reasons. First, it’s often the bottleneck in conversation. When neither person can listen, understanding ceases and conversation can break down. Second, it’s how we learn to speak. Every infant learns to speak by hearing the sounds, rhythm, and syntax of their native language. When we train to listen, we begin intuitively to learn how to articulate ourselves.

每当我教授正念沟通时，我通常会先介绍一些倾听技巧，然后再发言，原因有二。首先，倾听往往是对话的瓶颈。如果双方都无法倾听，理解就会中断，对话也会陷入僵局。其次，这是我们学习说话的方式。每个婴儿都是通过聆听母语的语音、节奏和句法来学习说话的。当我们训练自己倾听时，我们就会自然而然地开始学习如何清晰地表达自己。

Now let’s talk about the other side of the equation: self-expression. How do we say what we mean? To say what we mean requires knowing what we mean. We must be able to listen inwardly and get clear about our experience. What do we want the other person to know? And how can we communicate that fully and authentically, in a way that they can hear?

现在我们来谈谈等式的另一面：自我表达。我们如何表达自己的想法？要表达自己的想法，首先要知道自己想表达什么。我们必须能够倾听内心的声音，清晰地了解自己的体验。我们想让对方知道什么？我们又该如何以对方能够理解的方式，完整而真诚地传达这些信息呢？

The core of Rosenberg’s Nonviolent Communication model—observations, feelings, needs, and requests—offers a powerful template to investigate our own experience, thoughts, and emotions and to determine the essential components we wish to communicate. Before discussing our feelings and needs, we may need to get on the same page about the events in question. Making observations helps us talk about the context of a situation. When we don’t make observations, we can end up arguing about stuff that doesn’t matter or just feeling confused about the topic of discussion.

罗森伯格非暴力沟通模式的核心——观察、感受、需求和请求——提供了一个强有力的模板，帮助我们审视自身的经历、想法和情绪，并确定我们想要沟通的关键要素。在讨论感受和需求之前，我们可能需要就相关事件达成共识。观察有助于我们探讨情境的背景。如果我们不进行观察，最终可能会陷入无关紧要的争论，或者对讨论的主题感到困惑。

In this chapter we shift our attention in the communication dance from listening to speaking. We’ll explore the role of making observations in conversations, look at some tools for training our attention to observe clearly, and learn how to translate judgments into useful feedback.

本章我们将沟通的重点从倾听转移到表达。我们将探讨在对话中进行观察的作用，学习一些训练我们清晰观察能力的工具，并学习如何将判断转化为有用的反馈。

What Are You Adding?

你要添加什么？

The Buddhist teacher Sylvia Boorstein tells the story of calling a Zen meditation center to register for an upcoming retreat (this was in the days before online registration). She reached the receptionist, who explained she would need to speak with a man named Steve who had already left for the day. She called back the following day, only to find that she had just missed Steve again, and was told to try back tomorrow when Steve would be in by 9:00 a.m. The next day she dutifully called shortly after 9:00 a.m. only to be told by the receptionist, “I’m so sorry. Steve is stuck in traffic.”

佛教老师西尔维娅·布尔斯坦讲述了她打电话给一家禅修中心报名参加即将举行的静修活动的故事（那时还没有网上报名）。她接通了前台，前台解释说她需要和一位名叫史蒂夫的男士通话，但他当天已经下班了。第二天她再次致电，却发现自己又错过了史蒂夫，被告知第二天早上9点史蒂夫会来，再打过去。第二天早上9点刚过，她就准时打了过去，前台却说：“非常抱歉，史蒂夫堵车了。”

Feeling frustrated, Sylvia exclaimed, “Well, I guess this means I’m not supposed to sit this retreat!” The receptionist replied rather dryly, “No, it means Steve’s not here.”

西尔维娅感到很沮丧，她喊道：“好吧，看来我不应该参加这次静修活动了！”接待员语气冷淡地回答说：“不，意思是史蒂夫没来。”

We can jump to conclusions so quickly! Joseph Goldstein describes an interview with a student on a meditation retreat who had been noticing tension in his jaw. He began to weave a story, telling Joseph, “I’m such an anxious person, always so tense and uptight.” Joseph responded, “It sounds like you noticed your jaw was tight.” The student continued, “I’ve always been high-strung. That’s probably why my relationships never last. I’ll never have a long-term relationship because I’m so anxious…I’ll always be alone.” Again, Joseph pointed out, “It sounds like you experienced a feeling of tightness in your jaw; the rest is thinking.”

我们很容易妄下结论！约瑟夫·戈德斯坦讲述了他与一位参加冥想静修的学生的访谈，这位学生注意到自己下巴有些紧绷。他开始讲述自己的经历，告诉约瑟夫：“我是一个特别焦虑的人，总是那么紧张不安。”约瑟夫回应道：“听起来你只是感觉到了下巴紧绷。”学生继续说道：“我一直都很神经质。这可能就是为什么我的感情总是无法长久的原因。我永远不可能拥有长久的感情，因为我太焦虑了……我注定孤独终老。”约瑟夫再次指出：“听起来你只是感觉到了下巴紧绷；其他的都是你的臆想。”

Experience is one thing; what we add to it is another. Knowing the difference between these two is the key to talking about what happened in a way that builds understanding.

经验是一回事，我们在此基础上添加的东西又是另一回事。了解这两者之间的区别，是能够以增进理解的方式谈论已发生的事情的关键。

Principle: Stating clearly what happened, without judgment or evaluation, makes it easier for someone to hear us and to work toward a solution.

原则：清楚地陈述所发生的事情，不加评判或评价，会让别人更容易听进去，也更容易找到解决办法。

Have you ever tried to have a conversation only to find yourself in the middle of an argument in less than one sentence? Maybe you begin, “I wanted to talk about how messy the kitchen’s been lately—” and before you can get another word out the person is defending themselves or accusing you of being a neat freak. “What just happened?” you wonder.

你有没有过这样的经历：想和人好好聊聊天，结果不到一句话就陷入了争吵？也许你刚开口说：“我想说说最近厨房有多乱——”还没等你说完，对方就开始为自己辩解，或者指责你有洁癖。“刚才发生了什么？”你疑惑地问。

If we lead with a subjective interpretation that the other person doesn’t share, they’re likely to challenge it. The blame game thrives on interpretations: “messy, ignored, attacked.” Clear observations allow us to discuss events with less chance of an argument.

如果我们一开始就提出对方不认同的主观解读，他们很可能会质疑。互相指责的风气往往建立在各种解读之上：“一团糟”、“被忽视”、“被攻击”。清晰的观察能让我们更理性地讨论事件，减少争论的可能性。

You also may have had a corollary experience: someone approaches you and launches into a diatribe, visibly upset. You’re confused, caught off guard. You may think to yourself, “What are they talking about?”

你可能也有过类似的经历：有人走过来，情绪明显激动，开始滔滔不绝地抱怨。你感到困惑，措手不及。你可能会想：“他们在说什么？”

Without an observation, we are left on our own to puzzle things out. Observations provide a shared reference point. They give us a context to talk about our feelings and needs in a way that the other person is more likely to recognize without needing to argue.

如果没有观察，我们就只能独自摸索。观察提供了一个共同的参照点，让我们能够在一个语境下谈论自己的感受和需求，这样对方更容易理解，而无需争论。

An observation is a concrete, specific, and neutral statement of an event, of what we see or hear in our environment, distinct from evaluation or interpretation.

观察是对事件、对我们周围环境中所见所闻的具体、明确和中立的陈述，与评价或解释不同。

Referring to what happened clearly and neutrally makes it easier to get on the same page. We can cover a lot ground in dialogue just by sifting through interpretations, judgments, and evaluations and building a shared understanding of events.

清晰客观地描述事件经过，更容易达成共识。通过梳理各种解读、判断和评价，并建立对事件的共同理解，我们可以在对话中取得很大进展。

Seeing Clearly

看得清楚

My good friend Hanuman knows something about separating observations from interpretations. One afternoon in Boston, he met an attractive young woman while waiting at a crosswalk. They had a short but warm connection, and they exchanged numbers. A few days later he called and left a message. After a couple of weeks, when he didn’t hear back, he decided to call again. More time passed with no response. Hanuman stuck with his observations: he’d felt a genuine connection when they met; he’d left a few messages and hadn’t heard back. That’s all he knew.

我的好友哈努曼深谙区分观察与解读之道。一天下午在波士顿，他在人行横道等红灯时，邂逅了一位年轻貌美的女子。两人短暂而亲切地交谈了几句，并互留了电话号码。几天后，他打电话留言。几周过去，杳无音信，他又打了一次。时间一分一秒地过去，依然没有回应。哈努曼坚持自己的观察：初次见面时，他确实感受到了彼此间的真挚情谊；他留了几次言，却始终没有收到回复。这就是他所知道的一切。

Over the next few months, he called a few more times, leaving short, friendly messages with an open invitation to connect. Months later, the phone rang. She’d been doing her residency, pulling all-nighters, and said she was so glad he kept calling. They went kayaking and ended up dating for over three years.

接下来的几个月里，他又打了几次电话，每次都留下简短友好的留言，热情地邀请她联系。几个月后，电话响了。她当时正在做住院医师，经常熬夜，她说很高兴他一直打电话来。他们一起去划皮划艇，最终发展成了恋爱关系，这段关系持续了三年多。

It’s natural to interpret and draw conclusions from our experience; it’s part of how we navigate life. Our brains continually evaluate, discerning safety from danger, friend from foe. Clear discernment is useful. Reactive, automatic, or habitual judgment is not. The problem is when we evaluate without awareness, mistaking our interpretations for reality. Conflating observations and evaluations creates stress internally and can wreak havoc in our relationships. We can interpret a single facial expression to mean anything, spinning an entire narrative of antagonism without even checking if we understood in the first place. The mind jumps so quickly from an event to an interpretation that we easily miss the fact that these are two separate things.

我们自然会从经验中解读并得出结论，这是我们应对生活的方式之一。我们的大脑不断进行评估，辨别安全与危险、朋友与敌人。清晰的辨别力固然重要，但被动的、自动的或习惯性的判断则不然。问题在于，当我们无意识地进行评估，将自己的解读误认为现实时。混淆观察和评估会造成内在压力，并可能破坏我们的人际关系。我们可能将一个简单的面部表情解读成任何含义，甚至在确认自己是否真正理解之前，就编造出一整套敌对的故事。我们的思维如此迅速地从事件跳转到解读，以至于我们很容易忽略这两者之间的区别。

Mindfulness is often defined as awareness free from distortion or bias. It illuminates the process of interpretation, clarifying the difference between our direct experience and the stories we tell about it. One Buddhist text enjoins the practitioner to discern “in the seen, just what is seen; in the heard, just what is heard.” 1 We can use mindfulness to deconstruct our beliefs and interpretations. Applying careful attention, we tease apart the actual events—specific data in our environment—from the added layers of thought, perception, and reactivity.

正念通常被定义为不带任何扭曲或偏见的觉察。它能照亮诠释的过程，厘清我们直接体验与我们讲述的关于体验的故事之间的区别。一部佛教经典告诫修行者要“所见即所见，所闻即所闻”。我们可以运用正念来解构我们的信念和诠释。通过细致的觉察，我们可以将实际发生的事件——我们环境中的具体数据——与附加的思维、感知和反应层层区分开来。

Clearly knowing this difference can be profound. Many of our most painful core beliefs and psychological patterns are rooted in unseen, unquestioned stories about who we are, how others see us, or what life can offer.

清楚地认识到这种区别意义深远。我们许多最痛苦的核心信念和心理模式都根植于那些我们从未察觉、从未质疑过的关于我们是谁、别人如何看待我们，或者生活能提供什么的固有观念中。

The basic building block of this process is to identify what happened as directly as possible. To determine if something is an observation, ask yourself, “Could this be caught on film?” A camera registers movement and sound. It can’t record someone “behaving coldly.” It can’t demonstrate someone “never” or “always” doing anything. Does a video camera record someone “ignoring me,” or does it record one person walking past another while looking ahead?

这个过程的基本要素是尽可能直接地识别发生了什么。要判断某件事是否属于观察，问问自己：“这件事能被拍下来吗？”摄像机记录的是动作和声音，它无法记录某人“冷漠”的行为，也无法证明某人“从不”或“总是”做某事。摄像机记录的是某人“无视我”，还是记录的是一个人看着前方走过另一个人？

Another key metric for making an observation is the likelihood that it might bring up defensiveness. Remember, if we’re interested in creating understanding, our overall aim is to use language that leads to connection. How might you state this neutrally, so that the other person can recognize it without taking issue? “When I saw you walk in and turn on the TV” is less likely to trigger an argument than “When you ignore me.”

另一个衡量观察结果的关键指标是它是否可能引发对方的防御心理。记住，如果我们想要建立理解，我们的最终目标是使用能够促进沟通的语言。如何用中立的语气表达，才能让对方理解并接受，而不会产生异议呢？“当我看到你走进来打开电视”比“当你无视我”更不容易引发争吵。

The classical form of NVC for training attention to make observations is, “When I see / hear…” Beginning with the pronoun “I” rather than “you” shifts the focus from the other person to our direct experience. Verbs such as “see” and “hear” help us focus on the specific event rather than our interpretations. (This also indicates that we might remember events differently.)

非暴力沟通中训练注意力进行观察的经典形式是：“当我看到/听到……”。以代词“我”而非“你”开头，可以将焦点从对方转移到我们自身的直接体验。“看到”和“听到”等动词有助于我们关注具体事件，而非我们自身的解读。（这也表明我们对同一事件的记忆可能存在差异。）

Here are a few pointers on making observations:

以下是一些观察技巧：

• Use mindfulness to discern the raw data of what happened.

• 运用正念去辨别所发生的事情的原始数据。

• Separate what you actually know from assumptions or interpretations.

• 将你实际知道的事情与假设或解释区分开来。

• To check, ask yourself, “Could this be caught on film?”

• 为了验证这一点，问问自己：“这能被拍下来吗？”

• Avoid words that exaggerate or interpret: always, never, ever, whenever, rarely.

• 避免使用夸张或带有特殊含义的词语：总是、从不、永远、每当、很少。

• State your experience in the first person, “When I see / hear / notice…” rather than “When you said / did…”

• 用第一人称陈述你的经历，“当我看到/听到/注意到……”，而不是“当你说/做……”

• Determine if you are confident the other person would recognize this without growing defensive. If not, refine it further.

• 判断你是否确信对方能够理解这一点而不会产生防御心理。如果不能，则需要进一步完善措辞。
