Below are some examples of the difference between an evaluation and an observation. Evaluative terms are indicated in italics. Which is more or less likely to build understanding?

以下是一些评价和观察之间区别的例子。评价性术语以斜体字标出。哪种方法更有可能或更不可能增进理解？

Evaluation

评估

Observation

观察

“You rarely come home on time.”
“You’re always late. ”

“你很少按时回家。”“你总是迟到。”

“I noticed you came home twenty minutes after you said you would…”

“我注意到你比约定的时间晚了二十分钟才到家……”

“You’re so amazing.”

“你太棒了。”

“When I see the things you’ve accomplished…”

“当我看到你所取得的成就时……”

“When you’re rude to me…”

“当你对我无礼时……”

“When I hear you say that…”
“当我听到你说……”
“When I hear you say, ‘Whatever’ and look away…”
“当我听到你说‘随便’然后把目光移开……”
“When I see this certain expression on your face…”
“当我看到你脸上这种表情……”

Once we’ve made an observation, we link that to our own internal experience—our feelings and needs—to share where we’re at inside. These three components—an observation, a feeling, and a need—provide a simple map to say what we mean, discerning inwardly and sharing outwardly how we’re doing. What happened? How do you feel about it? Why? Training our attention to identify these specific components gives us clear and powerful information to state our experience.

一旦我们做出观察，就会将其与自身的内在体验——感受和需求——联系起来，从而表达我们内心的状态。这三个要素——观察、感受和需求——构成了一幅简洁的图景，帮助我们清晰地表达自己的想法，辨别内在感受，并向外分享我们的状态。发生了什么？你对此有何感受？为什么？训练我们集中注意力去识别这些具体的要素，就能让我们获得清晰而有力的信息来陈述自己的体验。

PRACTICE : Getting Concrete

实践：获取混凝土

Think of a recent situation that has some significance, positive or negative. Consider the following questions:

回想一下最近发生的一件对你来说意义重大的事情，无论是积极的还是消极的。思考以下问题：

OBSERVATION : WHAT HAPPENED ? Try to be as specific as possible. If you were to state this to the other person, would they agree with your description or get defensive?

观察：发生了什么？尽量具体描述。如果你把这件事告诉对方，他们会同意你的描述还是会感到抵触？

FEELINGS : HOW DO YOU FEEL ? What emotions are in your heart? See blaming thoughts or false-feeling words as information to uncover your emotions.

感受：你感觉如何？你内心深处有哪些情绪？把责备的想法或虚假的感受表达看作是揭示你真实情绪的信息。

NEEDS : WHAT MATTERS ? For each emotion, listen inwardly and connect it to your needs. Try to become conscious of what matters in terms of what you do want rather than what you don’t want.

需求：什么最重要？对于每一种情绪，倾听内心的声音，并将其与你的需求联系起来。试着觉察你真正想要的是什么，而不是你不想要的是什么，这才是最重要的。

Does doing this reflection give you more clarity or shift how you might discuss these events with the other person?

这样的反思是否让你思路更清晰，或者改变了你与对方讨论这些事件的方式？

Part of making observations is recognizing that there is often more than one perspective on a situation and that our observations will almost always be colored by our subjective experience. A well-known Buddhist allegory illustrates just how limited our perspectives can be. A king gathered a group of blind men, asking each to feel a different part of an elephant’s body. One held the ear, another the tusk, a third the tail, and so on. When asked if they knew what they touched, each responded with confidence: “It’s a basket…” “It’s a plowshare…” “It’s a rope…” 2

观察的一部分在于认识到，对于同一情况往往存在多种视角，而且我们的观察几乎总是会受到主观经验的影响。一个著名的佛教寓言生动地说明了我们视角的局限性。一位国王召集了一群盲人，让他们分别触摸大象的不同部位。一个摸了耳朵，一个摸了象牙，一个摸了尾巴，以此类推。当被问及是否知道自己摸到了什么时，每个人都自信地回答：“这是个篮子……”“这是个犁铧……”“这是根绳子……”

We can be so certain of our observations, assuming that we see the whole picture. This goes beyond the personal level, in which our vantage points differ based on our subjective individual experience, to the collective level, in which our differing experiences of systemic oppression, power, and privilege can yield divergent observations. My own privilege, for instance, can blind me to certain group dynamics. 3 At one conference, a female colleague gently pointed out how my quickness to speak first reflected a lack of awareness of the power dynamics inherent in my position in society. I observed that there was a period of silence, and then I spoke. She observed that none of the people of color present had spoken yet, and a white male spoke following a temporary silence. I only saw things from the individual perspective, while she observed through a wider lens. Given the dominance of white male voices in almost all aspects of society, my choice to speak first can be seen and understood very differently from a systemic perspective than from an individual one.

我们之所以对自己的观察如此确信，是因为我们认为自己看到了全貌。这不仅体现在个人层面（在个人层面，我们的视角会因主观的个人经验而有所不同），也体现在集体层面（在集体层面，我们对系统性压迫、权力以及特权的不同体验会导致不同的观察结果）。例如，我自身的特权可能会让我对某些群体动态视而不见。 3 在一次会议上，一位女同事委婉地指出，我急于第一个发言反映出我对自身社会地位所固有的权力动态缺乏认识。我注意到有一段时间的沉默，然后我开口了。她注意到在场的有色人种都还没有发言，而一位白人男性在短暂的沉默后发言。我只从个人的角度看待问题，而她则以更广阔的视角进行观察。鉴于白人男性的声音在社会几乎所有方面都占据主导地位，从系统性的角度和从个人的角度来看，我选择第一个发言的意义和含义截然不同。

Not only do our observations vary, but our interpretations of their impact —the meaning we assign them—also differ greatly depending on the context. A female student of mine recently complained of an ongoing situation at her legal firm in which a peer, male colleague regularly offers her unsolicited feedback. He observes his actions on the personal level, loosely aware of an intention to contribute. She experiences his actions within the context of a lifetime of being treated as inferior by men and from the collective, historical perspective of patriarchal oppression of women. She can see his intentions, but he is blind to the impact of his actions. To fully build mutual understanding and address the situation, he may need to acknowledge her frame of reference and understand his actions in a wider context. Similarly, some may view the success of an African American individual (Barack Obama, Oprah Winfrey) as proof of the American dream and the eradication of racism, while others understand the same observation as an exceptional accomplishment within a larger context of struggle. Bringing humility to the way we view an event and recognizing the possibility of other perspectives can help widen our view and open the door for more understanding.

不仅我们的观察各不相同，我们对观察结果影响的解读——我们赋予它们的意义——也会因语境而异。我的一位女学生最近抱怨她所在律师事务所里一位男同事经常未经允许就给她提供反馈。他从个人层面看待自己的行为，隐约意识到自己是想表达意见。而她则是在长期被男性视为低人一等的背景下，从父权制压迫女性的集体历史视角来看待他的行为。她能理解他的意图，但他却对自身行为的影响视而不见。为了真正建立相互理解并解决问题，他或许需要了解她的视角，并在更广阔的背景下理解自己的行为。同样，有些人可能将非裔美国人的成功（例如巴拉克·奥巴马、奥普拉·温弗瑞）视为美国梦和种族主义消除的证明，而另一些人则认为，这仅仅是在更广泛的斗争背景下取得的非凡成就。以谦逊的态度看待事物，并认识到其他观点的可能性，可以帮助我们拓宽视野，打开通往更深层次理解的大门。

The Ladder of Inference

推理阶梯

When we’re unaware of our interpretations (and the context upon which we base them), we tend to state them as facts, presenting our way of seeing things as reality. This can spark arguments and leave little room for dialogue.

当我们不了解自己的解读（以及解读的依据）时，我们往往会将其当作事实陈述，把我们看待事物的方式当作现实。这会引发争论，并留下对话的空间。

To communicate effectively, we need to investigate the very process of perception whereby our feelings and needs color events. Just as we bring a keen observing attention to the specific events around us, we can bring a radical honesty to the interpretations we add to an experience. The more aware we are of our judgments and evaluations, the more flexibility we have with how we express ourselves.

为了有效沟通，我们需要探究感知过程本身，即我们的情感和需求如何影响我们对事件的理解。正如我们敏锐地观察周围发生的具体事件一样，我们也可以对自己的经历做出彻底的解读。我们越了解自己的判断和评价，就越能灵活地表达自己。

Chris Argyris, a prominent business theorist and author connected to Harvard Business School, devised a visual metaphor called the Ladder of Inference to map the process of how we make interpretations and jump to conclusions. 4

与哈佛商学院关系密切的著名商业理论家和作家克里斯·阿吉里斯（Chris Argyris）设计了一个名为“推理阶梯”的视觉隐喻，用来描绘我们如何进行解读并得出结论的过程。

You can see a version of his model in figure 6. At the bottom of the ladder is all observable data: the wealth of images, sounds, thoughts, feelings, and sensations that constitute our life. (Internal events, such as thoughts and feelings, are also part of this data, since observing our internal experience is essential for skillful communication.) From this pool of information, our mind naturally selects certain data as more or less relevant. For example, if we’re having a conversation in a restaurant, we focus on the words of our interlocutor and filter out other conversations and ambient sounds.

图 6 展示了他模型的一个版本。在阶梯的最底层是所有可观察的数据：构成我们生活的丰富图像、声音、思想、情感和感觉。（内部事件，例如思想和情感，也是这些数据的一部分，因为观察我们的内部体验对于熟练的沟通至关重要。）从这些信息库中，我们的大脑会自然而然地选择一些相关性较高的数据。例如，如果我们在餐厅里与人交谈，我们会专注于对方的话语，而忽略其他人的谈话和环境噪音。

However, we tend to select data based on our views and biases. The negativity bias, whereby we attend more to perceived threats in the environment, is one example. In the classic roommate dynamic, the person who likes things neat usually notices only the behaviors of their roommate that don’t match their preferences for cleanliness and overlooks times they are tidy or make contributions in other ways. This selection process itself is a form of interpretation, skewing our perspective.

然而，我们往往会根据自身的观点和偏见来选择数据。消极偏见就是一个例子，它让我们更关注环境中感知到的威胁。在典型的室友关系中，喜欢整洁的人通常只会注意到室友不符合自己清洁偏好的行为，而忽略了室友保持整洁或做出其他贡献的时刻。这种选择过程本身就是一种解读，会影响我们的视角。

An essential part of strengthening romantic relationships is countering these tendencies by bringing attention to the goodness that exists, building what psychologist and author John M. Gottman calls a system of “fondness and admiration.” 5 Are there positive aspects of our partner’s behavior, actions, or personality that we take for granted? What would be the effect of paying more conscious attention to those attributes instead of focusing solely on the difficulties or irritants? As we explored in the last chapter, savoring the good also improves mental health, resilience, and emotional well-being.

巩固恋爱关系的关键在于克服这些倾向，关注伴侣身上存在的美好，从而建立心理学家兼作家约翰·M·戈特曼所说的“喜爱与欣赏”体系。我们是否常常忽略伴侣行为、举止或性格中的积极方面？如果我们更多地关注这些特质，而不是仅仅关注困难或令人不快之处，又会产生怎样的效果呢？正如我们在上一章探讨的那样，品味美好也有助于改善心理健康、增强韧性并提升情绪幸福感。

From the specific events and data we’ve selected, our mind begins making assumptions and meanings. Sylvia says, “I guess this means I’m not supposed to sit this retreat.” The meditator shares, “I’ve always been high-strung.” The process continues climbing up the ladder, as effortless as a monkey in a tree. We draw conclusions, form fixed views, and then speak or act based on those beliefs.

从我们选择的具体事件和数据出发，我们的思维开始做出假设并赋予意义。西尔维娅说：“看来我不应该参加这次静修。”冥想者说：“我一直都很敏感。”这个过程不断向上攀升，就像猴子爬树一样毫不费力。我们得出结论，形成固定的观点，然后根据这些信念说话或行动。

This whole process generally happens automatically, usually under the radar of our awareness. We are, by definition, ignorant of our assumptions. Mindfulness practice teaches us to look more closely at these inner workings of perception; it draws back the curtain to see the wizard of consciousness manipulating and forming our experience into the neat categories that structure our life.

整个过程通常是自动发生的，往往在我们意识不到的情况下进行。从定义上讲，我们对自己的假设是无知的。正念练习教导我们更仔细地观察这些感知机制的内在运作；它揭开帷幕，让我们看到意识的魔法师如何操纵和塑造我们的体验，将其归纳成构建我们生活的清晰类别。

What’s more, as you can see in the diagram, the process has feedback loops. Our views and beliefs make it more likely that we will select certain data. Our very choices and actions affect what data we have access to, determining who we spend time with, what events or activities we attend, and so forth.

此外，正如您在图中看到的，这个过程存在反馈回路。我们的观点和信念会影响我们选择某些数据的可能性。而我们的选择和行动又会影响我们能够获取哪些数据，进而决定我们与谁共度时光、参加哪些活动等等。

This process occurs collectively as well. The news and entertainment media are powerful societal filtering mechanisms, selecting and presenting data based on what sells. The algorithms driving social media create online filter bubbles in which we are exposed only to information that confirms our preexisting views. The effects of these biases become lodged in our consciousness. Consider the effect on a young gay person when none of their school classes celebrate examples of LGBTQI adults or the effect on people coming from impoverished families of seeing only stories of financial success on TV.

这个过程也以集体形式发生。新闻和娱乐媒体是强大的社会过滤机制，它们根据市场需求选择和呈现数据。驱动社交媒体的算法会制造出网络信息茧房，让我们只能接触到那些印证我们既有观点的信息。这些偏见的影响会根深蒂固地存在于我们的意识中。试想一下，如果一个年轻的同性恋者所在的学校课堂上没有提及LGBTQI成年人的榜样，这对他/她会造成怎样的影响；或者，如果来自贫困家庭的人们只能在电视上看到经济成功的案例，这对他们又会造成怎样的影响。

The implications of how this process operates in our lives are dramatic and far reaching. These filters narrow our views, fueling fear and antagonism by eliminating opportunities to build diverse relationships. As Martin Luther King Jr. said in a speech in 1962:

这一过程在我们生活中的运作方式影响深远，意义重大。这些过滤机制使我们的视野狭隘，扼杀了建立多元关系的机会，从而加剧了恐惧和敌意。正如马丁·路德·金在1962年的一次演讲中所说：

I am convinced that men hate each other because they fear each other. They fear each other because they don’t know each other, and they don’t know each other because they don’t communicate with each other, and they don’t communicate with each other because they are separated from each other. 6

我深信，人之所以彼此憎恨，是因为他们彼此恐惧。他们彼此恐惧，是因为他们不了解彼此；他们不了解彼此，是因为他们不交流；他们不交流，是因为他们彼此分离。

We can use the Ladder of Inference to catalyze our awareness. When we are embroiled in conflict, we are often high up on the ladder, locked in views about one another, our motives, or intentions. Painful emotions also can drive us up the ladder, as we attempt to make sense of another’s actions. The specific distinctions between various “rungs” is less important than becoming aware of how high up we are on the ladder and growing skilled at traveling back down so we can make observations that the other person will recognize.

我们可以运用推理阶梯来提升自我认知。当我们深陷冲突时，我们往往处于推理阶梯的高位，固守着对彼此、动机或意图的固有看法。痛苦的情绪也会驱使我们攀升至更高的位置，试图理解他人的行为。不同“阶梯”之间的具体区别并不重要，重要的是意识到自己所处的位置，并学会如何向下移动，从而做出对方能够理解的观察。

PRACTICE : Using the Ladder

练习：使用梯子

As you move through your day, pay attention to your inner narrative of thoughts. When you notice interpretations about yourself or others that are higher up on the ladder, see if you can come back down. What are the actual events to which you are reacting?

在日常生活中，留意你内心的想法。当你注意到自己或他人的解读过于主观时，试着冷静下来，分析一下你所关注的事件究竟是什么。

Pay attention to conversations. Notice when you or others are higher up on the ladder. What are the specific data points in question? What would be the effect of shifting the dialogue to these specifics rather than the interpretations?

注意倾听对话。留意你或其他人何时处于更高的地位。具体讨论的数据点是什么？如果将对话的重点从解读转移到这些具体数据上，会产生什么影响？

Translating Negative Judgments

翻译负面判断

Coming down the ladder isn’t always easy, especially with strong, negative interpretations. In their raw form, such reactive judgments are likely to embroil us in argument. We can release ourselves from their grip and step out of the blame game by uncoupling judgments from specific observations, our feelings, and the needs associated with them. This gives us more options to talk with the other person and can transform the narrative of blame that often makes it difficult to hear one another.

放下成见并非易事，尤其是在面对强烈的负面解读时。未经深思熟虑的此类反应性判断很容易让我们陷入争论。我们可以摆脱这种束缚，跳出互相指责的怪圈，方法是将判断与具体的观察、自身的感受以及与之相关的需求脱钩。这让我们有更多与对方沟通的选择，也能改变那种常常阻碍彼此倾听的互相指责的叙事模式。

Principle: Translating judgments into observations, feelings, and needs can yield valuable information about what is and isn’t working and provide clues for how to move forward.

原则：将判断转化为观察、感受和需求，可以产生有关哪些有效哪些无效的宝贵信息，并为如何前进提供线索。

In training ourselves to make observations, we are cultivating a commitment to honesty. When we consider the difference between an observation and an evaluation, which is true? Is he really “being rude” or would it be more truthful to say that he did or said something that you didn’t enjoy, that didn’t meet your need for respect? Is it accurate to say that “you’re never affectionate” or that “you’re not as affectionate as I would like”? When we’re honest in this way, there’s less to argue about and more room to hear one another.

我们训练自己进行观察，就是在培养诚实的品质。当我们思考观察和评价之间的区别时，哪个才是真相？他真的“无礼”吗？或者更准确地说，他做了或说了些让你不高兴、没有得到你应有尊重的事情？说“你从来不亲昵”更准确，还是说“你没有我想象中那么亲昵”更准确？当我们以这种方式坦诚相待时，争论就会减少，彼此倾听的空间也会更多。

The first step to translating negative judgments is to recognize our judgment, honoring it as a vital piece of information. Judgments and evaluations are just one way we’ve learned to communicate what’s happening inside. They are reflections of our own unmet needs.

转化负面评价的第一步是认识到我们自身的评价，并将其视为至关重要的信息。评价和评估只是我们用来表达内心感受的一种方式，它们反映了我们自身未被满足的需求。

PRACTICE : Transforming Judgments and Evaluations

实践：转变判断和评价

Use this exercise to work with judgments you may hold about yourself or someone else. Begin with a situation that isn’t too difficult, to get a feel for the process. You can use this activity to prepare for a conversation or, as it becomes more familiar, during the flow of a conversation.

利用这个练习来处理你可能对自己或他人抱有的评判。先从一个不太复杂的情境开始，熟悉一下整个过程。你可以用这个练习来准备谈话，或者随着练习的深入，也可以在谈话过程中运用。

Begin by settling your mind and becoming aware of your breathing. As genuinely as possible, connect with your intention to come from curiosity and care. Call to mind a situation in which you have some judgments you’d like to transform, then:

首先，静下心来，觉察自己的呼吸。尽可能真诚地与你的意图建立连接，即出于好奇和关怀。回想一下你曾经有过的一些评判，并希望改变它们，然后：

NAME THE JUDGMENT : Say the judgment aloud or write it down. Let yourself really feel it. If there are many, choose just one to explore. Remember that this is a valuable piece of information that expresses something that matters to you.

说出你的判断：大声说出你的判断，或者把它写下来。让自己真正地感受它。如果有多个判断，选择其中一个来深入探究。记住，这是一条宝贵的信息，它表达了对你而言重要的事情。

INVESTIGATE : What was the actual event, the one direct observation to which you are reacting? If there are several, choose one on which to focus first.

调查：实际发生的事件是什么？你所观察到的唯一直接现象是什么？如果有多个事件，请选择一个作为首要关注点。

OBSERVE : Can you make an observation, as clearly and neutrally as possible? Could this be caught on film? Would the other person recognize this without arguing?

观察：你能否尽可能清晰、客观地做出观察？这能否被拍摄下来？对方能否在不争辩的情况下理解这一点？

FEELINGS : What emotions do you feel in relation to this event? Take some time here, allowing yourself to feel fully. If the original judgment returns or new judgments arise, acknowledge them and return to feeling your emotions.

感受：你对这件事有什么感受？请花些时间，让自己充分感受。如果最初的评判再次出现，或者产生了新的评判，请承认它们，然后继续感受你的情绪。

NEEDS : Listen inwardly for your needs. What matters to you here? What is it you do want rather than what you don’t want? Are there different needs connected to different emotions? Sift through things until you arrive at one or two core needs. For what do you long?

需求：倾听内心的声音，探寻你的需求。对你而言，什么最重要？你真正想要的是什么，而不是你不想要的是什么？不同的需求是否与不同的情绪相关联？仔细梳理，直到找到一到两个核心需求。你渴望的是什么？

REFLECT : Review your observation, feelings, and needs. How does this affect your experience of the event? Repeat this process for any other judgments you have, one at a time.

反思：回顾你的观察、感受和需求。这如何影响你对事件的体验？对其他任何判断，逐一重复此过程。

Ideally we do the work of translating our evaluations into observations, feelings, and needs before we speak. Sometimes, particularly if we are in a lot of pain, we’re unable to do that work of translation. In these situations, it can be helpful to seek empathy from a friend or mentor. Sometimes, a trusted companion can help us identify our emotions and the powerful values being stimulated underneath those feelings.

理想情况下，我们应该在开口之前，先将自己的评估转化为观察、感受和需求。但有时，尤其是在我们承受巨大痛苦的时候，我们无法完成这项转化工作。在这种情况下，向朋友或导师寻求共情会很有帮助。有时，一位值得信赖的伙伴可以帮助我们识别自己的情绪，以及隐藏在这些情绪之下的深层价值观。

If we still can’t get to an observation (or if we don’t have the time or energy to do so), we can take responsibility for our evaluations by acknowledging their subjectivity, which leaves room for the other person’s experience. In other words, we can make an observation of our own evaluation. Here are a few examples of how we might separate observations and evaluations, taking responsibility for an evaluation or judgment (indicated in italics):

如果我们仍然无法进行观察（或者我们没有时间或精力进行观察），我们可以通过承认评估的主观性来承担评估的责任，这为对方的经验留出了空间。换句话说，我们可以对自己的评估进行观察。以下是一些如何区分观察和评估，以及承担评估或判断责任的例子（以斜体字标出）：

• “When I hear you say that, I’m telling myself that you’re judging me. ”

• “当我听到你这么说的时候，我就觉得你是在评判我。”

• “When I hear that you offered to help, I think that you are being too kind. ”

• “听说你要帮忙，我觉得你太善良了。”

• “ I’ve rarely seen him make a decision without changing it at least once.”

“我很少看到他做出决定后不至少改一次。”

• “ I find him attractive .”

• “我觉得他很有魅力。”

• “ I think she’s great. We get through the agenda when she facilitates the meetings.”

• “我觉得她很棒。在她主持会议的情况下，我们都能顺利完成议程。”

• “ I don’t think he’ll stay in the job more than a few weeks.”

“我认为他这份工作干不了几个星期。”

• “ I can’t remember a time when he followed through without a reminder.”

• “我记不清他什么时候在没有提醒的情况下完成过什么事。”

Praise, Feedback, and Gratitude

表扬、反馈和感激

Translating judgments into observations, feelings, and needs is a flexible template that can bring clarity, richness, and meaning into many domains of our lives. Praise is a common form of positive judgment. While it may feel pleasant, we learn very little from being praised. What’s more, praise places one person in a position of power over another, determining the value or worth of another’s actions. Instead, we can name the specific actions we are celebrating and which needs of ours have been met.

将判断转化为观察、感受和需求，是一种灵活的模式，可以为我们生活的许多领域带来清晰、丰富和意义。赞扬是一种常见的正面判断形式。虽然赞扬会让人感到愉悦，但我们从中能学到的东西却很少。更重要的是，赞扬使一个人凌驾于另一个人之上，决定着他人行为的价值或意义。相反，我们可以具体指出我们所赞扬的行为，以及我们自身的哪些需求得到了满足。

PRAISE : “Great job! You’re so amazing.”

TRANSLATION : “When I heard you got the job, I felt so amazed at what you’ve been able to accomplish.” [colloquially sharing needs for growth or meaning]

赞扬：“干得好！你太棒了！” 翻译：“当我听说你得到这份工作时，我对你所取得的成就感到非常惊讶。” [口语化地表达对成长或意义的需求]

We also can use this format to give one another accurate feedback, sharing what did or didn’t work (the observation) and why (our needs). In professional situations, it’s often most useful to frame the needs in terms of a team’s shared values or goals.

我们还可以利用这种形式互相提供准确的反馈，分享哪些方面有效或无效（观察结果）以及原因（我们的需求）。在专业场合，通常最好将需求与团队的共同价值观或目标联系起来。

Principle: When giving feedback, be specific about what is and isn’t working and why, which makes it easier to learn.

原则：在提供反馈时，要具体说明哪些方面有效，哪些方面无效以及原因，这样更容易学习。

In intimate relationships, we may express our enjoyment and care for one another with the tender words “I love you.” While this can express a certain depth of feeling or strength of commitment, it can be even more meaningful to elaborate. What do we mean? Are there specific traits, words, or actions to which we’re responding? How do we actually feel, and why? Consider the richness of a statement such as, “When you hold my hand I feel so safe, warm, and at ease. I’m so glad to have you as a companion in my life.”

在亲密关系中，我们可能会用“我爱你”这句温柔的话语来表达对彼此的喜爱和关爱。虽然这句话本身就能表达出一定的情感深度或坚定的承诺，但如果能更详细地阐述，意义会更加丰富。我们究竟是什么意思？我们是在回应对方的哪些特质、言语或行为？我们内心真正的感受是什么？为什么会有这种感受？不妨思考一下这样一段话：“当你牵着我的手时，我感到无比安全、温暖和自在。我很高兴生命中有你这样的伴侣。”

When our needs are met, we have the opportunity to express the fullness of our gratitude. This practice gives us a method for doing that, for opening our heart and celebrating our relationship by sharing the details of how someone else has contributed to our life. We may have to stretch beyond our comfort zone to speak so openly and authentically, but it pays off in an enriching quality of connection.

当我们的需求得到满足时，我们就有机会充分表达我们的感激之情。这种练习为我们提供了一种方法，让我们敞开心扉，通过分享他人如何为我们的生活做出贡献的细节来庆祝彼此的关系。我们或许需要走出舒适区才能如此坦诚真挚地表达，但这会带来更丰富的情感联结。

PRACTICE : Expressing Gratitude

练习：表达感激之情

The next time someone does something you enjoy, let them know. Instead of saying “Thank you,” take a risk and share the fullness of your appreciation. Be specific about what they said or did, how you feel, and why. Speak from your heart. Focus on conveying why this mattered or how it contributed to you (as opposed to simply following the structure of the form).

下次如果有人做了让你开心的事，一定要让他们知道。不要只是简单地说声“谢谢”，而是要大胆地表达你由衷的感激之情。具体说说他们说了什么或做了什么，你的感受是什么，以及为什么。发自内心地表达。重点在于阐明这件事对你的意义或它如何帮助你（而不是仅仅遵循形式）。

As we learn these tools, it’s common to start to think that there is a “right” way to communicate. “Stop praising me…That’s an evaluation, not an observation! You’re using a false feeling!” The more we think there is a right and a wrong way to speak, the further we move away from genuine curiosity and care.

当我们学习这些技巧时，很容易开始认为存在一种“正确”的沟通方式。“别再夸我了……那是评价，不是观察！你这是在用虚假的情感！”我们越是认为说话有对错之分，就越会远离真正的好奇心和关怀。

The point of these practices, the ultimate aim of refining our thoughts and crafting our words, is to create understanding and connection in service of meeting needs. If you find yourself wondering, “Is this an observation? Can I say this in mindful communication?” take a step back and reconnect with your intention. Consider, “How might the other person hear this? Is it likely to lead to connection and build understanding?” If the answer is yes, go for it! If not, find another way to express yourself authentically that the other person is more likely to hear.

这些练习的最终目的，即精炼思想、润色言辞，是为了在满足需求的同时，建立理解和联结。如果你发现自己在思考：“这算是一种观察吗？我能用正念沟通的方式表达出来吗？”不妨退后一步，重新审视你的意图。想想：“对方会如何理解这句话？它有可能促进联结和理解吗？”如果答案是肯定的，那就大胆说出来！如果不是，那就寻找另一种更真诚、更易于对方接受的表达方式。

The Courage to Speak

勇敢发声

It’s not always easy to speak up and say our piece. We may have had difficult experiences of not feeling seen or heard or even may have been actively silenced. It can take patience, courage, and support from loving friends and community to find our voice.

表达自己的想法并非易事。我们或许曾有过不被关注、不被倾听，甚至被刻意噤声的艰难经历。我们需要耐心、勇气，以及来自挚友和社区的支持，才能找到自己的声音。

Recognizing the source of these challenges—internally or structurally—can be freeing. Karen works internationally around issues of sustainability and rural development. She’s good at what she does, but she can find it challenging to identify her needs and express herself at work. After one coaching session, she realized that growing up, her family consistently dismissed her point of view. She had learned to mistrust her own experience. This insight helped her begin to heal the pain beneath her frustration, opening new possibilities of self-expression.

认识到这些挑战的根源——无论是内在的还是结构性的——都能带来解脱。凯伦在国际上从事可持续发展和农村发展方面的工作。她工作能力很强，但她发现很难识别自己的需求，也难以在工作中表达自己的想法。一次辅导之后，她意识到，在她成长的过程中，家人总是忽视她的观点。她学会了不信任自己的经验。这一领悟帮助她开始疗愈挫败感背后的伤痛，并开启了自我表达的新途径。

I’ve mentioned my own struggles with speaking up. I learned to sing and play the guitar around the same time that I encountered NVC. These worked together synergistically, helping me find my voice literally and figuratively. As I sang, I could feel the constriction in my throat and chest begin to loosen. The relaxation carried over into the interpersonal domain, giving me the courage to share my feelings and needs and bridge the chasm between myself and another.

我之前提到过自己难以开口表达的困境。我学习唱歌和弹吉他的时间，差不多也是我接触到非暴力沟通（NVC）的时候。这两者相辅相成，帮助我从字面意义和象征意义上都找到了自己的声音。唱歌的时候，我能感觉到喉咙和胸口的紧绷感开始放松。这种放松感也延伸到了人际交往领域，让我有勇气分享自己的感受和需求，并弥合彼此之间的鸿沟。

Personal challenges to self-expression are often compounded by structural issues. When we belong to a group that has been historically oppressed, we often internalize the impact of generations being systematically ignored, punished, and even murdered for speaking up. Tragically, this can leave those of us in society whose voices most need to be heard least equipped to speak up, which continues the cycle of invisibility and oppression.

个人表达所面临的挑战往往会因结构性问题而加剧。当我们属于一个历史上遭受压迫的群体时，我们常常会内化几代人因敢于发声而被系统性地忽视、惩罚甚至杀害的影响。悲剧的是，这会导致社会上那些最需要被倾听的人反而最缺乏发声的能力，从而使隐形和压迫的恶性循环持续下去。

Having a critical awareness of the context of our individual life experiences can bring powerful inspiration and insight to free ourselves from any sense of personal failure. We can seek support to heal the inner pain of this legacy and work with others to transform the systems that perpetuate the dynamics that prevent us from being heard. It takes time, and it requires steady support to transcend the external and internal obstacles. Despite it all, even deep-seated patterns can change, giving way to a great freedom and clarity of self-expression and a commitment to everyone’s liberation.

对自身生活经历的背景保持批判性的觉察，能够带来强大的灵感和洞察力，帮助我们摆脱任何个人失败感。我们可以寻求支持，疗愈过往经历带来的内在创伤，并与他人携手，共同改变那些阻碍我们发声的固有体制。这需要时间，也需要持续的支持，才能超越内外的重重障碍。尽管如此，即使是根深蒂固的模式也能改变，从而带来极大的自由和清晰的自我表达，以及对每个人解放的承诺。

PRINCIPLES

原则

Stating clearly what happened, without judgment or evaluation, makes it easier for someone to hear us and to work toward a solution.

客观地陈述事情经过，不加评判或评价，能让别人更容易听进去，也更容易找到解决办法。

Translating judgments into observations, feelings, and needs can yield valuable information about what is and isn’t working and provide clues for how to move forward.

将判断转化为观察、感受和需求，可以产生有关哪些有效哪些无效的宝贵信息，并为如何前进提供线索。

When giving feedback, be specific about what is and isn’t working and why, which makes it easier to learn.

给出反馈时，要具体说明哪些方面有效，哪些方面无效以及原因，这样更容易学习。

KEY POINTS

要点

Tips for making observations:

观察技巧：

• Use mindfulness to discern the raw data of what happened.

• 运用正念去辨别所发生的事情的原始数据。

• Separate what you actually know from assumptions or interpretations.

• 将你实际知道的事情与假设或解释区分开来。

• To check, ask yourself, “Could this be caught on film?”

• 为了验证这一点，问问自己：“这能被拍下来吗？”

• Avoid words that exaggerate or interpret: always, never, ever, whenever, rarely.

• 避免使用夸张或带有特殊含义的词语：总是、从不、永远、每当、很少。

• State your experience in the first person, “When I see / hear / notice…,” rather than “When you said / did…”

• 用第一人称陈述你的经历，“当我看到/听到/注意到……”，而不是“当你说/做……”。

• Determine if you are confident the other person would recognize this without growing defensive. If not, refine it further.

• 判断你是否确信对方能够理解这一点而不会产生防御心理。如果不能，则需要进一步完善措辞。

• Use the Ladder of Inference to consider whether you are observing or evaluating.

• 使用推理阶梯来思考你是在观察还是在评价。

QUESTION & ANSWER

问答

Q: I have one relative who gets really aggressive and yells whenever they’re upset. How can I make an observation without them getting even angrier?

问：我有一位亲戚，他一生气就会变得非常暴躁，大声吼叫。我怎样才能在不让他更生气的情况下观察他？

I’m hearing how much you’d like to find a way to talk with this person that minimizes the chance of angering them. No matter how we say something, we can’t control another person’s reaction. All we can do is come from a wholesome intention and approach the situation as skillfully as possible.

我听得出你很想找到一种既能与对方沟通又能尽量避免惹恼对方的方法。无论我们怎么说，都无法控制对方的反应。我们所能做的，就是怀着善意，尽可能巧妙地处理这种情况。

You may want to begin by getting empathy from a friend. If you feel heard and understood, you can bring more clarity and balance to the situation. Then find a time to talk about the pattern when it’s not happening, which increases the likelihood they’ll be able to hear you. I suggest leading with something that you enjoy about the relationship or framing the conversation in terms of what you’d like to build on. For example, “I’d so like for us to be able to spend time together at family gatherings in an easeful way.”

你或许可以先从朋友那里获得一些同理心。如果你感到被倾听和理解，就能更清晰、更平衡地看待问题。然后找个时机，在问题没有出现的时候谈谈这件事，这样他们更容易听进去。我建议你先从这段关系中你喜欢的部分入手，或者围绕你想进一步发展的方向来展开对话。例如，“我非常希望我们以后能轻松地一起参加家庭聚会。”

When dealing with patterns, begin with a specific instance. To make an observation, you could describe their behavior in reference to your own manner or preferences: “Some of the ways you expressed yourself were very difficult for me to hear. I felt scared and overwhelmed. Can we talk about how we handle things when we disagree?” Listen to their side of things and see if you can brainstorm how to navigate the dynamic together.

处理行为模式时，要从具体事例入手。为了更好地观察，你可以用自己的方式或偏好来描述对方的行为：“你有些表达方式让我很难接受。我感到害怕和不知所措。我们能不能谈谈意见不一致时该如何处理？” 认真倾听对方的想法，看看你们能否一起集思广益，找到应对这种情况的方法。

Q: I feel really awkward when I state an observation, a feeling, and a need. Even when I manage to get it out, it’s so unnatural that it leads to less connection rather than more!

问：当我表达自己的观察、感受或需求时，我感觉非常尴尬。即使我设法表达出来，也感觉很不自然，反而会拉近彼此的距离！

The form is a skeleton, not a script; there’s no need to follow it rigidly. Use the components in whatever order feels authentic, recognizing that it takes time to make this your own. We are retraining our attention to see more clearly. In the beginning, feel free to stick to the principles and just track these components silently.

表格只是一个框架，并非固定的脚本；无需严格遵循。您可以根据自己的感觉，以任何顺序使用这些组件，但要知道，这需要时间才能真正形成自己的风格。我们正在重新训练自己的注意力，以便看得更清楚。一开始，您可以先遵循这些原则，然后默默地跟踪这些组件的进展。

Marshall Rosenberg was fond of saying, “Don’t confuse what’s habitual with what’s natural.” I believe it is more natural for us to be conscious of feelings and needs than to blame one another. We learn to blame and judge. When infants are hungry or in pain, they cry; they don’t blame their parents. The words feel unnatural because we haven’t practiced.

马歇尔·卢森堡常说：“不要把习惯和天性混淆。” 我认为，比起互相指责，我们更自然地去觉察自己的感受和需求。指责和评判是我们后天习得的。婴儿饿了或疼了，会哭，不会责怪父母。责怪父母的话语之所以显得不自然，是因为我们没有练习过。

Q: What if I can’t translate a judgment? I see that I’m evaluating, I’m even aware of my feelings and needs to some extent, but I’m still blaming the other person inside. How do I deal with being stuck like that?

问：如果我无法理解自己的判断怎么办？我知道自己在评判，甚至在某种程度上也意识到自己的感受和需求，但内心深处仍然在责怪对方。我该如何摆脱这种困境？

Blame feels so true sometimes, doesn’t it? The power of a judgment is directly proportional to the intensity of our feelings and needs. The stronger our emotions and the deeper our needs, the fiercer the judgment. It’s our mind and heart’s way of letting us know, “Hey! This is really important!”

责备有时听起来确实如此，不是吗？评判的力量与我们感受和需求的强度成正比。我们的情绪越强烈，需求越深，评判就越激烈。这是我们的大脑和心灵在告诉我们：“嘿！这真的很重要！”

Getting empathy is one of the best ways to transmute that energy. Find someone who can really listen and offer a genuine reflection of your experience, without agreeing, reassuring, or trying to fix, solve, or strategize. In some cases, depending on the relationship, you might be able to get that support from the person you’re judging. If they have some tools, acknowledge that you’re stuck in a judgment and ask for their help. If they’re able to listen and offer empathy, it can be very healing.

获得同理心是转化这种负面情绪的最佳途径之一。找到一个真正能够倾听并真诚地回应你经历的人，而不是试图附和、安慰你，或者试图帮你解决问题、制定策略。在某些情况下，根据你们之间的关系，你或许能从你评判的人那里获得这种支持。如果他们有一些方法，不妨承认你陷入了评判的泥潭，并向他们寻求帮助。如果他们能够倾听并给予同理心，这将带来极大的疗愈。

Q: How do you deal with people who won’t acknowledge certain facts, who have different data or “alternative facts”? How do you have a conversation when part of the issue is that you can’t even agree on an observation?

问：如何应对那些不承认某些事实、持有不同数据或“另类事实”的人？当问题的一部分在于你们甚至无法就某个观察结果达成一致时，如何进行对话？

If these tools only work when we agree, they would be very limited. Their power is in the possibility of creating connection in any circumstances. Focus on the needs. Getting alignment on shared values is what enables us to have meaningful conversations. The real work is in establishing that mutual framework, criteria for the solutions we devise. For example, if we are policy makers and can’t agree on the science of climate change, we can still explore our requirements for a viable economy, a wise use of resources, and so forth. 7

如果这些工具只有在我们达成共识时才能发挥作用，那么它们的作用将非常有限。它们的力量在于能够在任何情况下建立联系。关注需求。在共同价值观上达成一致，才能让我们进行有意义的对话。真正的工作在于建立共同的框架，以及我们制定解决方案的标准。例如，如果我们是政策制定者，无法就气候变化的科学原理达成一致，我们仍然可以探讨我们对可持续经济、合理利用资源等方面的需求。

When we care deeply about the issues, such dialogues are by nature challenging. It’s therefore important to do as much inner work as we can ahead of time. Get empathy for any pain, fear, despair, or anger you have about the impact of the other person’s views. Then try to see their humanity. Stretch your heart with empathy. Try to make sense of their choices, to reach for the deeper needs behind what may seem incomprehensible on the surface. This can create an important bridge in hearing one another and can protect us from devolving into reactivity.

当我们对某些议题深感关切时，这类对话本身就充满挑战。因此，事先做好充分的自我反思至关重要。要体谅对方观点可能带来的痛苦、恐惧、绝望或愤怒。然后，试着去理解他们的人性。敞开心扉，去感受他们的同理心。尝试理解他们的选择，探寻那些看似难以理解的背后更深层次的需求。这能搭建起彼此倾听的重要桥梁，也能避免我们陷入过激反应。

You also can explore the disagreement directly. You might inquire, “I’m guessing we both care about having accurate information, and that we share the view that good data can help us make more informed decisions?” I imagine most folks would agree. You might continue, “I know for me, one of my concerns is the belief that your data is biased, and I’m guessing you have the same concern about what I’m presenting?” From there, you might have a richer conversation about your shared concerns and strategies for examining the data.

你也可以直接探讨分歧所在。你可以问：“我猜我们都重视信息的准确性，也都认为可靠的数据能帮助我们做出更明智的决策？” 我想大多数人都会同意。你可以继续说：“就我个人而言，我担心你的数据可能存在偏差，我猜你对我提供的数据也有同样的顾虑？” 这样，你们就可以就彼此的担忧以及分析数据的策略展开更深入的讨论。

Q: Sometimes I’m not willing to make neutral observations, especially if someone has caused harm. If someone said something racist or made a microaggression, I don’t care if they get upset or defensive. Why should I go out of my way to make it easy for them to hear me?

问：有时候我不愿意保持中立，尤其是当有人造成伤害时。如果有人说了种族歧视的话或者做出了微侵犯行为，我不在乎他们是否会生气或辩解。我为什么要刻意让他们更容易听到我的话呢？

I’m hearing your fierce commitment to being fully authentic, as well as the clear recognition that you’re not responsible for their feelings or reactions. I’m guessing all of that is heightened by the historical dynamics of racism beneath the personal level in that sort of interaction.

我感受到你对保持真诚的坚定承诺，以及你清楚地认识到自己无需为他人的感受或反应负责。我猜想，在这种互动中，个人层面之下根深蒂固的种族主义历史因素，会加剧所有这些感受。

Making neutral observations doesn’t mean tamping down one’s authenticity or “being nice.” Nor is it about taking care of the other person or tiptoeing around their feelings. Saying things neutrally is a strategy to meet needs—needs for understanding, clarity, connection.

保持中立并不意味着压抑自己的真实想法或“表现得友善”。这也不是为了照顾他人或小心翼翼地顾及他们的感受。中立的表达方式是一种满足需求的策略——理解、清晰的认知和联结的需求。

If your goal is to give this person some honest feedback or change their behavior through dialogue, then the question becomes, what’s most effective? What’s most likely to create understanding and inspire change? When someone has done something that hurts us, our tendency is to react—to throw that pain right back at them. These tools offer a method to share your experience in a way that opens the other person’s heart and catalyzes a shift in their consciousness. The aim is to be fully authentic and caring at the same time, sharing the depth of your feelings without blame. Making an observation can serve that end.

如果你的目标是给予对方一些真诚的反馈，或者通过对话改变他们的行为，那么问题就变成了：什么方法最有效？什么方法最有可能促进理解并激发改变？当有人做了伤害我们的事时，我们往往会做出反应——把这种痛苦反过来伤害他们。这些方法提供了一种分享自身经历的方式，能够打开对方的心扉，并促使他们意识发生转变。其目的是做到既真诚又关怀，坦诚地分享你的感受，而不加指责。提出观察就能达到这个目的。

11

if you want something, ask for it

如果你想要什么，就开口要。

The human hand must open to receive, but also to give, and to touch. The heart must open as well to give and to touch another heart.

— LYNNE TWIST

人的手必须张开才能接受，才能给予，才能触摸。人的心也必须张开，才能给予，才能触动另一颗心。——琳恩·特威斯特

A LITTLE WHILE ago I was speaking with Laela, a meditation student who has chronic pain. She lives with her parents, who were in the process of moving. She needed to pack her belongings but was in the midst of a flare, her joints and muscles burning with pain. Just lying down hurt, let alone packing boxes or lifting things.

不久前，我和莱拉聊了聊，她是一位冥想学员，患有慢性疼痛。她和父母住在一起，他们正在搬家。她需要收拾行李，但当时正值疼痛发作期，关节和肌肉都像火烧一样疼。就连躺下都疼，更别提打包或搬东西了。

After listening and offering some empathy, I inquired, “Laela, may I ask you a question? Why don’t you ask for some help from your folks or a friend?” Strange as it may seem, she had never thought to ask. We spent the rest of our conversation exploring the assumptions and beliefs that had kept this most basic, simple possibility hidden from her awareness. I could relate to her resistance. Having often felt invisible as a child at our family dinners, it took me many years to muster the courage to speak up and ask for someone to listen.

听完她的倾诉并表示理解后，我问道：“莱拉，我可以问你个问题吗？你为什么不向父母或朋友寻求帮助呢？” 听起来或许有些奇怪，但她从未想过要开口求助。接下来的谈话中，我们探讨了那些让她忽略了这种最基本、最简单的可能性的假设和信念。我能理解她的抗拒。小时候，我常常在家庭聚餐中感到自己像个隐形人，我花了多年才鼓起勇气开口，请求别人倾听。

Being able to make requests is the last core component of training our attention to focus on what matters. In conversations, requests move things forward one step at a time, building understanding and proposing solutions that may work for everyone. In this chapter we’ll explore the different kinds of requests we can make and some of the conditioning that gets in the way.

能够提出请求是训练我们专注于重要事项的最后一个核心要素。在对话中，请求能够一步步推动事情进展，增进彼此的理解，并提出可能对大家都适用的解决方案。本章我们将探讨我们可以提出的不同类型的请求，以及一些阻碍我们提出请求的固有观念。

The Gift of Needs

满足需求的礼物

“I don’t want to impose. I’d rather not burden them.”

“I can handle it; I’ll be okay.”

“It’s no big deal. I wouldn’t want them to feel obligated…”

“我不想给他们添麻烦。我不想给他们增加负担。” “我可以应付，我会没事的。” “没什么大不了的。我不想让他们觉得有义务……”

Sometimes it can feel easier to shoulder a burden on one’s own than try to navigate the awkwardness, fear, or discomfort of asking for help. Our intentions may be quite wholesome: we genuinely don’t want others to feel obligated. We respect their autonomy, time, and energy and want to ensure that they feel free to say no.

有时候，独自承担重担似乎比克服寻求帮助时的尴尬、恐惧或不适感要容易得多。我们的初衷或许是好的：我们真心不想让别人感到有义务。我们尊重他们的自主权、时间和精力，并希望确保他们能够自由地说“不”。

These values needn’t prevent us from making requests. In fact, they enable us to make truly effective requests that support collaboration. When we’re unable to take into account another person’s needs, we make demands. It is our lack of skill in expressing these values and navigating the responses that trips us up. Similarly, if we can’t come up with more than one strategy to resolve a situation, our request may bear a quality of desperation that challenges the other person’s sense of choice. Beneath all of this, our fears, beliefs, and vulnerability can stop us from asking.

这些价值观并非阻止我们提出请求的障碍。事实上，它们使我们能够提出真正有效的请求，从而促进合作。当我们无法顾及他人的需求时，我们就会提出要求。正是我们表达这些价值观和应对他人反应的能力不足，才导致我们犯错。同样，如果我们无法提出多种解决问题的策略，我们的请求可能带有绝望的意味，从而挑战对方的选择权。归根结底，我们的恐惧、信念和脆弱感都可能阻止我们提出请求。

Making a request is about finding a way to meet needs. To ask is to acknowledge our interdependence, which opens us up to disappointment or rejection. We may have had experiences that have taught us it can be dangerous, shameful, or futile to ask for what we need—so why bother? Alternatively, we may have learned that giving is the only way to get our needs met or that help from another can only come laced with hidden agendas and strings attached.

提出请求是为了找到满足自身需求的方法。开口求助意味着承认我们彼此依赖，这也意味着我们可能面临失望或被拒绝的风险。我们或许有过一些经历，让我们觉得提出需求是危险的、可耻的，甚至是徒劳的——所以何必呢？或者，我们可能已经习以为常，认为付出才是满足自身需求的唯一途径，或者认为来自他人的帮助总是暗藏着不可告人的目的和附加条件。

As we’ve explored, our belief in cultural myths of self-sufficiency or the idealization of individual achievement can further limit our ability to seek support. On the collective level, entrenched systems can give rise to feelings of futility and despair or make violence seem like a viable strategy. These messages and experiences often leave us with complex and confusing relationships around how to meet our own and others’ needs or how to work for change.

正如我们所探讨的，我们对自给自足文化神话的迷信或对个人成就的理想化，会进一步限制我们寻求支持的能力。在集体层面，根深蒂固的体制会引发无力感和绝望感，甚至使暴力看起来像是一种可行的策略。这些信息和经历常常让我们在如何满足自身和他人的需求，以及如何推动变革方面，产生复杂而困惑的关系。

My heart breaks to see how our culture, society, and upbringing twists and complicates one of our most basic, beautiful, and natural impulses: the impulse to give and receive. Spend time with a child (who is rested and well-fed) and you know the joy they feel at giving, sharing, and helping those around them. 1

看到我们的文化、社会和成长环境如何扭曲和复杂化我们最基本、最美好、最自然的本能之一：给予和接受的冲动，我感到无比痛心。花些时间和一个（休息充足、吃饱喝足的）孩子在一起，你就会明白他们给予、分享和帮助身边人时所感受到的快乐。

Contributing to one another is one of our most fundamental drives; doing so brings joy. Consider the ease or uplift you feel when engaging in simple acts of kindness such as holding the door, smiling, or greeting someone. Recollect the last time you helped a friend in need—not because you had to but simply because you could. Felt pretty good, right?

互相帮助是我们最基本的驱动力之一；这样做会带来快乐。想想当你做一些简单的善举，比如帮人开门、微笑或问候时，你会感到多么轻松愉悦。回想一下你上次帮助有需要的朋友是什么时候——不是因为你不得不这样做，而是因为你有能力这样做。感觉很棒，对吧？

Rather than being a burden, needs can be gifts. When we are able to negotiate the dance of choice and willingness, respecting the limits of one another’s time and energy, all needs become invitations to experience the joy of giving and receiving.

需求与其说是负担，不如说是馈赠。当我们能够协商选择与意愿，尊重彼此的时间和精力限制时，所有需求都会变成体验给予和接受之乐的邀请。

PRACTICE : Reflection on Giving and Receiving

实践：反思给予与接受

Reflecting on how it feels to give and receive can transform your relationship with asking for what you need and helping others. Take some time to settle into your body and allow your attention to gather with the sensations of breathing. When you feel ready, reflect on the following questions.

反思给予和接受的感受，可以改变你对索取所需和帮助他人的态度。花些时间感受你的身体，让注意力集中在呼吸的感觉上。准备好后，思考以下问题。

Recall a specific time when you helped someone in your life, not because you felt obligated but simply because you wanted to. Contemplate how it felt to lend a hand. How does it feel to remember it now? How would it have felt if you learned later that they needed help but didn’t reach out?

回想一下你生活中曾经帮助过别人的具体时刻，不是出于义务，而是出于自愿。想想当时伸出援手是什么感觉。现在回想起来感觉如何？如果你后来才知道他们需要帮助却没有主动寻求帮助，你会作何感想？

Next, recall a time when you needed help and someone was there for you, a time when you trusted that they were helping not because they felt obligated but because they genuinely chose to help. How did it feel to receive their support? How does it feel now recalling this?

接下来，回想一下你需要帮助时，有人伸出援手，而你相信他们帮助你并非出于义务，而是真心实意地想要帮助你。当时你接受他们的帮助是什么感觉？现在回想起来，你又是什么感受？

Recognizing how it feels to give and receive freely, what gets in the way of asking for help when you need it?

体会过自由付出和接受的滋味后，是什么阻碍了你在需要帮助时寻求帮助呢？

A Little Secret

一个小秘密

In my early twenties, a good friend passed along a piece of advice he’d received from his dad. Upon graduating from high school, his father had said, “I’ll tell you a little secret to life: if you want something, ask for it.”

二十出头的时候，一位好友跟我分享了他父亲给他的一条建议。他父亲在他高中毕业时说：“我告诉你一个人生秘诀：如果你想要什么，就开口要。”

This is the central principle behind making requests.

这是提出请求的核心原则。

Making clear requests is fairly uncommon. Listen to any conversation and see how often a speaker ends a statement by asking for what they’d like to hear back or see happen next. How many times have you shared something important, only to have the other person take the conversation in a totally different direction? Without telling someone what we’d like to hear back, they are left to guess or to respond however they please.

明确提出要求并不常见。随便听听任何一段对话，你会发现说话者经常会在说完一句话后询问对方接下来想听到什么或看到什么。你是不是也曾分享过一些重要的事情，结果对方却把话题引向了完全不同的方向？如果我们不告诉对方我们想听到什么，他们就只能靠猜测或者随意回应。

Principle: The clearer we are about what we want and why, the more creative we can be about how to make it happen.

原则：我们越清楚自己想要什么以及为什么想要，就越能创造性地实现它。

By contrast, following a statement with a request lets others know how they can help and offers a concrete idea for where to go next in the conversation. It’s illuminating to see the power of making requests. As one student of mine commented, “What was most frustrating was realizing that I wasn’t getting what I wanted simply because I wasn’t letting others know what I needed.”

相比之下，在陈述之后提出请求，可以让对方知道如何提供帮助，并为接下来的对话指明方向。提出请求的力量令人大开眼界。正如我的一位学生所说：“最令人沮丧的是，我意识到自己得不到想要的东西，仅仅是因为我没有让别人知道我的需求。”

A request is a question about one’s willingness to perform a specific action to meet needs. Requests are strategies and are distinct from demands.

请求是询问某人是否愿意采取特定行动来满足需求。请求是一种策略，与要求截然不同。

“No Spilling”: Making Requests

“不洒漏”：提出请求

Some time ago, I was at an airport waiting to board a plane and saw a mother with two little girls. The older child, no more than five or six years old, was holding a large drink with a straw. The mother said to her, with agitation in her voice, “Don’t spill it!” I watched the young girl’s body tighten with anxiety, trying to figure out how to prevent further rebukes by “not spilling” the drink.

前段时间，我在机场候机，看到一位母亲带着两个小女孩。年纪稍大的孩子，大概五六岁，手里拿着一大杯插着吸管的饮料。母亲语气焦急地对她说：“别洒了！”我看到小女孩紧张地绷紧了身体，努力想着怎样才能不洒出饮料，避免被母亲责骂。

How might it have been had the mother said, “Sweetie, that’s a big drink and I’m concerned it might spill. Can you hold it carefully with two hands? ” With such a request, the daughter would have had specific instructions for what to do, making it clearer and easier to meet the request.

如果妈妈说：“宝贝，这饮料好多啊，我怕洒出来。你能用双手小心地拿一下吗？” 这样一来，女儿就能得到具体的指示，更容易理解和执行妈妈的要求。

Requests gauge another’s willingness to help or agree to our strategy. To make this as clear as possible, it’s best to formulate requests with three qualities:

请求可以衡量他人是否愿意提供帮助或同意我们的策略。为了尽可能清晰地表达这一点，最好在提出请求时考虑以下三个方面：

1. Positive: Requests state what we do want rather than what we don’t want.

1. 积极的：请求表达的是我们想要什么，而不是我们不想要什么。

2. Specific: Requests are concrete and doable rather than vague or abstract.

2. 具体：要求具体可行，而不是模糊或抽象。

3. Flexible: Requests are distinct from demands; they offer a suggestion for how to move forward, with openness to other ideas.

3. 灵活：请求与要求不同；它们为如何前进提供建议，并对其他想法持开放态度。

Making requests can be challenging, but we’ve already been developing the skills to do so. Our ability to make a request positive is based on our capacity to identify needs and then to offer a strategy that might meet them. Making a request that is specific rests upon our ability to find clear observations, concrete behaviors we are seeking. And the flexibility that is at the heart of a request comes from understanding our needs, being sensitive to the needs of others, and being creative enough to find more than one strategy to meet all of the needs present. Here are a few examples that illustrate these qualities.

提出请求可能充满挑战，但我们一直在培养这方面的技能。能否提出有效的请求，取决于我们能否识别需求，并提出可能满足这些需求的策略。提出具体的请求，则取决于我们能否清晰地观察并找到我们所期望的具体行为。而请求的核心在于灵活性，这种灵活性源于我们理解自身需求、体察他人需求，以及具备足够的创造力，找到多种策略来满足所有需求。以下是一些能够体现这些特质的例子。

NOT POSITIVE : “Don’t talk to me that way!”

AS A REQUEST : “Would you be willing to lower your voice, or can we take a break?”

NOT SPECIFIC : “Will you love me more?”

AS A REQUEST : “When you come home, can you try to remember to look me in the eyes and say hello? It would mean so much to me.”

NOT FLEXIBLE : “We have to talk.”

REQUEST : “Can we find some time to sit down together and talk about things? Or, if not, do you have ideas about how we can sort this out?”

不肯定：“别那样跟我说话！” 作为请求：“你能小声点吗？或者我们能不能休息一下？” 不具体：“你会更爱我吗？” 作为请求：“你回家的时候，能不能尽量看着我的眼睛说声你好？这对我来说意义重大。” 不灵活：“我们必须谈谈。” 作为请求：“我们能不能找个时间坐下来好好谈谈？或者，如果不行，你有什么办法解决这个问题吗？”

PRACTICE : Listening for Requests

练习：倾听请求

As you move through your day, pay attention to the presence or absence of requests. How often do people (yourself included) let others know what they’d like to hear back? When is it implicit? When a person does make a request, is it positive, specific, and flexible?

在你日常生活中，留意一下是否有人提出请求。人们（包括你自己）多久会明确告诉别人自己希望得到怎样的回应？什么时候是隐晦的？当有人提出请求时，请求是否积极、具体且灵活？

Kinds of Requests: Asking for Empathy

请求的种类：寻求同理心

There are two basic kinds of requests in conversation: requests that aim for connection and requests that propose a solution. Connection requests check that the line hasn’t dropped, in effect saying, “You still there?” They complete a cycle of communication, confirm that the message sent was received, and water the seeds of trust and goodwill. Solution requests propose concrete strategies to address both of our needs and make agreements about going forward.

对话中有两种基本类型的请求：建立联系的请求和提出解决方案的请求。建立联系的请求是为了确认线路是否中断，实际上是在问“你还在吗？”。这类请求完成了一个完整的沟通循环，确认对方已收到信息，并有助于建立信任和友好关系。提出解决方案的请求则会提出具体的策略来满足双方的需求，并就未来的合作达成一致。

In simple situations, solution requests may be sufficient. “How about this? Any way you could find time for XYZ?” With more challenging issues we need to lay some groundwork before discussing solutions. After all, another person’s willingness to collaborate is based on the quality of understanding and connection we’ve established. In chapter 7 , we touched on the importance of building understanding, trust, and goodwill before proposing solutions.

在简单的情况下，提出解决方案请求就足够了。“这样如何？您能抽出时间做XYZ吗？” 对于更复杂的问题，我们需要在讨论解决方案之前做一些准备工作。毕竟，他人是否愿意合作取决于我们之间建立的理解和联系的质量。在第七章中，我们探讨了在提出解决方案之前建立理解、信任和善意的重要性。

Principle: The more we understand one another, the easier it is to find solutions that work for everyone. Therefore, establish as much mutual understanding as possible before problem solving.

原则：我们越了解彼此，就越容易找到对大家都适用的解决方案。因此，在解决问题之前，应尽可能建立相互理解。

When it’s not clear from the context or body language that the other person has understood, when things are particularly charged, or if it’s important for us to feel understood, it can be helpful to ask for a reflection. Here are a few examples.

当无法从上下文或肢体语言中判断对方是否理解，当气氛特别紧张，或者当我们非常需要被理解时，请求对方反馈可能会有所帮助。以下是一些例子。

Connection Requests That Ask for a Reflection / Empathy

请求反思/同理心

• “Can you tell me what you’re getting (from what I said)?”

• “你能告诉我你从我的话中得到了什么吗？”

• “I’m not sure I was totally clear. What are you understanding?”

• “我不太确定我是否完全表达清楚了。您理解的是什么？”

• “Could you tell me your understanding of what matters to me? Knowing that would really help me to feel understood.”

• “您能告诉我您对我的价值观的理解吗？如果能知道这一点，我会感觉自己被理解了。”

• “I’d like to make sure we’re on the same page. What are you taking away from this?”

• “我想确保我们理解一致。你从中得到了什么启示？”

If we have a sense that the other person is with us, we may simply want to know how they’re responding.

如果我们感觉对方与我们在一起，我们可能只是想知道他们的反应如何。

Connection Requests That Ask for a Response / Information

请求回复/信息的连接请求

• “How is it for you to hear all of this?”

• “听到这些，你感觉如何？”

• “What do you think? How do you feel about that?”

• “你怎么看？你对此有何感想？”

• “What can I say or do that would help you to feel more understood?”

• “我能说什么或做什么才能让你感到更被理解？”

Making connection requests isn’t always easy and doesn’t necessarily come naturally. It can feel awkward at first, and it takes practice. Yet with time, letting others know that we’re interested in hearing one another can be a powerful way to come together.

发出好友请求并非易事，也并非总是自然而然。起初可能会感到尴尬，需要练习。然而，随着时间的推移，让别人知道我们有兴趣倾听彼此，可以成为建立联系的有效途径。

In my twenties, my father and I grew quite close thanks to my persistent use of these tools. I explained how I wanted him to know more about my life and how meaningful it would be to have him just listen. He would agree but then inevitably interrupt to offer advice or to explain why I “shouldn’t feel that way.” I patiently heard these replies as expressions of his care and then reminded him that what would be most nourishing to me was his listening attention. He would listen, and I would check every now and then to see if he was still with me. Periodically, I asked how he felt about what I’d shared. After feeling heard, I usually was more open to his advice.

二十多岁的时候，我和父亲的关系变得非常亲密，这要归功于我坚持不懈地运用这些方法。我向他解释说，我希望他更多地了解我的生活，如果他能静静地倾听，对我来说意义非凡。他会同意，但总是会打断我，给出建议，或者解释我“不应该有这种感觉”。我耐心地把这些回应当作他关心我的表达，然后提醒他，对我来说最有益的，是他的倾听。他会听，我会时不时地确认他是否还在认真听。我也会定期询问他对我的分享有何感想。在感到被倾听之后，我通常更容易接受他的建议。

My attempts at creating connection with family weren’t always so graceful. Another casualty of my early attempts at NVC was my paternal grandfather. Sabba, as I called him, grew up in Poland and moved to what was then British Palestine in his late teens. When I knew him, he was mostly blind, living in the house he had built for his family.

我尝试与家人建立联系，但并非总是那么顺利。我早期尝试非暴力沟通的另一个受害者是我的祖父。我叫他萨巴，他在波兰长大，十几岁时搬到了当时的英属巴勒斯坦。我认识他的时候，他几乎失明，住在自己为家人建造的房子里。

One of the last times I saw Sabba, I sat by his bedside as my dad translated. I shared how much I loved him, and how much I would miss him when I went back home. I carefully ended each sentence with a request, asking him what he’d heard me say. After a short time, my grandfather’s face became very dour, clearly upset. “What’s wrong,” I inquired? My father explained, “He says he’s not a child; he understands what you’re saying.”

我最后一次见到萨巴时，坐在他床边，爸爸帮我翻译。我告诉他我有多爱他，回家后我会多么想念他。我每说完一句话，都会小心翼翼地问他是否听懂了。过了一会儿，爷爷的脸色变得很阴沉，显然很不高兴。“怎么了？”我问。爸爸解释说：“他说他不是小孩子了，他听得懂你在说什么。”

In my zeal to build connection, the awkwardness of translation, and communicating across cultures, I failed to recognize that he was hearing me just fine. I hadn’t developed an intuitive feel for when to ask for a reflection, when to ask for a response, and when to trust my gut and just let things be. If I could go back, I would have simply spoken from my heart and then asked him two questions (both connection requests). First, “How is it for you to hear all of this, Sabba?” And then, “Is there anything you’d like me to know?”

我急于建立联系，加上翻译的不便和跨文化交流的障碍，让我忽略了他其实已经听得很清楚了。我还没有培养出那种直觉，不知道什么时候该征求他的反馈，什么时候该寻求回应，什么时候该相信自己的直觉，顺其自然。如果可以重来，我会坦诚地表达自己的想法，然后问他两个问题（都是建立联系的请求）。第一个问题是：“萨巴，你听了这些感觉如何？”第二个问题是：“你有什么想让我知道的吗？”

In the end, we sorted it out. I apologized and explained where I was coming from. I believe he heard how much his strange American grandson loved him.

最后，我们解决了这个问题。我道了歉，并解释了我的出发点。我相信他能感受到他那古怪的美国孙子有多爱他。

PRACTICE : Making Connection Requests

练习：发出连接请求

When speaking, consider what you would like from the other person. Do you want to be heard and understood? Do you trust that’s happening sufficiently? If not, try venturing a request for a reflection. This could be as simple as “Do you know what I mean?” or as specific as “What are you getting from what I just said?” If you want information about how the other person is responding inside, ask.

说话时，想想你希望对方如何回应。你希望被倾听和理解吗？你相信对方能充分做到这一点吗？如果答案是否定的，不妨尝试请求对方的反馈。这可以很简单，比如“你明白我的意思吗？”，也可以很具体，比如“你从我刚才说的话中理解了什么？”。如果你想了解对方内心的感受，那就直接问。

Trust your ability to gauge the level of understanding and connection that is present, reading cues of eye contact, facial expression, and body language. When you make a connection request, do so in a way that is natural and authentic to you. If it’s someone close to you, you might even tell them you’re experimenting with something new and ask if they would be willing to give it a try with you.

相信自己能够判断彼此的理解程度和联系感，通过眼神交流、面部表情和肢体语言来解读这些信息。当你提出建立联系的请求时，要以自然真诚的方式进行。如果对方是你亲近的人，你甚至可以告诉他们你正在尝试一些新的东西，并询问他们是否愿意和你一起尝试。

When we’re unable to arrive at a deeper level of personal connection, it’s still essential to discuss the underlying needs and objectives in a situation before hammering out specific strategies. Without an understanding of what’s at stake for both of us, the solutions we create are less likely to address all of the factors or to come from a place of true willingness. The transition from building mutual understanding to problem solving is therefore key.

当我们无法建立更深层次的个人联系时，在制定具体策略之前，讨论问题的根本需求和目标仍然至关重要。如果我们不了解彼此的利害关系，那么我们提出的解决方案就不太可能面面俱到，也不太可能出于真正的诚意。因此，从建立相互理解到解决问题的过渡至关重要。

Requests That Move toward a Solution

推动解决方案的请求

• “Is there more? Anything else you’d like me to understand?”

“还有其他问题吗？还有什么你想让我明白的吗？”

• “Would this be an okay time to shift to talking about where we go from here?”

• “现在是不是可以转而讨论一下我们下一步该怎么做了？”

• “Do you have any ideas about what might work for both of us?”

• “你有什么想法，或许对我们双方都有利？”

When exploring strategies, the more creative we can be, the more likely we are to find a viable solution. If and when you reach an agreement, to maximize the chances of success, be sure to check if the other person has any concerns or reservations.

在探索策略时，我们越有创意，就越有可能找到可行的解决方案。如果达成协议，为了最大限度地提高成功率，务必确认对方是否有任何顾虑或保留意见。

Principle: Have ideas for strategies that meet as many needs as possible, which invites others to look for creative solutions.

原则：提出能够满足尽可能多的需求的策略想法，从而鼓励其他人寻找创造性的解决方案。

Flowers for My Table

餐桌上的鲜花

The most essential component of a request is the intention behind it. A request contains an inner orientation of flexibility that takes another’s needs into account and is distinct from a demand. Essentially it is a proposal: “How about this?” It is a continuation of the conversation, our best guess at where to go from here. A demand, on the other hand, is the end of a conversation; it’s how we use force or coercion to get our way when we don’t see other options. Requests invite collaboration; demands threaten consequences. We can indicate the collaborative nature of a request with the inflection of our voice or with specific words, signaling our willingness to explore other options and our desire for information about the other person’s needs. Here are a few examples of ways you might begin a request:

请求最关键的要素在于其背后的意图。请求蕴含着一种灵活的内在倾向，它考虑到了对方的需求，这与要求截然不同。本质上，请求是一种提议：“这样如何？”它是对话的延续，是我们对下一步走向的最佳设想。而要求则意味着对话的终结；它是我们在别无选择时，为了达到目的而诉诸武力或胁迫的方式。请求旨在促进合作；要求则会带来后果。我们可以通过语气或措辞来表明请求的合作性质，表明我们愿意探索其他方案，并渴望了解对方的需求。以下是一些提出请求的常用方法：

• “Would you be willing to…?”

• “你愿意……吗？”

• “Could it work for you to…?”

• “这对你来说可行吗……？”

• “How would it be for you to…?”

• “如果你这样做……你会怎么想？”

Marshall Rosenberg had a poetic way of capturing the spirit of making requests: “Ask others to meet your needs like flowers for your table, not air for your lungs.” If I ask you to do something with desperation, how much choice will you feel? How much joy in agreeing? How will it feel if I ask with openness and ease, as if to say, “Wouldn’t this be nice?” This depends on transforming our relationship to our needs and framing our requests around the joy of meeting them. Returning to the classic examples of roommates or romantic partners, notice the differences between the requests below:

马歇尔·卢森堡曾用诗意的方式概括了提出请求的精髓：“请求他人满足你的需求，就像请求鲜花点缀餐桌，而不是请求空气呼吸一样。” 如果我带着绝望的心情请求你做某事，你会感到多少选择余地？答应之后又会有多少喜悦？如果我以一种坦诚轻松的语气提出请求，仿佛在说：“这岂不是很好吗？” 你会作何感想？这取决于我们转变与自身需求的关系，并将满足需求的喜悦融入到请求的框架中。让我们回到室友或伴侣的经典例子，请注意以下请求之间的区别：

• AIR FOR LUNGS : “Would you please wash your dishes and wipe the counters? I need more order in this house!”

• 呼吸新鲜空气：“请你洗碗并擦拭台面好吗？我需要家里更整洁一些！”

• FLOWERS FOR TABLE : “Would you be up for washing your dishes and giving the counter a quick wipe down after you eat? I feel so much more relaxed when the kitchen’s clean and tidy.”

• 餐桌鲜花：“您愿意在饭后洗碗并快速擦拭一下台面吗？厨房干净整洁时，我会感觉放松很多。”

• AIR FOR LUNGS : “I need more time together. When are we going out again?”

• 呼吸新鲜空气：“我需要更多时间在一起。我们什么时候再出去？”

• FLOWERS FOR TABLE : “It’s so sweet for me when we have quality time. Could we look at our calendars and see when we can schedule another date?”

• 餐桌鲜花：“我们能有这样的美好时光，我感到非常甜蜜。我们能看看彼此的日历，安排一下下次见面吗？”

Even when the needs at stake are pressing, we have more leverage when we can create connection and make requests that consider the other person. A female NVC practitioner awoke in the middle of the night with a strange man standing in her bedroom. Trained in nonviolence, one of her first thoughts was, “My safety and this man’s safety are interconnected.” Refusing to see this person as an enemy, understanding that their safety depended on her ability to create connection, she spontaneously asked him what time it was. Caught off guard, the intruder looked at his watch and replied with the time. “How did you get in?” she asked him. A window had been unlocked. Trying to make sense of his breaking in, she ventured a guess, “Oh, it must be cold outside tonight?”

即使情况紧急，如果我们能够建立联结并提出考虑到对方的请求，我们就能拥有更大的优势。一位非暴力沟通（NVC）实践者半夜醒来，发现一个陌生男人站在她的卧室里。作为一名接受过非暴力训练的女性，她首先想到的是：“我的安全和这个男人的安全息息相关。”她拒绝将这个人视为敌人，因为她明白对方的安全取决于她能否与他建立联结，于是她主动问他几点了。这个闯入者有些措手不及，看了看手表，告诉了她时间。“你是怎么进来的？”她问他。原来是窗户没锁。她试图弄明白他为什么闯入，于是猜测道：“哦，今晚外面一定很冷吧？”

They spoke in that tense situation for a few minutes. She learned that he had nowhere to go. Eventually she explained that there was a guest bedroom down the hall, linens in the closet. He could spend the night if he wanted, and if he left in the morning before she was up, she would not call the police. They agreed, and he left her room. This is an extreme example, and few of us know how we would respond in such a situation. I’m not advocating this approach in a potentially dangerous situation without significant training in nonviolence! Yet the example is instructive with regard to how radical the effects of intentional communication can be: in the face of fear and potential violence, she remained able to see his humanity and make requests that accounted for both of their needs.

在那种紧张的气氛下，他们交谈了几分钟。她得知他无处可去。最后，她解释说走廊尽头有一间客房，衣柜里有床单。如果他愿意，可以留宿一晚；如果他在早上她起床前离开，她就不会报警。他们达成了一致，他离开了她的房间。这是一个极端的例子，我们大多数人都不知道在这种情况下会如何应对。我并不是提倡在没有接受过充分的非暴力训练的情况下，在潜在危险的情况下采用这种做法！然而，这个例子很有启发性，它展现了有意识的沟通可以产生多么巨大的影响：面对恐惧和潜在的暴力，她仍然能够看到他的人性，并提出兼顾双方需求的请求。

Providing Context

提供背景信息

Whenever we make a request, if the other person doesn’t understand why we’re asking or how it will contribute, they’re less likely to want to help. This is as true for connection requests as it is for solution requests, for mundane situations as for substantive ones. If it’s not already clear, we need to let the other person know why we’re asking; we need to give them a reason to say yes.

当我们提出请求时，如果对方不理解我们请求的原因或请求的意义，他们就不太可能愿意帮忙。无论是请求建立联系还是寻求解决方案，无论是日常琐事还是重大问题，都是如此。如果对方还不清楚我们请求的原因，我们就需要让他们明白，我们需要给他们一个答应的理由。

A simple example: My partner asks me in the morning, “Are you going to eat this for lunch?” I feel confused. Depending on the context, my response would differ. “I’d really like to take this for lunch today, were you planning on eating it?” is a different question from “I’m afraid this is going to spoil. Will you eat it, or shall I?”

举个简单的例子：早上，我的伴侣问我：“你午饭要吃这个吗？”我感到很困惑。根据语境的不同，我的回答也会有所不同。“我今天很想带这个当午饭，你打算吃吗？”和“我怕这个会坏掉。你吃还是我吃？”是截然不同的问题。

Here’s another example. Notice the difference between asking for a reflection with and without context:

这里还有另一个例子。请注意，在有上下文的情况下请求反思与在没有上下文的情况下请求反思之间的区别：

WITHOUT CONTEXT : “Can you tell me what you heard?”

WITH CONTEXT : “I just said a lot and I’m not sure it all came out the way I meant. Can you tell me what you heard?”

不带上下文：“你能告诉我你听到了什么吗？” 带上下文：“我刚才说了很多，但我不确定我的意思表达得是否准确。你能告诉我你听到了什么吗？”

WITHOUT CONTEXT : “Could you tell me your understanding of what matters to me?”

WITH CONTEXT : “I’d really like to feel heard right now. Could you tell me your understanding of what matters to me?”

不带语境：“您能告诉我您认为我重视的是什么吗？” 带语境：“我现在真的很想被倾听。您能告诉我您认为我重视的是什么吗？”

A Complete Way of Communicating

完整的沟通方式

Observation, feeling, need, request; what happened, how we feel about it, why, and a suggestion for what’s next—this is the classical structure of Nonviolent Communication. It provides a road map to say what we mean and to hear others. The first three components—observations, feelings, and needs—answer the basic question, “How are you?” In sharing this we invite one another into our felt experience: “Here is what’s happening for me.” Requests answer the question, “How can I help?”

观察、感受、需求、请求；发生了什么，我们对此有何感受，为什么会发生，以及对下一步的建议——这是非暴力沟通的经典结构。它为我们提供了表达自己想法和倾听他人的路线图。前三个组成部分——观察、感受和需求——回答了“你好吗？”这个基本问题。通过分享这些，我们邀请彼此进入我们的感受体验：“这就是我目前的感受。” 请求则回答了“我能帮上什么忙？”这个问题。

Expressing an observation, a feeling, and a need carries a lot of weight. If we share that level of detail without making a request, the other person is likely to hear blame regardless of our intentions or words. Consider the following statements with and without a request.

表达观察、感受和需求都非常重要。如果我们分享如此详细的信息却不提出请求，无论我们的意图或措辞如何，对方都可能感到被责备。请思考以下包含请求和不包含请求的陈述。

WITHOUT A REQUEST : “When I heard you wouldn’t be home until eight, I felt so disappointed and frustrated. It’s really important to me to have some time together in the evening.”

WITH A REQUEST : “When I heard you wouldn’t be home until eight, I felt so disappointed and frustrated. It’s really important to me to have some time together in the evening. Can we talk some about how to balance your responsibilities at work with my hopes for our relationship?”

不提出要求：“听说你八点才能回家，我感到非常失望和沮丧。晚上能和你一起待一会儿对我来说非常重要。” 提出要求：“听说你八点才能回家，我感到非常失望和沮丧。晚上能和你一起待一会儿对我来说非常重要。我们能不能谈谈如何平衡你的工作责任和我对我们关系的期望？”

WITHOUT A REQUEST : “I heard music coming from your apartment last night around eleven, and I got pretty frustrated. My earplugs didn’t help. I work early and need to get a good night’s rest.”

WITH A REQUEST : “I heard music coming from your apartment last night around eleven, and I got pretty frustrated. My earplugs didn’t help. I work early and need to get a good night’s rest. Would you be willing to turn the music down or use headphones after ten on weeknights?”

未提出要求：“我昨晚大约11点听到你公寓里传来音乐，这让我很烦躁。我的耳塞也没什么用。我早上要早起上班，需要好好休息。” 提出要求：“我昨晚大约11点听到你公寓里传来音乐，这让我很烦躁。我的耳塞也没什么用。我早上要早起上班，需要好好休息。请问您能否在工作日晚上10点以后把音乐声调小一些或者戴上耳机？”

Our intentions appear vague in the absence of a request, leaving the other person to figure out what we would like from them. Most of us are so conditioned to hear blame that that’s the first interpretation we make. Offering a request lets the other person know why we’re bringing this up and proposes how they can be helpful in this moment.

如果没有明确提出要求，我们的意图就会显得模糊不清，让对方自行揣测我们想要什么。我们大多数人习惯于听到指责，所以这往往是我们首先想到的解释。提出要求可以让对方明白我们为什么提起这件事，并说明他们此刻可以如何提供帮助。

Demands, Hearing and Saying No

要求、倾听和说“不”

The difference between a request and a demand isn’t in our words; it’s in how we respond when the other person says no. If we can meet a no with curiosity—“Oh, why not? What do you need?”—then we were genuinely making a request. If we respond with anger, self-righteousness, or a guilt trip, then we weren’t really asking in the first place, were we?

请求和命令的区别不在于措辞，而在于当对方拒绝时我们的反应。如果我们能以好奇心回应“哦，为什么不行？您需要什么？”，那么我们才是真正地提出请求。如果我们以愤怒、自以为是或道德绑架来回应，那么我们一开始就不是在请求，不是吗？

As we’ve explored, using guilt, blame, or demands to meet our needs comes at a cost in goodwill, trust, and the quality of relationship. Even if we get what we want in the short term, we pay a price in the long term. Most people respond to demands by reacting: submit or rebel. Neither is based on true freedom and autonomy. Even if they agree, their inherent motivation will likely be compromised. Here, asking ourselves Rosenberg’s two key questions can dissuade us from making demands and guide us to a more collaborative approach rooted in curiosity and care:

正如我们所探讨的，利用内疚、责备或强求来满足自身需求，会损害善意、信任和人际关系的质量。即使短期内我们如愿以偿，长远来看，我们也付出了代价。大多数人对要求的反应是：要么顺从，要么反抗。这两种反应都不是建立在真正的自由和自主之上的。即使他们同意，他们内在的动机也可能受到损害。在此，问问自己罗森伯格提出的两个关键问题，可以劝阻我们提出要求，并引导我们采取一种基于好奇心和关怀的、更具合作性的方法：

• What do I want them to do?

• 我希望他们做什么？

• Why do I want them to do it? What do I want their reasons to be?

• 我为什么要他们这样做？我希望他们给出的理由是什么？

This second question is not an attempt to control the other person or manipulate them. It’s a way of reconnecting with our deeper intentions of curiosity and care, of remembering how good it feels when others choose to meet our needs because they understand how it will contribute to us.

第二个问题并非试图控制或操纵对方，而是为了重新唤起我们内心深处的好奇和关怀，让我们再次感受到当别人因为理解我们的需求而选择满足我们时，那种美好的感觉。

Our ability to hear (and say) no without losing connection is essential. Hearing no can be one of the most vulnerable parts of making a request, especially when we are asking for something important. For beneath any request, however small, is a hidden question: “Do I matter?” Hearing no can challenge our sense of agency, frustrate our hopes, stimulate disappointment, or touch painful wounds.

我们能否在不失去联系的情况下听取（和拒绝）“不”至关重要。听到“不”可能是提出请求时最脆弱的环节之一，尤其是在我们请求重要的事情时。因为任何请求，无论多么微小，背后都隐藏着一个问题：“我重要吗？”听到“不”会挑战我们的自主感，挫败我们的希望，引发失望，甚至触及我们内心深处的伤痛。

In these instances, the practice of self-empathy is an important component in having the resilience to stay engaged and not take things personally when someone says no. If we can pause, sense our needs and any deeper longing to know that we matter, we can bring more openness, patience, and curiosity to the dialogue.

在这些情况下，培养自我同理心至关重要，它能帮助我们保持韧性，在别人拒绝时不至于耿耿于怀。如果我们能够停下来，感受自己的需求，以及内心深处渴望被重视的愿望，就能以更加开放、耐心和好奇的态度投入到对话中。

The ability to say no is a sign of a healthy relationship. If someone always says yes, we can’t know if they are genuinely agreeing or doing so out of fear, shame, or obligation—all of which can lead to resentment, mistrust, or lack of follow-through. On the contrary, when someone says no, we can trust that they mean it when they say yes!

能够说“不”是健康关系的标志。如果一个人总是说“是”，我们就无法判断他们是真心同意，还是出于恐惧、羞愧或义务——所有这些都可能导致怨恨、不信任或食言。相反，当一个人说“不”时，我们可以相信，当他们说“是”时，他们是真心实意的！

We can also view no as a source of information rather than a dead end. After all, saying no is in and of itself a strategy to meet some need; it indicates that there is something else more important preventing them from saying yes to our request. Instead of taking it personally, we can listen for the yes behind their no. This doesn’t mean assuming that they are saying yes to our request. It means that they are saying yes to something else that is more important to them. If we can identify what that is, we have more options to work together creatively. To what other needs are they saying yes? Can we find another strategy that meets all of the needs present or a way to sufficiently address their needs such that they can say yes to our request?

我们也可以将“不”视为信息的来源，而不是死胡同。毕竟，说“不”本身就是一种满足某种需求的策略；它表明有更重要的事情阻止他们答应我们的请求。与其将“不”视为针对个人的攻击，不如倾听他们“不”背后的“是”。这并不意味着我们假定他们就是在答应我们的请求。而是意味着他们正在答应对他们来说更重要的事情。如果我们能找到答案，就能有更多创造性的合作方式。他们还在答应哪些其他需求？我们能否找到另一种策略来满足他们所有的需求，或者找到一种能够充分满足他们需求的方法，从而让他们最终答应我们的请求？

PRACTICE : Hearing No

练习：听证会否

When someone says no, try to get curious. Check if you are open to other strategies to meet your needs and if you genuinely want the outcome to work for the other person. Here are some ideas for additional requests to continue the conversation:

当对方拒绝时，试着保持好奇心。想想你是否愿意接受其他方法来满足你的需求，以及你是否真心希望对方也能满意。以下是一些可以继续对话的建议：

• “I’m curious to know why not? Could you share more?”

• “我很想知道为什么不行？您能详细说说吗？”

• “What’s leading you to say no?”

• “是什么让你说不呢？”

• “Can we take some time to brainstorm ideas that could work for both of us?”

• “我们能否花点时间集思广益，想出一些对我们双方都有利的方案？”

• “Do you have other ideas?”

• “你还有其他想法吗？”

• “What would you need to know, or what could I do, to make it possible for you to say yes?”

• “您需要知道什么，或者我可以做些什么，才能让您答应下来？”

You may find yourself on the other side of the spectrum, struggling to honor your own limits and say no to requests. Overriding your own needs to help others can lead to burnout, depression, resentment, or lopsided relationships. This can come about for many reasons. You may fear disappointing others, want to avoid the discomfort of a difficult conversation, or have trouble trusting that your own needs matter. You may genuinely want to help but chronically overestimate your inner resources.

你可能发现自己处于另一个极端，难以尊重自己的底线，也难以对别人的请求说“不”。为了帮助他人而压抑自己的需求，可能会导致精疲力竭、抑郁、怨恨，或者人际关系失衡。这种情况的出现有很多原因。你可能害怕让别人失望，想要逃避棘手的谈话带来的不适，或者难以相信自己的需求也同样重要。你可能真心想帮助别人，但却总是高估自己的能力。

There are ways of saying no that maintain connection, honor your needs, and protect against misunderstanding. If you say no without affirming their needs in some way, the other person may interpret your response as not caring about them. Instead, try to separate your response to their strategy from your care for their needs ; that is, share your understanding of their needs and express your interest in finding a way to meet them. Let them know why you are saying no and propose an alternative, or invite them to do so.

拒绝的方式有很多种，既能维系彼此的联系，又能尊重自身需求，还能避免误解。如果你在拒绝时没有以某种方式肯定对方的需求，对方可能会觉得你漠不关心。因此，你应该尝试将你对他们策略的回应与你对他们需求的关心区分开来；也就是说，你要表达你理解他们的需求，并表示愿意找到满足这些需求的方法。让他们知道你拒绝的原因，并提出替代方案，或者邀请他们提出自己的方案。

PRACTICE : Saying No

练习：如何说“不”

The next time someone asks something of you and you’re not willing to agree, try to stay engaged in the process of dialogue. Here are a few examples of ways to say no while maintaining connection:

下次当有人向你提出请求而你又不想答应时，试着继续参与对话。以下是一些既能拒绝又能保持沟通的例子：

• “I’d like to say yes, and here’s what’s getting in the way of that right now.”

• “我很想答应，但目前阻碍我的是以下几点。”

• “I hear how important this is to you, and I’m not seeing how I can make it work given that I also have a need for…Could we explore some other options that might work for you?”

• “我知道这件事对你很重要，但我也不知道该如何兼顾……我们能否探讨一些其他可能适合你的方案？”

• “I can’t agree to that without a significant cost to myself in terms of…[my other commitments, my need for rest…]. Would it work for you if we tried this instead?”

• “如果那样做，我会付出很大的代价，比如影响我的其他安排、休息时间等等……。如果我们换个方式，你觉得可以吗？”

A Cycle of Giving and Receiving

给予与接受的循环

When we’re able to make requests, hear no, and gently persist with care, beautiful things can happen. I used what I learned from Sabba to help my student Laura find closure with her grandmother.

当我们能够提出请求、接受拒绝，并温柔而谨慎地坚持下去时，美好的事情就会发生。我运用从萨巴那里学到的方法，帮助我的学生劳拉与她的祖母和解。

Laura teaches mindfulness, and her ninety-two-year old grandmother had been an important source of inspiration throughout her life. Every time Laura tried to share her appreciation, her grandmother would grow uncomfortable, change the subject, or gently deflect Laura’s words. In her humility and desire to make space for others, she was unavailable to receive Laura’s gratitude.

劳拉教授正念冥想，她九十二岁的祖母是她一生中重要的灵感来源。每当劳拉试图表达感激之情时，祖母都会感到不自在，要么转移话题，要么委婉地回避劳拉的话。出于谦逊和想要为他人留出空间的愿望，她无法接受劳拉的谢意。

I coached Laura to reframe the conversation from trying to give something to her grandmother to making a request. “Grandma, there are some things I’d really like to share with you. It would be so meaningful to me to have you listen. Would you be willing to sit with me for a bit? It would be such a gift.” Her grandmother was delighted to offer this simple gesture of presence. Laura spoke of how meaningful their relationship was and of how her grandmother had been a role model for her all these years. They shared some tender moments of appreciation and even a few tears. By making a request, Laura had helped her grandmother see how receiving appreciation was a gift to both of them.

我引导劳拉把谈话的重点从想给奶奶送东西转移到提出请求。“奶奶，有些事我想跟您说说。如果您能听我说，对我来说意义非凡。您愿意陪我坐一会儿吗？这对我来说就是一份珍贵的礼物。”奶奶欣然接受了这个简单的陪伴。劳拉讲述了她们之间深厚的感情，以及奶奶这些年来一直是她的榜样。她们分享了一些温馨的感激时刻，甚至有人感动落泪。劳拉的请求让奶奶明白，接受别人的感激对她们俩来说都是一种馈赠。

PRINCIPLES

原则

The clearer we are about what we want and why, the more creative we can be about how to make it happen.

我们越清楚自己想要什么以及为什么想要，就越能创造性地实现它。

The more we understand one another, the easier it is to find solutions that work for everyone. Therefore, establish as much mutual understanding as possible before problem solving.

我们越了解彼此，就越容易找到对大家都适用的解决方案。因此，在解决问题之前，尽可能地建立相互理解。

Have ideas for strategies that meet as many needs as possible, which invites others to look for creative solutions.

要有能够满足尽可能多的需求的策略想法，这样才能鼓励其他人寻找创造性的解决方案。

KEY POINTS

要点

In conversations, requests move things forward one step at a time, building understanding, connection, and proposing solutions that may work for everyone. To transform our relationship with making requests and receiving them, we can see requests in the following ways:

在对话中，请求能一步步推动事情进展，增进理解和联系，并提出可能对双方都适用的解决方案。为了转变我们提出请求和接受请求的方式，我们可以从以下几个方面看待请求：

• Making a request is about working together to meet one another’s needs.

提出请求是为了共同努力满足彼此的需求。

• Needs are gifts, invitations to experience the joy of giving and receiving.

• 需求是礼物，是体验给予和接受的快乐的邀请。

• Expressing our needs through requests lets others know how they can help and offers a concrete idea for where to go next in the conversation.

• 通过请求表达我们的需求，可以让其他人知道如何提供帮助，并为接下来的对话提供具体的想法。

• Being skilled at making requests includes supporting others in asking for what they need, being sensitive to and intuiting requests they may have.

• 善于提出请求包括支持他人提出他们的需求，对他人的需求保持敏感和直觉。

• Hearing (and saying) no can be a sign of a healthy relationship and points to information about other needs that are preventing someone from saying yes.

• 听到（和说）“不”可能是健康关系的标志，并表明还有其他需求阻止某人说“是”。

We can say no and still maintain connection, honor our needs, and protect against misunderstanding by:

我们可以通过以下方式说“不”并维持联系、满足自身需求并避免误解：

• Affirming another’s needs

• 肯定他人的需求

• Sharing our understanding of their needs and expressing our interest in finding a way to meet them

• 分享我们对他们需求的理解，并表达我们有兴趣找到满足他们需求的方法。

• Letting them know why we are saying no and proposing an alternative or inviting them to do so

• 向他们解释我们拒绝的原因，并提出替代方案或邀请他们提出替代方案。

QUESTION & ANSWER

问答

Q: I’ve been using these tools, and I am getting a lot of feedback that I’m being self-centered, controlling, or pushy. What am I doing wrong?

问：我一直在使用这些工具，但收到很多反馈说我以自我为中心、控制欲强或咄咄逼人。我到底做错了什么？

When we become aware of our needs and start making requests, we can sound a bit demanding. Check if your requests are flexible. Are you coming from an attitude of “You should do this”? Also check that the other person understands that you’re genuinely willing to hear no.

当我们意识到自己的需求并开始提出要求时，我们可能会显得有些强势。请检查你的要求是否灵活。你是否抱着“你应该这样做”的态度？同时，也要确保对方明白你真心愿意接受拒绝。

When we have these tools, we also take on an extra role in conversation. We’re no longer solely an advocate for our own needs. We simultaneously become a facilitator, advocating for the other person’s needs as well—because we value their needs as an integral part of a healthy relationship, recognize our own needs for compassion and contribution, and understand that their willingness is a key ingredient in the success of any agreements we make.

当我们拥有这些工具时，我们在对话中也扮演着额外的角色。我们不再仅仅是自身需求的倡导者，同时也成为了沟通的协调者，维护对方的需求——因为我们珍视对方的需求，将其视为健康关系不可或缺的一部分；我们也意识到自身对同情和付出的需求，并明白对方的意愿是我们达成任何协议成功的关键因素。

You may need to make an extra effort to communicate as clearly as you can that you are genuinely interested in finding something that works for both of you. We can’t control others’ perceptions, but we can do our best to let them know that we would like to take their needs into consideration. Explicitly invite them to share: “I’d love to hear more about what’s important to you. What would work for you here?” Find requests that make it easy for them to say no or that invite them to share more information.
