For example: “I only want you to say yes if it really works for you…” or “I don’t want you to feel obligated; it’s okay if you say no.”

你可能需要格外努力，尽可能清晰地表达你真心想找到一个对双方都合适的方案。我们无法控制他人的看法，但我们可以尽力让他们知道，我们愿意考虑他们的需求。明确地邀请他们分享：“我很想了解对你来说最重要的是什么。你觉得怎样做才合适？” 提出一些容易让他们拒绝或鼓励他们分享更多信息的要求。例如：“我希望你只有在真的觉得合适的时候才答应……”或者“我不想让你感到有义务，如果你拒绝也没关系。”

Q: I’d like to be able to make requests, but things happen so quickly I kind of freeze. Even when there’s space, I wouldn’t know what to ask for.

问：我很想提出要求，但事情发生得太快，我常常不知所措。即使有空位，我也不知道该提什么要求。

There is a certain amount of retraining our nervous system to feel more ease in conversation. Start by using the tools of presence to handle your inner experience and find the courage to speak. Feel your feet on the ground and bring some attention to your posture, which can boost your strength. Start small, building confidence in less challenging situations.

我们需要对神经系统进行一定程度的重新训练，才能在交谈中感到更加自在。首先，运用正念技巧来掌控你的内心感受，并找到开口说话的勇气。感受双脚踏实地的感觉，并注意你的姿势，这可以增强你的力量。从小事做起，在不太棘手的情境中逐步建立自信。

To make a request, we have to be aware of our needs too, to know what we want. Try memorizing two or three simple requests that you can use any time. Find an authentic way of making a basic connection request for a reflection or a response, and practice until you can say it without thinking. Try rehearsing a request for some time to think, such as “There’s something I’d like to say. Can you give me a moment to gather my thoughts?”

提出请求之前，我们也要意识到自己的需求，知道自己想要什么。试着记住两三个简单的请求，以便随时使用。找到一种真诚的方式，提出基本的沟通请求，例如寻求反馈或回应，并反复练习，直到能够脱口而出。试着练习一下请求，给自己一些思考的时间，例如：“我有些话想说，您能给我一点时间整理一下思路吗？”

Q: “Would you be willing…” sounds so formal and stilted. Why not just say “Please”?

问：“您是否愿意……”听起来太正式、太生硬了。为什么不直接说“请”呢？

Remember, it’s not about what you say but where you’re coming from. The words help train our attention to stay aligned with the intention of the principles. “Please” can carry a lot of connotations. Most of us are socialized to say “please” and “thank you” whether or not we actually mean it. Sometimes “please” codes as a veiled demand. For these reasons, I suggest you find other ways to indicate your flexibility, such as “Would you / could you” or “How would it be for you…?” These phrases tend to carry less cultural baggage.

记住，重要的不是你说什么，而是你的出发点。措辞有助于我们集中注意力，使之与原则的初衷保持一致。“请”这个词可能包含很多含义。我们大多数人从小就被教导要说“请”和“谢谢”，无论我们是否真的想表达这些意思。有时，“请”甚至会变成一种隐晦的要求。因此，我建议你寻找其他方式来表达你的灵活，例如“您愿意/可以吗？”或者“您觉得怎么样……？”这些表达方式通常不会带有太多文化包袱。

Q: How do I tell the difference between when to bring something up and make a request and when to just let go or deal with it on my own?

问：我如何判断什么时候应该提出要求，什么时候应该放手或自己处理？

I’m interested in flexibility, cultivating the capacity to do both. Letting go isn’t mutually exclusive with making requests. I hope it’s clear that the less attached we are to getting our way, the more room we actually have to make requests and engage in dialogue.

我感兴趣的是灵活性，以及培养兼顾两者的能力。放手并不等同于提出要求。我希望大家明白，我们越不执着于事事如意，就越能腾出空间提出要求并进行对话。

Consider your conditioning and practice going in the other direction. If you’re someone who tends to work everything out on your own inside, risk speaking up and inviting others to hear what’s in your heart. If you’re more vocal and tend to look outside for resolution, balance that with some introspection. See if you can find some spaciousness inside and how that changes your perspective on the situation.

不妨反其道而行之，反思一下你的习惯。如果你习惯于独自在内心解决所有问题，那就大胆地敞开心扉，让别人倾听你的心声。如果你更善于表达，倾向于向外寻求解决方案，那就需要进行一些内省，以平衡这种习惯。看看你是否能在内心找到一些空间，以及这会如何改变你对问题的看法。

Q: What about when someone isn’t interested in engaging? I’ve made several requests and it’s either “No” or radio silence.

问：如果对方没有兴趣参与怎么办？我提过好几次请求，要么是“不”，要么就是杳无音信。

It can be so painful when the other person is not willing to engage in dialogue. It seems to touch some ancient, deep-rooted need for belonging, even a fear of exile from the tribe. I think most of us need a lot of tenderness and care in times like that.

当对方不愿沟通时，那种感觉真的非常痛苦。这似乎触及了我们内心深处某种古老而根深蒂固的归属感需求，甚至是害怕被群体放逐的恐惧。我想，在这样的时刻，我们大多数人都需要温柔的关怀和照顾。

We can try to empathize with the feelings or needs behind their silence which, in effect, has become their only message. In some circumstances, this can create the conditions to reengage in dialogue. In my own life, I’ve seen that sometimes we just have different expectations. The other person may need more time before they are ready to talk. For me, it’s been incredibly important in such situations to get support and to turn inward and call upon my own resources for healing and resolution. With patience, we can find a lot of compassion for ourselves and forgiveness for others. In the end, the process can be deeply freeing.

我们可以尝试去理解他们沉默背后的感受或需求，因为沉默实际上已经成为他们唯一的表达方式。在某些情况下，这可以创造重新开启对话的条件。就我个人而言，我发现有时我们只是期望不同。对方可能需要更多时间才能准备好开口。对我来说，在这种情况下，获得支持、反思自身、调动自身资源进行疗愈和解决问题至关重要。只要有耐心，我们就能对自己充满慈悲，也能宽恕他人。最终，这个过程会带来深刻的解脱。

# ↩

part four

# ↩

第四部分

bringing it all together

将所有内容整合在一起

WHEN THE THREE steps to effective conversation are functioning together, dialogue can feel like dancing. We relax. We take turns speaking and listening with ease, shifting our attention back and forth as if to the rhythm of music. Leading with presence grounds us and gives us more choice in how we relate. Coming from care and curiosity, we create the conditions for collaboration and understanding. Focusing on what matters, we identify what’s actually important.

当有效对话的三个步骤协同运作时，对话便如同翩翩起舞。我们放松下来，轻松地轮流发言和倾听，注意力在彼此间自如切换，如同音乐的节奏。以专注的态度引领对话，让我们脚踏实地，并赋予我们更多沟通方式的选择。出于关怀和好奇，我们创造合作与理解的条件。专注于真正重要的事情，我们才能认清真正重要的事物。

Other times, conversation feels more like mountain climbing than dancing! We trudge uphill with a heavy load, picking our way around obstacles, stumbling over dicey terrain. We interrupt, skip ahead, or jump from one topic to another.

有时候，谈话与其说是跳舞，不如说是登山！我们背负重担艰难跋涉，小心翼翼地绕过障碍，跌跌撞撞地走过险峻的地形。我们打断对方，跳过某些话题，或者从一个话题跳到另一个话题。

Life is complicated and messy, and learning to be light on our feet takes practice—whether we’re dancing or climbing a peak. We need to be prepared to lose the rhythm, rub sore feet, tend to a few blisters, and stumble every now and again.

生活复杂多变，学会轻盈起舞需要练习——无论是在跳舞还是攀登高峰。我们需要做好准备，随时可能失去节奏、揉搓酸痛的双脚、处理水泡，以及时不时地跌倒。

In the last part of this book, we’ll explore how things fit together in the arc of a conversation and how to handle challenging situations. We’ll learn how to move nimbly, knowing when to dance, when to trek uphill, and when to stop and rest. We’ll also learn how to follow the larger movements of a conversation, how to shift and move with the changing focus from me to you, and how to manage the different threads of information that can arise.

本书最后一部分，我们将探讨对话的各个环节如何衔接，以及如何应对棘手的情况。我们将学习如何灵活应对，懂得何时该轻快地展开对话，何时该奋力攀登，何时该停下来休息。我们还将学习如何把握对话的整体走向，如何随着对话焦点从“我”转移到“你”而调整，以及如何处理对话中可能出现的各种信息线索。

# ↩

12

the flow of dialogue

对话流程

This life is a thump-ripe melon, so sweet and such a mess.

—GREG BROWN

人生就像一颗熟透的甜瓜，甜美又混乱。——格雷格·布朗

A GOOD FRIEND of mine, Amanda, called me to ask for some advice about a tricky conversation. She’d recently spent some time with a friend. After a week of camping and a rushed departure, Amanda’s four-year-old son had a meltdown in the car on their way to the airport. The friend intervened (without permission) and later emailed Amanda some unsolicited parenting advice.

我的好朋友阿曼达打电话给我，想就一个棘手的谈话向我寻求一些建议。她最近和一位朋友一起度过了一段时间。露营一周后，她们匆匆离开，阿曼达四岁的儿子在去机场的路上在车里突然大哭大闹。那位朋友未经允许就介入了，之后还给阿曼达发了一些她并不需要的育儿建议。

I offered Amanda some empathy for how frustrated she might be feeling and asked if she longed for more respect for her choices as a parent. Then we took things apart and strategized how best to approach the conversation. There were several layers: their friendship, the other woman’s genuine desire to contribute, Amanda’s need to receive support in a way and at a time that works for her. We identified each of the different topics, clarified her needs, the requests she could make, and finally discussed some ways to open the conversation to start off on the right foot.

我向阿曼达表达了对她可能感到沮丧的理解，并询问她是否渴望作为父母的选择能得到更多尊重。然后我们一起分析了事情的来龙去脉，并制定了最佳的谈话策略。这其中涉及多个层面：她们之间的友谊、对方真诚的帮助意愿，以及阿曼达希望以适合她的方式和时间获得支持。我们逐一梳理了不同的话题，明确了她的需求和可以提出的要求，最后探讨了一些开启对话、确保对话顺利进行的方法。

The three steps to effective conversation—lead with presence, come from curiosity and care, and focus on what matters—form the foundation for how we show up, the way we engage, and what we discuss. It’s also important to be able to zoom out and have a broader view of the conversation as a whole. Where do we start? How do we shift from one topic to another or from my perspective to yours?

有效对话的三大步骤——以专注的态度引领、出于好奇和关怀、聚焦于重要事项——构成了我们如何展现自我、如何参与互动以及我们讨论内容的基础。同样重要的是，要能够跳出固有思维，从更广阔的视角看待整个对话。我们从哪里开始？如何从一个话题过渡到另一个话题，或者如何从我的视角转换到你的视角？

The Steps of the Dance

舞蹈的步骤

Dialogue is a lot like dancing. It takes time to learn the basics, but when we are conversing smoothly with someone else, it can be magical. Old friends and new lovers can talk for hours, moving effortlessly through the steps of that ancient dance. We speak, we listen, we dwell together in contemplation or wonder, in celebration or mourning.

对话很像跳舞。学习基本技巧需要时间，但当我们与他人流畅地交谈时，那感觉简直妙不可言。老朋友和新恋人可以畅谈数小时，毫不费力地跳着这古老的舞蹈。我们说话，我们倾听，我们一起沉思或惊叹，一起庆祝或哀悼。

Just as the in- and out-breath anchor our awareness in meditation, just as feelings and needs ground our attention in conversation, three basic “positions” choreograph our dance of dialogue. I mentioned these briefly in chapter 1 , and I’d like to return to them now with the added richness of all that you’ve learned.

正如呼吸在冥想中锚定我们的意识，正如感受和需求在对话中使我们的注意力集中，三种基本的“位置”编排了我们对话的节奏。我在第一章中简要提及了这些位置，现在我想结合你们所学到的知识，更深入地探讨它们。

In any given moment of a conversation, we can speak, listen, or rest in presence. We express : we speak from the heart, sharing observations, feelings, needs, or requests openly and honestly, with as little blame as possible. We receive : we listen from the heart, with curiosity and care, hearing the human feelings and needs beneath another person’s words. We rest : we bring presence to the whole process, pausing to settle and integrate as needed.

在对话的任何时刻，我们都可以说话、倾听或保持临在。我们表达：我们发自内心地说话，坦诚地分享观察、感受、需求或请求，尽可能避免指责。我们接受：我们用心倾听，带着好奇和关怀，聆听对方话语背后隐藏的人性情感和需求。我们休息：我们全程保持临在，根据需要停下来，让自己平静下来，整合信息。

These are the basic moves of the dance. All communication comes back to these three options: express honestly, receive empathically, or return to presence. 1

这些是沟通的基本步骤。所有沟通最终都归结为这三个选项：坦诚表达、同理心接纳或回归当下。

It can be healing to feel that rhythm of give-and-take and work through a challenge. We find a flow as we shift attention back and forth, hearing one another and allowing things to settle. Many students report how transformative just one successful conversation can be. In sensing the rhythm of that dance, something in our nervous system learns how to participate in the process of creating understanding with another human being.

感受这种有来有往的交流节奏，并共同克服挑战，本身就是一种疗愈。当我们来回转移注意力，倾听彼此，让一切沉淀下来时，便能找到一种流畅感。许多学生都表示，一次成功的对话就能带来巨大的改变。在感知这种交流节奏的过程中，我们神经系统中的某些部分学会了如何参与到与他人建立理解的过程中。

PRACTICE : The Dance of Dialogue

实践：对话之舞

Simplify your focus in conversation and return to the basics. Allow the details of all that you’ve learned so far to be in the background. Lead with presence, come from curiosity and care, and consider the choice points between speaking, listening, and resting with presence. Can you find the rhythm of give-and-take in conversation, the dance of speaking, listening, and resting?

简化对话的焦点，回归基本。把你之前学到的所有细节都放在一边。以专注的态度引导对话，怀着好奇和关怀，并带着专注思考说话、倾听和休息之间的选择。你能在对话中找到互动的节奏，找到说话、倾听和休息之间的和谐律动吗？

Framing a Conversation

构建对话框架

Beginnings are delicate. How we start a relationship or a conversation can have a significant effect on its trajectory. (Starting a date with “You’re late” will probably influence how the night unfolds.) Yet so many factors feed into any one moment that it can be hard to know where to start.

开头总是微妙的。我们如何开启一段关系或一段对话，会对它的走向产生重大影响。（约会以“你迟到了”开场，很可能会影响当晚的进展。）然而，任何一个瞬间都受到诸多因素的影响，以至于我们很难知道该从何开始。

The behaviors of complex, dynamic systems are highly sensitive to what are known as initial conditions, the value of certain variables at the beginning of a process. Human beings are complex, dynamic systems; the pre- and perinatal periods of a child’s life can have dramatic impact on their long-term psychological and physiological health. A conversation is also a complex, dynamic system. It’s a living, breathing process. We can use a tool called framing to set the initial conditions for a successful exchange.

复杂动态系统的行为对所谓的初始条件（即过程开始时某些变量的值）高度敏感。人类是复杂动态系统；儿童的孕前和围产期对其长期的心理和生理健康有着显著的影响。对话也是一个复杂动态系统，它是一个鲜活的、不断发展的过程。我们可以利用一种称为“框架”的工具来设定成功交流的初始条件。

Framing summarizes an issue or area of discussion in a broad and neutral way, often in terms of any shared needs, goals, or values.

框架是指以广泛和中立的方式概括某个问题或讨论领域，通常是根据共同的需求、目标或价值观来概括的。

Framing gives someone a general indication of the territory we’d like to discuss in a neutral or positive way. Like putting up the scaffolding for a house, it provides structure and outlines areas to be filled in later. Framing can be particularly helpful when the issues are loaded, and specific observations are likely to embroil us in the heat of a challenge. It also can provide an opportunity to gauge another person’s willingness to converse, align us with one another, or introduce a metalevel discussion concerning how we’re going to talk about things.

框架构建能以中立或积极的方式，大致勾勒出我们想要讨论的领域。就像搭建房屋的脚手架一样，它提供了结构框架，并勾勒出后续需要填充的内容。当问题充满争议，具体的观察结果可能会让我们陷入困境时，框架构建就显得尤为重要。它还能帮助我们评估对方的沟通意愿，使彼此达成共识，或者引出关于我们如何讨论问题的更深层次的讨论。

The first and most essential aspect of setting initial conditions is agreeing to have the conversation. If we are too focused on the issues, we can forget to negotiate this most basic aspect of relating. Is this the right time to talk? Is it a good place? Here are two examples of introducing a topic with and without framing.

设定初始条件的首要且最关键的一点是双方同意进行对话。如果我们过于关注问题本身，就可能忽略了协商这一最基本的沟通方式。现在是谈话的合适时机吗？地点合适吗？以下是引入话题时使用和不使用框架的两个例子。

WITHOUT FRAMING : “When I heard you say ‘stop being so self-centered’ I felt so hurt. I really wanted you to know how much it would mean to me if you came to the event. Can you understand how I might have felt?”

不加修饰地表达：“当我听到你说‘别这么以自我为中心’时，我感到非常受伤。我真的很想让你知道，如果你能来参加这个活动，对我来说意义有多么重大。你能理解我的感受吗？”

WITH FRAMING : “I wanted to talk about the conversation we had yesterday to see if we could understand where we each were coming from a little better. Would you be up for that?”

（引导语）：“我想谈谈我们昨天的对话，看看我们能否更好地理解彼此的观点。你愿意吗？”

Instead of quoting the most painful observation, the speaker refers to the conversation more generally, suggests some shared needs, and frames things in terms of “we.” Each of these aspects can create alignment and togetherness at the outset of a dialogue. Here are two more examples of an initial request for dialogue:

与其直接引用最令人痛心的言论，不如将话题引向更广泛的层面，提出一些共同的需求，并以“我们”的视角来构建对话。这些做法都能在对话伊始就建立起共识和凝聚力。以下是另外两个发起对话的例子：

• “Would you be willing to take some time to have a conversation with me about…?”

• “您是否愿意抽出一些时间和我谈谈……？”

• “Could we sit down and look at what we both need, to see if we can find a way to work this out?”

• “我们能不能坐下来，看看我们双方的需求，看看能不能找到解决办法？”

There are many ways to frame a conversation to create a sense of togetherness and shared purpose. Depending on the context, different facets may be more or less useful.

有很多方法可以构建对话框架，从而营造团结感和共同目标感。根据具体情况，不同的方法可能效果各异。

Options for Framing

装裱方案

BROAD VIEW : State the situation in a broad, neutral way that lets the other person make an informed decision about entering the conversation without getting into potentially contentious details.

概括性陈述：以概括、中立的方式陈述情况，让对方在不涉及可能引起争议的细节的情况下，做出是否加入对话的知情决定。

FEELINGS : Share your vulnerability, naming feelings that may stimulate compassion.

感受：分享你的脆弱，说出可能激发同情心的感受。

SHARED NEEDS : Include any shared needs, goals, or benefits of the dialogue. State things in terms of “we” rather than “I.”

共同需求：包括任何共同的需求、目标或对话益处。用“我们”而不是“我”来表述。

APPRECIATION : Are there bonds you share that would support goodwill, curiosity, and care? Begin with appreciation for the other person, what you enjoy about them or your relationship.

欣赏：你们之间是否存在能够促进善意、好奇心和关怀的纽带？首先要欣赏对方，欣赏你喜欢对方的哪些方面，或者欣赏你们之间的关系。

Here are some examples of how you might use each of these options.

以下是一些如何使用这些选项的示例。

FRAMING FEELINGS : “Some of our interactions recently were a bit difficult for me. I’m struggling to sort them out, and wonder if we could take some time to talk about what happened?”

表达感受：“我们最近的一些互动让我感到有些困难。我正在努力理清思绪，想知道我们是否可以花些时间谈谈发生了什么事？”

FRAMING SHARED NEEDS : “Could we revisit that last interaction? I’d love to find a way for us to both feel understood and supported.”

明确共同需求：“我们能再回顾一下上次的交流吗？我希望能找到一种让我们双方都感到被理解和支持的方式。”

FRAMING APPRECIATION : “Our friendship is so important to me; I really appreciate having you in my life. What happened last week was difficult for me and I’d like to find some resolution. Would you be up for talking?”

表达感激之情：“我们的友谊对我来说非常重要；我真的很感激生命中有你。上周发生的事情让我很难过，我想找到解决办法。你愿意谈谈吗？”

Each of these examples offers a different way of creating alignment as you enter a conversation. Use discernment to determine which tool is best suited to any given situation.

这些例子分别展示了在对话中达成共识的不同方法。运用判断力，确定哪种工具最适合具体情况。

Principle: Stating how a conversation can contribute to both of us helps create buy-in and willingness.

原则：阐明对话如何对我们双方都有益处，有助于建立认同感和意愿。

Tracking in Conversations

对话中的跟踪

Navigating a conversation can feel like trying to follow an overgrown trail through the woods. It takes patience and careful observation. You lose the path periodically, only to pick it up again later. While every conversation is unique, there are certain universal patterns. To shepherd a dialogue toward resolution, we track its process —what kind of conversation we’re having, where we are in that, who has the center of attention—and we track its content —the specific topic we are discussing and if it’s complete.

引导对话有时就像在树林里沿着杂草丛生的小径前行。这需要耐心和细致的观察。你会时不时地迷失方向，但之后总能重新找到方向。虽然每次对话都独一无二，但其中也存在一些普遍的模式。为了引导对话走向解决，我们需要追踪对话的过程——我们正在进行什么类型的对话，对话进行到什么阶段，谁是关注的焦点——以及对话的内容——我们正在讨论的具体主题以及讨论是否完整。

Tracking means following specific pieces of process or content in a conversation.

跟踪是指跟踪对话中的特定过程或内容。

At the most basic level, there are two kinds of conversations— relational and logistical ; they often coexist as layers of a single conversation. The relational domain includes our quality of connection, our emotions, and the ways in which we’re relating. The logistical domain encompasses whatever problem we are trying to solve concretely and any agreements we make. In Amanda’s situation, the relational conversation was about how she felt in response to her friend’s interventions, the kind of trust and support she wanted, and her friend’s motivation for giving advice. The logistical conversation was about what to do next time a parenting issue arose.

从最基本的层面来说，对话分为两种——关系型对话和逻辑型对话；它们通常以对话的不同层面并存。关系型对话涵盖了我们彼此联系的质量、我们的情绪以及我们互动的方式。逻辑型对话则包括我们试图具体解决的问题以及我们达成的任何协议。在阿曼达的例子中，关系型对话是关于她对朋友介入的感受、她想要的信任和支持类型，以及她朋友提供建议的动机。逻辑型对话则是关于下次遇到育儿问题时应该怎么做。

Trying to resolve a logistical conversation without addressing underlying relational issues can be confusing and complicated. We’re discussing something concrete but keep getting snagged because there’s an unnamed subtext of emotions. If Amanda only discussed strategies about parenting practices without acknowledging her underlying concerns, the conversation would likely feel tense and edgy. (At times, we may choose to focus solely on the logistical level because there is insufficient trust, safety, or willingness to address the relational domain. In these cases, having internal clarity about the relational issues can bring more balance and centeredness to how we interact.)

试图在不解决潜在关系问题的情况下解决实际操作层面的对话，可能会令人困惑且复杂。我们讨论的是具体的事情，却总是陷入僵局，因为其中隐藏着难以言说的负面情绪。如果阿曼达只讨论育儿策略而不提及她内心深处的担忧，那么对话很可能会变得紧张而剑拔弩张。（有时，我们可能选择只关注实际操作层面，是因为彼此缺乏信任、安全感或意愿去处理关系层面的问题。在这种情况下，如果能更清晰地认识到关系问题，就能让我们的互动更加平衡和稳定。）

Similarly, mistaking a logistical issue for a relational one can lead to confusion. My mother was visiting recently, and I asked Evan if she would help make the guest bed. She promptly walked into the other room and began doing something else! Puzzled (and slightly annoyed), I went to help my mother make the bed myself. I later learned that she simply hadn’t heard me. Had I mistaken this logistical miss for something relational, I might have created painful interpretations or sparked an argument.

同样，把后勤问题误认为是人际关系问题也会导致误会。我母亲最近来访，我问埃文能不能帮忙铺客房的床。她立刻走进另一个房间，开始做别的事情！我感到困惑（也有些恼火），于是自己去帮我母亲铺床。后来我才知道，她根本没听到我的话。如果我把这种后勤上的小插曲误认为是人际关系问题，我可能会产生一些令人不快的误解，甚至引发争吵。

It’s generally helpful to try to deal with relational issues first. In complex situations, if we need to shift back and forth, being clear internally about which we are discussing can help us navigate the changes with more ease.

通常来说，先处理人际关系问题是有帮助的。在复杂的情况下，如果我们需要在两者之间来回切换，那么事先明确我们正在讨论的是哪一方面，可以帮助我们更轻松地应对这些变化。

As we’ve already seen, successful conversations also have two main phases: building mutual understanding and problem solving. There can be a lot of pressure to jump prematurely to solutions. Let’s just figure this out already! Whether we are dealing with a relational issue or a logistical one, the more understanding and trust, the easier it will be to create a lasting solution.

正如我们之前所见，成功的对话也包含两个主要阶段：建立相互理解和解决问题。人们常常会迫于压力过早地寻求解决方案。“咱们赶紧把问题解决掉吧！”无论我们处理的是人际关系问题还是实际操作问题，理解和信任越多，就越容易找到持久的解决方案。

We can track which phase of the conversation we are in and study when and how to make transitions. Before moving from mutual understanding to problem solving, we ensure that we’ve gathered enough information to understand one another. Usually, there is a sense of settling or renewed energy when it’s time to brainstorm solutions. Here are some questions to consider before problem solving:

我们可以追踪对话所处的阶段，并研究何时以及如何进行过渡。在从相互理解过渡到解决问题之前，我们会确保收集到足够的信息来相互理解。通常，当需要集思广益寻找解决方案时，会有一种平静下来或重新焕发活力的感觉。以下是一些在解决问题之前需要考虑的问题：

• Do you have all the information you need?

• 您是否已掌握所需的所有信息？

• Are both of us clear about the needs and objectives that are present?

• 我们双方是否都清楚当前的需求和目标？

• Is there an overall sense of both people feeling heard or understood?

• 双方是否都感到被倾听或被理解？

• Does the other person trust that you are genuinely interested in what will work for them?

• 对方是否相信你是真心关心什么对他们有效？

Here are some requests we can use in making this transition, which build on the “Requests That Move toward a Solution” in chapter 11 :

以下是一些我们可以用于实现这一转变的请求，这些请求建立在第 11 章“推动解决方案的请求”之上：

• “Do you have a sense that I understand what matters to you here? That I get your side of things?”

• “你觉得我理解你在这里最看重的是什么吗？我明白你的想法吗？”

• “Is there anything else you think would be important for us to consider?”

• “您认为还有其他什么重要的事情需要考虑吗？”

• “I’d like to find something that works for both of us. Can you sense that?”

• “我想找到一个对我们俩都合适的办法。你能感受到吗？”

Establishing trust is crucial. If we can show that we’re genuinely interested in collaborating, there will be more willingness and creativity to brainstorm. We build this kind of trust one step at a time, showing empathy, hearing and reflecting the other person’s feelings and concerns.

建立信任至关重要。如果我们能展现出真诚的合作意愿，就能激发更多合作的意愿和创造力，从而更好地进行头脑风暴。这种信任的建立需要循序渐进，展现同理心，倾听并回应对方的感受和顾虑。

PRACTICE : Tracking Process in Conversation

练习：跟踪对话中的过程

The next time you are trying to work something out, consider what kind of conversation you are having: Is this a purely logistical matter, or are there relational aspects? If both are present, see if you can sort out the relational before handling the logistical level. When moving between the two, try to be clear inside about what you are discussing.

下次当你试图解决某个问题时，思考一下你们正在进行的是哪种类型的对话：这仅仅是一个后勤问题，还是也涉及人际关系方面？如果两者都存在，试着先解决人际关系问题，然后再处理后勤问题。在两者之间切换时，尽量确保你内心清楚你们正在讨论的内容。

Focus on building as much understanding as possible before transitioning to problem solving. Bring particular attention to that shift from one phase to another, checking to ensure you are both ready to look at solutions.

在进入问题解决阶段之前，应尽可能多地加深彼此的理解。尤其要注意从一个阶段过渡到另一个阶段的过程，确保双方都已准备好探讨解决方案。

Who Has the Floor?

谁先发言？

Tracking what kind of conversation we are having and where we are in that conversation are broad, macro level skills. To flow with the dance of a dialogue, we also need to be able to track smaller movements. The most basic of these is tracking what I call the center of attention, or who has the floor.

追踪我们正在进行的对话类型以及对话进行到哪个阶段，是宏观层面的技能。为了顺畅地融入对话，我们还需要能够追踪更细微的动态。其中最基本的一点就是追踪我所谓的“注意力中心”，或者说谁在发言。

In every conversation there is a center of gravity that shifts back and forth between the interlocutors. This is broader than just who’s speaking or listening. It’s about sensing which person most needs to be heard in any given moment and bringing awareness to how we navigate those changes. If we are careless about shifting the center of attention, grabbing it back and forth between us, this can lead to mistrust, complexity, and a lack of empathy.

每一次对话中，焦点都会在对话双方之间来回转移。这不仅仅关乎谁在说话或倾听，更关乎感知在特定时刻谁最需要被倾听，以及我们如何应对这些变化。如果我们不注意转移注意力中心，随意地在彼此之间转移，就可能导致不信任、关系复杂化和缺乏同理心。

In conversation, the center of attention is the party on whom attention is focused in any given moment, the one who “has the floor.”

在谈话中，注意力的中心是当下注意力集中的那一方，也就是“拥有发言权”的那一方。

The general guideline is to listen first. Whenever possible, offer the center of attention to the other person. Shift the focus back to yourself after they feel heard and complete, when they’re more likely to have space to listen. 2

总的原则是先倾听。尽可能地将注意力集中在对方身上。等到对方感到被倾听、被理解之后，当他们更有可能静下心来倾听时，再将注意力转移到自己身上。

Using empathy, you can build understanding and check if the other person feels understood. Keep asking two basic questions: “Did I get it? Is there more?” You may need to offer several rounds of empathy before someone feels heard enough to give you the floor and listen. Check if the person is willing to shift the focus by making a request:

运用同理心，你可以增进理解，并确认对方是否感到被理解。反复询问两个基本问题：“我明白了吗？还有什么需要补充的吗？”你可能需要多次表达同理心，对方才会感到被充分倾听，愿意把话筒交给你。通过提出请求，确认对方是否愿意转换话题：

• “Is there anything else you’d like me to understand?”

• “还有什么你想让我明白的吗？”

• “I’d like to share a little about how I’m feeling. Do you have some space to listen?”

• “我想跟你分享一下我的感受。你现在有空听我说吗？”

Taking care with this transition can go a long way to building trust and repairing damage in difficult conversations.

谨慎处理这一过渡环节，对于建立信任和修复困难对话中造成的伤害大有裨益。

Principle: Whenever possible, check if the other person feels understood before moving on to a new topic or shifting the center of attention to your own experience.

原则：尽可能先确认对方是否理解自己的意思，然后再进入新的话题或将注意力转移到自己的经历上。

Of course, our patience and empathy have limits. If we lose the ability to listen, we can respectfully bring the center of attention back to ourselves. Remember, there are no hard rules in communication. Our job is to stay grounded and present, connected to our good intentions, and to respond to what’s happening as skillfully as possible. This is about using mindfulness to be aware of what’s happening in our own internal process. Are we still present? Are we able to stay connected to a genuine intention to understand? If not, what do we need to do to reconnect? Would shifting the center of attention help?

当然，我们的耐心和同理心都是有限度的。如果我们失去了倾听的能力，我们可以礼貌地将注意力重新集中到自己身上。记住，沟通中没有硬性规定。我们的任务是保持清醒和专注，与我们的善意保持联结，并尽可能巧妙地应对正在发生的事情。这需要我们运用正念来觉察自身内在的变化。我们是否依然专注？我们是否能够保持真诚的理解意愿？如果不能，我们需要做些什么来重新建立联结？转移注意力是否会有帮助？

We can lose the ability to listen for many reasons. There may be more information than we can follow, we may begin to feel full and lose the ability to track our own thoughts or feelings, or there may be something so pressing inside that we need to speak to get some relief before we can listen more. If we can’t listen, that’s what’s most important. If we can’t hear the other person, pretending to continue to listen won’t serve either of us.

我们失去倾听能力的原因有很多。可能是信息太多，我们无法全部理解；可能是感到心绪纷乱，无法追踪自己的想法或感受；也可能是内心有迫切的事情需要倾诉，以求得片刻的平静，之后才能继续倾听。如果我们无法倾听，这才是最重要的。如果我们听不到对方的声音，假装继续倾听对我们双方都没有好处。

In these instances, we need to interrupt—not because we don’t want to listen but rather because we do want to listen; we recognize that if we don’t interrupt we won’t be able to do so. The more heated the conversation, the more care needs to be taken when interrupting. To reduce the chances that the other person will take offense, we lead with our intention to connect. Here are a few examples of interrupting skillfully—notice how each begins with an affirmation of the connection:

在这种情况下，我们需要打断——不是因为我们不想听，而是因为我们想听；我们意识到，如果我们不打断，就无法真正倾听。谈话越激烈，打断时就越需要谨慎。为了减少对方感到被冒犯的可能性，我们首先要表明建立联系的意图。以下是一些巧妙打断的例子——请注意，每个例子都是以肯定彼此联系开始的：

• “I want to hear the rest of what you’re saying and I’m starting to lose track. Would it be all right if we paused so I can summarize what I’m hearing so far?”

• “我想听完你接下来的话，但我开始有点跟不上节奏了。我们能不能暂停一下，让我总结一下我目前听到的内容？”

• “I want you to continue, but I’m a bit confused. May I ask a question?”

• “我想让你继续，但我有点困惑。我可以问个问题吗？”

• “I want to keep listening, and I’m having trouble because there’s something I want to clarify. May I respond for a moment?”

• “我想继续听下去，但我遇到了一些问题，因为我想澄清一下。我可以插一句吗？”

In the first two examples, even though we are interrupting, the center of attention stays with the other person. In the third example, we propose shifting the center to ourselves by letting the other person know that we need to express something before we can continue listening.

在前两个例子中，即使我们打断了对方，注意力仍然集中在对方身上。在第三个例子中，我们建议将注意力转移到自己身上，让对方知道我们需要先表达一些想法才能继续倾听。

If we have the floor and the other person shifts the focus back to themselves, we have two options. We can follow their lead, letting go of our piece for a moment as we listen and offer them some understanding, or we can acknowledge the shift and request to keep the focus with us: “I hear that, and I’d like to finish what I was saying first. Could we take a few more minutes to complete this piece before moving on?”

如果我们发言，而对方又把话题转回到自己身上，我们有两种选择。我们可以顺应对方的思路，暂时放下自己的话，认真倾听并表示理解；或者我们可以承认对方的转移，并请求对方把注意力集中在我们身上：“我明白了，我想先把我刚才说的话说完。我们能不能再花几分钟时间把这部分说完再继续？”

PRACTICE : Tracking the Center of Attention

练习：追踪注意力中心

Who has the floor? Notice when the center of attention shifts from one person to another. What is the effect when that shift happens smoothly with consent or abruptly without consent? Practice shifting the focus consciously by checking if the other person feels complete, by making a request, or by interrupting skillfully if necessary.

谁在发言？注意观察注意力从一个人转移到另一个人的情况。如果这种转移是自然而然地、双方同意的，或者突然而未经同意的，会产生什么效果？练习有意识地转移注意力，例如询问对方是否感到被关注，提出要求，或者在必要时巧妙地打断对方。

Tracking Content

跟踪内容

Most conversations have more than one piece of content to discuss. In Amanda’s case, she’d had several interactions with her friend around parenting, including an email exchange, and needed to discuss the relational issues at play. Tracking all of that can be tricky. The course of a conversation often seems more like a labyrinth than a trail. It twists and turns, breaks off, and loops back on itself.

大多数对话都包含不止一个讨论内容。就阿曼达而言，她和朋友就育儿问题有过多次交流，包括电子邮件往来，她需要讨论其中涉及的关系问题。要理清所有这些内容并非易事。对话的走向往往更像是一个迷宫，而非一条清晰的路径。它曲折蜿蜒，时而中断，时而又回到原点。

If we’re unable to track these elements, we can find ourselves entangled in a mess. Tracking skills help us keep an eye on both the general trajectory of the conversation (what phase of dialogue are we in; who has the floor) as well as the actual content we’re examining. To do this, there are a few more tracking skills to flow with the dance of dialogue.

如果我们无法追踪这些要素，就会陷入混乱。追踪技巧能帮助我们把握对话的整体走向（我们处于对话的哪个阶段；谁在发言），以及我们正在分析的实际内容。为此，我们还需要掌握一些追踪技巧，才能更好地融入对话的节奏。

Just as someone may jump ahead to problem solving, many times people will introduce new topics before completing the one that’s already on the table. I call this splintering because it’s a way that conversations can fracture and break apart. We start talking about one thing that then diverges into two, then three or four, and soon we can’t even remember where we began.

就像有人会直接跳到解决问题上一样，很多时候人们会在还没讨论完当前话题之前就引入新的话题。我称之为“分裂”，因为它会让对话变得支离破碎。我们一开始讨论一件事，然后话题就分成两件，再分成三件甚至四件，很快我们就忘了最初是从哪里开始的。

When a conversation splinters, it gets complicated quickly. Issues rarely get resolved because there are too many things on the table at once without any of them being completed. If we get off topic or jump ahead, we need to be able to redirect the conversation—to gently guide it back on course. In challenging conversations, this requires extra care and sensitivity to minimize the chance that the other person will interpret our efforts as controlling or as a challenge to their autonomy.

当谈话偏离主题时，情况很快就会变得复杂。问题往往难以解决，因为同时讨论的事情太多，却没有一件得到解决。如果我们偏离主题或跳跃式地展开讨论，就需要能够重新引导谈话——温和地将其拉回正轨。在棘手的谈话中，这需要格外谨慎和敏感，以尽量避免对方将我们的努力解读为控制或对其自主权的挑战。

Splintering introduces new pieces of content before the current topic is complete.

分裂是指在当前主题完成之前引入新的内容。

Redirecting gently guides a conversation back to a chosen phase or topic.

巧妙地引导对话回到选定的阶段或主题。

Redirecting is similar to interrupting skillfully. First, we affirm or acknowledge what the other person has said so they don’t think we are dismissing their point. Then we state our desire to return to the previous topic. Here are a few examples of redirecting:

巧妙地转移话题类似于巧妙地打断对方。首先，我们肯定或认可对方所说的话，以免他们觉得我们忽略了他们的观点。然后，我们表明希望回到之前的话题。以下是一些转移话题的例子：

• “Thank you. I’m glad you mention that. Before we go there, I’d like to say one or two more things about…”

“谢谢。很高兴你提到这一点。在我们继续讨论之前，我还想再补充一两点……”

• “I appreciate you bringing that up. I want to discuss that in a minute, but first I’d like to touch on a few more things related to…”

• “感谢你提出这个问题。我稍后会讨论这个问题，但首先我想再谈谈与此相关的其他一些事情……”

• “Yes, that’s important. Can we finish talking about this first, and come back to that in a moment?”

• “是的，这很重要。我们能先把这件事说完，过一会儿再谈那个吗？”

The basic tool of reflecting before we respond to complete a cycle of communication helps prevent splintering. Instead of letting a topic hang in the air, we use empathic reflections to ensure that understanding is happening. When we apply this consistently in conversation, we build a sense of momentum and cooperation.

在回应之前进行反思，是完成沟通循环的基本工具，有助于防止沟通出现分歧。与其让话题悬而未决，不如运用同理心反思来确保彼此理解。当我们在对话中始终如一地运用这种方法时，就能建立起沟通的动力和合作氛围。

Just as we feel a somatic shift when we complete one cycle of communication, we often experience a felt change when we complete a larger topic or thread in conversation. There can be a sense of settling, an outbreath, or a spontaneous feeling of energy when we both recognize “Okay, that’s that! This is a good place to pause or to shift.” Even if an area isn’t completely resolved, we feel it when we arrive at a place of some shared understanding around an issue.

就像我们完成一次沟通循环后会感受到身体的变化一样，当我们结束一段较长的对话或讨论时，也常常会感受到一种变化。当我们都意识到“好了，就到此为止吧！现在是时候停下来或者转换话题了”，我们可能会感到一种平静、长舒一口气，或者涌起一股能量。即使某个问题没有完全解决，当我们就某个问题达成某种共识时，我们也能感受到这种变化。

PRACTICE : Tracking Content

实践：跟踪内容

When there’s more than one issue on the table, pay attention to which piece of content is being discussed. If the conversation splinters, jumping ahead or introducing a new thread in a way that doesn’t seem helpful, try redirecting. Affirm the importance of what’s been said and gently request to return to the previous issue.

当讨论涉及多个议题时，要注意当前讨论的是哪个议题。如果谈话偏离主题，跳到下一个话题或以看似无益的方式引入新的主题，请尝试引导谈话回到之前的议题。强调已讨论内容的重要性，并委婉地请求回到之前的议题。

As you discuss an issue, reflect before you respond in order to complete the cycle. Try to close each loop in a conversation, seeing if you’re on the same page before moving on to a new area.

在讨论问题时，为了完成讨论循环，请在回应前先思考。尽量在对话中完成每个环节，确保你们的理解一致后再进入下一个话题。

Say What You Mean: The Power of Being Succinct

言简意赅：简洁的力量

The last tracking skill is essential in creating understanding: being clear about what and how much we say. When we feel passionate about something, or if we don’t feel heard, we often repeat ourselves. Yet the more words we use, the less understanding we usually get. We all know what it’s like to be on the receiving end of a monologue, how easy it is to feel overloaded and lose the ability to digest what the other person is saying.

最后一项追踪技巧对于建立理解至关重要：清晰地表达我们所说的话以及表达的量。当我们对某事充满热情，或者感觉自己的声音没有被倾听时，我们常常会重复自己的话。然而，我们说的话越多，通常得到的理解就越少。我们都体会过被长篇大论轰炸的感觉，也知道那种感觉有多容易让人不堪重负，以至于无法理解对方的意思。

Principle: We have more clarity and power when we use fewer words with more sincerity. Speaking in short, succinct chunks makes it easier for others to understand us.

原则：言简意赅、真诚表达，能让我们更清晰、更有力量。言简意赅的说话方式，更容易让别人理解我们。

We can distinguish between two types of self-expression, chunking and flooding. Flooding is the experience of opening the gates and letting it all pour out! Our inner world doesn’t gather and collect before we share. We may speak for several minutes at a clip without taking a break or checking if the other person is still with us. Chunking is the ability to share information in manageable pieces, one or two at a time. This makes it easier for the other person to take things in and gives us the opportunity to check for understanding and complete the cycle.

我们可以区分两种自我表达方式：分块表达和倾泻式表达。倾泻式表达就像打开闸门，让所有情绪倾泻而出！我们的内心世界不会在分享之前积蓄能量。我们可能会一口气说上好几分钟，中间不休息，也不确认对方是否还在听。分块表达则是指将信息分成易于理解的小块，一次只说一两句。这样更容易让对方理解，也让我们有机会确认对方是否理解，从而完成整个表达过程。

Flooding is when we repeat ourselves, try to say everything all at once, or share more information than the other person can process at once.

信息过载是指我们重复自己的话，试图一次性说完所有事情，或者分享的信息量超过对方一次能够处理的信息量。

Chunking is when we speak one piece of content at a time, in small, manageable parts.

分块讲解是指我们一次只讲一个内容，将其分成小的、易于管理的部分。

We each have different ways of expressing ourselves. Some of us prefer to know what we want to say before we begin, others of us like to discover what we mean through the process of dialogue. In my Jewish family of origin, we often show our love by interrupting one another. In my Buddhist community, we tend to express care through speaking more slowly or pausing. Regardless of our personal style or culture, it’s helpful to be conscious of the amount we’re sharing and the other person’s capacity to take it in, so we can adjust accordingly.

我们每个人都有不同的表达方式。有些人喜欢在开口之前就想好要说什么，而有些人则喜欢在对话的过程中慢慢领悟自己的意思。在我原生的犹太家庭里，我们常常通过打断对方来表达爱意。在我的佛教社群里，我们倾向于通过放慢语速或停顿来表达关心。无论我们的个人风格或文化背景如何，意识到自己分享的信息量以及对方的接受能力都非常重要，这样我们才能做出相应的调整。

To be succinct rests upon the ability to discern what we want to communicate and on the capacity to be self-aware as we speak. The discernment aspect of speech is a training in understanding and organizing our inner world. This begins with deliberate practice and culminates in more spontaneous, clear communication. The act of verbal expression (literally to “push out” words) is a process whereby something gathers within and is then offered without. It is to comprehend our inner life, allowing thoughts and feelings to coalesce and form into discrete words and phrases. 3

简洁表达的关键在于辨别我们想要传达的信息，以及在说话时保持自我觉察的能力。辨别能力是理解和组织我们内心世界的一种训练。这始于刻意练习，最终达到更加自然、清晰的沟通。语言表达（字面意思是“说出”词语）是一个将内在的想法凝聚起来并表达出来的过程。它旨在理解我们的内心世界，让思想和情感凝聚成形，最终形成清晰的词语和短语。

Give yourself time to gather your thoughts, discern your feelings and needs, and formulate what it is you wish to express. Recall that we communicate to create understanding, to “make common” what is unique and personal. Instead of asking yourself, “What do I want to say?” you might consider, “What do I want the other person to understand?” The clearer you can be about what specifically you would like them to know or hear, the easier it will be to articulate in chunks. Eventually you will learn to do this in real time.

给自己一些时间整理思绪，辨别自己的感受和需求，并构思你想表达的内容。记住，我们沟通是为了增进理解，将独特而私人的事物“化为共识”。与其问自己“我想说什么？”，不如思考“我希望对方理解什么？”。你越清楚自己想让对方知道或听到什么，就越容易将想法分步骤地表达出来。最终，你将学会实时做到这一点。

To curtail the runaway train of words that can tumble out of our mouths, we use presence to track our own level of stimulation. This internal tracking can remind us to pause periodically and check with the other person to see where they’re at.

为了控制我们脱口而出的话语，我们需要运用临场感来追踪自身的兴奋程度。这种内在的追踪可以提醒我们定期停下来，询问对方的感受。

When we can chunk information and stay attuned to completing the cycle, we begin to enter the flow of dialogue. We speak, check, and build understanding. When listening, we can guide the conversation with that same rhythm, interrupting to stay connected, helping to ensure that the other person gets the understanding they want and need.

当我们能够将信息分块处理并保持专注，完成整个流程时，我们就进入了对话的流畅状态。我们发言、确认，并逐步加深理解。在倾听时，我们可以用同样的节奏引导对话，适时打断以保持联系，帮助对方获得他们想要和需要的理解。

There is a wonderful saying (often attributed to Albert Einstein) that gets at this skill: “Everything should be made as simple as possible—but not simpler.” Tracking the content of a conversation is about paring away what’s extraneous and attending to the essence of what’s being expressed by ourselves or another.

有一句很棒的格言（通常被认为是爱因斯坦说的）恰好概括了这种能力：“凡事都应该尽可能简单——但不能过于简单。” 把握对话内容的关键在于剔除无关信息，抓住我们自己或他人所表达的本质。

PRACTICE : Chunking Information

练习：信息分块

To increase the chances that you’ll get the understanding you seek, consider what it is you’d like the other person to understand before you speak. If there is more than one point you’d like to make, or more than one thing for which you’d like empathy, break it down into chunks. When you speak, track the amount of information you’re sharing. Stay grounded with presence, pausing periodically to check if the other person is still with you.

为了提高获得对方理解的几率，在开口之前，先想想你希望对方理解什么。如果你想表达多个观点，或者希望对方理解你的想法，那就把它们拆分成几个部分。说话时，注意控制你分享的信息量。保持专注，时不时停顿一下，看看对方是否还在认真听。

Entering the Flow of Dialogue

进入对话流程

The third step to better conversation is focusing on what matters. To do this, we need to train our attention to notice and identify the range of possibilities of what might matter in each moment. Which of the three basic positions in dialogue is needed: expressing clearly, receiving empathically, or returning to presence? Within the specifics of the conversation, is there an observation to clarify, a feeling to express or receive, a need to acknowledge, or a request to make? What’s needed to keep things on track? Do we need to redirect or interrupt so that we can stay connected? Or do we need to practice chunking, breaking something complex down into more basic components so that we can get to the heart of what matters?

提升对话质量的第三步是聚焦于重要事项。为此，我们需要训练自己的注意力，去发现并识别每个当下可能重要的各种可能性。对话中需要采取三种基本策略中的哪一种：清晰表达、同理心接收，还是回归当下？在具体的对话中，是否存在需要澄清的观察、需要表达或接收的感受、需要确认的需求，或是需要提出的请求？如何才能让对话保持正轨？我们需要引导或打断对方以保持沟通吗？或者我们需要练习分块处理，将复杂的问题分解成更基本的组成部分，从而直击问题的核心？

It can seem like a lot, but the practice boils down to one central question: What is most salient? In each moment, at each step of the way, what’s most important? If we’ve taken the time to train our attention to notice each of these components of conversation, what matters will be clear.

这看起来似乎很多，但这种做法归根结底可以归结为一个核心问题：什么最重要？在每个时刻，在每个步骤中，什么才是最重要的？如果我们花时间训练自己去注意对话中的每一个组成部分，那么真正重要的事就会变得清晰明了。

When Amanda spoke with her friend, she started by framing the situation more broadly and getting agreement to have the conversation. She made some observations, shared how she felt and why, and asked for understanding. Though she didn’t receive the empathy she had hoped for, having clarity about her needs helped her navigate the conversation. Her friend got a little defensive, but Amanda was able to address the relational side of things enough to make some logistical requests around the advice-giving in a respectful and caring way. Her friend understood and agreed to do her best to honor Amanda’s wishes.

阿曼达和朋友谈话时，她先从更广泛的角度描述了情况，并征得了对方的同意。她提出了一些看法，分享了自己的感受和原因，并请求对方理解。虽然她没有得到预期的同理心，但明确自己的需求帮助她更好地引导了谈话。她的朋友起初有些抵触，但阿曼达能够从人际关系的角度出发，以尊重和关怀的方式提出一些关于提供建议的具体要求。她的朋友理解了，并同意尽力满足阿曼达的意愿。

You don’t have to have it all figured out or even know what to say next. You just need to show up, come from curiosity and care, and focus on what matters. Trust what you notice and use the tools as a road map to proceed.

你不必事事都想清楚，甚至不必知道接下来该说什么。你只需要出现，怀着好奇和关怀，专注于真正重要的事情。相信你的观察，并将这些工具作为前进的路线图。

Try to relax and find the flow of dialogue, that rhythm of moving between basic presence, speaking, and listening in a fluid and natural way. Lead with presence and trust your genuine intention to understand. Let this be your guide. Continue to train your attention in the tools and practices I’ve shared, but don’t be afraid to let go and trust the principles behind them. Conversation is a living, dynamic activity. Trust the process and follow what’s alive in the moment.

试着放松，找到对话的节奏，在基本的临场感、说话和倾听之间流畅自然地转换。以临场感为先，相信你真诚的理解意图。让这种意图指引你。继续练习我分享的技巧和方法，但不要害怕放手，相信它们背后的原则。对话是一个鲜活的、动态的过程。相信这个过程，跟随当下鲜活的感受。

PRINCIPLES

原则

Stating how a conversation can contribute to both of us helps create buy-in and willingness.

说明对话如何对我们双方都有益处，有助于获得对方的认同和意愿。

Whenever possible, check if the other person feels understood before moving on to a new topic or shifting the center of attention to your own experience.

尽可能先确认对方是否理解自己的意思，然后再进入下一个话题或将注意力转移到自己的经历上。

We have more clarity and power when we use fewer words with more sincerity. Speaking in short, succinct chunks makes it easier for others to understand us.

当我们用更少的文字表达更真诚时，我们的表达会更清晰有力。简短精炼的语句更容易让别人理解我们。

KEY POINTS

要点

In conversation, notice how you can shift between speaking, listening, and resting in presence. Learn to track the different parts of a conversation:

在对话中，注意如何在说话、倾听和保持专注之间切换。学会追踪对话的不同阶段：

• Relational level: your connection, emotions, and how you’re getting along

• 关系层面：你们之间的联系、情感以及相处情况

• Logistical level: any concrete problem you’re trying to solve

• 后勤层面：你试图解决的任何具体问题

• The center of attention (who has the floor?)

• 关注的焦点（谁有发言权？）

• The specific topic or thread you are discussing

• 您正在讨论的具体主题或话题。

• The tendency to splinter (introducing new topics) and the possibility of redirecting (returning to complete the previous topic)

• 容易出现话题分裂（引入新话题）以及有可能重新回到之前的话题继续讨论（返回完成之前的话题）

QUESTION & ANSWER

问答

Q: I get tripped up by the speed of conversations. I find it difficult to switch between listening and trying to be aware of what I’m feeling.

问：我经常被谈话的语速搞得晕头转向。我很难在倾听和觉察自身感受之间切换。

It takes time to learn how to shift back and forth with the flow of conversation. It’s a little like learning to drive a manual transmission. At first there are so many things happening; every time you try to shift gears the car starts jerking back and forth! Over time your feet, hands, eyes—your whole mind and body—learn how to work together to operate the vehicle. It’s the same with these tools. If it feels overwhelming, just stick to the basics: lead with presence, come from curiosity and care, and focus on one thing that matters. From there, you can slowly add in the other components.

学习如何在对话中灵活转换需要时间。这有点像学习驾驶手动挡汽车。一开始会感觉很混乱；每次换挡，车子都会左右摇晃！但随着时间的推移，你的脚、手、眼睛——你的整个身心——会学会如何协同工作来操控车辆。使用这些工具也是如此。如果感觉不知所措，那就坚持基本原则：以专注的态度引导对话，保持好奇心和关怀，并专注于一件重要的事情。之后，你可以慢慢地添加其他要素。

Q: Sometimes it’s easier to pretend that I’m listening than to interrupt and deal with the awkwardness of telling the other person I’m not interested. What would you recommend?

问：有时候假装在听比打断别人说话、尴尬地告诉对方我不感兴趣要容易得多。您有什么建议？

We’re not always interested to listen, even with the people we love. The question is, what kind of relationships do you want in your life? Do you want them to be based on mutual trust and honesty or on some level of deceit, however minor? If someone were pretending to listen to you, would you rather they carry on the ruse or be real with you? Our time, attention, and energy are some of the most precious resources we have in life. Why waste them pretending to listen? Is it really worth the price to avoid the discomfort of interrupting?

我们并非总是乐于倾听，即使是对我们爱的人也是如此。问题是，你想要什么样的关系？你想要建立在互信和诚实之上的关系，还是建立在某种程度上的欺骗之上的关系？如果有人假装在听你说话，你宁愿他们继续装模作样，还是希望他们对你坦诚相待？我们的时间、注意力和精力都是人生中最宝贵的资源。为什么要浪费它们去假装倾听呢？为了避免打断别人的尴尬，真的值得付出这样的代价吗？

There’s a balance between being honest and showing care. If possible, discuss the dynamic when it’s not happening so that you’re not feeling impatient or frustrated while talking about something sensitive. Begin by framing the conversation with shared needs or appreciation. Talk about the quality of connection you’d like to experience and some ideas for how you can create that together. Or, if you’re no longer interested in spending time together, have the difficult conversation with as much tenderness and compassion as you can.

坦诚和关怀之间需要找到平衡。如果可能，在关系出现问题时就进行沟通，这样在谈论敏感话题时就不会感到不耐烦或沮丧。可以先从共同的需求或欣赏开始，以此作为谈话的切入点。谈谈你希望建立怎样的亲密关系，以及你们可以一起创造这种关系的一些想法。或者，如果你不再想和对方共度时光，那就尽可能温柔体贴地进行一次艰难的谈话。

Q: What about when interrupting is seen as disrespectful? I can do that with my American friends, but in other cultures it would be regarded very poorly if I interrupted someone.

问：如果打断别人说话会被视为不尊重人呢？我可以和我的美国朋友这样做，但在其他文化中，如果我打断别人说话，会被认为非常不礼貌。

Interrupting is intended to reestablish connection. If it has the opposite effect culturally, then it’s not the right tool. Focus on the principle: how you can work within the customs of the culture to reconnect. Is there a way of indirectly asking for what you need that they would understand?

打断的目的是为了重建联系。如果打断在文化上产生了相反的效果，那就说明这种方法不合适。重点在于：如何在文化习俗的框架内重建联系。有没有一种委婉的方式提出你的需求，对方又能理解呢？

Cross-cultural communication can be quite complex, especially since each of us often carries multiple layers of cultural conditioning. One simple way of thinking about it is that one always has three options. You can learn about and adapt to the other person’s culture, they can learn about and adapt to yours, or together you can have a metalevel conversation about your cultural differences and work together. In this latter option, once you’ve acknowledged the different expectations, you might risk breaking a norm in a way that minimizes any offense. Begin with a gentle apology, “Forgive me…” or “I’m so sorry to interrupt…” and then venture your request.

跨文化沟通可能相当复杂，尤其因为我们每个人都往往受到多种文化因素的影响。一个简单的理解方式是，我们通常有三种选择：你可以了解并适应对方的文化，对方可以了解并适应你的文化，或者你们可以就彼此的文化差异进行深入的探讨，并共同努力。在后一种情况下，一旦你意识到彼此的期望不同，你或许会冒着打破常规的风险，但要尽量避免冒犯。可以先温和地道歉，比如“对不起……”或“很抱歉打扰您……”，然后再提出你的请求。

Q: Listening is easy for me. I’ve been trying to speak up for myself more, but it’s challenging. I feel as if I have to be forceful or sharp to speak. Do you have any suggestions for finding a balance?

问：我很容易就能听懂别人说话。我一直想多表达自己的想法，但这对我来说很难。我感觉自己必须语气强硬或尖锐才能开口。您有什么建议可以帮助我找到平衡点吗？

We all have different conditioning; some find it easier to speak, some to listen, others find it easiest to be alone! It’s great that you’re noticing the pattern and working to expand your comfort zone so you can have as much flexibility as possible.

我们每个人的习惯都不同；有些人觉得说话更容易，有些人觉得倾听更容易，还有些人觉得独处更自在！你注意到这种规律并努力拓展自己的舒适区，从而拥有更大的灵活性，这真是太好了。

If we’re not used to expressing ourselves, it can feel awkward or strident at first. If we haven’t developed this capacity, it can take a lot of exertion to get to a baseline. I would encourage you to let things come to equilibrium on their own. Don’t be too concerned with how it sounds coming out. If you’re skilled at listening, you can clean up the mess if you express yourself in a way that’s brusque.

如果我们不习惯表达自己，一开始可能会觉得尴尬或刺耳。如果我们还没有培养出这种能力，就需要付出很多努力才能达到基本状态。我建议你顺其自然，不要太在意说出口的话听起来如何。如果你善于倾听，即使你的表达方式比较生硬，你也能弥补由此造成的混乱。

In relationships where there’s more trust, let the other person know this is something you’re working on, which reduces anxiety and gives you a forum to practice. Over time, the more you speak up, the more your nervous system will learn to trust that you know how to advocate for yourself. Once that trust is established internally, the pressure and urgency to speak will begin to fade and your words will flow with more ease.

在信任度较高的关系中，让对方知道你正在努力克服这个问题，可以减轻焦虑，并为你提供练习的机会。随着时间的推移，你越是勇于表达，你的神经系统就会逐渐信任你，相信你有能力维护自己的权益。一旦这种信任在内心建立起来，说话的压力和紧迫感就会开始消退，你的表达也会更加流畅自然。

# ↩

13

running the rapids

穿越激流

We don’t rise to meet our expectations;

we fall to our level of training.

—BRUCE LEE

我们不会超越自己的期望，而是会跌落到自己的训练水平。——李小龙

DIFFICULT, TENSE CONVERSATIONS are a normal part of life. Skillful communication doesn’t necessarily prevent those situations. Rather, it helps us handle difficult conversations when they arise and try again when we blow it.

艰难而紧张的对话是生活中的常态。娴熟的沟通技巧并不能完全避免这种情况的发生，但它能帮助我们应对棘手的对话，并在我们搞砸之后重新尝试。

The difference between ordinary conversations and challenging ones is a bit like the difference between canoeing on open water and running rapids. Both involve paddling with balance, but the stakes are much higher and the skills more demanding in white water.

普通对话和棘手对话之间的区别，有点像在开阔水域划独木舟和在激流中漂流之间的区别。两者都需要划桨保持平衡，但激流漂流的风险更高，对技巧的要求也更高。

Think of a terrible argument you had with someone or a time when you tangled with a coworker. Intense emotions, personal blind spots, and mistaken assumptions can make high-stakes conversations unproductive and even explosive. The boat capsizes, your gear gets soaked, and you wash up on shore somewhere downstream. I once smashed a chair in my grandmother’s living room, remember?

想想你和某人发生过的激烈争吵，或者你和同事发生冲突的经历。强烈的情绪、个人的盲点和错误的假设会让重要的对话变得毫无成效，甚至引发冲突。就像船翻了，你的装备被水浸透，然后你被冲到下游的某个地方。记得吗？我曾经在我奶奶家的客厅里砸坏过一把椅子。

Fortunately, you’ve already learned the tools you need to handle white water. In this chapter I’ll offer guidelines for how to prepare for a difficult conversation, practices to balance your nervous system, and some ideas for starting over when your words fall short of your intentions.

幸运的是，你已经掌握了应对棘手情况所需的技巧。在本章中，我将提供一些指导原则，帮助你为艰难的谈话做好准备，练习一些方法来平衡你的神经系统，以及当你的言辞未能达到预期效果时，如何重新开始。

Navigating Tough Conversations

如何应对棘手的对话

Preparing ahead of time for difficult conversations helps clarify what’s important, reduces reactivity, and increases the likelihood that we will be able to engage in a way that is in line with our intentions. Paramount to this is our internal preparation, which includes:

提前做好应对棘手对话的准备有助于明确重点，减少情绪反应，并提高我们以符合自身意愿的方式进行沟通的可能性。其中至关重要的是我们的内部准备，包括：

• Nourishing yourself

• 滋养自己

• Investigating what’s at stake

• 调查利害关系。

• Humanizing the other person

• 将对方人性化

Nourishing Yourself

滋养自己

Nourishing yourself before a difficult conversation can help you feel clear, balanced, and well resourced. This means getting some empathy for any pain, anger, or upset you may feel. Empathy can reduce reactivity and create more space to hear the other person. Find someone you trust and be explicit about the kind of support you’d like. Ask them to listen and reflect what they hear matters to you. Later, if it helps, you can move on to analyzing, brainstorming, or getting feedback with your friend.

在进行艰难的谈话之前，好好照顾自己，能让你感到头脑清醒、情绪平衡，并拥有充足的精力。这意味着要理解并体谅自己可能感受到的任何痛苦、愤怒或不安。同理心可以减少你的过激反应，让你有更多空间去倾听对方。找到一个你信任的人，明确地告诉他们你需要什么样的支持。请他们倾听，并反馈他们听到的内容对你来说是否重要。之后，如果这有帮助，你可以和朋友一起分析、集思广益或寻求反馈。

You can also use the self-empathy process in chapter 9 to sort through your emotions and identify your needs. (Sometimes this is the only option.) To find some space inside, try to connect with the more universal aspect of your needs. Can you sense them as complete and whole, as a natural part of your humanity, rather than as a something lacking or unfulfilled?

你也可以运用第九章中的自我同理心方法来梳理你的情绪，并识别你的需求。（有时这是唯一的选择。）为了找到内心的空间，试着与你需求中更普遍的层面建立联系。你能否感受到它们是完整而圆满的，是你人性中自然而然的一部分，而不是某种缺失或未得到满足的东西？

Investigating What’s at Stake

调查利害关系

Investigating what’s at stake helps us recognize the most important aspects of a complicated or intense situation and can inform our choices about how to proceed. Pay attention to any blame or judgments that you hold. Avoid indulging or bypassing them. Instead, regard your judgments as valuable information about your heart. If you’re high up on the ladder of inference, try to descend to more specific observations. Look deeper and ask, “What’s holding this story together? What feelings and needs are expressing themselves as judgments?”

探究利害关系有助于我们认清复杂或紧张局势中最关键的方面，并指导我们采取何种行动。注意你心中任何责备或评判。避免沉溺其中或忽略它们。相反，将你的评判视为了解你内心的宝贵信息。如果你已经陷入高层次的推断，试着深入观察，进行更具体的思考。深入探究，问问自己：“是什么将这个故事串联起来？哪些感受和需求以评判的形式表达出来？”

In this process of investigation, consider if there are other things at stake in the situation. Is your self-image involved, wanting to be seen in a certain way? What expectations, views, or beliefs do you have? Are you avoiding some feedback?

在调查过程中，思考一下这件事是否还牵涉到其他方面。你的自我形象是否受到影响，你是否希望别人以某种特定的方式看待你？你有哪些期望、观点或信念？你是否在逃避某些反馈？

When canoeing, if one comes to an unfamiliar set of rapids the best practice is to pull ashore to scout the river and determine if it’s safe. In challenging situations, consider if your goals are realistic. Do you have the capacity to have the conversation in the way you’d like? Does the other person? Is this the right time to have the conversation or even the right person with whom to talk? Are you asking someone to resolve something that they don’t have the power to do?

划独木舟时，如果遇到不熟悉的急流，最好的做法是靠岸观察河道，判断是否安全。在遇到棘手的情况时，要考虑你的目标是否现实。你有能力以你想要的方式进行沟通吗？对方也有这样的能力吗？现在是进行沟通的合适时机吗？或者说，你是在要求别人解决他们无力解决的问题吗？

To further determine how to approach things, investigate what parts of the conversation are relational and what parts are logistical. For example, my argument with my brother (when I smashed the chair) wasn’t really about the logistics of sharing house chores. I had a relational desire to be seen, to receive empathy for how desperate and alone I felt with my emotions. Had I recognized this, I would have understood that my brother wasn’t the right person to talk to at that time.

为了进一步确定处理问题的方式，需要探究对话中哪些部分是人际关系方面的，哪些部分是实际操作方面的。例如，我和哥哥的争吵（我砸了椅子）实际上并非关乎家务分工的问题。我当时渴望被理解，渴望得到同情，渴望有人能理解我当时的绝望和孤独。如果我当时意识到这一点，我就会明白，哥哥并不是我当时应该倾诉的对象。

The knowledge gleaned from investigating the stakes can inform your approach. What do you want from the conversation? Understanding? Resolution? Are you entering with a range of ideas that might work for both people? What specific requests can you make to move forward?

通过调查利害关系所获得的知识可以指导你采取策略。你希望从对话中获得什么？理解？解决问题？你是否提出了一系列可能对双方都有利的想法？为了推动对话向前发展，你可以提出哪些具体要求？

Humanizing the Other Person

将他人人性化

Humanizing the other person requires the humility and empathy to step outside of your own story and consider other perspectives. If you can put yourself in their shoes and imagine, even for a moment, what might be going on for them, it can have a profound effect on the conversation. 1 Whatever the situation, however confusing or harmful another’s actions, there is some internal logic behind their choices. Use the empathy map from chapter 9 to explore their feelings and needs. Decide how you want to show up in this conversation and focus on that, rather than on proving a point or being right.

要真正理解他人，需要谦逊和同理心，跳出自己的视角，考虑他人的想法。如果你能设身处地地为他人着想，哪怕只是一瞬间，也能对对话产生深远的影响。无论情况如何，无论他人的行为多么令人困惑或有害，他们的选择背后都有其内在逻辑。运用第九章的同理心地图来探索他们的感受和需求。决定你想在对话中如何表现自己，并专注于此，而不是试图证明自己的观点或证明自己是对的。

We want to be right, to feel vindicated, to win the argument. Try to look honestly at this. How often has being “right” ever helped to resolve relationships or problems? Would you rather win or find real resolution? Would you rather be right or be free?

我们都想证明自己是对的，想得到肯定，想赢得争论。但请诚实地审视一下这个问题。“正确”究竟有多少次真正帮助我们解决人际关系或问题？你更想赢还是寻求真正的解决方案？你更想证明自己是对的还是获得自由？

Entering a difficult conversation, one can get totally hung up on being right and fail to see that this is a strategy to meet some deeper need. If the other person concedes that you are right, does that truly give you what you seek? Do you want empathy or acknowledgment for how their actions affected you? Do you long to know that they care? To find peace or healing? To affect a change in their behavior?

进入一段艰难的对话时，人们很容易执着于证明自己是对的，却忽略了这其实是一种满足内心深处某种需求的策略。如果对方承认你是对的，这真的能满足你的渴望吗？你想要的是对方的同理心，还是对他们的行为如何影响你的认可？你渴望知道他们关心你吗？渴望获得平静或疗愈吗？渴望改变他们的行为吗？

When you get clear on what you’d like, reflect on the conditions that would bring about that result. What intentions are most likely to support resolution? How can you create a quality of connection sufficient to disentangle this situation?

当你明确自己想要什么之后，思考一下哪些条件能够促成这个结果。哪些意图最有可能促成问题的解决？你如何才能建立起足以化解这种局面的良好关系？

Be humble enough to consider in what ways, if any, you’ve contributed to the problem through action or omission. Nothing occurs in a vacuum; all relationships are cocreated. Can you be honest about that with yourself? Can you stretch your empathy further and try to see yourself and your actions through their eyes? Taking responsibility for your part frees your heart from defensiveness and invites the other person to reciprocate.

要谦逊地反思，你是否以某种方式（如果有的话）通过行动或不作为加剧了问题。世事无常，所有关系都是相互建构的。你能坦诚面对自己吗？你能进一步拓展你的同理心，尝试从对方的角度看待自己和自己的行为吗？承担起自己的责任，能让你放下防备，也能促使对方做出回应。

PRACTICE : Guidelines for Preparing

实践：准备指南

Explore as many of these suggestions as you find supportive.

尽可能多地采纳这些建议，选择对你有帮助的。

NOURISH YOURSELF : Seek the support of a trusted friend or take time for self-empathy. Explore your own feelings, needs, and values. Can you connect with the universal aspect of your needs to find some space inside?

滋养自己：寻求值得信赖的朋友的支持，或抽出时间进行自我关怀。探索自己的感受、需求和价值观。你能否与自身需求的普遍性层面建立联系，从而找到内心的空间？

INVESTIGATE : Identify what’s at stake for you:

调查：确定对你而言利害攸关的事情：

• Honor any judgments, blame, assumptions, or views you have. Translate them into observations, feelings, and needs.

• 尊重你所有的判断、指责、假设或观点。将它们转化为观察、感受和需求。

• Consider your own and the other person’s capacity to have the conversation. Is this the right time, the right person?

• 考虑一下你和对方进行对话的能力。现在是合适的时机吗？是合适的人选吗？

• What parts of the conversation are relational and what parts are logistical?

• 对话中哪些部分是人际关系方面的，哪些部分是后勤方面的？

• What requests do you have? Do you have creative solutions in mind?

• 您有什么要求？您是否有好的解决方案？

HUMANIZE THE OTHER : Step outside of your story and consider alternative perspectives:

设身处地为他人着想：跳出自己的固有思维模式，考虑其他视角：

• Stretch your imagination to empathize with the other person.

• 发挥你的想象力去理解对方。

• Consider your needs behind the desire to be right.

• 在想要证明自己正确的同时，也要考虑自身的需求。

• What intentions will be most supportive to have this conversation?

• 哪些意图最有利于进行这次对话？

Redirecting the River

改道河流

Conflict can send a cascade of physiological effects through our body. Our breathing changes, stress hormones release, and (if we lack skills to meet this swell of energy) our cognitive function alters.

冲突会引发一系列生理反应，波及我们的身体。呼吸会发生变化，压力激素会释放，而且（如果我们缺乏应对这种能量激增的能力）认知功能也会发生改变。

Every time we respond by blowing up, running away, or shutting down, we retrace and strengthen the neural networks for that behavior, like floodwaters carving a riverbed into a hillside. Inundated with stimuli, our sympathetic system prompts us to react with aggression, fear, or confusion, and we fall back on one of the four learned conflict behaviors (avoidance, confrontation, passivity, and/or passive aggression).

每当我们以爆发、逃避或封闭的方式回应时，我们都会重新审视并强化与这种行为相关的神经网络，就像洪水在山坡上冲刷出河床一样。当受到大量刺激时，我们的交感神经系统会促使我们以攻击性、恐惧或困惑来回应，于是我们退回到四种已习得的冲突行为之一（回避、对抗、被动和/或被动攻击）。

So how can we deal with the unhelpful physiological streams that we’ve fed within our nervous system? While it’s not possible to control our life circumstances, we can make educated choices about how to navigate the rapids.

那么，我们该如何应对神经系统中那些我们自己灌输的有害生理信号呢？虽然我们无法控制生活环境，但我们可以做出明智的选择，来应对人生中的种种挑战。

With mindful presence and skill, we can shift these patterns by carving new conduits into the hillside of our mind and body, creating different streams for that energy to follow. Progress is incremental, but every drop we redirect deepens the new riverbed, attracting more and more water to change the course of the river of consciousness.

凭借正念和技巧，我们可以改变这些模式，在身心的山坡上开辟新的通道，为能量创造不同的流向。进步是渐进的，但我们引导的每一滴水都会加深新的河床，吸引越来越多的水流，从而改变意识之河的流向。

If we don’t remember to be mindful in difficult conversations, we’re less likely to access our wisdom or good intentions, let alone any of the tools we’ve learned. And in tough situations, the main thing to be mindful of is our nervous system.

如果我们不注意在艰难的对话中保持觉察，我们就更难运用自身的智慧或善意，更遑论运用我们所学的任何技巧。而在困境中，最需要注意的是我们自身的神经系统。

Principle: Attending to our own reactivity, noticing the rise of activation and supporting the calm of deactivation, can help us make wiser choices about what to say and when.

原则：关注我们自身的反应，注意到情绪的激活和抑制的平静，可以帮助我们更明智地选择说什么以及何时说。

Working with our nervous system to handle reactivity and redirect the river has three stages that flow naturally from one to the next, just like breathing in and breathing out:

运用我们的神经系统来处理反应并引导情绪发展分为三个阶段，这三个阶段自然地从一个阶段过渡到下一个阶段，就像吸气和呼气一样：

• Recognizing activation

• 识别激活

• Riding the waves

• 乘风破浪

• Supporting deactivation

• 支持停用

Recognizing Activation

识别激活

Under ordinary circumstances, our body and mind naturally ebb and flow through activation and deactivation, arousal and settling, like waves rocking a boat. Breathing itself follows this rhythm. The elasticity of our nervous system, its resilience, is our ability to navigate this cycle with ease, tolerating the stress of sympathetic arousal, allowing the settling of parasympathetic deactivation, and returning to a baseline state of oriented awareness. This shows up as a relaxed alertness, an easy readiness with dynamic tone that can respond appropriately to changing circumstances. 2 When something unusual occurs in the environment—positive or negative—we enter a temporary state known as sympathetic activation or arousal . 3 For example, say you see an old friend unexpectedly: everything animates, your face flushes, you breathe in deeply and perk up. Or, if you hear a loud sound: your body tenses for a moment—“Am I in danger?” Your head turns toward the sound, trying to determine its origin and meaning.

在正常情况下，我们的身心会像波浪摇晃小船一样，自然地经历激活与抑制、兴奋与平静的起伏。呼吸本身也遵循着这种节奏。我们神经系统的弹性，或者说它的韧性，使我们能够轻松地驾驭这个循环，承受交感神经兴奋带来的压力，让副交感神经抑制平静下来，最终回归到一种定向意识的基线状态。这表现为一种放松的警觉，一种轻松的准备状态，以及一种动态的语调，能够对不断变化的环境做出恰当的反应。当环境中出现异常情况——无论是积极的还是消极的——我们都会进入一种被称为交感神经激活或兴奋的暂时状态。例如，假设你意外地见到一位老朋友：一切都变得生动起来，你的脸颊泛红，你深吸一口气，精神振奋。或者，如果你听到一声巨响：你的身体会瞬间紧张起来——“我遇到危险了吗？”你循声望去，试图确定声音的来源和含义。

The degree of arousal—how fast the flood rages—depends on the intensity of the stimulation (actual or perceived). In a healthy nervous system, when the cause for stimulation passes (we meet the challenge; a threat vanishes; we lose interest), aspects of the parasympathetic system come back online to “calm the waters” in our mind and body. The system comes to rest as the cycle of activation completes, and we paddle along on open water.

唤醒程度——也就是情绪爆发的速度——取决于刺激的强度（实际的或感知到的）。在健康的神经系统中，当刺激源消失（我们克服了挑战；威胁消失了；我们失去了兴趣）时，副交感神经系统的部分功能会重新激活，使我们的身心“平静下来”。随着激活周期的完成，系统恢复平静，我们便能像在开阔水域中划桨一样自由前行。

During interpersonal conflicts, the sympathetic arousal can snowball. Danger signals get amplified, and—to use a very precise, technical term—we lose it. Our ability to access higher cognitive function in the prefrontal cortex declines and we’re along for the ride, like losing our paddle in white water. We explode, flee, collapse, or check out. We may even enter a dissociative state as a form of self-protection. If the level of stimulation exceeds our capacity to respond, we freeze.

在人际冲突中，交感神经的过度激活会像滚雪球一样越滚越大。危险信号被放大，用一个非常精准的专业术语来说，我们会失去理智。我们运用前额叶皮层高级认知功能的能力下降，就像在激流中失去桨一样，任由情绪左右。我们会爆发、逃跑、崩溃或神游物外。我们甚至可能进入一种分离状态，作为一种自我保护机制。如果刺激强度超过了我们的反应能力，我们会僵住不动。

To redirect the river, we start by recognizing our nervous system activation patterns. With mindfulness we sense the changes of sympathetic arousal in real time. We get to know more intimately how activation feels both in the ordinary flow of life and in difficult situations. As we learn to catch its signals earlier we have more choices to handle it.

为了引导情绪的走向，我们首先要识别自身神经系统的激活模式。通过正念练习，我们可以实时感知交感神经兴奋的变化。我们能够更深入地了解这种激活状态在日常生活和困境中带来的影响。当我们学会更早地捕捉到这些信号时，我们就拥有了更多应对的选择。

PRACTICE : Monitoring Activation

实践：监测激活

This activity builds on the chapter 5 practice, “Just say ‘Oh!’ ”

这项活动建立在第 5 章的练习“只需说‘哦！’”之上。

As you move through your day, study what happens when your nervous system is activated. Whenever something of any significance occurs—you get some good news, you almost miss the train, someone cuts you off in traffic—notice the physiological effects in your body. Does your heart rate increase? Does your breathing change? Do you feel warmer? Try to maintain an attitude of curiosity and care rather than judgment. These are natural responses preparing you to meet a challenge or pursue a goal.

在日常生活中，留意一下神经系统被激活时的反应。每当发生一些重要的事情——比如收到好消息、差点错过火车、被人突然插队——都要留意身体的生理反应。心跳加快了吗？呼吸有变化吗？感觉身体发热了吗？试着保持好奇和关注的态度，而不是评判。这些都是自然的反应，它们在帮助你迎接挑战或追求目标。

Extend this exploration to the interpersonal sphere. Pay attention to even small shifts in your nervous system when something stimulating occurs (positive or negative). Look for changes in breathing, heart rate, perspiration, muscle tone, jaw tension, or bodily sensation.

将这种探索延伸到人际交往领域。当受到刺激（无论是积极的还是消极的）时，要注意神经系统哪怕最细微的变化。观察呼吸、心率、出汗、肌肉张力、下颌紧张或身体感觉的变化。

For advanced practice, see if you can observe these changes in others. Watch for shifts in posture, body language, color of skin, muscle tone, jaw tension, breathing, facial expression, tone of voice, pace, or volume.

为了进行更深入的练习，试着观察他人身上的这些变化。注意观察姿势、肢体语言、肤色、肌肉张力、下颌紧张程度、呼吸、面部表情、语调、语速或音量的变化。

Riding the Waves

乘风破浪

Feeling activated is completely natural. It’s ethically neutral and inherently benign. Mindfulness doesn’t aim to suppress activation or achieve some imaginary neutral state. The goal is to become aware and adept at riding life’s waves.

感到兴奋是完全自然的。它在伦理上是中立的，本质上也是良性的。正念的目的并非抑制这种兴奋感，也不是要达到某种虚构的中立状态。它的目标是觉察并能自如地驾驭人生中的起伏。

We each already know something about how to ride the waves and handle activation without reacting impulsively. Ever felt the inner agitation of wanting to say something but needing to wait for the right moment to interject? That’s an experience of sympathetic arousal. Anytime you relate to that internal pressure wisely—taking a breath, shifting your weight, making a mental note—you’re handling the activation. Doing it for even a split second can yield more choice about what to say and when.

我们每个人都已经懂得如何驾驭情绪波动，如何在不冲动行事的情况下应对情绪激活。你是否曾有过这样的感受：内心躁动不安，想要开口却又不得不等待合适的时机？这就是一种交感神经兴奋的体验。任何时候，当你明智地应对这种内在压力——比如深呼吸、调整重心、在心中默念——你就是在控制情绪激活。哪怕只是一瞬间，也能让你在选择说什么、何时说方面拥有更多选择。

In effect, awareness lends the ability to steer. It is through mindfulness that we can pause, track the reactivity in our body, and ride the wave rather than be capsized by it. Your ability to ride a wave of activation depends on your capacity to tolerate discomfort. In contemplative practice, every time you observe an itch, a knee or back pain, without immediately jerking, you are developing the inner balance to respond rather than react. If the wave is too big, step back, feel the energy in your body, and allow it to dissipate.

实际上，觉察赋予我们掌控局面的能力。通过正念，我们可以停下来，觉察身体的反应，并顺势而为，而不是被它所吞噬。你驾驭这种情绪波动的能力取决于你承受不适的能力。在冥想练习中，每次你觉察到瘙痒、膝盖或背部疼痛时，不要立即做出反应，你就是在培养一种内在的平衡，从而能够做出回应而不是反应。如果情绪波动太大，就退后一步，感受身体中的能量，让它消散。

The paired practices of pausing and grounding are especially helpful in difficult conversations. Pausing—anything from a micropause to a full breath to a break in the conversation—creates the space to recognize activation. Then, grounding in the body provides an anchor to steady your attention instead of losing your center.

暂停和扎根练习相结合，在棘手的对话中尤为有效。暂停——无论是短暂的停顿、深呼吸，还是对话中的短暂中断——都能创造空间，让你意识到自己正处于紧张状态。然后，扎根于身体则能为你提供一个锚点，稳定你的注意力，避免失去平衡。

The mindfulness exercises in chapter 3 are excellent ways to develop these skills. Use whichever reference point is most available. The feeling of gravity can stabilize your awareness. The upright sense of the centerline may lend clarity and attentiveness, while the rhythm of breathing can soothe intensity. If the activation is strong, shift attention to the periphery of your body, feeling the sensations in touch points such as your hands or feet, or orient to sounds or physical space. These reference points widen awareness, which can provide much needed relief in challenging moments.

第三章的正念练习是培养这些技能的绝佳方法。选择最容易获得的参照点。重力感可以稳定你的意识。保持身体中线的直立感有助于提升清晰度和专注力，而呼吸的节奏则可以舒缓紧张感。如果情绪过于强烈，可以将注意力转移到身体的边缘，感受手脚等接触点的感觉，或者留意声音或空间。这些参照点可以拓宽你的意识，在充满挑战的时刻为你提供急需的慰藉。

As you become more familiar with tracking activation in your body, you’ll start to notice when you approach your tolerance threshold—maybe a quickening of the breath, a scattering of the mental process, or an intimation of rising energy. The key here is to learn how to slow down the conversation or pause it altogether before you hit that threshold.

随着你越来越熟悉如何追踪身体的激活状态，你会开始注意到自己何时接近耐受阈值——也许是呼吸加快、思维变得混乱，或是能量开始上升。关键在于，你要学会如何在达到阈值之前放慢谈话节奏，甚至完全暂停谈话。

In white-water canoeing, building skill slowly is essential: start small in class 1 rapids, taking time to learn. When the waters are dangerous or the rapids beyond your skill level, pull ashore, unload the gear, and portage to safer waters.

在激流皮划艇运动中，循序渐进地提升技能至关重要：从一级激流开始，慢慢学习。当水流危险或激流超出你的技能水平时，应靠岸，卸下装备，然后搬运皮划艇前往更安全的水域。

The guidelines for difficult conversations are the same. Whenever possible, do your best to take things slowly so your system can adjust. This might mean breaking a difficult conversation into parts, having it via written correspondence, or asking someone else to be present. If the waters are too choppy—if the sympathetic arousal exceeds your capacity to handle it—the wisest response is to gracefully exit the conversation until you recover (see “Pausing” in chapter 3 ).

处理棘手对话的原则是一样的。尽可能放慢节奏，让你的大脑有时间适应。这可能意味着将棘手的对话分成几个部分，通过书面沟通，或者请其他人在场。如果情况过于紧张——如果情绪激动到你无法承受——最明智的做法是优雅地结束对话，直到你恢复过来（参见第三章“暂停”部分）。

PRACTICE : Riding the Waves of Activation

练习：驾驭激活的浪潮

When you notice sympathetic arousal in conversation, practice subtly pausing and grounding to track the activation. Use whatever method(s) you’ve found most helpful and authentic to pause: a deep breath, a gesture, or a verbal request. Choose a reference point for grounding awareness in your body: gravity, the centerline, breath, touch points in your hands or feet. Experiment with widening your attention by orienting to sounds or the space around you.

当你在谈话中察觉到情绪激动时，练习轻微地停顿和调整状态，以追踪这种情绪的激活。使用你觉得最有效、最自然的方式来停顿：深呼吸、做个手势或提出一个口头请求。选择一个身体上的参照点来调整意识：重力、身体中线、呼吸、手脚的接触点。尝试通过关注周围的声音或空间来扩展你的注意力。

Supporting Deactivation: Settling Downstream

支持停用：下游稳定

Riding the rapids of activation means being with the whole process, the up and the down. Just as we learn to recognize and attend to the arousal, we can also train ourselves to notice, feel, and support any calming. This can occur at many points, in small ways, during and after a conversation. If we’re skilled, we’re sensing it all along, continually enhancing these naturally occurring intervals in our nervous system.

驾驭情绪激荡意味着全程参与，包括情绪的起伏。正如我们学会识别并关注兴奋状态一样，我们也可以训练自己去觉察、感受并支持任何平静的迹象。这种平静可以在对话过程中和对话结束后以细微的方式在很多时刻发生。如果我们足够熟练，就能始终感知到它，并不断增强我们神经系统中这些自然发生的间歇。

How do we notice and take advantage of deactivation amid churning waters? This requires getting skilled at choosing where to place our attention. Focusing on irritants—such as judgments, negative feelings, or displeasing aspects of another’s words and actions—tends to fuel our reactivity, increasing nervous system activation. We can begin deactivating by attending to any calming, soothing, or simply less irritating aspects of experience. Developing our ability to notice how these feel in our body can bring our nervous system back into balance.

在纷乱的情绪中，我们如何觉察并利用那些可以暂时放下烦恼的事物呢？这需要我们学会如何选择关注点。专注于那些令人烦躁的事物——例如评判、负面情绪，或是他人言行中令人不快的部分——往往会加剧我们的反应，增强神经系统的活跃度。我们可以通过关注那些令人平静、舒缓或不那么烦躁的体验来开始放下烦恼。培养觉察这些感受的能力，可以帮助我们的神经系统恢复平衡。

This is different than our normal way of being. We are accustomed to attending to whatever is most interesting, most intense, even if it’s unpleasant. Like playing with a loose tooth, our mind is magnetically drawn to the point of greatest intensity.

这与我们通常的行事方式截然不同。我们习惯于关注那些最有趣、最刺激的事物，即便它们并不令人愉快。就像玩弄一颗松动的牙齿一样，我们的注意力会被最强烈的事物所吸引。

Deactivation occurs both literally and figuratively as an outbreath. Any shift in the state of our nervous system is reflected in the breath’s pace, depth, duration, or rhythm. We exhale. Muscle tension releases, our jaw slackens, our shoulders relax, our gaze softens, our breathing slows or deepens. We can train ourselves to notice these physiological signs. They’re occurring continually in small ways all day long.

神经系统的放松，无论是字面意义上的还是比喻意义上的，都如同呼气一般。我们神经系统状态的任何变化都会反映在呼吸的节奏、深度、持续时间和韵律上。我们呼气，肌肉紧张释放，下颌放松，肩膀舒展，目光柔和下来，呼吸减慢或加深。我们可以训练自己去觉察这些生理信号。它们以细微的方式，整天都在持续发生。

Activation is easy to spot; deactivation takes a more refined attention. It may not seem that interesting. It’s subtle. It’s what happens afterward, the outbreath, the cooldown. By deepening our sensitivity, we cultivate a taste for the soothing effects of the downward phase of the cycle.

激活状态很容易察觉；而消退状态则需要更细致的观察。它或许看起来并不那么引人注目，因为它很微妙。它体现在之后发生的事情，呼气，以及冷却的过程。通过加深我们的感知，我们就能体会到循环中下降阶段带来的舒缓效果。

This period, however brief, is the phase of healing, integration, and regeneration. To notice deactivation, we must become interested in the lull, a passing phase, or an “empty” moment. If we begin to inhabit these spaces, they calm our mind and body.

这段时期，无论多么短暂，都是疗愈、整合和再生的阶段。要觉察到这种低迷状态，我们必须关注平静期、过渡期或“空虚”时刻。如果我们开始体验这些状态，它们就能使我们的身心平静下来。

When we give mindful awareness to a feeling of ease or relaxation, it amplifies like a bell ringing, like the stroke of a bow resonating through the body of a cello. Taking small moments to feel the soothing quality of this deactivation nourishes us and strengthens resilience, in conversation and in life.

当我们用心感受轻松或放松的感觉时，这种感觉会像钟声一样放大，就像琴弓的拉弦声在琴身中回荡。花些时间感受这种平静舒缓的特质，能够滋养我们，增强我们在交谈和生活中的韧性。

As we develop the art of attention and being mindful of our nervous system, we grow skilled at transforming ordinary moments, the spaces between things, into sources of rest and comfort. Sometimes we notice the deactivation first, and that gives way to a moment of quiet. Other times we notice the moment and the settling comes after. Still other times we sense our need for deactivation and intentionally create the space to settle with a word, gesture, or action. When the gaps are missing, we learn to create them.

随着我们逐渐掌握专注的艺术，并觉察到自身的神经系统，我们便能熟练地将平凡的瞬间，那些事物之间的空隙，转化为休憩和舒适的源泉。有时，我们先注意到某种放松状态，随之而来的是片刻的宁静。有时，我们先注意到那一刻，平静随后到来。还有些时候，我们感受到放松的需求，便会刻意地用言语、手势或行动来创造平静的空间。当这些空隙缺失时，我们便学会创造它们。

In conversations, find the transitional space between exchanges or phrases, pauses or breaks in the flow of dialogue. Notice any settling when you complete a cycle of communication. In difficult conversations, even the smallest amount of agreement, acknowledgment, goodwill, or concession can provide a momentary raft in the flood of words and emotions. If those moments aren’t apparent, seek them out. Shift your attention to sound or the space in the room, or use your creativity to insert a pause or take a break.

在对话中，寻找交流或短语之间的过渡空间，也就是对话流程中的停顿或间歇。注意完成一个沟通循环后，对方情绪是否有所缓和。在棘手的对话中，哪怕是最微小的赞同、认可、善意或让步，都能在纷乱的言语和情绪洪流中提供一丝喘息之机。如果这些时刻并不明显，那就主动去寻找。你可以将注意力转移到周围的声音或房间的空间，或者发挥你的创造力，插入一个停顿或休息一下。

Shepherding a challenging dialogue to some resolution relies on our ability to find (or insert) these moments and to make the most of them. We can do this internally, with our own attention, and/or relationally, drawing out small successes by naming and appreciating them.

引导一场充满挑战的对话走向解决，关键在于我们能否发现（或促成）这些契机，并充分利用它们。我们可以通过内在的自我关注，以及/或者通过人际关系，指出并赞赏那些微小的成功，从而做到这一点。

PRACTICE : Attending to Deactivation

实践：处理停用事宜

Silent Practice

静默练习

Find a quiet place, close your eyes, and take a few minutes to settle your mind and body. Allow your attention to gather with the sensations of breathing in and breathing out. As you breathe in, can you notice any increase in energy or vitality in your body? That’s a subtle form of sympathetic activation. As you breathe out, can you notice any settling, calming, or soothing? That’s deactivation.

找个安静的地方，闭上眼睛，花几分钟时间让身心平静下来。将注意力集中在呼吸的吸气和呼气上。吸气时，你是否感觉到身体的能量或活力有所提升？这是一种微妙的交感神经激活。呼气时，你是否感觉到身体平静下来，或者感到舒缓放松？这就是交感神经系统的抑制。

Next, call to mind a slightly challenging conversation (past or future). Begin to feel the physiological effects of activation in your nervous system. Then put the issue aside, turning your attention back to a neutral reference point: gravity, the centerline, the breath, touch points in your hands or feet, sound, or space. As the arousal dissipates, pay close attention to any deactivation in your body: settling, loosening, calming, and any corollary changes in your breath.

接下来，回想一下一段略带挑战性的对话（过去或将来皆可）。开始感受神经系统被激活后的生理反应。然后，将这件事放在一边，把注意力重新集中到一个中性的参照点上：重力、身体中线、呼吸、手脚的接触点、声音或空间。随着兴奋感的消退，密切注意身体的任何放松状态：平静、放松、舒缓，以及呼吸的任何相应变化。

Interpersonal Practice

人际实践

During conversations, begin to look for and attend to any settling or ease you experience in the flow of dialogue. Try paying more attention to the outbreath. Look for natural pauses, breaks, or shifts. Feel any sensations of relaxation, release, ease, or settling in your body or breath.

在交谈中，留意对话过程中任何让你感到平静或轻松的时刻。试着更加关注呼气。寻找自然的停顿、间歇或转换。感受身体或呼吸中任何放松、释放、轻松或平静的感觉。
