As you practice with these stages—recognizing activation and riding the waves, noticing deactivation and allowing the churning waters to subside—you will learn to use them in other situations and in shorter periods of time. Simply notice what’s happening: the seeing itself creates the possibility for shifting the pattern.

当你练习这些阶段——识别激活状态并顺势而为，觉察消退状态并让翻腾的波涛平息——你将学会如何在其他情境中以及更短的时间内运用它们。只需觉察正在发生的事情：觉察本身就创造了改变模式的可能性。

Over time, your body will begin to feel the potential for a new way of relating. You may experience a different order of being in tense situations, as new messages flow through your nervous system: “Ah, maybe I don’t need to defend, attack, or try to disappear.” Slowly your capacity to deal with more difficult situations will grow. You can learn to trust your ability to hear someone else without losing yourself and to have a voice without trying to control or overpower another.

随着时间的推移，你的身体会逐渐感受到一种新的相处模式。在紧张的情境中，你可能会体验到一种不同的状态，因为你的神经系统会接收到新的信息：“啊，也许我不需要防御、攻击，或者试图消失。” 慢慢地，你应对更棘手情况的能力也会增强。你可以学会信任自己倾听他人而不迷失自我的能力，学会表达自己的想法而不试图控制或压制他人。

Rehearsing

排练

Another practical, effective way to prepare for a difficult conversation is to test things out with role-play. It can feel a little awkward if you’ve never done this before, but the potential benefits are great. Rehearsing a difficult conversation can teach you to stay balanced, yield insight, and support healing.

另一种应对棘手对话的实用有效方法是进行角色扮演练习。如果你以前从未这样做过，可能会感觉有点尴尬，但它的潜在益处是巨大的。演练棘手的对话可以帮助你保持冷静，获得洞察力，并有助于疗愈。

Use the role-play instructions below, concentrating on one or two tools. Being clear about what you’re practicing helps focus your attention and enhances learning. To lead with presence and support deactivation, make a point to take a break (“in character” or not) whenever you notice yourself feeling reactive. This is a powerful way to build confidence and expand your nervous system’s capacity for calming and grounding. To come from curiosity and care, reflect not only on what you say but also on how you say it. Recollect any helpful intentions you’ve identified, for example: being patient, building trust, or trying to collaborate.

按照以下角色扮演指导，专注于一到两种工具。明确练习内容有助于集中注意力，提升学习效果。为了更好地展现临在感并支持情绪放松，每当您感到情绪激动时，无论是否“保持角色扮演”状态，都要记得休息一下。这是一种建立自信、增强神经系统平静和稳定能力的有效方法。为了以好奇和关怀的态度表达，不仅要反思您说了什么，还要反思您是如何说的。回想一下您想到的任何有益意图，例如：保持耐心、建立信任或尝试合作。

PRACTICE : Rehearsing

练习：排练

To Practice on Your Own

自行练习

Find a quiet place and take a few minutes to settle your mind and body. Imagine having the conversation with a third person whom you respect in the room: a mentor, an elder, even a historical or religious figure. How would it feel to have the conversation in their presence? How might you speak or act differently? If they were in your shoes, what might they say?

找个安静的地方，花几分钟时间让身心平静下来。想象一下，房间里还有一位你尊敬的第三人：一位导师、一位长者，甚至是一位历史人物或宗教人物。在他们面前进行对话会是什么感觉？你的言行举止会有何不同？如果他们处在你的位置，他们会说什么？

To Practice with Someone Else

与他人一起练习

Invite a friend or colleague to role-play with you. Describe the situation and one or two things about how the other person might respond. Choose the tools you want to practice. To focus your learning, limit the role-play to five or six minutes. If you get charged up, take breaks to let your nervous system settle.

邀请一位朋友或同事与你进行角色扮演。描述一下情境，并设想对方可能会做出的一两点反应。选择你想练习的工具。为了集中学习，角色扮演的时间限制在五到六分钟。如果情绪激动，可以休息一下，让神经系统平静下来。

Afterward, reflect on what you learned and get feedback from your friend. Ask for specific observations about what you did that helped. Did they trust you? Did they hear blame or criticism at any point? What ideas or suggestions might they have? Role-playing a second time can be a helpful way to integrate feedback.

之后，反思你所学到的东西，并向朋友征求反馈意见。询问他们对你哪些做法有帮助的具体看法。他们是否信任你？他们是否在任何时候听到过责备或批评？他们有什么想法或建议？再次进行角色扮演可以帮助你更好地吸收反馈意见。

The Real Conversation

真正的对话

Do your best to start things off on the right foot. If you have choice over where and when to talk, try to set supportive initial conditions: time, place, who’s present. Consider how you can lay a foundation of curiosity and care prior to the conversation. For instance, a kind email or a few simple words can be a generous gesture that sets things in a good direction. Let the other person know that you’re looking forward to talking and working together to figure things out.

尽你所能，让一切有个好的开始。如果你可以选择谈话的地点和时间，尽量营造一个有利的初始条件：时间、地点、在场人员。想想如何在谈话前建立起好奇和关心的氛围。例如，一封友好的邮件或几句简单的问候就能起到很好的效果，让事情朝着好的方向发展。让对方知道你期待着与他们交谈，并共同努力解决问题。

How you open the conversation itself can be incredibly important. If you’ve initiated the dialogue, show respect for the other person by inquiring, “Is now still a good time?” This can create a sense of agreement and mutual respect from the start. Review the tools for framing ( chapter 12 ). As much as possible, work to present things in a balanced way and name any shared goals or objectives.

对话的开场方式至关重要。如果你主动发起对话，请以尊重对方的方式询问：“现在方便吗？”这样可以从一开始就建立起共识和相互尊重。回顾一下框架构建技巧（第12章）。尽可能以平衡的方式陈述事实，并明确双方的共同目标或目的。

Lead with presence. Pay particular attention to pausing and the pace of the conversation. Things tend to move quickly in heated dialogue; a lot of the work is about slowing down. The more you can find ways to naturally pause and deactivate, the easier it will be to stay clear, hear one another, and respond wisely. Taking time to reflect before you respond naturally downshifts the pace of a conversation. If you do it consistently, it can even create a rhythm of give-and-take that the other person picks up on and mimics, offering back their understanding for whatever you’ve shared.

以专注的态度引领对话。特别注意停顿和谈话的节奏。激烈的对话往往节奏很快；关键在于放慢速度。你越能自然地停顿和放松，就越容易保持思路清晰，倾听彼此，并做出明智的回应。在回应之前花点时间思考，自然就能放慢谈话的节奏。如果坚持这样做，甚至可以形成一种你来我往的节奏，对方会感知并模仿，从而对你分享的内容表达出他们的理解。

Next, come from curiosity and care and try genuinely to understand. This will show up in your body language, your tone of voice, and other nonverbal communication that supports an atmosphere of goodwill and collaboration. When appropriate, state your intention explicitly: “I’d really like to understand where you’re coming from…” or “I’m committed to figuring this out in a way that works for both of us.” Such statements can shift the entire tone of a conversation. If you lose the capacity to listen, interrupt skillfully and ask if they can hear you for a bit. (If neither of you are able to listen, put the conversation on hold for a while.)

接下来，要带着好奇心和关心，真诚地尝试理解。这会体现在你的肢体语言、语气和其他非语言沟通中，从而营造出友好合作的氛围。在适当的时候，明确表达你的意图，例如：“我真的很想了解你的想法……”或者“我致力于找到一个对我们双方都合适的解决方案。”这样的表述可以改变整个对话的基调。如果你无法集中注意力倾听，可以巧妙地打断对方，询问是否可以暂时听听你的想法。（如果双方都无法集中注意力，那就暂时搁置对话。）

Focus on what matters and keep your attention flexible. Instead of belaboring the story of “what happened,” listen for what matters to both of you. If you’re hearing demands, internally translate them into requests and respond in a way that honors the other person’s needs. When you can identify needs, you have more room to hear one another and think creatively about solutions.

专注于真正重要的事情，并保持灵活的注意力。与其纠缠于“发生了什么”，不如倾听对你们双方都重要的事情。如果听到的是要求，请在内心将其转化为请求，并以尊重对方需求的方式回应。当你们能够识别出彼此的需求时，就能更好地倾听对方，并创造性地思考解决方案。

As you weave these steps together, the fundamental orientation is to discern what matters most to each involved, to identify the needs and get them all out on the table, side by side. To do this requires being firmly rooted in a genuine intention to understand. Hold that angle of orientation in the conversation, applying some energy to counter the pull of less helpful, automatic reactions (protect, defend, judge, attack). Keep making that radical internal shift to curiosity and care. Demonstrating your care and commitment to collaboration usually helps the other person relax and engage more flexibly.

在将这些步骤串联起来的过程中，最根本的导向是辨别每位参与者最关心的事情，明确他们的需求，并将所有需求并列摆在桌面上。要做到这一点，需要始终怀着真诚的理解意愿。在对话中保持这种导向，并努力克服那些无益的、自动的反应（例如保护、辩护、评判、攻击）。不断进行这种根本性的内在转变，转向好奇和关怀。展现出你的关心和对合作的承诺，通常有助于对方放松下来，更灵活地参与其中。

Finally, if the situation is complex, consider breaking it down into multiple conversations on different days. Your initial pass might just focus on empathy, trying to listen and hear the other person. Next time, share your side and endeavor to build mutual understanding. For the final pass, explore strategies for moving forward.

最后，如果情况比较复杂，可以考虑分几天进行多次谈话。第一次谈话可以着重于同理心，尝试倾听对方。下次谈话时，再分享自己的观点，努力建立相互理解。最后一次谈话，则探讨下一步的行动策略。

The Do-Over

重来一次

Life is messy. In spite of our preparations, training, and best intentions, we all blow it from time to time. In the heat of the moment, an emotion or reaction gets the best of us. A wave of arousal rises, lifts us up, and we crash onto the rocks.

人生难免混乱。即便我们做好了准备，进行了训练，并且怀着美好的愿望，我们还是会时不时地犯错。在情绪激动的时候，某种情绪或反应会让我们失去理智。一股兴奋的浪潮涌起，将我们高高举起，然后我们却重重地摔在礁石上。

Where I grew up, we would play ball in the street on long summer days until daylight faded. Whenever there was a dispute about the game, if any kid called out “Do-over!” we’d stop arguing and redo the play. We can do something similar as adults.

在我长大的地方，夏日漫长的日子里，我们会在街上玩球，直到天黑。每当比赛中出现争执，只要哪个孩子喊“重来！”，我们就会停止争吵，重新开始。我们成年人也可以这样做。

A do-over is like pressing the reset button. We acknowledge where things went awry, restate our intentions, and ask the other person if they’d be gracious enough to let us try again. We can own our part for something as small as a single remark or as broad as an entire conversation. When we take responsibility for losing it, most people are happy to give us a second chance. It’s rarely too late to ask for a do-over.

重来一次就像按下重启键。我们承认哪里出了问题，重申我们的意图，并请求对方宽容地给我们一次机会。无论是一句小小的失言，还是整场对话，我们都可以承担自己的责任。当我们勇于承担责任时，大多数人都乐意给我们第二次机会。请求重来，永远不会太晚。

Depending on the situation, this may be as simple as making a request. Here are a few examples of how you might ask for a do-over during or after a conversation:

根据具体情况，这可能就像提出请求一样简单。以下是一些在对话中或对话后请求重来的例子：

• “That didn’t come out quite right. Can I try that again?”

• “刚才那句话好像不太对劲。我可以再试一次吗？”

• “I’m concerned some of the things I said aren’t helping. Can we start over?”

• “我担心我说的一些话可能没有起到帮助。我们能重新开始吗？”

• “Things didn’t really go the way I was hoping when we talked. Could we rewind and try having the conversation again?”

• “我们谈话的时候，事情并没有像我希望的那样发展。我们能不能倒回去，再谈一次？”

A dear friend and fellow NVC trainer spoke with me recently about a challenging email she’d received. In exploring how she might respond, I suggested offering an empathic reflection. She laughed and said, “That’s ‘Empathy 101’ but I didn’t even think of it!”

最近，一位挚友兼非暴力沟通（NVC）培训师跟我聊起她收到的一封棘手的邮件。在探讨她该如何回应时，我建议她尝试进行同理心反思。她笑着说：“这可是‘同理心入门’啊，我竟然没想到！”

When we’re triggered, we’re all beginners. In challenging situations, our most important and reliable skills are empathy and reflecting before we respond. These tools build trust, understanding, and connection. Be prepared to offer an empathic reflection more than once. This bears repeating: we might need to empathize three or four times before someone feels adequately understood around a single point. It can take great patience and fortitude to do this, but it can have dramatic effects. We balance empathy with a strong commitment to our own authenticity, shifting carefully between listening and expressing our side of things.

当我们情绪被触发时，我们都是新手。在充满挑战的情境中，我们最重要、最可靠的技能是同理心和在回应前进行反思。这些技巧能够建立信任、理解和联结。要做好准备，多次进行同理心反思。这一点值得重申：我们可能需要反复表达同理心三四次，才能让对方感到被充分理解。这需要极大的耐心和毅力，但却能产生显著的效果。我们要在同理心和坚持自身真实性之间找到平衡，谨慎地在倾听和表达自身观点之间切换。

Principle: When in conflict, if we aim to listen to the other person first it increases the chances that they will be willing to listen to us.

原则：当发生冲突时，如果我们首先尝试倾听对方的意见，就能增加对方愿意倾听我们意见的可能性。

I’ve mentioned my friend Sarah, whose mom passed away suddenly. During that same period, she had a difficult conversation with her brother. Having some flexibility in her life at that time, she had agreed to put personal projects on hold and move back to her hometown to look after their elderly father and sort through her mother’s belongings. As so often happens in such times, tensions began to surface and trust began to erode between Sarah and her brother.

我之前提到过我的朋友莎拉，她的母亲突然去世了。就在那段时间，她和哥哥进行了一次艰难的谈话。当时她的生活比较灵活，于是同意暂停个人计划，搬回老家照顾年迈的父亲，并整理母亲的遗物。就像这种时候经常发生的那样，莎拉和哥哥之间开始出现矛盾，信任也逐渐瓦解。

The conversation started off in a pretty rocky way. Sarah’s feelings of helplessness and anger showed up as blame and reactivity. Having taken some of my classes, she recognized what was happening, apologized, and stated her desire to work together. She listened, reflecting his feelings and needs. At one point, when things got tense, she asked if he would give her a minute to breathe and handle some of her feelings, to which he agreed.

谈话一开始并不顺利。莎拉感到无助和愤怒，并将这种情绪转化为指责和过激反应。由于她上过我的一些课，她意识到了问题所在，并向我道歉，表示希望与我合作。她认真倾听，并体谅我的感受和需求。谈话一度变得紧张，她请求我给她一点时间冷静一下，处理一下自己的情绪，我同意了。

That pause transformed the conversation. She considered her own needs and spoke openly and vulnerably about the issue, sharing that she wanted to clear up any conflict as soon as possible because it was important to her that they be able to trust each other during this difficult period. Her sincerity touched him; he wanted the same thing. As they hashed out the details, Sarah summarized the conversation and their agreements with regard to future conversations, which they knew might be challenging. They ended by appreciating each other, their good qualities, and how they’d stuck with a difficult interaction and come through to the other side.

那次停顿改变了谈话的走向。她开始考虑自己的需求，坦诚而脆弱地谈论这个问题，表示她想尽快消除任何冲突，因为对她来说，在这个艰难时期彼此信任至关重要。她的真诚打动了他；他也同样渴望如此。在他们讨论细节的过程中，莎拉总结了谈话内容以及他们就未来可能充满挑战的对话所达成的共识。最后，他们互相欣赏对方的优点，并赞扬他们如何坚持完成了这次艰难的沟通，最终渡过了难关。

We don’t need to be perfect, and it’s rarely too late to recover from a misstep. If we can slow down, remember the principles, and come from our genuine good intentions, deep transformation and understanding are possible.

我们无需追求完美，而且从错误中吸取教训也往往为时不晚。如果我们能够放慢脚步，牢记原则，并秉持真诚的善意，那么深刻的转变和理解就成为可能。

PRINCIPLES

原则

Attending to our own reactivity by noticing the rise of activation and supporting the calm of deactivation can help us make wiser choices about what to say and when.

关注我们自身的反应，注意情绪的激活状态，并支持情绪的平静消退，可以帮助我们更明智地选择说什么以及何时说。

When in conflict, if we aim to listen to the other person first it increases the chances that they will be willing to listen to us.

当发生冲突时，如果我们首先尝试倾听对方的意见，就能增加对方愿意倾听我们意见的可能性。

KEY POINTS

要点

Prepare for a difficult conversation by:

为应对棘手的谈话做好准备：

• Nourishing yourself with empathy or self-empathy

• 用同理心或自我同理心滋养自己

• Investigating what’s at stake

• 调查利害关系。

• Humanizing the other person with empathy

• 用同理心将他人人性化

• Rehearsing with a role-play

• 通过角色扮演进行排练

QUESTION & ANSWER

问答

Q: How do I talk to people who have a very different communication style than I do? They speak quickly, more loudly, and don’t have patience for pausing, expressing feelings, or processing.

问：我该如何与那些沟通方式与我截然不同的人交流？他们语速很快，声音很大，而且没有耐心停顿、表达感受或思考。

Mastering these skills means finding the balance between authenticity and flexibility. The kind of situation you’re describing includes an implicit request to relate more in their style. In fact, you may share many of the same needs: ease, flow, comfort, safety. The dance is about acknowledging your different preferences and finding a way to hear one another. Honor your own needs and be willing to let go and adjust.

掌握这些技巧意味着在真诚和灵活之间找到平衡。你描述的这种情况隐含着一种希望以对方的方式与你交流的愿望。事实上，你们可能有很多共同的需求：轻松、流畅、舒适和安全。关键在于承认彼此不同的偏好，并找到倾听对方的方式。尊重自己的需求，并愿意放手和调整。

Keep in mind that it’s common to stumble or take longer to express ourselves when learning these tools. Just like learning a language, it can be hard to keep up with the pace of things until we’re fluent. In the process, some will be more or less patient with us!

请记住，学习这些工具时，磕磕绊绊或表达速度变慢是很正常的。就像学习一门语言一样，在熟练掌握之前，我们很难跟上学习的节奏。在这个过程中，有些人会比有些人更有耐心，有些人则会比较缺乏耐心！

Q: How do you deal with situations where there is a power imbalance, such as if you’re talking to a supervisor or someone with more power than you?

问：当遇到权力不对等的情况时，例如与上级或比你权力更大的人交谈时，你会如何处理？

When we have less power than the other person, these tools become even more important. If we’re unwilling to use violence to meet our needs (which I hope is the case), dialogue is an essential tool. 4 Our capacity to create meaningful human connection becomes our leverage.

当我们处于弱势地位时，这些工具就显得尤为重要。如果我们不愿诉诸暴力来满足自身需求（我希望如此），对话便成为必不可少的工具。我们建立有意义的人际关系的能力，就成为了我们的筹码。

How you approach the conversation depends on the situation. One avenue is to align with them by identifying any shared goals or purposes. Another useful angle can be to help them see how meeting your needs will contribute to them, directly or indirectly. The last option is to share your own vulnerability and appeal to the person’s natural sense of care, compassion, or generosity. This may mean opening their eyes and heart to the human or moral cost of their current behavior or inspiring them to see the goodness and benefit of contributing in the way that you’d like.

如何展开对话取决于具体情况。一种方法是与对方建立联系，找出共同的目标或目的。另一种有效途径是帮助他们理解满足你的需求将如何直接或间接地对他们有所裨益。最后一种方法是坦诚地表达自己的脆弱，唤起对方与生俱来的关怀、同情或慷慨之心。这可能意味着让他们意识到自身行为所造成的道德或人性代价，或者启发他们看到以你所期望的方式做出贡献的益处和意义。

Q: What about when the other person doesn’t have these tools or when they just want to fight?

问：如果对方没有这些工具，或者他们只是想打架呢？

We cocreate our relationships; it takes two of us to dance. Regardless of whether or not the other person is familiar with these ideas and practices, you can shift the dialogue by how you relate. In martial arts, if you tense up or resist and your opponent is more skilled than you, they can easily take you down. Fighting back immediately puts you in the realm of struggle and power dominance—and right there you’ve already lost something important. You lose balance, your own equilibrium and responsiveness. But if your mind and body stay flexible and dynamic, you can redirect their energy and things can take a different course.

我们共同创造彼此的关系；共舞需要两个人。无论对方是否熟悉这些理念和实践，你都可以通过互动方式来转变对话走向。在武术中，如果你紧张或抗拒，而你的对手比你更熟练，他们很容易就能将你击败。反击会立刻让你陷入争夺和权力控制的境地——而就在那一刻，你已经失去了一些重要的东西。你失去了平衡，失去了自身的平衡感和反应能力。但如果你的身心保持灵活和动态，你就能重新引导能量，事情就会朝着不同的方向发展。

You can learn to respond to others without resisting or igniting more ire and to set limits and express yourself without tensing up or becoming rigid. When someone comes toward you with aggressive, blaming energy, if you respond with empathy, meeting their intensity in an authentic way, the game stops there. Try to see their behavior as a strategy to meet their needs. What do they want? If you can connect with that, you can start to defuse the situation.

你可以学会如何回应他人而不抗拒或激怒对方，如何设定界限并表达自己而不紧张或僵硬。当有人带着攻击性和指责的情绪接近你时，如果你以同理心回应，真诚地回应他们的情绪，那么冲突就到此为止了。试着把他们的行为看作是满足自身需求的一种策略。他们想要什么？如果你能理解这一点，就能开始缓和局面。

14

conclusion

结论

charting your course

规划你的路线

Words that come from the heart will enter the heart. But words that come from the tongue will not pass beyond the ears.

—ABŪ AL-NAJĪB SUHRAWARDĪ

发自内心的话语会进入内心，而口中说出的话语却无法传出耳朵。——阿布·纳吉布·苏赫拉瓦迪

WE ’ VE COVERED A lot of ground in these pages. It can seem like a lot, and in many ways it is. Communication is rich and complex, and we’ve explored many of its dimensions. The three steps to effective conversation provide a framework that encapsulates all we’ve explored and hopefully serves as a guide to say what you mean—to find your voice, speak your truth, and listen deeply. As this particular conversation comes to a close, I’d like to share a few reflections with you on how to integrate what you’ve learned and where to go from here.

我们已经探讨了很多内容。这看起来很多，在很多方面也确实如此。沟通既丰富又复杂，我们已经探索了它的许多维度。有效对话的三个步骤提供了一个框架，概括了我们所探讨的所有内容，并希望能指导你如何表达自己的想法——找到自己的声音，说出自己的真心话，并认真倾听。随着这次对话的结束，我想和大家分享一些关于如何整合所学知识以及未来发展方向的思考。

Turning the Ship

调转船头

Life is not two-dimensional. As I mentioned when we first started, you can no more learn to communicate solely from a book than you can learn to swim from an instruction manual. Eventually you have to get wet.

生活并非二维的。正如我一开始提到的，你不可能只靠一本书就学会沟通，就像你不可能只靠一本游泳说明书就学会游泳一样。最终，你必须下水实践。

Hopefully you’ve been experimenting with these tools all along, putting them into practice whenever possible and seeing what works. You’ve probably had some awkward moments or confusing exchanges along the way. You may have even had one or two spectacular crashes! Hopefully you’ve also had a few successes. When you’re learning something new, it doesn’t matter how many times you fall down. What matters is whether or not you get back up.

希望你一直以来都在尝试使用这些工具，尽可能地付诸实践，看看哪些有效。在此过程中，你可能遇到过一些尴尬的时刻或令人困惑的交流。你甚至可能经历过一两次惨痛的失败！希望你也取得了一些成功。学习新事物时，跌倒多少次并不重要，重要的是你是否能重新站起来。

I want to return to the image of turning a large ship at sea as a metaphor for shifting our communication habits. We each carry a massive amount of momentum that’s been barreling ahead in one direction, speaking and relating in set ways for decades. It only takes two things to turn that ship and alter its course: adjust the rudder and hold the angle. For a ship leaving from London headed to New York, a mere two-degree change in its course at the outset of the journey will alter the destination by 195 nautical miles—putting that ship in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, or Chesapeake Bay, Virginia, depending on whether it was an increase or decrease in angle!

我想再次用在海上调转巨轮的意象来比喻改变我们的沟通习惯。我们每个人都带着巨大的惯性，几十年来一直朝着一个方向疾驰，以固定的方式说话和交流。要改变这艘船的航向，只需要两件事：调整舵并保持角度。对于一艘从伦敦驶往纽约的船来说，航程开始时航向仅仅改变两度，就能使目的地改变195海里——根据角度是增加还是减少，这艘船可能会停泊在新罕布什尔州的朴茨茅斯，或者弗吉尼亚州的切萨皮克湾！

In that vein, I encourage you to take what you’ve learned from this book and hold fast to it. Identify what you’ve found most helpful and stick with it. Our brains learn through repetition. To make these tools second nature, to have them available at a moment’s notice, we need to keep practicing, using them in small ways every day.

因此，我鼓励你把从这本书中学到的知识牢记于心。找出对你最有帮助的部分，并坚持下去。我们的大脑通过重复来学习。为了让这些技巧成为你的第二天性，让你能够随时运用，我们需要不断练习，每天都以小的方式使用它们。

PRACTICE : Integration

实践：整合

Sit comfortably with your eyes closed and take some time to quiet your body and mind. If you like, let your awareness settle with the sensations of breathing in and breathing out.

舒适地坐下，闭上眼睛，花些时间让身心平静下来。如果愿意，可以感受一下呼吸的节奏，让注意力集中在吸气和呼气上。

Reflect on what you’ve absorbed over the course of reading this book. As you cast your mind back, over weeks or chapters, what stands out? What has been most useful for you? Allow your thoughts to roam freely as you consider these questions.

反思一下你在阅读本书过程中吸收了哪些内容。回想过去几周或几章的阅读过程，哪些内容让你印象深刻？哪些内容对你最有帮助？思考这些问题时，让你的思绪自由驰骋。

Finally, distill these reflections to their essence. What specific practices, tools, or principles would you like to integrate into your life?

最后，将这些思考提炼成其本质。你希望将哪些具体的做法、工具或原则融入到你的生活中？

Next Steps

后续步骤

There are many ways to continue your communication practice. You can review the principles and practices in this book, using them as an outline for further study and practice. Explore one practice each week, then review and move on to the next one.

有很多方法可以继续练习沟通技巧。你可以回顾本书中的原则和方法，并以此为框架进行更深入的学习和练习。每周练习一种方法，然后回顾总结，再进行下一种方法。

As I mentioned at the beginning, having a dedicated practice buddy is a huge support. If there isn’t someone in your life who shares your interest, check online forums, local groups, or classes to find an empathy buddy with whom you can speak regularly and practice these skills.

正如我开头提到的，拥有一个固定的练习伙伴会给你带来巨大的帮助。如果你生活中没有志同道合的人，可以去网上论坛、本地社群或课程中寻找一位同理心伙伴，定期与他/她交流并练习这些技巧。

Finally, seek out community. Communication is by definition relational, and the more opportunities we have to practice it in real time, the more we learn. I teach courses online and in person here in the United States. While there are, at present, very few people teaching mindful communication in the ways that I have shared with you, there are many retreats, classes, and trainings in Nonviolent Communication happening all over the world. I highly encourage you to attend such programs, which share many of the same principles and practices in this book. (See the “Further Resources” section for more.)

最后，要积极寻求社群。沟通的本质是关系性的，我们越有机会实时练习沟通，就能学到越多。我在美国开设线上和线下课程。虽然目前很少有人像我一样教授正念沟通，但世界各地有很多关于非暴力沟通的静修营、课程和培训。我强烈建议你参加这些项目，它们与本书中的许多原则和实践不谋而合。（更多信息请参见“更多资源”部分。）

Look Inside

查看详情

In closing, I want to emphasize one point. If it’s not already clear, mindful communication is not about what we say. It’s not in the words. All of the tools—the technical pointers, tips, and principles—are designed to help you create more understanding in yourself and with those around you. If we get too hung up on the language, too narrowly focused on “saying it right,” the magic of human connection gets lost.

最后，我想强调一点。如果这一点还不清楚的话，那么我要强调：用心沟通的关键不在于我们说了什么，也不在于措辞。所有工具——技术要点、技巧和原则——都是为了帮助你增进自己和他人的理解。如果我们过于执着于语言，过于狭隘地关注“如何正确表达”，那么人与人之间联结的魔力就会消失殆尽。

To communicate well, to create understanding through awareness, begins and ends with what is inside you. Listen to others with genuine openness and humility. Really try to understand. To say what you mean, look inside. What is true for you? How do you actually feel, in this moment? What do you need? What matters? What is it you would like this person to understand or know about your experience? How would you like to invite them to join you in the interdependent dance of giving and receiving called life?

良好的沟通，通过觉察建立理解，始于你的内心，也终于你的内心。以真诚的开放和谦逊倾听他人，真正尝试去理解。要想表达你的意思，首先要审视内心。对你而言，什么是真实的？此刻，你真实的感受是什么？你需要什么？什么才是最重要的？你希望对方理解或了解你经历的哪些方面？你希望如何邀请他们加入你，一同体验这名为“生命”的相互依存、给予与接受的舞蹈？

# ↩

summary of principles

# ↩

原则概述

The Three Steps to Effective Conversation

有效对话的三个步骤

1. Lead with presence.

1. 以身作则。

2. Come from curiosity and care.

2. 源于好奇心和关爱。

3. Focus on what matters.

3. 专注于重要的事情。

The First Foundation: Presence

第一基础：临在

Effective communication requires presence.

有效的沟通需要亲临现场。

• Given the complexity of communication, transformation occurs most readily through small shifts sustained over time.

• 鉴于沟通的复杂性，变革最容易通过长期持续的小幅变化来实现。

• Presence lays the ground for connection.

• 存在感为建立联系奠定了基础。

• Lead with presence; begin conversation with awareness, return to and strive to maintain that awareness, and be honest with oneself about what’s happening.

• 以专注的态度引领；以觉察力开始对话，回归并努力保持这种觉察力，并对自己正在发生的事情保持诚实。

• The more aware we are, the more choice we have.

• 我们越了解情况，就越有选择。

• Leading with presence includes mutuality, seeing the other person as an autonomous individual, and uncertainty, acknowledging and accepting the unknown, both of which create new possibilities in dialogue.

• 以临在感为主导包括相互尊重，将对方视为自主的个体，以及不确定性，承认并接受未知，这两点都能在对话中创造新的可能性。

The Second Foundation: Intention

第二基础：意图

Intention determines direction.

意图决定方向。

• Our intentions, views, and experiences reinforce each other: views determine intentions, intentions shape experiences, and experiences confirm our views. Shifting our view therefore can change our intentions and our experience.

我们的意图、观点和经验相互强化：观点决定意图，意图塑造经验，经验印证我们的观点。因此，改变我们的观点可以改变我们的意图和经验。

• Being aware of our habitual conflict styles allows us to transform the underlying beliefs and emotions that hold them in place and to make different choices.

• 意识到我们习惯性的冲突方式，可以让我们转变维持这些方式的潜在信念和情绪，并做出不同的选择。

• The less blame and criticism, the easier it is for others to hear us.

• 指责和批评越少，别人就越容易听我们说话。

• Everything we do, we do to meet a need.

• 我们所做的一切，都是为了满足某种需求。

• People are more likely to listen when they feel heard. To build understanding, reflect before you respond.

人们在感到被倾听时更愿意倾听。为了增进理解，请在回应前先思考。

The Third Foundation: Attention

第三基础：注意

Attention shapes experience.

注意力塑造体验。

• The more we are able to differentiate between our strategies and needs, the more clarity and choice we have.

• 我们越能区分我们的战略和需求，我们就越能清晰地了解情况并做出选择。

• The more we understand one another, the easier it is to find solutions that work for everyone. Therefore, establish as much mutual understanding as possible before problem solving.

• 我们越了解彼此，就越容易找到对大家都适用的解决方案。因此，在解决问题之前，尽可能建立相互理解。

• Being aware of our emotions supports our ability to choose consciously how we participate in a conversation.

• 了解自己的情绪有助于我们有意识地选择如何参与对话。

• The more we take responsibility for our feelings, connecting them to our own needs rather than to others’ actions, the easier it is for others to hear us.

• 我们越是对自己感受负责，并将感受与自身需求而非他人行为联系起来，别人就越容易理解我们。

• The more we hear others’ feelings as a reflection of their needs, the easier it is to understand them without hearing blame, needing to agree, or feeling responsible for their emotions.

• 我们越能将他人的感受视为他们需求的反映，就越容易理解他们，而不会感到被责备、需要同意或对他们的情绪负有责任。

• Having empathy for ourselves increases our capacity to listen to others, whether or not they have the space to listen to us.

• 对自己有同理心，就能提高我们倾听他人的能力，无论他们是否有时间倾听我们。

• Stating clearly what happened, without judgment or evaluation, makes it easier for someone to hear us and to work toward a solution.

• 清楚地陈述所发生的事情，不加评判或评价，会让别人更容易听我们说话，并努力找到解决方案。

• Translating judgments into observations, feelings, and needs can yield valuable information about what is and isn’t working and provide clues for how to move forward.

• 将判断转化为观察、感受和需求，可以产生有关哪些有效哪些无效的宝贵信息，并为如何前进提供线索。

• When giving feedback, be specific about what is and isn’t working and why, which makes it easier to learn.

• 提供反馈时，要具体说明哪些方面有效，哪些方面无效以及原因，这样更容易学习。

• The clearer we are about what we want and why, the more creative we can be about how to make it happen.

• 我们越清楚自己想要什么以及为什么想要，就越能创造性地实现它。

• Have ideas for strategies that meet as many needs as possible, which invites others to look for creative solutions.

• 提出能够满足尽可能多的需求的策略想法，从而鼓励其他人寻找创造性的解决方案。

• Stating how a conversation can contribute to both of us helps create buy-in and willingness.

• 说明对话如何对我们双方都有益处，有助于获得认同和意愿。

• Whenever possible, check if the other person feels understood before moving on to a new topic or shifting the center of attention to your own experience.

• 尽可能在进入新话题或将注意力转移到自己的经历之前，确认对方是否感到被理解。

• We have more clarity and power when we use fewer words with more sincerity. Speaking in short, succinct chunks makes it easier for others to understand us.

• 当我们用更少的词语表达更真诚时，我们的表达会更清晰有力。简短精炼的语句更容易让别人理解我们。

• Attending to our own reactivity, noticing the rise of activation and supporting the calm of deactivation, can help us make wiser choices about what to say and when.

• 关注我们自身的反应，注意到情绪的激动和激动，并支持情绪的平静和放松，可以帮助我们更明智地选择说什么以及何时说。

• When in conflict, if we aim to listen to the other person first it increases the chances that they will be willing to listen to us.

• 当发生冲突时，如果我们首先尝试倾听对方的意见，就能增加对方愿意倾听我们意见的可能性。

# ↩

useful communication phrases

# ↩

常用沟通短语

Requests for Dialogue

对话请求

• “Would you be willing to take some time to have a conversation with me about [topic]?”

• “您是否愿意抽出一些时间和我谈谈[话题]？”

• “Could we sit down together and look at what we both need to see if we can find a way to work this out?”

• “我们能不能坐下来一起看看我们双方的需求，看看能不能找到解决办法？”

Offering Empathy

展现同理心

• “Let me see if I’m understanding. What I’m getting is…?”

• “让我看看我理解得对不对。我理解的是……？”

• “I want to make sure I’m getting it. It sounds like…?”

“我想确认一下我理解对了。听起来好像是……？”

• “Here’s what I’m hearing…Is that right?”

• “我听到的是这样……是这样吗？”

Eliciting Information

获取信息

• “Tell me more.”

• “请告诉我更多。”

• “Anything else you’d like me to understand about this?”

“关于这件事，你还有什么想让我明白的吗？”

Requests for Empathy

请求同理心

• “What would be most helpful for me is just to be heard. Would you be willing to listen for a bit and tell me what you’re hearing?”

• “对我来说，最有帮助的就是有人倾听。您愿意听一会儿，然后告诉我您听到了什么吗？”

• “I just said a lot and I’m not sure it all came out the way I was intending. Could you tell me what you got from all that?”

• “我刚才说了很多，但我不确定我的意思表达得是否完全符合我的预期。你能告诉我你从中得到了什么吗？”

• “What I just said is really important to me. Would you be willing to tell me what you’re getting?”

• “我刚才说的话对我来说非常重要。您愿意告诉我您会得到什么吗？”

Inserting a Pause

插入停顿

• “I’d like a moment to gather my thoughts.”

• “我需要一点时间整理一下思绪。”

• “I’m not sure. Let me think about that.”

“我不太确定，让我想想。”

• “This sounds important. I’d like to give it some time.”

• “这听起来很重要。我想花点时间考虑一下。”

• “I’d like some time to take that in. Can we pause here for a moment?”

• “我需要一些时间来消化一下。我们能在这里暂停一下吗？”

Taking a Break: To Pause a Conversation

休息一下：暂停谈话

• “I’d really like to continue our conversation, and I’m not in the best frame of mind to do that right now. Can we take a break and come back to this…?”

• “我很想继续我们的谈话，但我现在状态不太好。我们能休息一下，过段时间再继续吗……？”

• “I’d really like to hear what you have to say, and I’m feeling a little overwhelmed, so I don’t think I’ll be able to listen well. Could we take a break and continue tomorrow?”

• “我很想听听你的想法，但我现在感觉有点不知所措，所以恐怕没法好好听。我们能不能休息一下，明天再继续？”

• “I’m committed to figuring this out together and don’t quite have the space to think clearly now. Can we put this on hold until…?”

• “我决心和你们一起想办法解决这个问题，但我现在实在没有精力冷静思考。我们能不能先把这件事搁置一下，等到……？”

• “I want to finish our conversation, and I don’t think anything else I say right now will be useful. Could we take a break until…”

“我想结束我们的谈话，我觉得我现在再说任何话都没用了。我们能不能休息一下，等到……”

• “I’d really like to hear what you have to say, but the way you’re saying it is making that very difficult. I wonder if you’d be willing to…

• “我很想听听你的想法，但你说话的方式让我很难听懂。不知道你是否愿意……”

…try explaining what’s happening for you in a different way?”

……试着用另一种方式解释一下你遇到的情况？

…take a break until we’ve both had a chance to reflect on this?”

……不如我们先休息一下，等我们俩都好好想想这件事？”

…let me have a moment to tell you what’s going on for me?”

……请允许我花一点时间跟你说说我的情况？

Interrupting

打断

• “Let me make sure I’m still with you…”

• “让我确认一下，我还在你身边……”

• “I want to make sure I’m getting everything you said. Can we pause for a moment so I can make sure I’m following it all?”

• “我想确认一下我是否完全理解了您说的所有内容。我们能暂停一下吗？这样我才能确保我都听懂了。”

• “I want to hear the rest of what you’re saying, and I’m starting to lose track. Can I summarize what I’m hearing so far?”

• “我想听完你接下来的话，但我快要听不清了。我可以总结一下我目前听到的内容吗？”

• “I want you to continue, but I’m a bit confused. May I ask a question?”

• “我想让你继续，但我有点困惑。我可以问个问题吗？”

• “I want to keep listening, and there’s something I want to clarify. May I respond for a moment?”

• “我想继续听下去，而且我还有一件事想澄清一下。我可以先回答一下吗？”

Redirecting

重定向

• “I’m glad you mention that. Before we go there, I’d like to say one or two more things about…”

“很高兴你提到这一点。在我们讨论这个问题之前，我还想再补充一两点……”

• “I appreciate you bringing that up. I want to discuss that in a minute, but first I’d like to touch on…”

• “感谢你提出这一点。我稍后会讨论这个问题，但首先我想谈谈……”

• “Yes, that’s important. Can we finish talking about this first, and come back to that in a moment?”

• “是的，这很重要。我们能先把这件事说完，过一会儿再谈那个吗？”

Hearing No

听证会否

• “I’m curious to know, why not? Could you share more?”

• “我很好奇，为什么不行？您能多分享一些吗？”

• “What’s leading you to say no? Do you have other ideas?”

• “是什么让你拒绝呢？你还有其他想法吗？”

• “Can we take some time to brainstorm ideas that could work for both of us?”

• “我们能否花点时间集思广益，想出一些对我们双方都有利的方案？”

• “What would you need to know, or what could I do, to make it possible for you to say yes?”

• “您需要知道什么，或者我可以做些什么，才能让您答应下来？”

Saying No

拒绝

• “I’d like to say yes, and here’s what’s getting in the way of that right now.”

• “我很想答应，但目前阻碍我的是以下几点。”

• “I’m hearing how important this is to you, and I’m not seeing how I can make it work given that I also have a need for…Could we explore some other options that might work for you?”

• “我知道这件事对您很重要，但我也不知道该如何兼顾……我们能否探讨一些其他可能适合您的方案？”

• “I can’t agree to that without a significant cost to myself in terms of…[other needs]. Would it work for you if we tried…instead?”

• “如果那样做，我会在其他方面付出很大的代价……（其他需求）。如果我们换一种方式，您觉得可以吗？”

Requests for Do-Overs

请求重做

• “That didn’t come out quite right. Can I try that again?”

• “刚才那句话好像不太对劲。我可以再试一次吗？”

• “I feel like we got off to the wrong start. Could we start over?”

• “我觉得我们一开始就走错了方向。我们能重新开始吗？”

• “I’m concerned some of the things I said aren’t helping. Would you be willing to let me try again?”

• “我担心我说的一些话可能没有起到帮助。您愿意让我再试一次吗？”

• “Things didn’t really go the way I was hoping when we talked. Could we try having the conversation again?

• “我们谈话后，事情并没有像我希望的那样发展。我们能再谈一次吗？”

Chapter 1: The Center of Our Lives

第一章：我们生活的中心

1. Human beings are social creatures that meet many needs interdependently. We evolved living in small bands, groups, and communities that engaged collaboratively to meet needs for shelter, food, and safety for the tribe. These origins express themselves in many ways. Within a human life, the need for social connection changes over time. It has been well established by researchers that people have a physiological need for connection (safe, healthy human touch and social engagement) beginning with birth and throughout the early years of life. The proper growth and development of the human brain and nervous system depend on continued contact and social engagement with healthy, well-regulated adults.

人类是社会性动物，需要相互依存地满足诸多需求。我们进化成以小型部落、群体和社群的形式生活，彼此协作，共同满足部落的住所、食物和安全等需求。这种起源以多种方式体现出来。在人的一生中，对社会联结的需求会随着时间而变化。研究人员已经充分证实，人类从出生起，在生命早期就存在生理上的联结需求（安全、健康的肢体接触和社会互动）。人类大脑和神经系统的正常生长发育依赖于与健康、情绪稳定的成年人持续的接触和社会互动。

As we grow, social connection becomes relevant for the development of empathy and emotional intelligence. During adolescence it manifests psychologically, in terms of identity formation and the development of ego strength, as well as biologically, for procreation. In adulthood, the need for social connection remains relevant in many of these ways (including spiritually, through the exploration of consciousness and subject-object duality) and simultaneously becomes a strategy to work together to meet other needs interdependently when desired or necessary.

随着成长，社会联系对于同理心和情商的发展至关重要。在青春期，它体现在心理层面，例如身份认同的形成和自我意识的增强；也体现在生理层面，例如繁衍后代。成年后，社会联系的需求在许多方面依然重要（包括精神层面，例如对意识和主客体二元性的探索），同时，它也成为一种策略，使我们能够在需要或想要的时候，与他人合作，相互依存地满足其他需求。

2. As social creatures, we are keenly attuned to what our nervous systems are telling us about other people and our surroundings. Social engagement can calm or activate the nervous system, depending on the circumstances and each individual’s internal state.

2. 作为社会性动物，我们对神经系统传递的关于他人和周围环境的信息非常敏感。社交活动可以使神经系统平静下来，也可以使其活跃起来，这取决于具体情况和每个人的内在状态。

3. Key aspects of our communication are animated by the vagal system (a constellation of nerves including the vagus and trigeminal nerves). The inner ear filters out extraneous sounds and attunes to the human voice; facial muscles express emotion and other signals; the larynx controls vocal tone and helps articulate verbal communication. These form part of the human social engagement system, a third branch of the autonomic nervous system, distinct in its evolutionary trajectory as well as in its neural architecture. These ideas were proposed by Stephen Porges in his groundbreaking work on polyvagal theory. See Stephen W. Porges, The Polyvagal Theory: Neurophysiological Foundations of Emotions, Attachment, Communication, and Self-Regulation (New York: W. W. Norton, 2011).

3. 我们沟通的关键方面由迷走神经系统（包括迷走神经和三叉神经在内的一组神经）驱动。内耳过滤掉无关的声音，并适应人声；面部肌肉表达情绪和其他信号；喉部控制音调，并帮助我们清晰地表达语言。这些构成了人类社会参与系统的一部分，该系统是自主神经系统的第三个分支，其进化轨迹和神经结构都独具特色。这些观点由斯蒂芬·波格斯在其开创性的多迷走神经理论著作中提出。参见斯蒂芬·W·波格斯，《多迷走神经理论：情绪、依恋、沟通和自我调节的神经生理学基础》（纽约：W·W·诺顿出版社，2011年）。

4. Stephen W. Porges, “Neuroception: A Subconscious System for Detecting Threats and Safety,” Zero to Three 24, no. 5 (May 2004): 19–24.

4. Stephen W. Porges，“神经感知：一种用于检测威胁和安全的潜意识系统”，《零至三岁》24，第 5 期（2004 年 5 月）：19-24。

5. Traditional understandings of the autonomic nervous system identify two main branches: the sympathetic branch, responsible for basic physiological homeostasis and the fight-or-flight mechanism, and the parasympathetic branch, responsible for the rest-and-digest functions of the body. Sympathetic activation (or “arousal”) marshals energy in the body for action, regulates functions such as the heartbeat, and prepares us to meet a threat. The parasympathetic branch slows the flow of that energy, helping us to relax, unwind, and downshift from the arousal of sympathetic activation. (Porges’ polyvagal theory introduced a third branch to the autonomic nervous system: social engagement, which is parasympathetic.)

5. 传统对自主神经系统的理解认为它包含两个主要分支：交感神经分支，负责维持基本的生理稳态和战斗或逃跑反应；以及副交感神经分支，负责身体的休息和消化功能。交感神经激活（或称“唤醒”）会调动体内的能量以进行行动，调节心跳等功能，并使我们做好应对威胁的准备。副交感神经分支则会减缓这种能量的流动，帮助我们放松、舒缓，并从交感神经激活带来的兴奋状态中恢复过来。（波格斯的迷走神经多支理论为自主神经系统引入了第三个分支：社交活动，它属于副交感神经支配。）

2. NVC encourages the practitioner to create connection sufficient to accomplish the task at hand. In personal and intimate relationships, connection can be an end in and of itself. In other arenas, connection is in service of some shared goal. We aim to create enough understanding and genuine connection to accomplish that goal. Failure to recognize this can lead to frustrating experiences in which the practitioner’s focus on connection is misattuned to their interlocutor. For example, if I ask for a glass of water, I’m not wanting empathy for my thirst!

2. 非暴力沟通鼓励实践者建立足以完成当前任务的联结。在个人和亲密关系中，联结本身就是目的。在其他领域，联结则服务于某个共同目标。我们的目标是建立足够的理解和真诚的联结来实现该目标。如果未能认识到这一点，可能会导致令人沮丧的经历，因为实践者对联结的关注与对话者的感受并不契合。例如，如果我要一杯水，我并不是想要对方体谅我的口渴！

Chapter 7: Getting Down to What Matters

第七章：直击要害

1. In the fields of mediation and conflict resolution, a similar distinction is made between positions (strategies) and interests or concerns (the needs at play).

1. 在调解和冲突解决领域，立场（策略）和利益或关注点（需求）之间也存在类似的区分。

2. To say that all needs are universal is a complex terrain philosophically. Are some needs—such as authenticity—more culturally specific? Some theorists, including Ken Wilber, have proposed a development model in which various needs become salient at different stages of development. The perspective I am presenting here, which is at the heart of Rosenberg’s method, is a pragmatic one: needs are more universal than strategies, and looking to the underlying motivations of our actions connects us with one another.

2. 认为所有需求都是普遍存在的，这在哲学上是一个复杂的问题。某些需求——例如真实性——是否更具文化特殊性？一些理论家，包括肯·威尔伯，提出了一种发展模型，其中各种需求在不同的发展阶段会变得突出。我在此提出的观点，也是罗森伯格方法的核心，是一种实用主义的观点：需求比策略更具普遍性，探究我们行为的深层动机能够将我们彼此联系起来。

3. Chilean economist and social theorist Manfred Max-Neef identifies nine basic categories of needs: subsistence, protection (safety), affection, understanding, participation, leisure, creation, identity, and freedom. See Manfred A. Max-Neef, Human Scale Development: Conception, Application and Further Reflections (New York and London: The Apex Press, 1991).

3. 智利经济学家和社会理论家曼弗雷德·马克斯-尼夫提出了九种基本需求：生存、保护（安全）、情感、理解、参与、休闲、创造、身份和自由。参见曼弗雷德·A·马克斯-尼夫，《人类尺度发展：概念、应用及进一步思考》（纽约和伦敦：Apex出版社，1991年）。

2. Some psychological systems draw distinctions between primary affect (bodily, not necessarily conscious), feelings (conscious), and emotions (more socially constructed and including stories).

2. 一些心理学体系区分了基本情感（身体上的，不一定是有意识的）、感觉（有意识的）和情绪（更多是社会建构的，包括故事）。

3. The nuances of classical Western philosophy in this area are complex, and the modern notion of emotion does not map neatly onto earlier concepts. The early Greeks (Plato in particular) had a system of thought in which reason, will, and desire worked together, with reason as the guiding principle. The Stoics suggested that “passions” on their own were dangerous and needed to be structured, organized, and understood by reason. These ideas were reinterpreted by early Christians and the church fathers (second and third century A.D.), who cast the passions as manifestations of Satan and evil forces, which in turn have informed the modern view of emotions as being dangerous and irrational. Personal communication, Rabbi Jack Bemporad, December 4, 2017. For more, see Jan Plamper, The History of Emotions (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2012); Peter Goldie, ed., The Oxford Handbook of Philosophy of Emotion (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2012); Anthony Damasio, Descartes’ Error: Emotion, Reason, and the Human Brain (New York: Penguin, 1994); and Kashtan, Spinning Threads of Radical Aliveness, 87–89.

3. 古典西方哲学在这一领域的细微差别十分复杂，现代情感概念与早期概念并非完全对应。早期希腊人（尤其是柏拉图）的思想体系中，理性、意志和欲望相互协作，理性是指导原则。斯多葛学派认为，“激情”本身是危险的，需要用理性来构建、组织和理解。这些观点被早期基督教徒和教父们（公元二至三世纪）重新诠释，他们将激情视为撒旦和邪恶力量的体现，这反过来又影响了现代人对情感的危险和非理性的看法。私人交流，杰克·本波拉德拉比，2017年12月4日。更多信息，请参阅简·普兰珀，《情感史》（牛津：牛津大学出版社，2012年）；彼得·戈尔迪编，《牛津情感哲学手册》（牛津：牛津大学出版社，2012年）。 Anthony Damasio，《笛卡尔的错误：情感、理性与人脑》（纽约：企鹅出版社，1994 年）；以及 Kashtan，《编织激进活力的线索》，第 87-89 页。

4. “Emotions can be explained as specialized states, shaped by natural selection, that increase fitness in specific situations. The physiological, psychological, and behavioral characteristics of a specific emotion can be analyzed as possible design features that increase the ability to cope with the threats and opportunities present in the corresponding situation.” See Randolph M. Ness, “Evolutionary Explanations of Emotions,” Human Nature 1, no.3 (1990): 261–289.

4. “情绪可以解释为由自然选择塑造的特殊状态，能够提高特定情境下的适应性。特定情绪的生理、心理和行为特征可以分析为可能的设计特征，这些特征增强了应对相应情境中存在的威胁和机遇的能力。”参见 Randolph M. Ness，“情绪的进化解释”，《人类本性》1，第3期（1990）：261-289。

5. Paul Eckman suggests that emotions evolved as a way for humans to solve dangerous problems quickly, without reliance on the relatively slower process of thinking. See Self Comes to Mind: Constructing the Conscious Brain (New York: Vintage, 2012).

# ↩

glossary

# ↩

词汇表

Activation: The stimulation of energy in the body to carry out an action in response to a desired goal or perceived threat in the environment; sympathetic arousal, including engagement of the fight-or-flight mechanisms.

激活：身体能量受到刺激，以执行对期望目标或感知到的环境威胁的反应；交感神经兴奋，包括启动战斗或逃跑机制。

Affect labeling: The cognitive process of naming emotions.

情感标签：命名情绪的认知过程。

Anchor: A reference point to which we return to strengthen mindful presence.

锚点：一个参照点，我们可以回到这个参照点来加强正念觉察。

Center of attention: The party on whom attention is focused in a conversation in any given moment; the one who “has the floor.”

关注中心：在谈话中，在任何特定时刻，注意力集中到的一方；“拥有发言权”的人。

Centerline: The midline of the torso, halfway between front and back, in the middle of the left and right sides of the body.

中心线：躯干的中线，位于前后方向的中间，身体左右两侧的中间位置。

Choice point: A moment of awareness in which we decide whether to speak or listen.

选择点：一个意识觉醒的时刻，在这个时刻，我们会决定是说话还是倾听。

Chunking: Speaking one piece of content at a time, in small, manageable parts.

分块讲解：一次只讲一个内容，分成小的、易于管理的部分。

Communication: A process of interaction or exchange creating understanding.

沟通：一种通过互动或交流产生理解的过程。

Connection: See social connection.

关系：参见社交关系。

Connection request: A question intended to confirm that message sent was message received, foster mutual understanding, and water the seeds of trust and goodwill. Connection requests also are used to determine if there is sufficient trust and understanding to move toward exploring solutions.

连接请求：旨在确认已发送信息已被接收，促进相互理解，并培育信任和善意的种子。连接请求还用于判断是否存在足够的信任和理解，以便继续探讨解决方案。

Deactivation: The settling of energy in the body in response to completing an action, meeting a need, or resolving a perceived threat; parasympathetic settling, or releasing of sympathetic arousal.

去激活：指身体能量在完成一项行动、满足一种需求或解决一种感知到的威胁后趋于稳定；副交感神经稳定，或交感神经兴奋的释放。

Emotional contagion: A phenomenon of having one person’s emotions stimulate similar emotions in others.

情绪传染：指一个人的情绪能够激发其他人产生类似情绪的现象。

Emotions: Multifaceted, affective experiences, felt in the body.

情绪：多方面的、情感上的体验，在身体中可以感受到。

Empathic distress: An emotional state characterized by the inability to tolerate the perceived pain of another.

同理心痛苦：一种无法忍受他人所感受到的痛苦的情绪状态。

Empathy: The capacity to understand or feel what another person is experiencing from their point of view.

同理心：能够从他人的角度理解或感受他人的经历的能力。

Empathy spectrum: The range of access to feeling empathy in human beings.

同理心谱系：人类感受同理心的程度范围。

Feelings: See emotions.

感受：查看情绪。

Flooding: Repeating ourselves, trying to say everything all at once, or sharing more information than the other person can process.

信息过载：重复自己，试图一次性说完所有事情，或者分享超出对方处理能力的信息。

Framing: Summarizing an issue or area of discussion in a broad and neutral way, often in terms of any shared needs, goals, or values.

框架：以广泛和中立的方式概括某个问题或讨论领域，通常从共同的需求、目标或价值观的角度出发。

Intention: The motivation or inner quality of heart that drives our words and actions.

意图：驱动我们言行的内在动机或品质。

LGBTQI: Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer (or questioning), and intersex.

LGBTQI：女同性恋、男同性恋、双性恋、跨性别者、酷儿（或性取向待定者）和双性人。

Logistical conversation: The aspects of a conversation that attempt to solve a problem concretely, including any agreements made.

逻辑性对话：对话中试图具体解决问题的各个方面，包括达成的任何协议。

Mindfulness: Being aware of what’s happening in the present moment in a balanced and nonreactive way. See also presence.

正念：以平衡且不带反应的方式觉察当下正在发生的事情。另见“临在”。

Needs: Core values that motivate our actions. They’re what matter most, the fundamental, root reasons for why we want what we want.

需求：驱动我们行动的核心价值观。它们是最重要的，是我们想要某些东西的根本原因。

Observation: A concrete, specific, and neutral statement of an event, of what we see or hear in our environment, distinct from evaluation or interpretation.

观察：对我们所处环境中所见所闻的事件进行具体、明确、中立的陈述，与评价或解释不同。

Orienting: Connecting to one’s environment through the senses.

定向：通过感官与周围环境建立联系。

Presence: Embodied awareness of our direct sensory, mental, and emotional experience. See also mindfulness.

临在：对我们直接的感官、心理和情感体验的具身觉察。另见正念。

Privilege: Special rights or advantages available to a particular person or group of people based on a certain attribute, status, or membership in that group. Privilege grants preferential treatment and/or enables access to resources due to legal and/or social norms, and it exists independently of any particular action or inaction by those who possess it. It often exists independently of any awareness on the part of the privileged individual or group of the presence of any disparity, the benefits to the privileged party, or the costs to others. (See note 5 of the introduction, page 257 .)

特权：指基于某种属性、地位或群体成员身份而赋予特定个人或群体的特殊权利或优势。特权因法律和/或社会规范而给予优先待遇和/或获取资源的途径，其存在独立于拥有特权者的任何具体作为或不作为。特权的拥有者往往意识不到自身所处地位的差异，也意识不到特权给自身带来的益处或给他人造成的损失。（参见导言第257页注释5。）

Protective use of force: The conscious, intentional, and temporary use of force to create safety, employed out of care, without malice or ill will.

保护性使用武力：有意识地、有意地、暂时地使用武力来创造安全，出于关心，没有恶意或敌意。

Redirecting: Gently guiding a conversation back to a chosen phase or topic.

重新引导：巧妙地将对话引导回选定的阶段或主题。

Reflection: A restatement of or inquiry about what’s been said to confirm understanding.

反思：对所说内容的重述或询问，以确认理解。

Relational conversation: The aspects of a conversation focused on the quality of connection, emotions, or how parties are relating.

关系型对话：对话中关注联系质量、情感或对话双方如何相处的各个方面。

Request: A question about one’s willingness to perform a specific action to meet needs. Requests are strategies and are distinct from demands.

请求：询问某人是否愿意采取特定行动来满足需求。请求是一种策略，与要求不同。

Social connection: The need for and experience of safe, healthy human contact and enjoyable social engagement. (This need changes in its manifestation throughout a human life, and in its relative significance on physiological, emotional, biological, psychological, and spiritual levels. For more, see note 1 of chapter 1 , page 258 ).

社会联系：对安全、健康的人际交往和愉悦的社交活动的需求和体验。（这种需求在人的一生中表现形式不断变化，其在生理、情感、生物、心理和精神层面的重要性也各不相同。更多信息，请参见第1章第258页的注释1。）

Solution request: A question proposing a concrete strategy or suggesting an agreement to attend to needs; a question offering an idea about how to move forward in a situation.

解决方案请求：提出具体策略或建议达成协议以满足需求的问题；提出在某种情况下如何前进的想法的问题。

Splintering: Digressing in a conversation by introducing new pieces of content before the current topic is complete.

跑题：在谈话中偏离主题，在当前话题结束之前引入新的内容。

Strategy: An attempt to meet needs tied to a specific person, place, action, time, or object.

策略：满足与特定人物、地点、行动、时间或物品相关的需求的尝试。

Touch points: Areas of strong sensation in the body such as the hands, feet, lips, or tongue.

触觉点：身体上感觉强烈的区域，例如手、脚、嘴唇或舌头。

Tracking: Following specific elements of process or threads of content in a conversation.

跟踪：跟踪对话中特定的流程要素或内容线索。

View: A particular perspective on, way of looking at or understanding something; it can be consciously chosen or unconsciously held.

观点：对某事物的特定视角、看待或理解方式；它可以是有意识地选择的，也可以是无意识地持有的。

关于作者

OREN JAY SOFER teaches meditation and Nonviolent Communication in both Buddhist and secular contexts. He first became interested in contemplative practice in high school, went on to complete a degree in comparative religion from Columbia University, and later spent two and a half years living as an anagarika (Buddhist renunciate) in the Ajahn Chah Thai Forest lineage. Today, his teaching combines classical Buddhist training with the accessible language of secular mindfulness.

奥伦·杰伊·索弗（OREN JAY SOFER）在佛教和世俗语境下教授冥想和非暴力沟通。他高中时开始对冥想修行产生兴趣，之后在哥伦比亚大学获得比较宗教学学位，并在阿姜查泰森林传承中以出家僧人（佛教弃世者）的身份生活了两年半。如今，他的教学融合了古典佛教训练和通俗易懂的世俗正念语言。

Oren is a member of the Spirit Rock Teacher’s Council, a Certified Trainer of Nonviolent Communication, and a Somatic Experiencing Practitioner for healing trauma. He also has served as the senior program developer at Mindful Schools, is the founder of Next Step Dharma ( nextstepdharma.org ), and is cofounder of Mindful Healthcare ( mindfulhealthcare.net ).

奥伦是灵岩教师委员会成员、非暴力沟通认证培训师，以及创伤疗愈躯体体验疗法执业者。他还曾担任正念学校的高级项目开发人员，是“下一步佛法”（nextstepdharma.org）的创始人，也是“正念医疗保健”（mindfulhealthcare.net）的联合创始人。
